By Lou Karney 

WACO, Tex. — Minyard 
Food Stores has unveiled a 76,- 
000-sq.-ft. combo called Sack ’N 
Save that combines a food ware- 
house store with a deep-dis- 
count drug store. It is a first for 
the industry. 

The 24-hour store, located in 
a former Woolco site 100 miles 
south of Dallas, has a — 
area of 55,000 sq. ft., with foo 
comprising 60% of the mix and 
nonfoods, including pharmacy, 
40%. Pharmacy hours are 9 
a.m. to 9 p.m. er to Satur- 
day, and 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. on 
Sunday. 

Minyard is playing a high- 
stakes game in the venture. Ac- 
cording to Joe Pat Smith, direc- 
tor of retail operations for Sack 
’"N Save, the store must gener- 
ate $8 per square foot a week to 


break even. That translates 
into almost $23 million a year. 

After the first year, the store 
is expected to be generating 
about $600,000 a week, or more 
than $30 million a year, drawing 
from a 30-mile ed oa “Not ev- 
ery consumer likes the con- 
cept—about half don’t,” Smith 
said. “That’s why we have to 
draw from such a wide radius.” 

While the store has been open 
only amonth, Minyard is so con- 
fident of its eventual success 
that it has drawn plans toopen a 
second 70,000-sq.-ft. unit in six 
months. 

Smith designed the concept 
for Sack ’N Save after criss- 
crossing the country for six 
months, studying other ware- 
house stores. Then he tested the 
waters. Two years ago he con- 
verted Minyard’s 22,000-sq.-ft.

_ Late News 


F. W. WOOLWORTH CO. is planning to open two deep- 
discount drug stores in Philadelphia in March on an “ex- 
perimental basis.” The variety store chain also plans to 

n three more deep discounters in 1986, but would not dis- 
close the sites. Industry sources said the diversification is 
seen as an effort by Woolworth’s to further decrease its reli- 
ance on the traditional “5¢ and 10¢”’ store concept. A Wool- 
worth spokesman said the chain chose deep discounting be- 
cause the industry isn’t dominated by national retailers and 
because operating costs are low.

SYRACUSE — Fay’s Drug 
has launched its first entry into 
the deep-discount field, a store 
called Jay Jay’s that it pur- 
chased from 4 M. Flickinger 
Co. of Buffalo. 

With about $1.2 million in in- 
ventory, the huge, 38,000-sq.- 
ft. (20,000 sq. ft. selling) out- 
let—a former roller gin 
rink—is one of the largest of all 
deep-discount units. 

Like most other deep-dis- 
count stores, gross margins are 


kept under 20%, discounts 
range up to 50%, and 80% of the 
buying is done on deal. When 
mature, the store could easily 
hit $10 million in annual sales. 
To maintain an entrepre- 
neurial spirit, Fay’s uses the 
talents of Abe Pereira, former 
vp merchandising for Lane 
Drug, to make the opportunis- 
tic buys that are the key to 
deep-discounting success. 
George Wadowiec, a Fay’s vet- 
eran, is general manager.

=—=News in brief== 


Woods quits NARD 


WASHINGTON — William E. Woods, the chief spokesman 
for the nation’s independent pharmacists over the past two de- 
cades, retired abruptly as executive vp of the National Associ- 
ation of Retail Druggists late last month. , 

_Ina terse announcement of the departure, the association 
disclosed that Charles West, executive vp of the Arkansas 
Pharmacists Association, had assumed command on an inter- 
im basis. 

According to the announcement, Woods played a key role in 
“shaping NARD” into a “pivotal force” in pharmacy circles and 
in developing the organization into a major association with a 
$4 million budget. 

Word of Woods’ departure caught other pharmacy and drug 
store industry leaders by surprise. } 

“Bill was one of the few constant and predictable factors in 
pharmacy,” one of his contemporaries at a rival industry asso- 
ciation toid Drug Store News. “It’s difficult to imagine NARD 
without Bill Woods.” he 

Over the years Woods’ sharp wit and even sharper tongue 
earned him a reputation as one of the most outspoken and con- 
troversial lobbyists in Washington. But even his detractors, 
many of whom were subjected to bitter criticism for disagree- 
ing with him on policy issues, rarely questioned his commit- 
ment to the interests of independent druggists. 

Toward the end of his tenure, however, Woods’ open hostil- 
ity to other pharmacy leaders, wholesale drug executives and 
industry association leaders who differed with him on pharma- 
cy crime legislation may have proved to be his undoing. 

Although NARD officials offered no explanation for Woods’ 
sudden retirement, the announcement was made following a 
nonpublic meeting of the association’s board, which had under- 
gone recent membership changes. 


Walter Feltman dies 


NEW ORLEANS — Walter Feltman, executive vice presi- 
dent and a director and member of the executive council of 
K&B Inc., died Oct. 16 while attending a NACDS SCOPE 
meeting in Kansas City. 

Feltman joined K&B on Oct. 3, 1966, as store operations di- 
rector, a position he maintained at the time of his death. 
Private funeral services were held in New Orleans on Oct. 19. 


McKesson net earnings rise 


SAN FRANCISCO — McKesson Corp. reported that net 
earnings for the third quarter ended Sept. 30 increased slight- 
y to $16.77 million from $16.69 million during the same period 
the previous year. 

e earnings figure for the third quarter this year includes 
income from discontinued operations of $34,000. The 1983 
quarterly figure includes income from discontinued operations 
of $767,000. 

Sales for the third quarter increased 14% to $1.17 billion 
from $1 billion in the third quarter in 1983. 

Earnings for the nine-month period ended Sept. 30 dropped 
slightly to $32.2 million from $32.4 million in 1983. The 1984 
figure includes income from discontinued operations of 
$725,000 and the 1983 figure includes income from discontin- 
ued operations of $805,000. 

Sales for the nine-month period rose 14%, increasing to $2.3 
billion from $2 billion during the same period in 1983. 

On a per-share basis third-quarter earnings increased to 88¢ 
from 87¢. For the nine-month period, earnings dropped to 
$1.67 from $1.68.

Genovese Drug Stores has un- 
veiled a new 20,000-sq.-ft. drug 
store here that showcases its 
latest efforts in the areas of 
home health care and automo- 
tive aftermarket retailing. 

Located in a strim shopping 
center only a few miles from its 
Melville, N.Y., headquarters, 
the Lindenhurst stor'e is among 
the largest ever operied by Gen- 
ovese. The store, formerly a 
Channel Home Center, repre- 
sents Genovese’s second ven- 
ture into home health care re- 
tailing, as well as its second 
effort with a full-line automo- 
tive ts department, called 
the Genovese Auto Warehouse. 

The Genovese Home Health 
Care Center is actually a sepa- 
rate entity fromthe drug store, 
although for the time being it is 
drawing custojers from the 


drug store entrance. Separate 
doors will be installed in the 
2,000-sq.-ft. home health care 
store, which will enable Geno- 
vese to operate the store during 
different hours from the drug 
store. In addition, the home 
health unit is supported by its 
own sales staff, and sales and 
profits are being treated sepa- 
rately from the drug store por- 
tion of the store. 

The automotive department, 
located in an alcove in the far 
corner of the store, carries ac- 
cessory items and chemicals 
and features a service counter 


for hard parts. As in the case of 


the Jackson Heights, N.Y., 
store, the only other Genovese 
location to contain an Auto 
Warehouse, the Lindenhurst 
store carries parts mainly for 
domestic cars. Parts can be or- 
dered for foreign cars and usu- 


ally received within one day. 

Unlike the home health care 
center, Genovese is treating 
the Auto Warehouse as it does 
other departments in the drug 
store. 

The remaining departments 
in the store resemble a conven- 
tional Genovese drug store, 
however, with some subtle 
changes in store decor and with 
more space allocated to depart- 
ments such as toys, stationery 
and greeting cards.

at NACDS conference

Chain drug executives attending 
this year’s NACDS Administra- 
tions/Operations conference 
here were able for the first time 
to visit exhibition booths manned 
by vendors displaying the latest 
in drug store technology. 

Another first for the confer- 
ence was the combining into one 
meeting of what in the past had 
been four separate meetings: 
the Human Resource Manage- 
ment Conference; the Loss Pre- 
vention Conference; the Man- 
agement Information Services 
Conference, and the SCOPE 
(systems, controls, operations, 
personnel and EDP) Confer- 
ence. 

Approximately 300 retailers 
attended the conference includ- 
ing chain executives specializ- 


ing in finance, loss prevention 
and human resources as well as 
management and operations in- 
formation services. 

The attendees were able to 
visit the exhibit areas during 
breaks in the workshop ses- 
sions. Many of the 27 vendors 
present were able to give 
‘hands-on” demonstrations of a 
new generation of equipment, 

Because of the show’s suc- 
cess, Vince Gardner, vp phar- 
macy and health affairs, said 
that the NACDS is considering

Hook’ s third-quarter earnings drop by 28.6% 


INDIANAPOLIS — Hook 
Drug reported that its third- 
uarter earnings fell 28.6% to 
$1.28 million from $1.8 million 
during the same quarter in 
1983. 

The company said that the 
earnings drop reflected in- 
creased expenses related to 
new store development, high- 
er-than-expected operating 
osts and a sales growth rate 
hat fell below the 12% pace tar- 


geted by the chain prior to the 
start of fiscal 1985. 

Hook’s sales for the third 
quarter, ended Sept. 30, to- 
taled $86.1 million, up 8.8% 
from the $79.2 million regis- 
tered in the third quarter of 
1983. 

On a per-share basis, earn- 
ings for the third quarter fell to 
29¢ per share from 41¢ in 1983. 

Through the first nine 
months of the fiscal year, 


Hook’s net income was off 
17.8% to $4.6 million from near- 
y $5.6 million earned during 
the first three quarters of last 
year. Nine-month earnings 
were down 18% to $1.29 from 
$1.06 last year. 

Hook’s nine-month sales rose 
9.4% to $254.5 million from 
$232.7 million the previous 
year. 

J. Douglas Reeves, Hook’s 
chairman, president and ceo, 


expressed confidence that the 
chain would be able to produce 
“favorable results” in the fourth 
quarter. 

Commenting on the results 
from the third quarter and previ- 
ous two quarters, Reeves said: 
“In mid-August as the dimen- 
sions of the situation became evi- 
dent, management designed an 
impressive corporatewide pro- 
gram of cost control and sales 
management. These measures 


were developed with the full par- 
ticipation of all employees.” 

Ithough Reeves did not dis- 
close the specific nature of the 
cost control and sales enhance- 
ment measures, he said that 
“most are now in place and are 
operational.” 

During the third quarter, the 
company also said that it 
opened four new stores, bring- 
+4 its total storé count up to 

12.

DRUG STORE NEWS, November 12, 1984 


MERCHANDISER 


Special report: 


Ethnic 
products 


| 


s the ethnic category continues to 

heat up, more and more drug re- 

tailers are increasing their com- 
mitment, and now even wholesalers are 
entering the fray for the first time. 

Most drug retailers report that they 
have added space and sku’s to their eth- 
nic sections in the past year, while sever- 
al major chains say they plan to intro- 
duce departments chainwide. 

The success of the category has also 
captured the attention of several major 
wholesalers, who say they will offer spe- 
cialized planograms to their customers. 

Among the major developments: 

@ SupeRx is creating its own plano- 
grams ranging from 3 ft. to 48 ft. and is 
working with the American Health & 
Beauty Aids Institute to develop a pro- 
gram for ethnic cosmetics. 

® Hook Drug has added over 50 ethnic 
hair care items to its warehouse in the 
past year. 

®@ Gray Drug last month began promot- 
ing ethnic products on a chainwide ba- 
sis. 

@ At least three major wholesalers— 


Stories by 
Gail Appleson 


McKesson, Bergen Brunswig and Fox- 
Meyer—have drawn up ethnic depart- 
ment planograms for their customers. 
@ Judith Lynn and Ben Sheftall are 
among the ethnic product distributors 
that have expanded their lines to include 
Hispanic. 

This burst of activity is indicative of 
the efforts not only to improve the mer- 
chandising of the ethnic mix, which can 
yield margins as high as 45% and turns 
of up to 19, but also to keep with the 
growing population of blacks and His- 
panics. 

In the past decade, the black popula- 
tion has shot up 18%—three times that 
of whites. Today blacks make up about 
12% of the entire population, and it is 
predicted they will account for 12.8% in 
1993. In 1980, blacks spent close to $400 
million on health & beauty aids and cos- 
metics. By 1983, that figure had grown 
to about $2 billion. 

Because of their special hair care 
needs, blacks spent most of their H&BA 
dollars on hair care. In 1983, 41% of 
those dollars—or $820 million—went 
for hair care products. Purchases of eth- 
nic products made up 27% of the entire 
$3 billion hair care market. 

The Hispanic market is also growing 
rapidly. It is estimated that the more 
than 22 million Hispanics who live in the 


Chains, wholesalers expand efnhnic lines 


United States spend more than $60 bil- 
tion annually. What’s more, the Hispanic 
population is increasing 6.5% faster 
than the population at large. 

A study released in September by 
Yankelovich, Skelly & White Inc., con- 
cluded there has been a distinct “blur- 
ring of differences” between U.S. His- 
panics of varying national origins and 
thus, “the marketer could consider all 
Hispanics in aggregate as [one] consum- 
er segment.” 

_On the other hand, the study showed 
that there has been a rise in Hispanic 
identification since 1981 and a greater 
desire by Hispanics to pass traditions 
along to their children. 

Because of their willingness to offer 
and promote full lines of ethnic prod- 
ucts, drug chains continue to be the pri- 
mary outlet for retail sales of these prod- 
ucts. In 1983, according to A. C. 
Nielsen, 58% of all ethnic hair care dol- 
lars were spent in drug stores, an 11% 
increase over 1982. In comparison, 24% 
of the dollars were spent in food stores 
(up 19%) and 18% in mass merchandis- 
ers (a 7% increase). 

As for unit sales, drug stores held 54% 
of the market, up 6%, while food stores 
had a 29% share (up 19%) and mass mer- 
chandisers, 17% (an 8% decrease). 

Because hair care is the dominant 


7 =. 


part of this category, the changes that 
are occurring and which are predicted 
are of particular importance to retailers 
and wholesalers. The most significant 
current questions: What will happen to 
the curl market, and is straightened hair 
the next strong trend? 


Hair care 


Between 1978 and 1983, the curl mar- 
ket generated $143 million in activator 
sales and $79 million in kit sales. Most 
industry sources say the market is still 
strong, but sales have leveled off and

many say the strength is regional. 

According to Karen Nelson, assistant 
product manager for M & M Products 
Co. in Atlanta, geography has a lot todo 
with the popularity of the curl. “In the 
South and West you see more curls. It’s 
a convenience because of the heat and 
humidity,” she said. “In the North and 
East, women have gone back to relaxing 
their hair.” 

Armand Jackson, senior product man- 
ager for the professional products divi- 
sion of Alberto Culver, makers of TCB, 
said that relaxers are definitely on the 
increase. “The cur! business is leveling 
off, but there are still a large number of 
people with curls. There are certain 
pockets where it is still doing quite 
well.” 

Walt Smith, general manager of 
Worlds of Curls, and Lou Parent, senior 
vp of Carson Products, also agreed 
there is a trend toward straightened 
hair for women and away from the curl. 
The manufacturers also said the wave 
has become popular for men. 

On the other hand, Beauty Enter- 
prises, an ethnic products distributor in 
Hartford, Conn., reported an increase 
in sales of curl kits and related mainte- 
nance products between October 1983 
and 1984. According to Rocky Piccirillo, 
director of operations, curl products 
made up 49.6% of their sales, up 6.8%, 
and wave products increased by 11%. In 
comparison, relaxers made up 10.9% of 
the rackjobbers’ sales, a 1.2% decrease. 

Yet, manufacturers are predicting 
these sales figures will begin to change 
in the next 12 to 24 months and are gear- 
ing up to meet new consumer demands. 

For example, TCB and Worlds of 
Curls will be among those manufactur- 
ers soon introducing new relaxer and 
grooming products. “That’s the direc- 
tion we’re moving,” said Smith of Worlds 
of Curls. 

Industry sources are now curious as 
to whether a trend toward straightened 
hair will mean better sales for ethnic 
mousses, a new subcategory that has 
been moving slowly in comparison with 
the mass-marketed product. 

Jackson said that TCB, which recent- 
ly introduced a mousse, was hopeful that 
with the trend toward straightened hair 
and an advertising campaign that began 
in October, sales would be good. 

Smith and Nelson said their compa- 
nies may be looking into mousse in the 
future, but Parent said his company had 
rejected the idea. “They just don’t seem 
to be catching hold in the ethnic mar-

products

2 


at 


ket,” he said. 

In another area of hair care, Parent 
said hair coloring was doing well. Car- 
son estimates that 25% of all black wom- 
en have tried it and 85% continue to buy 
hair coloring. He pointed out the biggest 
challenge was convincing chains to dis- 
play ethnic hair color with the mass mar- 
keted products. “When a woman wants 
color, she goes to where the color is.” 

Parent said lighter and brighter 
shades are now popular, and that the 
company was having a good response to 
its three new shades, light brown, fiery 
auburn and honey blonde. 


Cosmetics 


Another developing ethnic category 
is cosmetics. So far, all ethnic cosmetics 
sold in drug stores have been blister- 
packed and dominated by Posner, Ultra- 
Sheen, Zuri and Honey & Spice. Chain 
drug store buyers disagree over how 
well these cosmetics sell. There’s also no 
consensus about whether the problem 
lies with how they are displayea and pro-

Source: Business Trends Analysis 


moted or whether there just isn’t a mar- 
ket. 

“We're doing extremely well,” said 
Pat Duckworth, cosmetics buyer at Peo- 
ples Drugs, about the pegged ethnic cos- 
metics. She said the stores have 2- and 4- 
ft. ethnic cosmetics departments. 

Duckworth said the nail polish and 
lipstick are selling best, and that a new 
hot item this year is Honey & Spice’s ar- 
tificial fingernails. 

Peoples, which has ethnic depart- 
ments in 93 of its stores, does all its cos- 
metics planogramming in-house. “By of- 
fering stores a good mix with a lot of 
planograms, they’re more willing to get 
involved,” she said. 

She said that at one time Peoples did 
poorly with ethnic cosmetics because 
the stores weren’t carrying full lines. 
“One of the problems dealing with eth- 
nic cosmetics is that a lot of stores don’t 
understand what to carry. The ethnic 
sales are there. There’s no doubt about 
ae 

However, some buyers disagreed. 
One cosmetics buyer for a large South- 
ern chain said there are no strong ethnic 
cosmetics programs available to drug 
stores. “Black women still go to depart- 
ment stores for Fashion Fair and spend 
$10 when they could get Honey & Spice 
for $3.79.” 

Helen James, cosmetics buyer for 
Hook, said there doesn’t seem to be 
strength in any one brand of ethnic cos- 
metic. “Blacks still haven’t found what 
they want,” she said. 

Piccirillo of Beauty Enterprises said 
he felt sales in ethnic cosmetics were not 
stronger because many colors are dupli- 
cated in mass-marketed lines and be- 
cause the blister packs discourage im- 
pulse sales. 

He said his company usually recom- 
mends that stores limit space for ethnic 
cosmetics to 1 to 2 ft. We seldom recom- 
mend 4 ft. You’re just not going to get 
the turns.” 

Buyers agree that although blacks 
frequently use skin cream, most ethnic 
products are still not particularly strong 
movers. Soft Sheen’s Cocoa Creme But- 


ter, however, was frequently mentioned 
as a good seller. 


Skin care 


There has also been little movement in 
shaving aids, though Magic Shave Pow- 
der most often named as a best seller. 
Because a majority of blacks suffer from 
pseudofolliculitis, or razor bumps, they 
cannot use most mass-marketed shav- 
ing creams. Some buyers said they 
would like to see new entries in this area 
and were curious about a new advertis- 
ing campaign aimed at blacks by Selby 
Drugs, manufacturer of Peau de Soie, a 
shaving creme that has been targeted 
toward white women. (See related story 
in this special section. ) 

Piccirillo said his company has seen 
good sales of the specially made Ameri- 
can Safety Razor. He said that although 
the entire shaving subcategory makes 
up only about 2% of all sales, dollar sales 
rose 37% between 1983 and 1984. 


DRUG STORE NEWS, November 12, 1984 


MERCHANDISER 


Chains begin to target Hispanic market 


ith all the various nationalities 
W that make up the so-called His- 

panic culture, retailers have 
long worried that they would never be 
able to create an H&BA section with 
enough mass appeal to justify the in- 
vestment in space. 

But now a new study by Yankelovich, 
Skelly & White has exposed the flaw in 
that thinking. The study says that since 
1981 there has been a distinct “biurring 
of differences” among U.S. Hispanics of 
varying national origins. 

Yankelovich concluded that “the mar- 
keter should consider all Hispanics in 
aggregate as [one] consumer segment.” 


Special report: 


Ethnic 
products 


Although chains have been reluctant 
to establish Hispanic sections, a few, in- 
cluding SupeRx, have put in 3- and 6-ft. 
H&BA sections in selected stores, and a 
number of chains, including Walgreens, 
Eckerd and Gray, carry Hispanic cos- 
metics. 

Chains should also consider another 
Yankelovich finding that Hispanics 
want to preserve religious and national 
traditions, as well as their native lan- 
guage. This means there is probably a 
growing market for items in Spanish 
packaging imported from Mexico and 
other countries. These items may have 
been used by Hispanic consumers or 
their parents in their native countries. 

At least two rackjobbers, Judith 
Lynn and Ben Sheftall, are offering His- 
panic planograms and say these import- 
ed items are definitely doing well in ar- 
eas with large Hispanic populations. 
These items include shampoos, tonics, 
soaps, aspirin, antacids and rubbing al- 
cohol. Judith Lynn and Ben Sheftall 
both report that most of these items are 
imported from Mexico. 

According to Diana Warren of Judith 


Lynn’s one-year-old Tampico Division, 
stores with as little as 15% Hispanic 
traffic can support a separate depart- 
ment. 

“The need is there,” said Warren. 
“It’s so much like the ethnic market was 
years ago.” 

Judith Lynn offers a 3-ft. planogram 
with 79 sku’s and a 4-ft. planogram with 
86 sku’s. Larger planograms can be de- 
signed to meet the needs of individual 
stores, Warren said. 

Richard Eichholz, president of Ben 
Sheftall, said his company offers 2-, 3-, 
5-, 8- and 12-ft. planograms for Hispanic 
departments. Like Judith Lynn, Shef- 
tall can create larger planograms to 
meet greater needs, and the planograms 
are flexible enough to accommodate 
specially requested items, such as reli- 
gious candles and even Cuban coffee 
pots. 

Like ethnic planograms, there is also 
a need to merchandise regionally manu- 
factured products. For example, Miami 
area stores may want to carry the locally 
manufactured Mirthas hair and skin 
care products, said Eichholz. 

Cosmetics have also become a popular 
category in Hispanic merchandising. In 
fact, the second mass-marketed Hispan- 
ic line with bilingual packaging debuts 
this month. It is called Lindeza and it is 
being distributed by Mas Industries 
Inc. of Santa Monica, Calif. , along witha 
fragrance called Enamorada. The prod- 
ucts will first be introduced in the Miami 
market and will be available nationwide 
as Mas receives shipments from the 
manufacturer in Barcelona, Spain. 

Lindeza enters the market about one 
year after Belleza Internacionale Inc. of 
Lake Bluff, Ill. , began distribution of its 
qué Guapa cosmetic line. Qué Guapa is 
now in about 3,000 outlets including 
many Eckerd stores, said Leslie Niesse, 
marketing manager. 

Lindeza and qué Guapa items are sim- 
ilarly priced, averaging between $2.50 
and $3.50 and are all blister-packed. In- 
cluded in each line are eye shadow sin- 
gles and duos, nail polish, lipstick and 
blush. Distributors say retailers can 
achieve about 40% margins with both 
brands.

Unlike qué Guapa, the Lindeza line 
includes foundation and eye pencils. Mas 
is also offering the upscale Enamorada 
fragrance, which comes in a 3.4-0z. 
spray with a suggested retail price of 
$21.50 and a 1.7-0z. pour cologne with a 
suggested price of $15. 

Rita Moreno is the spokesman for 
Lindeza and Enamorada, and she is ap- 
pearing in a four-week Spanish televi- 
sion commercial campaign in the Miami 
market. She will also appear in mass- 
market television commercials as the 
products beceme more widely available. 

Mas has received orders from Wal- 
greens, Gray and SupeRx for their Mi- 
ami-area stores, said Stewart Brown, 
Mas vp. 

The same chains are also offering qué 
Guapa in selected stores, said Niesse. 

Currently the company is advertising 


on radio stations and in the Spanish edi- 
tions of such magazines as Harper’s Ba- 
zaar and Cosmopolitan. 

Belleza has also been working with re- 
tailers to promote qué Guapa, Niesse 
said. In addition to co-op dollars, Belleza 
has provided in-store Seagal aaad at 
such chains as Walgreens. 

“Walgreens has been one of our big- 
gest promoters,” Niesse said, compli- 
menting the chain for its work with cos- 
meticians and neighborhood flyers. 

Another new entry into Hispanic 
merchandise are novelty bath products 
featuring Menudo, the popular five- 
member Hispanic pop group. The bath 
accessories—soap,| bubble bath and 
sponges—are packaged to resemble au- 
dio equipment, They are available from 
Berdell Cosmetics, a subsidiary of CCA 
Industries. 


Study finds increase 
In Hispanic income 


ilies earning $20,000 or more in- 

creased from 28% to 36% be- 
tween 1981 and 1984, according to a 
study released by Yankelovich, Skel- 
ly & White Inc. 

This study also found that the aver- 
age Hispanic income has gruwn from 
$15,900 to $17,800, while those earn- 
ing less than $10,000 has decreased 
from 38% to 32%. 

Although Hispanics appear to have 
more money to spend—good news for 
retailers—-the study also suggested 
that Hispanics are becoming general- 
ly less responsive to new products 
and new stores. 

Since 1981 there has been a drop in 
the percentage of Hispanics who are 
looking for new foods, liquor and 
beer, laundry products, magazines 
and department and grocery stores. 

Yankelovich deduced that “appar- 
ently, along with other Americans, 
Hispanics are now more focused on 
coping with and winning in the more 
limited economic climate.” 

Like the 1981 study, Yankelovich 
found that a majority of Hispanics 
said they were paying more attention 
to how long a product lasts in relation 
to its price. And while they are not 
looking for new products, they will 
stay loyal to brand names they have 
previously used. In fact, 82% in both 
1981 and in 1984 agreed with the 


T he percentage of Hispanic fam- 


statement, “Once I find a brand I 
like, I stick with it.” 

Of the Hispanics surveyed, 38% 
said the “biggest, most popular 
brands are best,” compared with 22% 
of the generai United States public. 
The study showed that 40% of the 
Hispanics agreed that private-label 
products are as good as the nationally 
advertised brands, compared with 
61% of the total United States popu- 
lation. 

Another area of interest to retail- 
ers is that while Hispanics continue 
to hold more traditional views about 
sex roles, there are early signs of pro- 
gress for women. 

For example, in 1981 48% of those 
surveyed said a married women with 
children should be able to have a ca- 
reer. That percentage increased 
slightly to 50% in 1984. 

In 1981, 23% of those surveyed said 
that unless extra money is needed, a 
woman with children should not have 
an outside job. That figure dropped to 
21% in 1984. 

There was a greater drop in the 
number who said the man of the 
house should decide on buying expen- 
sive items like a television, car or 
house. That percentage dropped to 
46% in 1984, from 55%. 

The study was commissioned by 
SIN Television and is an update of a 
1981 survey of 775 respondents.

Exec 


fter two years of research, Rhea 

Palmer, national merchandise 

manager of H&BA for McKesson, 
is finally seeing her pet project—ethnic 
planogramming—become a reality. 

Not only is it a personal triumph for 
Palmer, it is also a breakthrough for 
McKesson, as the industry giant be- 
comes the first major full-line wholesal- 
er to field a national ethnic planogram 
program. 

Last month McKesson unveiled four 
different ethnic planograms ranging 
from 4 ft. to 16 ft. , the latter containing a 
maximum of 350 sku’s, including cos- 
metics. The wholesaler has also added 
some 200 new black hair care items to its 
inventory. 

A buyer for 18 years—most of that 
time with the Value Giant chain that was 
purchased by Pay Less—Palmer came 
to McKesson three years ago with the 
hope that the wholesaler would let her 
develop an ethnic planogram. 

“IT feel very close to this market. I 


don’t know if it’s because I’m black or be- - 


cause I knew there was so much poten- 
tial,” she said. 

Palmer said she knew there were 
many independents who weren’t doing 
the business in ethnic because they were 
trying to arrange facings without 
knowledgeable help. Or maybe, she 
said, they couldn’t afford rack jobbers, 
and so they weren’t even selling the 
products. 

As a consumer, Palmer was irritated 
because the products she needed were 
not available at neighborhood stores. 
And like other consumers, she stopped 
shopping the stores that didn’t carry 
what she needed. 

Palmer was optimistic McKesson 
would consider her observations and let 
her pursue her proposal. “McKesson is 
constantly exploring avenues of new 
business,” she said. 

And she was right. McKesson gave 
Palmer the go-ahead and soon she was 
engulfed in stacks of marketing and 
sales reports and taking part in rounds 
of meetings with manufacturers—in ad- 


Indies attracted 


Three giant wholesalers 


j| lead charge to ethnics 


holesalers are jumping into the 

ethnic section planogramming 

business, with at least three of 
the giants leading the way. 

McKesson, for example, this month 
launched a national program. FoxMeyer 
began a limited program in July, and 
Bergen Brunswig will be starting one 
shortly. 

The planogramming service is partic- 
ularly attractive to independents who 
either can’t afford a rackjobber or who 
want to control the section themselves. 
By using a wholesaler’s planogram, a 
store can order most of its stock—ethnic 
along with OTC and other H&BA— 
from one source. This eliminates the 
problems of large minimum orders ard 
dealing with many suppliers. 

Dealing with wholesalers may also 
mean a savings beeause the larger the 
overall order, the better the price. The 
wholesaler service is also relatively in- 
expensive. McKesson, for example, 
charges $25 a month. 

McKesson is now offering four differ- 
ent planograms—4 ft., 8 ft., 12 ft. and 16 


ft.—and these are available nationwide. 

FoxMeyer has three different plano- 
grams—4 ft., 8 ft. and 12 ft.—but they 
are only available in certain regions. The 
wholesaler introduced the planograms 
in July in the Memphis and Little Rock 
markets. In October, the program was 
expanded to St. Louis and this month, 
Cincinnati was added. 

Bergen Brunswig is just about ready 
to unveil its 12- and 16-ft. planograms, 
the latter containing 340 sku’s of HBA 
and cosmetics. 

“The market is there and we recog- 
nize it as a growing business and that 
many customers would like us to be the 
source for it,” said Thomas Allison, vp of 
merchandising for Bergen.

SUpeRX stocks, planog 


into warehousing and planogram- 

ming its own ethnic depart-

chain recognition from the American 
Health and Beauty Aids Institute for its 
aggressive merchandising efforts. 

SupeRx now has ethnic departments 
in over 400 of its 570 stores, and accord- 

«ing to David Wesloh, merchandise man- 
ager, the chain would like such depart- 
ments in all stores by 1985. 

SupeRx changed its approach about a 
year ago when it went from complete de- 
pendence on rackjobbers to join with 
Kroger in warehousing many items and 
creating in-house planograms. Now the 
Cincinnati-based chain uses rackjob- 


8 upeRx took the plunge this year 


Ethnic 
products 


bers to supplement departments 12 ft. 
and over. 

Planograms now range from 3 ft. to 48 
ft. A typical 12-ft. planogram contains 
300 sku’s. 

“One of our biggest challenges in the 
planograms is to allot space to local 
products,” Wesloh said. “We try to keep 
2 to 3 ft. for locally manufactured prod- 
ucts and that makes it difficult for a na- 
tional planogram.” 

Even in the smallest departments, 
about 18 in. are saved for regional prod- 
ucts. 

Wesloh, who developed the plano- 
grams with Bonnie Madill, buyer, and 
input from members of the AHBAI, 
said, “It’s been an experience for Bonnie 
and I. We haven’t perfected the alloca- 
tions and we recognize there needs to be 


more work.” 

One of the areas that AHBAI and Su- 
peRx are continuing to explore is ethnic 
cosmetics. 

“Cosmetics are confusing and less sta- 
ble than hair care,” Wesloh said. I don’t 
think anyone has a good handle on it. So 
we asked the AHBAI to help us with a 
planogram.” 

Wesloh said SupeRx hopes to have the 
cosmetics planograms in 20 stores by 
early next year. He said other stores will 
also continue to carry a smattering of 
ethnic cosmetics. 

According to Anthony Fanticola, di- 
rector of merchandising, the planogram 
will emphasize shades of colors. He said 
the chain is considering eliminating 
some of its slower-moving lines of mass 
marketed cosmetics to make room for a 
more extensive selection of ethnic cos- 
metic colors. 

Fanticola said SupeRx continues to 
work with the AHBAIT in determining 
whether the chain should allocate more 
space in individual stores fer ethnic sec- 
tions, and in some cases, whether the 
space should be reduced. 

In another development this year, 
Wesloh said SupeRx recently started 
promoting ethnic products on a chain- 
wide basis. 

SupeRx is also promoting ethnic 
products through in-store displays and 
endcaps. 

Wesloh said he and Madill have begun 
to attend ethnic trade shows to increase 
their understanding of the category. 

The successful experience with sepa- 
rate ethnic departments has encour- 
aged the chain to create separate His- 
panic sections in a few of its Florida 
stores. These departments are small, 3 
ft. and 6 ft., with 100 and 160 items, re- 
spectively. These few stores are also car- 
rying Hispanic cosmetics. 

“I think these departments really 
have a lot of potential in certain loca- 
tions,” Wesloh said.

Gray tightens belt 


to cut profit slide 


CLEVELAND — In an ef- 
fort to stop sliding profits, Gray 
Drug Fair has begun a cam- 
paign to cut corporate costs and 
stimulate sales by reducing its 
margins. The company is also 
looking to acquire a drug chain 
during the coming year. 

These were among the strat- 
egies described by officials from 
Sherwin-Williams, Gray Drug 
Fair’s parent company, during 
last month’s closed meeting 
with financial analysts in New 
York. 

According to analysts who at- 
tended the meeting, Mac Allen 
Culver, the drug chain’s new 
president, said the company 
was undertaking vigorous rem- 
edies following a $1.1 million op- 
erating loss for the drug chain 
during the third quarter ended

ORLANDO, Fla. — As the 
newly elected chairman of the 
National Wholesale Druggists’ 
Association, Laurie Du Ow, 
president of Lawrence Pharma-

chairman at last month’s annual 
meeting here, plans to start his 
year’s tenure by launching sev-

common denominator problems 
as we can find.”

days visiting a key manufactur- 
er.

it, will consist of companies 
from every segment of NWDA’s 
broad-based membership. Now 
that NWDA and the Drug

merged, the resulting member-

Retailers scout new goods 


Home health star of 


By Faye Brookman 

ROSEMONT. II. — Private- 
label pump toothpastes, incon- 
tinence items and equivalents 
of new shampoo introductions 
were the scene-stealers during 
the recent Private Label Trade 
Show. 

Drug chains attending the 
three-and-a-half-day event— 
sponsored by the Private Label 

anufacturers Association— 
said they were looking to boost 
total store-brand count 10% to 
15%. Their goal is to produce 
10% of total sales with their own 
labels. 

Many of the representatives 
of larger chains such as Supe- 
Rx, Hook, Walgreens and 
Fay’s already stock well over 
200 store brand sku’s and were 
there to scout for new catego- 
ries. Buyers from smaller 
chains including Ribordy, 
Wellby and Morgan Pharma- 
cies were seeking to round out 
their own mix. 

The area generating perhaps 
the greatest interest was home 
health care, particularly incon- 
tinence items. Manufacturers 
estimate that sales of inconti- 
nence products may be as high 
as $2.7 billion. Drug chains 
were anxious to get into that 
business because of high-gross 
margins and also because it is an 
effective way to tie the chain’s 
name to health care. 


“If there’s one thing we’re 
here to look at, itis incontinence 
items,” said SupeRx’s private- 
label buyer Bob Miles. 

Other chains agreed that the 
incontinence area is a prime pri- 
vate-label growth area. In fact, 
Medicare-Glaser, Thrifty and 
Thrift Drug already have intro- 
duced their own labels. Those in 
it suggest merchandising the 
items next to the national brand 
in a home health care area—not 
near feminine hygiene. 

Top level executives praised 
the private-label industry’s 
growing sophistication and 
cited its speed at producing a 


section to represent all mem- 
bers, no matter their size, their 
corporate configuration or their 
owner.” 

DuBow says that he has al- 
ready talked to more than a doz- 
en manufacturers who are ea- 
ger to participate. 

“You know,” he points out, 
“at some of our conventions we 
set aside part of a day for indi- 
vidual wholesalers and manu- 
facturers to sit down for 12 to 15 
minutes to go over their prob- 
lems and opportunities. This is 
good, but it’s not enough. To get 
a handle on the subject, you 
need more than 15 minutes or a 
half-hour, you need an all-day 
session. We have to learn from 
the manufacturers and the 
manufacturers have'to learn 
from us.” 

Possible subjects for such 
meetings, he suggests, include 
standardizing return goods pol- 
icies, doing a better job of ob- 
taining and dispensing new 
product information and deter- 
mining space allocation more ef- 
ficiently.

_ Earnings drop as Med-Glaser looks to future 


ST. LOUIS — A “conscious 
decision” by Medicare-Glaser to 
give up short-term earnings 
growth in order to gain market 
share and long-term profitabili- 
ty sent profits plummeting for 
the second quarter and first six 
months of fiscal 1985. 

The St. Louis-based drug 
chain reported that earnings for 
the second quarter ended Sept. 
30 fell 45% to $167,000, or 5¢ a 


share, for the comparable year- 
earlier period. Sales for the 
quarter were up 4.4% to $19.6 
million from $18.8 million. 

For the first six months, 
earnings declined 30% to 
$281,000 or 9¢ a share, from 
$402,000, or 17¢ a share, in the 
comparable period a year ago. 
Sales increased 4.3% to $39.2 
million from $37.6 million. 

The company reported that it 
had “embarked on a vigorous 


program of opening new stores, 

hile remodeling and enlarging 
existing stores. At the same 
time the company is broadening 
its product mix and enhancing 
its competitive posture.” 

The result, according to 
Medicare Glaser, has been “sig- 
nificant new store losses.” The 
company also said that results 
had been affected by the cost of 
adding to its management team 
to handle expected growth in its 


full-line drug stores as well as a 
diversification into home health 
care and deep discounting. 

In addition, Medicare-Glaser 
reported that it had made a 
“significant” investment in the 
development and marketing of 
its medical information subsid- 
iary, Professional Drug Sys- 
tems Inc. [PDS], in order to ac- 
celerate the subsidiary’s 
aay, gies growth. 

e company reported that 


during the second quarter PDS 
delivered a computerized phar- 
macy system to a major drug 
ehain, which added about 
$213,000 to net earnings for the 
period. 

At the close of the second 
quarter, the company was oper- 
ating 62 professional pharma- 
cies, 28 full-line drug stores, 12 
retail optical centers and a 
home health care center—all in 
Missouri, Illinois and Conn.

American puts muscle 


into ‘super chain’ plan 


By Bruce Buckley 
SALT LAKE CITY — With 
the sale of Rea and Derick un- 
der its belt, American Stores 
has begun to consolidate its re- 
maining drug store operations 
into a single super chain operat- 
ing stores coast to coast. 
The move, according to the 
company, is designed to achieve 
“significant economies” for the 
three operations—Skaggs, 
Osco and Sav-On. The 641 super 
stores operated by the three di- 


visions are estimated to ener- 
ate sales of more than bil- 
lion—the highest in the 


industry. 
Part of the move will involve 


merging the buying activities of 
the three chains in order to 
achieve the best possible prices 
based on volume buys. In addi- 
tion, American said, it will “pro- 
vide the company with greater 
flexibility and leverage in de- 
veloping its private-label pro- 
gram. 

Asked if the coordination of 
buying programs meant the 
creation of a single super buy- 
ing staff in Salt Eas or Chica- 
go, Michael T. Miller, sr. vp of 
American Stores, said, “Not at 
present.”

gaining greater market pene- 
tration and economies of scale,

with a robust 56% earnings

14.3% to $87.4 million. For

while sales rose 16.8% to 
$257.3 million.

Site changed for Pay Less d.c. 


_WILSONVILLE, Ore. — Pay Less NW has switched the 
site of its planned northern California distribution center from 
Stockton to Woodland. Construction of the 500,000-sq.-ft., fa- 
cility will begin in the spring of 1985, with completion sched- 
uled for the summer of 1986. 

The new Woodland facility will service 79 Pay Less stores in 
northern California. 

The major purpose of the new facility is to cut distribution 
costs to Pay Less stores in northern Cai ucing dis- 
tances from warehouse to stores by one-half. Currently, the 
central distribution center in Wilsonville ships from Oregon 
south to Bakersfield, a distance of 1,000 miles. The new d.c. 
will ship from Woodland to Bakersfield, a distance of 430 miles. 


Pay ess NW officials would not comment on the reasons for 
the site change. 


Genovese net income up 5% 

MELVILLE, N.Y. — Genovese Drug Stores Inc. reported 
that third-quarter net income rose 5% to $774,000 from 
$737,000 during the same period last year. Sales for the quar- 
ter, ended Nov. 9, were up nearly 19% to $50.8 million from 
$42.7 million in 1983. 

Through the first three quarters of the year, Genovese has 
posted earnings of nearly $2.5 million on sales of $163.5 million. 


Eckerd appoints Masters 
CLEARWATER, Fla. — Jack Eckerd Corp. has appointed 
Larry C. Masters, former chairman of Mav D&éF Department 
Stores in Denver, chairman and ceo of J yrons Department 
Stores, its 61-store junior department store subsidiary. 


Evans named ceo at Cullum Cos. 


DALLAS — Jack W. Evans has been named chief executive 
officer of Cullum Cos., the parent of Page Drug and Tom 
Thumb/Page. Evans retains the title of president. However, 
J. T. Hairston succeeds Evans as chief operating officer. 


Whitehall ordered to nix Advil ads 


NEW YORK — Whitehall Laboratories was ordered by a 
U. S. Distriet Court here to discontinue advertisements for 
Advil that the Upjohn Com said were deceptive and mis- 
leading. The court enjoined W hitehall from using a print and 
television ad that represented the hrown-celeved Advil as an 
orange tablet, which closely resembles the color of U pjohn’s 
prescription ibuprofen, Motrin. Whitehall also was ordered to 
discontinue an advertising copy line stating that Advil is “so ef- 
fective that doctors have already prescribed it over 130 million 
times.” Upjohn charged that the sentence in the ad could cause 
confusion to consumers, who might interpret the statement as 
referring to Upjohn’s Motrin rather than Whitehall’s nonpre- 
scription product, Advil. 


Perry opens new store 


PONTIAC, Mich. — Perry Drug has opened its first new 
store for its fiscal 1985, a 6,000-sq.-ft. Auto Works discount 
auto parts store in Sturgis, Mich. 

The chain now operates 146 drug stores, 157 auto parts 
stores, a clinical laboratory and a health-care facility in eight 
states. 


Revco to offer Rx info program 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — Revco D. S. next month will launch 
a new pharmacy information program designed to answer con- 
Sumer questions about prescription drugs and the growing 
number of OTC medications. Dubbed “PHARMassist,” the 
new in-store program will include special store signs and bro- 
chures, all of which are aimed at encouraging customers to ask 
Revco pharmacists questions concerning health care related 
products. 

Revco also has kicked off a new campaign promoting the ca- 
reer opportunities in the field of pharmacy. In addition to send- 
ing Revco personnel out to speak to high school students, 
Revco also will make presentations to pharmacy school stu- 
dents about the trends in the industry. 

Diane M. Tharp, R. Ph., manager, professional operations, 
will oversee Revco’s in-store pro for customers. H. Craig 
Darby and Joseph R. Sabino, both professional operations rep- 
——- will spearhead Revco’s pharmacist recruitment

Bogus OC’s traced to Panama 


ROCKVILLE, Md. — Food 
and Drug Administration in- 
vestigators traced at least one 
shipment of counterfeit Ovulen 
21 oral contraceptives to Pana- 
ma, but are downplaying specu- 
lation that a “Central American 
connection” may be responsible 
for the bogus OC 's, which began 
turning up in pharmacies and 
wRolesale drug warehouses 
over a month ago. 

The Panamanian shipment, 
destined for a Deer Park, N.Y.., 
wholesaler (Quality King), was 
ae by. a-sharp-eyed U.S. 

u 


st inspector at New 


York’ nedy International 


sy who became suspicious 
of laration indicating that 


the drugs were “re-entering” 
the United States. 
Acting on the Custems 


agent’s tip, F.D.A. officials 
seized 1,329 cartons (15,948 21- 
tablet units) of the counterfeit 
Searle OC from Quality King. A 
spokesman for the agency told 
Drug Store News that the pills 
ia ts Panamanian shipment 
appear to be from the same 
batch (‘Lot 489’’) that was 
traced earlier to a competing 
Long Island distributor, Inter- 
state 7 

F.D.A. investigators also 
disclosed a separate seizure of 
482 cartons of counterfeit “489” 
Ovulen (“complete with patient 
package inserts”) at McKes- 
son’s warehouse in Grand Prai- 
rie, Tex. The agency also seized 
4,100 units of ere OC’s from 
Memphis, Tenn.-based Wil- 
liams Generics. (Unlike the 
counterfeits obtained from 


McKesson and Quality King, 
the drugs seized in Tennessee 
were marked similarly to phony 
Ovulen tablets that had been 
earlier tracked to a third Long 
Island wholesaler, Interstate 
Drug Exchange.) 

Althou h officials at two of 
the New York wholesale drug- 
gists (Interstate Cigar and In- 
terstate Drug Exchange) told 
DrSN that they had purchased 
their Ovulen supplies from a 
Florida distributor (Lantor), 
Federal investigators refused 
to disclose any information con- 
cerning that company’s possible

Officials at Searle, which is 
conducting its own investiga- 
tion of the counterfeits, also re- 
fused to release any further in-

Three wholesalers post record sales, earnings 


NEW YORK — Three of the 
country’s five leading wholesal- 
ers reported record sales and 
earnings for the quarter ended 
Sept. 30. 

leo Standard Corp., head- 
uartered in Valley Forge, Pa., 
closed its fiscal year with earn-

1983. Primary earnings per 
share rose 14% to $2.87 from 
$2.52 the previous year. 
Alco’s revenues from con- 


tinuing operations were up 24% 
to $3.4 billion from $2.7 billion 
in 1983. 

For the three-month period 
ended Sept. 30, Alco recorded a 
7% decrease in net earnings as 
net income drop to $17.9 
million from $19.2 million dur- 
ing the fourth quarter of 1983. 
Revenues from the fourth quar- 
ter rose 24% to $381.3 million 
from $306.7 million in 1983.

leading wholesaler, reported 


that second quarter earnings 
rose 46% to $1.9 million from

In-store decisions: How the retailer can cash in 


Point of Purchase Advertising Institute of 

Fort Lee, N.J., in conjunction with the Du 
Pont Company, sent researchers out to inter- 
cept consumers as they shopped in 258 drug 
stores located in 40 of the country’s major met- 
ro markets. 

In the course of their research, the POPAI 
representatives interviewed an unprecedented 
12,131 consumers and recorded a total of 
27,282 purchases. 

The findings from these interviews, pub- 
lished in depth here for the first time, clearly 
show that the typical drug store shopper of the 
80’s is using his or her drug store as a place to 
make convenience purchases and that many of 
these purchases are initiated on the spur of the 
moment because of an attractive price, a high- 
traffic location, a pleasing display, a compelling 
sign or some other in-store variable. 

With two exceptions (prescriptions and cos- 
metics), the products most frequently bought 
in drug stores are not high ticket items. They 
are the little treats that people tend to buy for 
themselves every day and on which they usual- 
ly spend $1 or $2 or less. 


: n the early summer and late fall of 1983, the 


Departments ranking the highest in fre- 
quencies of purchase are candy and gum, 
greeting cards, stationery, tobacco and food 
and beverages. 

The common denominators of all of these 
categories, of course, are low price and high 
consumability. When a product is inexpensive, 
highly consumable, highly visible and well 
merchandised in a store, it is inevitably an inci- 
tor of impulse sales. For around a dollar or less, 
a shopper can pick up a candy bar or two, select 
a greeting card for a friend, buy a pack of ciga- 
rettes or treat themselves to a bag of chips and 
a can of soda. 

These same forces, however, can’t be count- 
ed on to spark purchases in the more tradition- 
al and nontraditional drug store categories like 
foot care or laxatives, barbecue items or jewel- 
ry. 

Here a retailer can’t usually count on a whim 
to spark a purchase. A shopper doesn’t buy 
toothpaste or a laxative the way she buys a can- 
dy or a greeting card. 

However the POPAI study does present evi- 
dence that price may be a factor in the incite- 
ment or nonincitement of these sales even 


though products like vitamins or cosmetics or 
antacids can’t be considered in a ticket class 
with 50¢ candies and 75¢ greeting cards. 

A shopper will yield to a candy bar or greet- 
ing card because it’s something they decide 
they want right at the point that they notice it 
and it isn’t going to cost them very much. But a 
shopper will yield to a vitamin or a laxative 
only a) if they know they’re going to be able to 
use it, b) if the price is attractive and c) if the 
retailer has done something creative to draw 
attention to the category and its pricing. 

Vitamins, for instance, are a pretty popular 
product in food stores. They’re advertised fre- 
quently by food stores and most shoppers who 
buy vitamins know that the prices are good, 
they’re competitive. You can see that many 
shoppers don’t immediately think of drug 
stores when they think of buying vitamins be- 
cause just 36% of all vitamin purchases in the 
POPAI survey were specifically planned. 

To increase the incidence of purchase of this 
product line, the retailer has to do more to 
make the category attractive. One part of the 
equation is price.

How fo use POPAI purchase frequency charts 


On the following pages of this report, you'll find a 
purchase frequency chart for most of the 40 major cat- 
egories and 300 subcategories analyzed in the POPAL 
Du Pont survey. For purposes of explanation we’ll use 
the cosmetics chart. 

_There are nine columns in the chart, each giving a 
piece of information that shows how well the category 
did in frequencies of purchase and how well the cate- 
gory performed in generating unplanned sales. 

e first column simply summarizes how popular 
the category is in today’s drug store. There were 
27,282 purchases recorded in the POPAI survey, and 
this column in each chart lets you see the percentage 
share captured by the 40 major departments. Cosmet- 
ics, for instance, captured a 4.4% share. 

_ The second column lets you see how the subcatego- 
ries within that department did. Of all cosmetic sales, 
for example, 29% were a by face makeup, 
26% by eye makeup and 37% by nail products. 


The third column, purchases per 100 shoppers, is a 
neat way of measuring sales against traffic, with 100 
shoppers being a unit of traffic. This is the column that 
tells you what will draw best with good in-store mer- 
chandising. 

The next five columns lets you get a fix on whether 
the consumer comes to your store with a specific pur- 
chase in mind or tends to buy on impulse either be- 
cause of a whim or strong merchandising aids. 

In cosmetics, for instance, only 34% of all sales are 
Specifically planned, meaning the typical consumer 
knows coming into the store that she wanted a specific 
brand and type of makeup. Another 14% are generally 
paar 9g" meaning the customer knows she wants a 

lush, but may mot be sure which brand or which 
shade. 

Another 7% consist of substitute sales, meaning 
that the customer goes into the store with a particular 
purchase in mind, but somewhere along the line de- 


cides to substitute another brand or even anothei 
product. A new product or shade attractively dis- 
played or a sharp price may be the factors. 

A striking 45% of all cosmetic purchases in drug 
stores are completely unplanned, which shows how 
important it is te capture the imagination of the 
browsers. 

The final column in our chart, the store decision in- 
dex, shows the degree to which in-store variables such 
as displays, signing, good location or price have an im- 
pact on sales. ' the case of cosmetics, 66% of all deci- 
sions are made after the shopper enters the store. 
That includes the 45% that are completely unplanned, 
oe the 21% that are either generally planned or 

rand and product substitutes. 

A 66% in-store decision should signal to a retailer 
that highlighting and dramatizing the category will 
pay off in incremental sales, assuming, of course, that 
pricing is competitive.

100 shoppers in a store. 

Most drug stores today need 
volume before they need any- 
thing, and these highly pur- 
chased incidence categories 
sport the products that can get 
that volume. 

In the last few years, drug 
stores have been advertising 
prescriptions with growing fre- 
quency, and the POPAI chart 
confirms that this is a logical 
trend. Scripts generate nearly 
10 purchases for every 100 
shoppers. 

Just recently some chains 
such as Walgreens have begun 
advertising greeting cards. 
Again POPAI’s charts show the 
logic behind the trend: the 
greeting card department gen- 
erates 15 purchases for every 
100 shoppers and cards them- 
selves spark 10 purchases per 
each 100 shoppers. 

As the retailer goes through 
the category charts on the sub- 
sequent pages of this report, he 
should be looking for those high 
purchase incidence categories 
to help give his advertising and 
promotional programs added 
spark. 

Readers should certainly 
look at the purchase per 100 
shoppers column for candies, 
scripts, greeting cards, statio- 
nery, tobacco, foods, bever- 


ages, shampoos, hair dressings, 
cosmetics, paper goods, tooth- 
paste and mouthwashes, soaps 
and deodorants, laundry and 
household cleaning imple- 
ments, batteries and skin care, 
cough/cold remedies, analge- 
sic‘ —particularly internal an- 
algesics,—baby supplies, film, 
shaving products, toys, first 
aid, vitamins, antacids, auto- 
motives and fragrances. 

Readers should also look 
carefully at the columns marked 
unplanned purchases and store 
decision rates because the per- 
centage numbers here hold sev- 
eral clues to how well a drug 
store is doing in motivating in- 
cremental sales among shop- 
pers already in the store. 

Just as the purchase per 100 
shoppers charts offer clues to 
products to advertise to bring 
shoppers into the store, the un- 
planned purchase and store de- 
cision columns offer clues as to 
how to coax multiple purchases 
out of consumers already in the 
store. 

As we said before the jewel- 
ry/leather goods department 
may be a neglected opportunity 
within today’s drug stores. So 
may seasonals and toys and gar- 
dening. 

The POPAI study definitely 
suggests that there is almost an 
unbounded opportunity for the 
average drug store to improve

sales through stronger mer- 
chandising. Out of 27,282 pur- 
chases, just 43% were specifi- 
cally planned by the consumer, 
meaning that in just four out of 
every 10 purchases did the con- 
sumer plan to buy that item be- 
fore they entered the drug 
store. 

The other six out of 10 sales 
came from merchandising aids 
visible in the store. In cases 
where consumers in the POPAI 
study rated particular stores 
“high” on merchandising ex- 
citement, dollar volumes for 
those stores were 15% to 20% 
higher than for stores rated av- 
erage in merchandising pizazz. 

In 6% of the cases where a 
consumer had a particular 
planned purchase in mind, and 
that particular product was not 
available in the store or was too 
hard to find or too high priced, 
they left the store without mak- 
ing any purchase. “2 

In an industry where the av- 
erage drug store does less than 
$1 million a year and where food 
and discount stores are eagerly 
vying for drug store customers, 
no one can afford those missed 
opportunities. 

“It’s unfortunately true,” 
says Howard Stumpf, president 
of POPAI, “that if the point-of- 
purchase materials in the store 
don’t leap out at the shopper, if 
they don’t get them to the point 
when they’re cruising the store, 
then the chances are that the re- 
tailer will miss the sale. Food 
stores know this, and that’s why 
you see so much merchandising 
activity in the aisles and on the 
ends.” 


he POPAI Du Pont Drug 

Store Shopper Study was 

implemented in the early 
summer and late fall of 1983. 

Point of Purchase Advertis- 
ing Institute researchers, 
working with a methodology 
developed by the Wilmington, 
Del.-based Du Pont company 
back in the early 1930's, ar- 
ranged to monitor shopper pur- 
chases in a total of 258 drug and 
mass-merchandiser stores with 
pharmacy services in 40 major 
metro markets. 

Through the cooperation of 
the National Association of 
Chain Drug Stores and the Na- 
tional Association of Retail 
Druggists, POPAI arranged to 
have both chains and high vol- 
ume indpendents included in 
the study. Among the chains 
which participated were Wal- 
greens, Eckerd, Genovese, 
Thrifty, CVS, SupeRx, Path- 
mark and Sentry. Over 200 
stores in the survey were 
chains; the rest were indepen- 
dents and mass-merchandisers. 

With the permission of the 
participating chains and own- 
ers, the researchers ap- 
proached shoppers as they en- 
tered the stores and asked them 
a series of demographic and 
promotional questions includ- 
ing what they planned to buy 
and whether they planned to 
make the purchase because of 
an ad, a coupon or a store circu- 
lar. 

A total of 12,131 consumers 
were interviewed over the 
course of the survey. As each 
shopper completed a shopping 
trip and checked out, the PO-

PAI reseachers recorded what 
they had actually purchased. 
They also noted whether it was 
a planned purchase, unplanned, 
a substitute and whether it was 
associated with a coupon, an ad 
or a store circular. 

POPAI had done a similar 
study of supermarket store 


shoppers back in 1978, and is 
now planning to do a follow up 
study in 1986 or 1987. 

The drug store survey, which 
cost $400,000, was supported in 
part by contributions from ma- 
jor brand manufacturers. PO- 
PAI’s own membership shoul- 
dered about half the cost.

Cosmetics 


_M@ ith mass merchandis- 
ers and food stores 
quickly gaining mar- 


ket share in the cosmetics cate- 
gory, drug chains are finding 
that promotions, particularly 
circulars and newspaper ads, 
are effective methods of pro- 
tecting their lion’s share. 

Drug chains have been ag- 
gressively touting their broad 
selection of cosmetics, depart- 
ment store line of fragrances 
and even their trained cosmeti- 
cians in circulars and ads. Ac- 
cording to the POPAI Du Pont 
study these promotions are 
having the desired effect with 
consumers using circulars in be- 
tween 10% and 22% of their cos- 
metics and fragrance pur- 
chases. 

These circulars are particu- 
larly influencial because many 
cosmetics are purchased on im- 
pulse and because there is a 
high level of in-store decisions. 
According to POPAI, women 


buying cosmetics made in-store 
decisions 66% of the time. Of 
these purchases, almost 45% 
were made completely on im- 
pulse. 

The impact of circulars clear- 
ly can be seen in nail products, 
which make up 37% of the cos- 
metics category. According to 
POPAI, circulars were used in 
15% of all nail polish sales and 
17% of nail enamel remover 
sales. These figures are note- 
worthy considering that 70% of 
all nail product purchases are 
decided in store and that more 
than 46% of these are impulse 
sales. Only 30% of nail product 
purchases are specifically 
planned and about 18% are gen- 
erally planned. 

Face makeup, the second 
largest cosmetics subgroup, 
was also frequently purchased 
with circulars. For example, 
consumers used circulars in 
12% of their lipstick and lipgloss 
purchase decisions. Newspaper 
ads were remembered in 11% of 
the purchases. The POPAI 
study showed that 61% of the 


make-up purchases were based 
on in-store decisions, and 44% 
of these were impulse 

The trend was repeated in 
eye make-up, where consumers 
used circulars in 17% of their 
mascara purchases and 11% of 
their purchases of eyebrow pen- 
cils, eye liners and false lashes. 
Newspaper ads were remem- 
bered in 13% of the mascara 
purchases. 


Hair care 


n the hair care category, 

which is constantly flooded 

with new entries and in 
which there is little brand loyal- 
ty, promotions make a big dif- 
ference in what shoppers buy. 

Advertising is particularly 
important in this category be- 
cause the availability of co-op 
dollars and the amount of na- 
tional exposure can influence 
retailers’ decisions on which 
new brands they carry and how 
much space they devote to 
them. 


In the POPAI Du Pont study, 


the impact of promotion can be 
seen across the board in the hair 
care category, with store circu- 
lars, coupons and newspaper 
ads having a high degree of in- 
fluence on shoppers. 

In the shampoo category, for 
example, newspapers, store 
eirculars and coupons had an 
impact on 35% of the purchases 
(newspaper ad recall 15%, in- 
store circular 15% and coupon 
5%). 

A similar trend was found in 
hair dressing. Of all the hair 
sprays purchased, promotions 
came into play 37% of the time 
(recalled a newspaper ad 16%, 
used circular 13% and used cou- 
pon 8%). 


Baby 


he logic of shaving margins 
on high-demand baby 


products like diapers and 
formulas in order to encourage 
sales of higher-profit categories 


like baby clothing, toys, rattles 
and pacifiers is borne out by the 
findings of the POPAI Du Pont 
study. 

The findings show a high de- 
gree of impulse for the accesso- 
ry products and a high degree of 
preplanning for the diapers and 
formulas. 

In fact, almost 8 out of 10 
shoppers who purchased dia- 
pers-or formulas came to the 
store specifically planning to 
buy those products. 

In contrast, 7 out of 10 shop- 
pers decided to buy a particular 
item of baby clothing or a toy 
only after entering the store. 

Their decisions, in other 
words, were triggered by some- 
thing in the store—in most 
cases, probably just the prox- 
imity of the baby accessory 
products to the already planned 
diapers or formulas. 

Other baby need products 
that had a higher degree of in- 
store decision making included 
cotton swabs (64%), baby wipes 
(69%), oils and lotions (56%) and 
powder (58%).

Analgesics 


hen it comes to analge- 
sics, most drug store 
shoppers know what 


they want and make sure they 
get it. 

According to the POPAI Du 
Pont shopper study, more than 
6 out of 10 analgesic purchases 
were specifically planned, while 
only 25% were made on im- 
pulse. 

The study also showed that 
coupon use is relatively high in 
the analgesic category, espe- 
cially for aspirin compounds 
(11% of the purchases involved a 
coupon) and non-aspirin prod- 
ucts (13%). In addition, in 19% 
of the aspirin and 15% of the 
non-aspirin purchases, shop- 


pers relied on a store circular. 
Newspapers also came into play 
in aspirin purchases (22% re- 
called seeing an ad for the prod- 
uct) and non-aspirin purchases 
(16%). 

More than 9 out of 10 (92.3%) 
of the aspirin purchases were 
for internal products; the rest, 
for external. Aspirin products 
claimed a 49% share of the total 
category and non-aspirin items 
36%. 


Dental 


hile 6 out of 10 tooth- 
paste purchases (57%) 
are specifically 


planned, according to the PO- 


PAI Du Pont study, the catego- 


ry is highly influenced by pro- 
motional activity. 

The study showed that con- 
sumers recalled newspaper ads 
for 22% of their toothpaste pur- 
chases, used an in-store circular 
for another 17% and turned ina 
coupon for 11%. That adds up to 
a total promotional influence 
factor of 50%. 

That’s important because the 
total dental products category 
generates a healthy 7.3 pur- 
chases per 100 shoppers, indi- 
cating that it’s a better traffic 
draw than most other catego- 
ries. 

Moreover, a toothpaste pur- 
chase is often the trigger for 
companion sales of other dental 
products that are more suscep- 
tible to impulse than tooth- 
paste, according to the study. 


For example, sales of mouth- 
washes/breath fresheners were 
specifically planned by 4 of 10 
shoppers and brushes/floss by 
only 3 of 10 shoppers. 

The impact of promotions 
was also evident in mouthwash 
sales. For example, consumers 
recalled a newspaper ad for 14% 
of the mouthwash purchases, 
used an in-store circular for 14% 
and handed in a coupon for 12%. 


Cough 


ince cold, sinus and aller- 
gy remedies are among 
the most heavily promot- 
ed drug store items, it stands to 
reason that they were the top 
subgroup in the cough/cold cat- 


egory, with 39% of sales. 

The POPAI Du Pont study 
also confirmed that most shop- 
pers buy cold remedies on an as- 
needed basis. It found that over 
70% of those purchases were ei- 
ther specifically or generally 
planned, and only 19% were 
bought entirely on impulse. 

Once inside the store, howev- 
er, shoppers changed their 
minds and bought a different 
brand or product about 10% of 
the time. 

As expected, cough drops, 
lozenges and gum purchases 
were made primarily on im- 
pulse, with more than half 
choosing to buy such a product 
without any plan in mind before 
entering the store. Only 31% of 
those purchases were specifi- 
cally planned.

Housewares 


rug retailers who have 

placed a greater empha- 

sis on housewares and 
household chemicals can take 
heart from the POPAI Du Pont 
Drug Store Shopper Study 
findings that placed both cate- 
gories in the top 15 in terms of 
percentage share of all drug 
store purchases. 

The housewares category— 
including glass/dishware/cook- 
ware; mops, brooms and 
brushes; kitchen gadgets and 
utensils, and yarn/sewing -no- 
tions—produced 5.1 purchases 
for every 100 shoppers. 

Pacing the category were 
kitchen gadgets, which ac- 
counted for 22% of the category 
purchase, glassware/dishware/ 
cookware—13.7%, and yarn/ 
sewing notions—13.7%. 

Despite the houseware cate- 
gory’s relatively strong show- 
ing, consumers rarely form the 
decision to purchase a house- 
wares product before entering 
the store. Only 31% of the pur- 
chases were specifically 
planned. Moreover, the store 
decision index, which tracks the 
incidence of consumers making 
or altering purchasing decisions 
in the store, was 68.9%. 

Of those purchases that were 
specifically planned, a signifi- 
cant percentage were influ- 
enced by either newspaper ads | 
or store circulars. 

As in the case of the house- 
wares category, the study re- 
vealed a high level of impulse 
purchases in the household 
cleaning aids category. Only 
38.5% of the purchases in this 
category were specifically 
planned. 

Among the category leaders 
with the highest degree of im- 
pulse purchases were kitchen/ 
bathroom products, laundry 
products and air fresheners/ 
deodorizers. The highest inci- 
dence of impulse purchases 
were recorded in the air fresh- 
ener/deodorizer category, 
which were unplanned in 63% of 
the cases. 

More than other categories, 
the paper goods category is 
heavily influenced by advertis- 
ing and promotion.

Stationery 


fforts by drug retailers to 

expand greeting cards and 

stationery presentations 
paid dividends as both catego- 
ries placed second and third, re- 
spectively, in the percentage 
share of all drug store pur- 
chases, according to the POPAI 
Du Pont study. 

The greeting cards catego- 
ry—defined as cards, special- 
occasion items, novelties and 
lottery tickets—generated 15.1 
purchases for every 100 drug 
store shoppers. That translated 
to a 6.8% share of total pur- 
chases, second only to candy/ 
gum, which posted a 7.7% share 
of total purchases. 

Stationery, which the POPAI 
Du Pont study described as in- 
ay stationery, school and 
upplies accounted for 


13.9 purchases for every 100 
shoppers. Overall, the statio- 
nery category represented a 
6.3% share of total purchases. 
Books and magazines, a relat- 
ed category, also turned in a 
strong performance, placing 
10th in the category list of per- 


centage share of all purchases 


with a 3.5% of total purchases. 
A total of eight purchases of 
books and magazines were 
made for every 100 shoppers in 
drug stores. 

A closer look at the greeting 
cards and stationery categories 
revealed that the purchases 
were either generally or specifi- 
cally planned in more than 50% 
of the cases. 

Overal], the purchases made 
from greeting cards depart- 
ments were either generally 
planned: specifically planned 
in nearly .1% of the cases. This 
high degree of planned pur- 
chases in the greeting cards cat- 


BEST AVAILABLE COPY 


egory supports the recent 
moves by many drug chains to 
relocate departments to the 
front end of the store, thus mak- 
ing it easier for customers to lo- 
cate the department and get in 
and out of the store as quickly as 
possible. 

Similarly, peripheral greet- 
ing card categories such as gift 
wraps and party supplies also 
followed a pattern of planned 
purchases, although the inci- 
dence of impulse purchases of 
these items was considerably 
higher. Other items that are 
generally merchandised along 
with greeting cards such as can- 
dles and novelties are for the 
most part impulse items. Of the 
purchases gf €andles and novel- 
ties, 53% and 58%, respectively, 
were unplanned. 

In addition to greeting cards, 
many drug retailers have at- 
tempted to increase the visibili- 
ty of their stationery, school and 


home office sections. And, as in 
the case of greeting cards, re- 
tailers have largely been re- 
warded by their moves. 

By expanding the stationery 
department and upgrading the 
overall merchandise mix, retail- 
ers have been able to take ad- 
vantage of the generally 
planned purchasing patterns of 
consumers who buy items such 
as writing instruments and 
writing paper and home office 
supplies. 

The POPAI Du Pont study re- 
vealed that of the purchases of 
writing implements, which ac- 
counted for 20% of the total cat- 
egory purchases, nearly 53% of 
the consumers had either gen- 
erally planned or specifically 
planned to make the purchase. 

Of the purchases in the writ- 
ing paper segment, which in- 
cludes writing tablets, pads, 
boxed stationery, typing paper 
and envelopes, approximately 


55% of the purchases were ei- 
ther specifically or generally 
planned. 

The findings from the POPAI 
study also indicate that sales in 
the stationery category are sig- 
nificantly influenced by adver- 
tising and promotion. In 36% of 
the cases where a writing paper 
product was purchased, con- 
sumers reported that they ei- 
ther recalled a newspaper ad or 
used a store circular. And in an 
average of 46% of the cases 
where a writing instrument was 
purchased, consumers who 
were surveyed said they re- 
called a newspaper ad or used a 
store circular. 

With the exception of news- 
papers, which are usually 
planned purchases, the books 
and magazines category gener- 
ally follows a pattern of impulse 
purchases. Of the magazines 
purchased, 54.6% were com- 
pletely unplanned.

Candy 
FOOdS 
Beverages 


hen consumers pur- 
chase candy, food or 
beverage items in a 


drug store, they are likely 
swayed into making those pur- 
chasing decisions by high-traf- 
fic merchandising, sharp pric- 
ing or some combination of the 
two. 

Collectively, candy/gum, 
beverages and food items ac- 
counted for 43.2 purchases for 
every 100 shoppers, according 
to the 1988 POPAI Du Pont 
Drug Store Shopper Study. 
However, of those purchases, 
only 37.4% were specifically 
planned. 

Not surprisingly, candy, 
which is generally merchan- 
dised in high-traffic areas of 
drug stores, inclading many 
checkstand locations, regis- 
tered the highest degree of un- 
planned purchases. Of the 17.1 
candy/gum purchases made by 


. every 100 shoppers, 63.4% were 


unplanned impulse purchases. 

Within the candy category, 
smaller-sized items such as 
bars, rolls and small boxes and 
bags were most frequently pur- 
chased without prior planning 
on the part of the shopper. How- 
ever, higher-ticket candy items 
and bulk-packed candy prod- 
ucts were less of an impulse buy, 
according to the study. In addi- 
tion, a high percentage of con- 
sumers who purchased items 
such as boxed candy and sea- 
sonal candy either used a store 
circular or recalled a newspaper 
ad. 

Chewing gum, like individual 
candy bars and bags, was also 
more frequently purchased on 
impulse. Of the total chewing 
gum purchases, which account- 
ed for a21% share of the catego- 
ry purchases, 61.4% were un- 
planned. 

The POPAI Du Pont study re- 
vealed that many food pur- 
chases in drug stores are un- 
planned. The study said that of 
the 13.2 purchases for every 100 
shoppers, 50.4% were un- 
planned. 

Snack foods and cereals and 


breakfast foods were among the 
most frequently purchased im- 
pulse items. Snack foods, which 
accounted for 51% of the catego- 
ry purchases, were actually 
planned purchases in only 32% 
of the cases. 

The POPAI Du Pont findings 
would also seem to indicate that 
consumers perceive a Savings in 
many food items carried in drug 
stores. In fact, in some food cat- 
egories such as dairy products 
(primarily milk); canned and 
jarred meats, fish and fruits, 
and jams, jellies, spreads and 
syrups, the percentage of 
planned purchases was surpris- 
ingly high. In the case of dairy 
products, which represented 
21% of the food category pur- 
chases, nearly 65% of the pur- 
chases were either generally 
planned or specifically planned. 

Advertising, whether in the 
form of newspaper ROP ads or 
through in-store circulars, 
played a major role in several of 
the planned food purchases. Of 
those purchases of canned and 
jarred vegetables, meats and 
fruits, the percentage of con- 
sumers recalling either a news- 
paper ad or store circular pro- 


moting the product was 
significantly higher than other 
food items. 

Of the three categories, can- 
dy/gum, food and beverages, 
the latter recorded the highest 
incidence of planned purchises. 
With the exception of fruit 
juices/mixes, coffee and tea, 
which tended to be impulse pur- 
chases, the majority of other 
beverage categories were more 
frequently either generally or 
specifically planned purchases. 

The alcoholic beverages were 
the leaders in terms of planned 
purchases. Liquor, which ac- 
counted for a 10.1% share of the 
beverage category purchases, 
were either generally or specifi- 
cally planned in nearly 75% of 
the cases. Beer, which repre- 
sented 17% of the category pur- 
chases, were planned purchases 
in nearly 70% of the instances. 

Wine more closely followed 
the patterns of soft drinks, 
which tended to be both 
planned and impulse. Of the to- 
tal wine purchases, approxi- 
mately 58% were generally or 
specifically planned and nearly 
38% were picked up on impulse 
in the stores. 


Soft drinks, including regular 
and diet beverages, accounted 
for more than 50% of the share 
of category purchases and tend- 
ed to be impulse buys in approx- 
imately 36% of the cases. The 
study revealed that soft drinks 
were either generally or specifi- 
cally planned 55% of the time. 


Pet food 


n the pet foods and supplies 
| department, food drives the 

volume and supplies gener- 
ates the margins, according to 
the POPAI Du Pont shoppers 
study. 

Of the total department pur- 
chases, almost 2 out of 3 were 
rung up in the pet foods catego- 
ry and the remainder in pet sup- 
plies. The lower margin food 
category, the study showed, 
had a lower degree of in-store 
decision making (65% of the 
purchases) than the higher- 
margin supplies (80% of the 
purchases). 

Cat food generated almost 
half (48%) of the total pet food 
purchases, with dog food com- 
ing in second (38%).

dex. The percentage of jewelry
