The drugstore industry faces numerous challenges today. The 
market is more complex than ever. To survive, store traffic must 
be increased; the potential of every shopper maximized; and traffic 
patterns translated into greater profits through impulse sales. 


What does it take to diagnose trends that will sell consumers? 


It takes the awesome, statistical data of THE POPAI/Du PONT 

_ DRUGSTORE CONSUMER BUYING HABITS STUDY — a $400,000 

| work of research in 258 stores, 12,000 plus shopper interviews 

| and 40 markets, coast-to-coast. The full-scale study profiles the 

_ drugstore: Who buys, What sells, How purchase decisions are 
influenced, Where to place media dollars and Why the drugstore 
is the greatest untapped profit potential. 


The data contained in this 500 plus page book is stunning the 

| business community with facts that greatly contradict traditional 
| merchandising and advertising strategies. It includes answers to 

_ these crucial questions: 


How can the selling potential of the shopper be maximized? 
How can traffic patterns be translated into greater profits? 
How do shoppers decide on products before and during the 
shopping trip? 

What are the impacts of couponing and advertising? 

How does age, income, household size, sex and shopping fre- 
quency affect final purchasing decisions? 

How can retailers use this information to tap greater profits? 
What is the incidence of purchase for the top selling products? 
What cross merchandising opportunities exist? 


What are the major advertising markets and how can they 
be sold?

Auto 


oth the automotive and 
hardware categories are 
driven more by specific 
planned need than by impulse 
appeal, according to findings 
from the POPAI Du Pont study. 

Collectively, the automotive 
and hardware categories gener- 
ated nearly seven purchases for 
every 100 shoppers. However, 
the incidence of unplanned pur- 
chases was lower than most oth- 
er drug store categories. Of 
those products purchased from 
the automotive category, nearly 
33% were unplanned. The per- 
centage of hardware impulse 
sales for every 100 purchases 
was 30%. 

There was a high degree of 
brand substitution within the 
automotive category, which in- 
cludes motor oil, waxes and pol- 


ishes, gasoline and oil additives 
and miscellaneous gadgets. Of 
those consumers who pur- 
chased auto products, 6% sub- 
stituted brand. 

Hardware products were also 
frequently substituted at the 
point of purchase. Of those 
hardware products purchased 
for every 100 shoppers, more 
than 5% substituted brand. 
Overall, the store decision in- 
dex in the hardware category 
was 63%, indicating a high level 
of in-store decision-making. 

The leading products in the 
hardware category by percent- 
age share of purchases were 
batteries, which accounted for 
51% of the category purchases. 
According to the study, there 
were nearly three battery pur- 
chases for every 100 shoppers. 
Of those purchases, 41% were 
specifically planned, 21% gen- 
erally planned and 29% were 
unplanned. 


DRUG STORE NEWS, December 10, 1984 


-POPAI Du Pont 


Drug Store Shopper Study

Electrical appliances 


Aiton and promo- 
tion are key factors in a 
consumer’s decision to 
purchase a consumer electron- 
ics product in a drug store, ac- 
cording to the POPAI Du Pont 
shopper survey. 

In nearly every one of the 
electronics and household appli- 
ance products categories from 
which purchases were made an 
overwhelming percentage of 
the consumers had their buying 
decisions influenced by cou- 
pons, newspaper ads and/or 
store circulars. 

Of those purchases involving 
watchs and clocks, consumers 
reported seeing a newspaper ad 
for the item in 62% of the cases. 
Thirty-one per cent said they 
used a store circular and nearly 
16% used a coupon. 


Sales of calculators, a popular 
drug store item, also were 
heavily influenced by promo- 
tion. The incidence of consum- 
ers who purchased calculators 
recalling a newspaper ad for the 
item was 72%. Thirty-six per 
cent indicated that they used a 
store circular. 

With purchases involving ra- 
dios and stereos, the percent- 
age of consumers who recalled 
being exposed to some form of 
advertising for the item was 
even greater. Eighty per cent of 
those consumers purchasing ra- 
dios said they recalled a news- 
paper ad for the product, 30% 
saw the item featured in a store 
circular and 15% used a coupon 
in their purchase. 

Because of the apparent im- 
pact of advertising involving a 


consumer electronics product 
or household appliance on the 
decision to purchase that prod- 
uct, the incidence of impulse 
buying in this category is sub- 
stantially lower than most other 
drug store categories. Higher 
price points for consumer elec- 
tronics, it should also be pointed 
out, would help account for the 
lower level of impulse buying in 
this category. 

Of those purchases involving 
electrical or household appli- 
ances or supplies, only 30% of 
the consumers indicated that 
the purchase was unplanned. 


Seasonal 


hile seasonal depart- 
ments generate both 
specifically planned 


purchases and impulse sales in 


drug stores, the overwhelming 
majority of consumers make the 
final buying decision regarding 
seasonal products in the store. 

For the most part, seasonal 
items are either generally or 
specifically planned. Consum- 
ers who purchase items such as 
gardening tools and hoses, fire- 
place logs, and pesticides usual- 
ly follow a planned purchase 
pattern. 

However, once in the store it 
is clear that consumers are 
prone to change their minds 
both with respect to brands and 
products. For instance: garden- 
ing tools and hoses and insecti- 
cides and pesticides are fre- 
quently planned purchases. Of 
those purchases involving hoses 
or tools, nearly 70% were either 
generally or specifically 
planned. Similarly, of those pur- 
chases of pesticides and insecti- 
cides, nearly 60% were either 


generally or specifically 
planned. But both eategories 
had a store decision index of 
nearly 70%. 

One can assume that consum- 
ers are frequently unfamiliar 
with seasonal items even 
though they know they want a 
certain product. This may be 
due in part to low brand recog- 
nition with products in the sea- 
sonal category. 

Among the products most 
likely purchased on an impulse 
basis, the POPAI study indicat- 
ed, are live plants, shrubs and 
flowers. Of those products pur- 
chased, nearly 70% were un- 
planned. 

Conversely, products such as 
plant food, fertilizer and grass 
seed are planned purchases. Of 
the products purchased in that 
category, more than 70% were 
either generally or specifically 
planned.

DRUG STORE NEWS, January 7, 1985 


2 
By Faye Brookman 


NEW YORK — Sparked by a dynamic resur- 
gence in the toy category, Christmas sales for the 
nation’s drug store retailers increased over those of 
last year’s robust selling season. Retailers’ spirits 
were dampened, however, by the reluctance of con- 
sumers to dig deep into their pockets for higher- 
ticket gift items. 

The net result for drug chains was a “good but not 
great” Yule season. Same-store sales increased 
only 8% to 10% over 1983, instead of the 12% to 15% 
retailers had targeted. Plus, overall sales peaked at 
12% to 15% and the increases were produced 
thanks to the extra two selling days sandwiched 
into the Yule season. Without those extra selling 
hours, chains would have registered sales gains of 
-— 5% over 1983. 

Sluggish Christmas sales were actually the cul- 
mination of a trend that started last summer. Even 


Category adds sparkle to holiday sales 


the day after Thanksgiving, according to Paine 
Webber, did not produce the volume drug chains 
had anticipated. 

“The zip just isn’t there,” complained Genovese 
Drug’s Don Gross about the shopping days just pri- 
or to Christmas. “We’re not seeing the pent-up de- 
mand witnessed last year.” 

Gross, along with representatives of chains in- 
cluding Fay’s, Begley, —— Revco, People’s 
and Harco, fi that softer s, coupled with 
promotionai markdowns needed to clean our heavy 
inventories, could trickle down to the bottom line. 

Many pointed out that they enacted last-minute 
lieth gg | measures to avert any earnings 
problems, while others took solace in the fact that 
even department stores were forced to drastically 
cut prices to boost volume. For the first time in its 
history, for example, Bloomingdale’s was forced to 
run a huge three-day sale before Christmas. 


Many retailers blame the anemic sales on cus- 
tomers shying away from high-ticket goods. Bob 
Begley, president and chairman of Begley, termed 
this year’s shopper as having a “casual attitude. We 
know there is disposable income out there, but we 
just didn’t see ive buying.” 

_Added Fay’s president Dan Herrmann, “We just 
didn’t see the movement of items like TVs, micro- 
waves or electronics.” 

And on top of cautious consumer buying pat- 
terns, drug chains complained about the sheer 
— of retailers now competing for the same 
shopper. 

“There’s more retail square footage than ever 
and they’re all selling the same thing,” Begley la- 
mented. 

The competition didn’t only come from other re- 
tail segments, but drug chains, too. Most major

FORT LAUDERDALE, 
Fla. — Shareholders attend- 
ing Pantry Pride’s annual 
meeting here last month have 
5 aged voted in favor of 
the current management 
team, ending temporarily a 
bid by dissidents to gain con- 
trol of the supermarket chain 
and specialty retailer. 

Pantry Pride, which last 
month acquired Adams Drug, 
said that a preliminary count 
of votes from the Dec. 7 annual 
meeting indicates that the 
company’s board of directors, 
led by Grant C. Gentry, chair- 
man and ceo, has been re- 
elected. The food and drug re- 
tailer, whose other holdings 
include Devon Stores, said its 


slate of directors received 
aid 61% of the shares vot- 
ed. 

The dissident group, led by 
Dwight Devon, the son of the 
late Philip Devon, who found- 
ed the Devon hard goods 
chain; Howard Gittis, a Phila- 
delphia attorney, and Patrick 
Rooney, chairman of the New 
York investment firm the 
Rooney Pace Group, received 
only 10.7 million votes of the 
27.2 million cast. The Devon 
family controls approximately 
10.4% of Pantry Pride’s out- 
standing stock as a result of 
the sale of the 89-store chain to 
Pantry Pride last year. 

At issue during the openly 
bitter proxy fight has been the 


slumping performance of Pan- 
try Pride. The dissidents con- 
tend that the company stock is 
undervalued. Moreover, they 
charged that the company’s 
top execs are earning salaries 
that do not reflect Pantry 
Pride’s poor earnings. Gen- 
try, a prime target of the dissi- 
dents, earned $520,000 in sala- 
ry and bonuses during fiscal 
1984. 

Although the dissidents 
have vowed to continue the 
battle to unseat the Pantry 
Pride management, analysts 
who have followed the proxy 
fight say it is doubtful they 
will be successful following 
their defeat at the annual 
meeting.

made.

DRUG STORE NEWS, January 7, 1985 
Chain execs’ economic predictions 


Mostly sunny skies with a chance of showers 


he economy, following 

President Reagan’s re- 

election, may be entering 
a slowdown phase, but retail 
and wholesale drug industry 
executives, trying to peer into 
their crystal balls for 1985, are 
relatively optimistic. 

In a survey of top retail and 
wholesale executives carried 
out just prior to the election, 
the mood of most industry ex- 
ecutives was upbeat. 

Although there were some 
reservations about the deficit 
and possible increases in both 
personal and corporate taxes, 
most retail chain and indepen- 
dent drug store operators and 


oy 808 peer | 


most wholesale executives felt 
the economy was going to con- 
tinue along reasonably well, 
with such key economic ba- 
rometers as inflation and in- 
terest rates either not chang- 
ing at all or increasing 
moderately. 

On the most positive plane, 
the majority of chain retail and 
wholesale executives felt that 
disposable income would in- 
crease at least moderately in 
1985. At the same time they 
and many independents aiso 
felt that unemployment would 
go down, probably moderate- 
ly. 

Their optimism seems to be 


closely connected to a faith in 
the President’s ability to con- 
trol the economy. But that op- 
timism is not so strong as to 
make them believe that the 
threat of inflation is entirely 
behind us or that potential 
problems with the growing 
deficit can be avoided. 

In looking at the overall eco- 
nomic picture for 1985, nearly 
half of all chain executives, 


plus a third of all wholesalers , 
and independents, said they | 


were “very confident” that the’ 
economy would continue to 
move through a recovery 
phase in 1985. 

Half of our respondents 


were at least “somewhat confi- 
dent” that the economy would 
continue to recover. 

Chain executives were the 
most optimistic, with 95% of 
all respondents expressing ei- 
ther a very or somewhat opti- 
mistic view of the economy. 
Eight out of 10 wholesale and 
independent respondents, 
were equally as confident. 

The big worries about the 
economy came in the areas of 
the deficit, inflation, interest 
rates and corporate and per- 
sonal taxes. 

Half of all independents and 
wholesalers and two-thirds of 
all chain executives felt infla- 


tion would rise in 1985. How- 
ever, they said that they felt 
that any increases would only 
be moderate. 

With inflation now running 
at 3% to 4%, most of the indus- 
try seems to feel that inflation 
will remain far below the dou- 
ble digit rate in 1985, probably 
at no more than 7% to 8%. 

The deficit, however, is an- 
other story. Right now the 
Government is estimating that 
the deficit will reach about 
$210 billion. This is already 
$35 billion more than Reagan 
was estimating the week of his 
election.

First they plan to construct or 
acquire more conventional

mainstay, and second, they

Use of computers 
fo grow in 1985 


Over the next two years, 
chain drug executives will be 
installing computers, scan- 
ners and other electronic 
a that could result in 

% of all chain companies op- 
erating stores with total in- 
store automation systems by 
the end of 1986. 

According to Drug Store 
News first drug store indus- 
try trends and operations 
study, pharmacy computers 
are already a fact of life in the 
majority of chain stores and in 
about half of all independently 
owned stores. 


Chain executives are plan- 
ning to keep their lead over in- 
dependents in computer utili- 
zation systems by moving 
aggressively to round out 
their installation of electronic 
point-of-sale cash registers, 
inventory scanners, checkout 
scanners and in-store mini or 
micro computers that are able 
to interact with front-end reg- 
isters. 


The 1985 survey shows that 
approximately 75% of the 
chain companies already are 
using electronic cash registers 
in their stores and that anoth- 
er 10% plan to install them in 
1985 and 1986. 


If that game plan is met, 
then 85% of the chains will 
have electronic cash registers 
in their stores by the end of 
1986. In addition, by 1986 70% 
of the chains should have in- 
ventory scanners in their 
stores and another 65% should 
have checkout scanners. 


Currently, the survey 
shows that 50% of the chains 
already do have inventory 
scanners in their stores, while 
another 25% have checkout 
scanners in at least some 
stores.

holds up, would put chain op- 
erators “ ahead of indepen- 
dents in the development of 
store-automated systems.

in their utilization of electron- 
ic cash registers.

$10 million.

won't compete with conven-

Chain drug stock decline counte 


NEW YORK — After a 
broad decline through the first 
six months of the year, chain 
drug stocks recovered some- 
what in the second half, but for 
many of the publicly held drug 
chains it was a case of too little 
too late. 

However, of the 15 leading 

ublic drug chains tracked by 

Store News, nine stocks 

did a to appreciate dur- 

ing 1984. But the gains posted 

were considerably smaller 

than the increases registered 
the previous year. 

The sharp reversal from 
1983 was particularly evident 
among many of the secondary 
chain drug issues. Genovese 


Drug, whose stock soared 
200% in 1983, fell 28.3% in 
1984. Fay’s Drug, up 110% in 
1983, declined 23.6% last 
year. Big B finished 1984 
down 17.3% after rising 104% 
the previous year. Hook Drug 
plunged 31% in 1984 after reg- 
istering an 86% gain in 1984. 
Although the declines were 
less dramatic, some of the 
large institutionally held drug 
chains also experienced a 
rough year in 1984. Revco, be- 
set by internal problems, 
posted the most significant 
slide: up 28% in 1983 and down 
30.3% in 1984. And even a 
takeover last year by outside 
investors failed to help Pay ’n

turned out to be “too difficult 
to implement.”

been finding it hard to find

targeted for sectioning. 

ray’s management began 
downsizing the typical 18,000- 
to 25,000-sq.-ft. Drug Fair 
stores two years ago and has 


already completed about 60 
remodels.

quarters in which sales and op- 
erating profits both increased, 
Gray hit a bumpy third quar- 
ter for the miner | ended Sept. 
30, management since has 
been rethinking its priorities. 

The new planning calls for 
both belt-tightening and ag- 
gressive sales growth. 

Some of the belt-tightenin 
is coming from personne 
changes and some is coming 
from anew vigorous assault on

Bergen posts record sales and earnings 


LOS ANGELES — Bergen 
Brunswig Corp. announced 
record sales and earnings for 
a first quarter ended Nov. 

Net earnings from continu- 
ing operations increased 17% 
to $6.2 million, or 49¢ a share, 
from $5.3 million, or 42¢ a 
share, in the same previous- 
year period. 

Sales and other revenues 


for the quarter rose 24% to 
$493 million from $397 million. 
Emil P. Martini Jr., chair- 
man and ceo, said revenue and 
ae profit increases 
were partly the result of the 
Oct. 1 acquisition of the Allen 
Co., based in Orlando. 
Martini also explained that 
the Medical/Surgical division 
results continued to be affect- 
ed by sluggishness in the 


health care and hospital indus- 
try. “Earnings,” he said, “are 
running behind the prior year. 
Development of new business 
with alternative sites for 
health care delivery is in prog- 
ress.” 

Martini said the compan 
was “especially pleased wit 
the excellent results from 
Commtron Corp., the compa- 
ny’s consumer electronics di- 


vision, which continues to run 
well ahead of the plan.” 

In a related development, 
Synergex Corp., which has 
signed a definitive agreement 

roviding for the merger of 
Synergex with a wholly 
owned subsidiary of Bergen 
Brunswig, announced results 
for the first fiscal quarter. 

Sales for the period in- 
creased 29% to $95.9 million 


from $74.2 million for the com- 
parable previous-year quar- 
ter. Net earnings for the quar- 
ter increased 48% to $1.4 
million from $917,000 a year 
earlier. Earnings per share 
were up 15% to 31¢ from 27¢. 

Under the terms of the 
merger agreement with Ber- 
gen Brunswig, Synergex 
shareholders will receive $18 
per share.

NEW YORK — When 
President Reagan signed the 
Drug Price Competition and 
Patent Term Restoration Act 
of 1984 into law, it was amid 
much confusion about its con- 
tents from many members of 
the pharmaceutical communi- 
ty. 

While much of that confu- 
sion remains, the bill will still 
have a major impact on gener- 
ic and brand name pharmaceu- 
tical manufacturers. 

Drug analyst Hermant 
Shah of Mabon, Nugent & Co. 
sees it as the most important 
piece of legislation to surface 
in over 30 years. 

“I believe this bill is the 
most important legislation af- 
fecting the branded and ge- 
neric pharmaceutical industry 
since the Food, Drug and Cos- 
metic Amendments of Kefau- 
ver-Harris in 1962,”’ said 


Special report: 
Generic drugs 


Shah. While portions of the act 
have been rewritten (see sto- 
ry page 31), F.D.A. Commis- 
sioner Frank Young called it 
only a “down payment” and 
promised there will be more. 

“The regulations are suffi- 
ciently flexible for us to still 
examine the mechanisms used 
to review and process new 
drug applications,”’ said 
Young. “We will explore addi- 
tional methods of drug ap- 
proval that depart substan- 
tially from this classical 
procedure, including a greater 
reliance on outside experts.” 

Young hopes through modi- 
fication of F.D.A.’s advisory 
system that F.D.A. will be 
able to experiment with dif- 
ferent models of product ap- 
proval. 

Young says that perhaps 
one area in which F.D.A. is 
lacking may be the way 
changes in regulations are 
handled. 

“In all candor, this process 
is frequently cumbersome and 
we need to examine whether 
other approaches might pro- 
vide more flexibility when we 
must act quickly,” said 
Young. “There may be other, 
better means to the same 
end.” 

As expected, the influx of 
Abbreviated New Drug Ap- 
plications (ANDA) from ge- 
neric companies came sieitbe 
On Nov. 26, the first = the 
ANDA portion of the Wax- 
man bill went into effect, 
F.D.A.’s Generic Drug divi- 
sion received approximately 


200 post-1962 ANDA applica- 
tions from approximately 15 
to 20 manufacturers. 

To handle the onslaught, 
the F.D.A. had to do some re- 
shuffling of staffs and respon- 
sibilities. This has led to more 
than 20 positions slotted for 


New law should spawn 
flurry of generic drugs 


the Generic division. 

In addition the agency has 
set up a steering committee 
under the direction of Deput 
Commissioner Mark N mame 
to coordinate all the changes 
that will have to be made in

agents may be required to suppress gouty attacks in some cases The aftacks usually become shorter 
and less severe after several months of therapy The mobilization of urates from tissue deposits which 
cause fluctuations in the serum uric acid levels may be a possible explanation for these eprsodes 
Even with adequate allopurinol therapy Mt may require severai months to deplete the uric acid poo! sut- 
ficiently to achieve control of the acute aftacks A fluid intake sufficient to yield a daily urinary Output 
of at least 2 liters and the maintenance of a neutral or. preferably, slightly alkaline urine are desirable to 
(1) avoid the theoretical possibility of formation of xanthine caiculi under the influence of allopurinol 
therapy and (2) help prevent renal precipitation ot urates in patients receiving Concomitant uricosuric 
Some patients with pre-ex renal disease or poor urate clearance have shown a rise in 
BUN during allopurinol admiristration ugh the mechanism responsible for this has not been es- 
tablished, patients with impaired renal function should be carefully observed during the early stages 
of allopurinol administration and do decreased or the drug withdrawn if increased abnormalities 
in renal function appear and persist. Renal failure in association with allopurinol administration has 
been observed among patients with hyperuricemia secondary to neoplastic diseases Concurrent 
conditions such as multiple myeloma and congestive myocardial disease were present among those 
patients whose renal dysfunction increased after allopurinol was begun al failure is also 
frequently associated with gouty nephropathy and rarety with allopurincl-associated hypersensitivity 
reactions. Albuminuria has been observed among patients who developed clinical gout following 
chronic glomerulonephritis and chronic pyelonephritis. Patients with decreased renal function 
require lower doses of allopurinol than those with normal renal function Lower than recommended 
doses should be used to initiate therapy in any patients with decreased renal function and they should 
be observed closely mm earty stages of allopurinol administration In patients with severely 
impaired renal function or decreased urate clearance. the half-life of oxipurinol in the piasma is greatly 
prolonged. Therefore, a dose of 100 mg. per day or 300 mg. twice a week, or perhaps less, may be 
sufficient to maintain adequate xanthine oxidase inhibition to reduce serum urate levels Bone mar- 
row depression has been reported in patients receiving allopurinol, most of whom received con- 
comitant drugs with the potential for causing this reaction. This has occurred as early as six weeks to 
as long as six years after the initiation of allopurinol therapy Rarety a patient may develop varying 
degrees of bone marrow depression, affecting one or more cell lines, while receiving allopurinol 
alone tntermation fer Patients: Patients should be informed of the following (1) They should be cau- 
tioned to discontinue allopurinol and to Consult their physician immediately at the first sign of a skin 
rash, paintul urination, blood in the urine, irritation of the eyes, or swelling of the lips or mouth. (2) 
They should be reminded to continue drug therapy prescribed for gouty attacks since optimal benefit 
of allopurinol may be delayed for two to six weeks (3) They should be encouraged to increase fluid 
intake during therapy to prevent renal stones. (4) If a single does of allopurinol is occasionally forgot- 
ten, there is no need to double the dose at the next scheduled time. (5) There may be certain risks 
associated with the concomitant use of allopurinol and dicumarol. sulfinpyrazone, mercaptopurine 
azathioprine, ampicillin, amoxicillin and thiazide diuretics, and they should follow the instructions of 
their physician (6) Due to the occasional occurrence of drowsiness. patients should take precaution 
when engaging in activities where alertness is mandatory (7) Patients may wish to take allopurinol 
after meals to minimize gastric irritation Tests: The correct dosage and schedule for 
maintaining the serum uric acid within the normal range is best determined by using the serum uric 
acid level as an index. In patients with pre-existing liver disease, periodic liver function tests are rec- 
ommended during the early stages of therapy (see WARNINGS section). Aliopurinol and its primary 
active metabolite oxipurinol are eliminated by the kidneys, therefore, changes in renal function have a 
profound effect on dosage. In patients with decreased renal function or who have concurrent ilinesses 
which can affect renal function such as hypertension and diabetes mellitus. periodic laboratory 
parameters of renal function. particularly BUN and serum creatinine or creatinine Clearance. should 
be performed and the patient's allopurino! dosage reassessed. The prothrombin time shoulc de reas- 
sessed periodically in the patients receiving dicumarol who are given aliopurino! Drug interactions: 
In patients receiwing mercaptopurine or azathioprine. the concomitant admunistration of 300-600 mg 
of allopurinol per day will require a reduction in dose to approximately one-third to one-fourth of the 
usual! dose of mercaptopurine or azathioprine. Subsequent adjustment of doses of mercaptopurine 
or azathioprine should be made on the basis of therapeutic response and the appearance of toxic ef- 
fects (see CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY). It has been reported that allopurinol prolongs the half-life of 
the anticoagulant dicumarol. The clinica! basis of this drug interaction has not been established but 
should be noted when allopurinol is given to patients already on dicumarol therapy. Since the excre- 
tion of Oxipurinol is similar to that of urate, uricosuric agents which increase the excretion of urate are 
also likety to increase the excretion of oxipurinol and thus lower the degree of inhibition of xanthine 
oxidase. The concomitant administration of uricosuric agents and allopurinol has been associated 
with a decreased in the excretion of hypoxanthine and xanthine anc an increase in urinary uric acid 
excretion compared with that cbserved with allopurinol alone. Although clinical evidence to date has 
not demonstrated renal precipitation of oxypurines in patients either on allopurinol alone or in combi- 
nation with uricosuric agents, the possibility should be kept in mind. The reports that the con- 
comitant use of allopurinol and thiazide diuretics may contribute to the enhancement of allopurinol 
toxicity in some patients have been reviewed in an attempt to establish a cause and effect relationship 
and a mechanism of causation. The review of these case reports indicates that the patients were 
mainly receiving thiazide diuretics for hypertension and that tests to rule out decreased renal function 
secondary to hypertensive nephropathy were not often performed in those patients in whom renal 
insufficiency was documented, however, the recommendation to lower the dose of allopurinol was 
not followed Although a causal mechanism and a Cause and effect relationship have not been estab- 
lished, current evidence suggests that renal function should be monitored in patients on thiazide 
diuretics and allopurinol even in the absence of renal failure. and dosage levels should be even more 
conservatively adjusted in those patients on such Combined therapy if diminished renal function ts 
detected An increase in the frequency of skin rash has been reported among patients receiving ampi- 
cillin or amoxicillin with allopurinol compared to patients who are not receiving both drugs The cause 
of the reported association has not been established. Enhanced bone marrow suppression by cyc- 
lophosphamide and other cytotoxic agents has been reported to be increased among patients with 
neoplastic disease, except leukemia, in the presence of allopurinol. However, in a well-controlled 
Study of patients with lymphoma on combination therapy, allopurinol did not increase the marrow tox- 
icity of patients treated with cyclophosphamide. doxorubicin, bleomycin, procarbazine and/or 
mechiorethamine. Tolbutamide's conversion to inactive metabolites has been shown to be catalyzed 
by xanthine oxidase from rat wer The clinical significance, if any. of this observation is unknown 
Chiorpropamide's plasma half-life may be prolonged by allopurinol. since allopurinol and chiorprop 
amide may compete for excretion in the renal tubule. The risk of hypoglycemia secondary to this

K mart offers $500 million for Pay Less NW 


y Bruce Buckley 

WILSONVILLE, Ore. — K mart Corp. began a 
tender offer to acquire Pay Less NW for $500 million 
in cash, the largest sum ever paid for a chain drug 
company. 

Pay Less chairman Ed Hart, who announced the 
merger agreement jointly with K mart chairman 
Bernard M. Fauber, said the present Pay Less man- 
agement would continue to operate the chain. 

In capping its diversification program with the 
Pay Less acquisition, K mart is acquiring one of the 
best-run drug chains in the country. 

The Wilsonville, Ore.-based company, which op- 
erates 164 drug stores in five Western states—al- 
most all of them super stores in the 30,000-sq.-ft. 
range—has been turning in outstanding perfor- 
mances for more than a decade. The results have 


the faltering economy in the Pacific Northwest. 

For the nine months ended Oct. 31, Pay Less’ 
earnings were up 27% to $15.3 million, or 83¢ ashare. 
Analysts who follow the chain predict that year-end 
cantiieann will come in at a minimum of $1.60 a share, 
or about 20% above last year. In the first nine 
months, K mart has recorded net earnings of $295 
million on sales of $14.2 billion.

News in brief 


Snowstorm dampens conference 


SAN ANTONIO— The first snowstorm to hit San Antonio 
“in 100 years” put a slight crimp in the turnout for this year’s 
NACDS Small Chain Conference. 

Just about 60 attendees, about 55% of those expected, bat- 
tled their way through closed airports and ivy roads to be at 
the conference, but those who'got there said it was well 
worth their trouble. : 

“I came down here to learn and I am learning,” said Bob 
Begley, president of Begley Drug. “This conference always 

rovides a good opportunity to meet and exchange ideas. 
his year I may be talking to less people, but I’m talking with 
them longer.” 

Among the highlights at the convention were the follow- 
ing: Revco’s Al Sebok, vp of store operations, analyzed ways 
to recruit and keep pharmacists while Murray Raphel of Mur- 
ray Raphel Advertising highlighted strategies for making re- 
tail ads “more provocative, appealing and effective.” 


Wellby opens Portland Combo 


PORTLAND, Me. — Wellby Super Drug Stores has opened 
its second convenience/drug combo. The 7,500-sq.-ft. unit was 
| opened recently in downtown Portland. About 5,000-sq.-ft. of 
the space is devoted to standard drug store fare; the rest of the 
space is allocate’ to convenience foods. 


Supermarkets General expands 


WOODBRIDGE, N.J. — Supermarkets General Corp.

half of which will be eon discounters. The company operates

land logos in Baltimore and New England, respectively. Also 
planned are five to seven Pathmark Super Center combo 
stores, three to five Purity Supreme supermarkets and one 
Purity Supreimie combo, and four to five Rickel Home Cen- 
ters.

Vol. 7, No. 3 February 4, 1985 


CHICAGO — Walgreens, the industry lead- 
er in computerization of store operations, 1s In- 
stalling microcomputers in store offices as part 
of a new administration system called WIN 
(Walgreens Information Network). 

The system is currently in operation in 100 
Chicago stores where it is being used to handle 
daily sales/cash reports, and payroll and time 
and attendance records. 

So far, savings are averaging between 15 to 
20 hours a week, management says. 

Fred Canning, Walgreens’ president, calls 
the time savings to date “real productivity” and 
he says Walgreens wants the WIN system in 
every store by 1989. 

“The communication capabilities of a system 
like this are very impressive,” he says. “And 
very important to a widespread operation like 
ours.” 

Walgreens was the first of the major drug 
chains to go on-line chainwide with interactive 
on-line pharmacy computers. 

Canning calls Walgreens’ Intercom pharma- 
cy computer system “one of the biggest steps 
we took this past decade. With it, we definitely 
crossed the chasm into the computer age.” 

Because each Walgreens’ prescription is re- 
corded in the company’s master computer in 


Chicago, a pharmacist in any store in the sys- 
tem can access a customer’s prescription re- 
cords from anywhere in the nation. 

In addition, customers in the nine markets 
where Walgreens has 24-hour stores can also 
get their prescription filled any hour of the day 
or night whether they patronize that store reg- 
ularlv or not. 

“Because of the computer,” says Canning, 
“pharmacists have every customer’s prescrip- 
tions at their fingertips.” 

In other technological innovations, Wal- 
greens is also rolling out a chainwide credit 
card system designed to speed credit card au- 
thorizations at the store level. Management 
says the system, which will use technological 
communications already in place, will provide 
“substantial reductions in annual credit card 
service fees.” 

Like a number of other retail drug chains, 
Walgreens also began testing scanning in 1984 
in cooperation with a national research firm. 


Walgreens is using the information gleaned 
from its participation in the test to study the 
feasibility of eliminating price marking as well 
as to learn how much more efficient scanning 
can be at capturing product movement infor- 
mation at the individual item level.

Rite Aid’s $136M offer opens bids for Hook 


Trump keeps tight rein 


By Jim Ricchiuti 

SHIREMANSTOWN, Pa. — Rite 
Aid’s unfriendly $31 a share offer to ac- 
quire Hook Drug could spark a biddin 
war involving other leading United 
States retailers. 

Rite Aid appears to be the leadin 
ose to acquire the 312-unit Hook 

store chain. If completed, the 
a would position Rite Aid as the No. 
1 chain in Indiana, where most of 
Hook’s stores are located. The chain 
also operates stores in Illinois, Ken- 
tucky and Ohio. 

However, the diversified retailer 
may end up paying as much as $36 a 
share to acquire Hook. At $31\a share, 
Rite Aid would already be paying 
nearly 17 times earnings. 

Through the first nine months of the 
fiscal year, Hook earned $4.6 million, 
or $1.09 a share, on sales of $254.5 mil- 
lion. That represented a nearly 18% 
drop in net earnings from the same pe- 


riod last year. Analysts expect the 
chain to earn $1.85 a share for 1984. 

Officials at Hook Drugs would not 
comment on the Rite Aid offer, which 
was set to expire on Feb. 28. Although 
Hook had enacted a number of antita- 
keover measures at its recent annual 
meeting in May, it appeared unlikely 
that management would attempt to 
block the takeover. 

With time running out, Hook chair- 
man and president J. Douglas Reeves’ 
only viable option may be to prod Rite 
Aid into sweetening the $136 million 
tender offer. 

Hook, through its investment bank- 
ers, Goldman Sachs, was said to be of- 
fering the chain to a number of bid- 
ders. But sources following the 
situation said that two United States 
drug retailers—Eckerd Corp. and 
Walgreens—declined to enter a bid- 
ding war for the 84-year-old chain.

Pay Less leases warehouse 
WILSONVILLE, Ore. — Pay Less NW has leased a 347,- 
000-sq.-ft. warehouse in Sacramento. The facility will service 
Pay Less’ 72 stores in northern California until the chain’s 
$22 million, 500,000-sq.-ft. distribution center in Woodland, 
Calif., (20 miles west of Sacramento) is completed in 1986. 


Drug Emporium opens discount 

WORTHINGTON, Ohio — Drug Emporium plans to open 
five deep-discount stores in Philadelphia this spring and sum- 
mer, with another 15 planned nationwide by 1986. 

The move is part of the company’s long-range goal to pene- 
trate the Middle Atlantic and New England regions, accord- 
ing to vp of operations Gary Wilber. 

“We want to go in there in an aggressive way, and I am con- 
fident about our prospects,” Wilber said. 


Skaggs changes names to Sav-On 


LA HABRA, Calif. — The nameplate of the 14 Skaggs 
aa Centers in southern California has been changed to 

v-On. 

Twelve of the stores are in Orange County and two are in 
Bakersfield (100 miles north of Los Angeles). Bakersfield 
served as the launch pad for Skaggs’ entry into southern Cali- 
fornia a dozen years ago. 

Originally, Sav-On had operated two stores in Bakersfield. 
However, the Mount Vernon unit—across from a Skag 
Drug Center—was closed, and in December 1984, “sy 
opened a new Sav-On store on White Lane (southwest Ba- 
kersfield). Thus, at the time of the name-change, there were 
two Skaggs Drug Centers and two Sav-On’s in Bakersfield. 


Bi-Mart president retires 


EUGENE, Ore. — Jack Phelan, president and one of the 
founders of the 33-store Bi-Mart membership discount drug 
division of Pay ’n Save, retired on Feb. 2, 1985. Marty Smith, 
Bi-Mart’s merchandise manager and Phelan’s right-hand 
man, is the new president. 

In 1955, Phelan and seven others founded Bi-Mart. The 
first store opened in Yakima, Wash. New customers still pay 


a one-time $2 membership fee. 
_ The division operates 28 stores in Oregon and five in Wash- 
ington.

Duane-Reade, Rite Aid cited 
In NY OTC drug-dating case 


NEW YORK — New York State Attorney 
General Robert Abrams has filed a civil suit 
against two major — store chains that oper- 
ate stores in New York City and its suburbs. 

Duane-Reade Corp. of Long Island City and 
Rite Aid Corp. of Shiresmantown, Pa., have 
been charged with violating state and Federal 
drug-dating laws. 

Five other nondrug store retailers and five 
national drug manufacturers signed agree- 
ments with the Attorney General to correct 
their practices, paying total fines of $42,000. 
Duane-Reade and Rite Aid both, according to 
the Attorney General’s office, also had the op- 
portunity to sign the agreement, but refused. 

The action followed a six-month investiga- 
tion of 145 retail stores that sell OTCs. 

—— to the Attorney General, investi- 
weeny found 93 stores selling a total of 284 out- 

ated products. More than 100 of these prod- 
ucts were at least a year out of date, 19 were 
three years old and one acne cream bore a date 
of September 1979. 

Marvin Sklamberg, counsel for the 25-store 
Duane-Reade chain said the chain has such a 
large turnover that there would be “no way 
that we could sell expired items.” He added 
that if store management did find an outdated 
item, it could send it back to the manufacturer 
for credit. 

Sklamberg would not discuss the specifics of 


the suit, except to say that Duane-Reade was 
not being sued for selling expired OTC prod- 
ucts. 

Both Duane-Reade and Rite Aid were 
charged with having “no expiration dates or in- 
conspicuous ones on their private-label prod- 
ucts and placing price stickers directly over the 
dates on national brands.” 

“Duane-Reade does not manufacture any 
OTC products,” said Sklamberg. “They are 
manufactured by major companies, and | 
would think that anything which appears on 
those cartons would meet all [labeling] require- 
ments.” 

The five retailers who signed an agreement 
and paid fines were: F. W. Woolworth, Path- 
mark, Alexander’s, The County Dump and 
J. W. Mays. They agreed to remove all expired 
OTC drugs from their inventory and to take 
reasonable steps to assure that no expired 
items will be sold in the future. 

The five manufacturers—Plough Inc., Nor- 
wich Eaton Pharmaceuticals, Burroughs Well- 
come Co., Thompson Medical Co. and Richard- 
son-Vicks Inc.—agreed to make expiration 
dates more legible and conspicuous, including 
redesigning packaging where necessary. 

All other retailers identified in the investiga- 
tion have been sent letters advising them that 
failure to comply may subject them to legal ac- 
tion in the future. 


Sav-On combos closed; 


Longs buys script files 


FRESNO, Calif. — Ameri- 
can Stores closed its five Sav- 
On food/drug combos in the 
San Joaquin Valley on Jan. 25 
after a two-week “going-out- 
of-business” sale. 

Longs Drugs, operating 17 
superdrug stores in the San 
Joaquin Valley (a 200-mile 
stretch from Bakersfield to 
Merced in central California) 
te genes aa the pharmaceu- 
tical stock and prescription 
files of the five stores. 

Lucky Stores is ons 
for the purchase of the Merce 
(47,500 sq. ft.) and Atwater 
(38,000 sq. ft.) stores, accord- 
ing to a Lucky spokesman. 

e five food/drug combos 
have been proce te profit- 
able since the first one opened 
in Merced in the fall of 1983. 
However, both sales and prof- 
its dropped during the last two 
months, after local newspa- 
pers reported that the combos 
were for sale. 

Why were the stores closed 
rather — peewee them 

n and perhaps getting a 
higtier price? A real estate 
exec in the Fresno area told 


Drug Store News: “No one 
was interested in buying 
them, so American dropped 
the price. Even then — 
were no takers. The stores 
had a lot of money tied up in in- 
ventory, so American decided 
that the merchandise would 
bring in more dollars with a 
close-out sale to customers 
rather than selling it at dis- 
tressed prices to the new buy- 
er. ” 

In a companion move, 
American has sold 19 of its 22 
conventional Alpha Beta su- 
ype in the San Joaquin 

alley to independent opera- 
tors and closed three. 

American will also sell the 
seven conventional Sav-On 
superdrug stores in the San 
Jose area—plus the drug/ 
home center combo in Sout 
San Francisco. Some of the 
proceeds from this sale—as 
well as the proceeds from the 
five San Joaquin combos—will 
be used as seed money to build 
60,000-sq.-ft. combos in 
northern California. 

The Sav-On combos in the 
San Joaquin were designed 


and opened by Jewel Cos., be- 
fore Jewel sold out to Ameri- 
ean Stores. All but Atwater 
(38,000 sq. ft.) are 47,500 sq. 
ft., whereas American’s 
Skaggs-Alpha Beta food/drug 
combos are 60,000 to 70,000 
sq. ft. However, none of the 
emia ha Beta combos 
are in the San Joaquin ven § 

The 60,000- to 70,000-sq.-ft. 
combo is the size Sam Skaggs 
has committed to because he 
feels it can generate maximum 
sales and profit due to the 
large mix of nonfoods.

Leucadia seeks to block Bergen 


LOS ANGELES — The 
battle over the proposed 
merger between Bergen 
Brunswig Corp. and National 
Intergroup Inc. is heating up. 

With shareholders of ott 
companies about to vote on the 
merger, Leucadia National 
Corp. has mounted a proxy 
fight to block the deal.

7.2% interest in National In-

Street Journal.

“Bergen Brunswig has made 


an offer you can refuse,” the 
ad urged NI shareholders to 
give their proxies to Leuca- 
dia. The New York-based 
holding company said that if it 
wins he fight it will attempt 
to persuade the National In- 
tergroup board to “begin an 
orderly disposition of its as- 
sets or seek higher offers for 
the company in its entirety.”

shareholders will receive 
1.225 shares of Bergen Class 
A common stock for every NI 
share they hold, favors Ber- 
gen over National Intergroup.

own full-page ad, this time in

and certainties of the merger 
far outweigh the uncertainties 
of following the Leucadia 
course.”

merged company, with its en- 
hanced cash flow, would have 
the resources to pursue the di- 
versifications efforts “with 


less risk to our present stock- 
holders.”

tribution services area, 
“which, experience shows, of- 
fers strong growth potential.”

Howard M. Love, chairman 
and ceo of National Inter- 
group, said: “We do not know 
why it is that Leucadia be- 
lieves there would be buyers 
for our steel business when 
they were not previously 
there.” It also noted that the 
company would not be able to

8.8 M Pay Less shares tendered 


TROY, Mich. — The First Fidelity Bank of North America 
has reported that approximately 8.8 million shares, or about 
49% of the outstanding shares of common stock of Pay Less 
Drug Stores Northwest Inc., had been tendered and accept- 
ed for payment under K mart’s offer for all outstanding 
shares of Pay Less. 

Payment of $27 per share will be made to tendering share- 
holders. 

The tender offer is the first step in the definitive merger 
agreement providing for the acquisition of Pay Less by 
K mart. 

It is expected that a special meeting of shareholders of Pay 
Less will be held in late March to consider and vote upon the 
merger proposal. 


Fazio’s launched in Dallas, 
largest U.S. deep-discounter 


MESQUITE, Tex. — John Fazio, a super- 
marketer for 40 years, opened the country’s 
largest deep-discount drug store in the hotly 
competitive Dallas area on Feb. 20. 

The 65,000-sq.-ft. store, called “Fazio’s,” 
opened in the former location of a Gibson’s Dis- 
ge” Center. Selling space accounts for 44,000 
sq. It. 

Sixty per cent of the store is devoted to OTC, 
pharmacy, H&BA, cosmetics and audiovisual, 
with the remaining 40% to promotional dry 
groceries, hardware, housewares, auto, and 
other general merchandise lines. 

Fazio’s approach to food differs from most 
deep-discounters, who usually stack it high in 
front to quickly establish a low-price image. 

“In this store,” says Chuck Fazio, store man- 
ager and vp of Jote, the corporation that con- 
trols the new store, “you won’t see food until 
you're 25% into the store. The message is that 
this is no supermarket—hbut a drug store.” 

John Fazio, president of Jote, is no stranger 
to deep-discount drug steres. He was ceo of 
Fisher Foods until the late 70’s when he sold his 
stock to Fisher and retired. 

In December 1982, he opened Jote, a deep- 
discount drug store in Cleveland, which he still 
owns. After Fazio sold out to Fisher, Fisher 
opened several deep-discount drug stores in 
the Cleveland area under the Jax logo. 

Gross margins at Fazio’s are in the 18%-20% 
range. Asked for the break-even point, Chuck 
Fazio said: “We won’t know until 12 months.” 
He did say his opening inventory was $4 million 
at cost. 

The new outlet has drug store fixtures rath- 
er than warehouse-type racks because, says 
Chuck Fazio, “we’re trying to project a retail 
atmosphere.” 


Fazio adds that there will be no advertising. 
“We’re depending on word-of-mouth,” he told 
Drug Store News. 

John Fazio says: “We’re not in it for money; 
we're in it for glory.” 

Fazio may get his glory, but he will also get 
wey! of competition because Dallas is a hot- 
‘en for deep-discounters and food/drug com- 

OS. 

Drug Emporium operates three deep-dis- 
counters in this area, with two more coming in 
Grand Prairie and Fort Worth. Almost a year 
ago, Texas Drug Warehouse opened a drug dis- 
counter. The operator was a former buyer with 
Sanger-Harris department store. And 
Safeway opened its Drug For Less in Dallas in 
April 1983, and has since added three more. 

Then there are the combos. The newest en- 
try is Albertson’s, with four 62,000 sq. ft., food/ 
drug combos onstream and four more coming 
in a few months. 

Albertson’s stunned the food/drug communi- 
ty by going with everyday discount prices 
across the board. According to exit interviews, 
Albertson’s is making its deepest inroads in the 
market share of Skaggs-Alpha Beta, pioneer in 
combos in Texas and former Albertson part- 
ner. Tom Thumb/Page is also a major combo 
force, as is Kroger. 

Then there’s Minyard’s and its Sack’n Save 
food warehouse stores with heavy emphasis on 
H&BA. Sack’n Save’s 76,000-sq.-ft. deep-dis- 
count combo in Waco, Tex., is one of the largest 
food/drug combos in the country. 

Also there are two conventional drug 
chains—Reveo and Eckerd—that won’t roll 
over for anyone. 

So begin the glory days in the Dallas-Fort 
Worth area.

DRUG STORE NEWS, March 4, 1985 


FINANCIAL 


SupeRx posts increase in sales and earnings 


CINCINNATI The 
Kroger Co. reported that Su- 
peRx Drug Stores had “signif- 
icant sales and earnings im- 
provement”’ for the year 
ended Dec. 29. 

Although pretax operating 
profits for the drug store divi- 
son increased only 4.4% to 
$28.4 million, Kroger pointed 
out that the operating profit 
included a $5.5 million pretax 
LIFO charge. SupeRx did not 
use the LIFO method in 1983. 

According to Kroger, Su- 
peRx sales for the year in- 
creased 8.8% to $859.5 million 
from $789.6 million the previ- 


ous year. 

Kroger wound up the year 
with 621 drug stores and ex- 
pects to build 30 SupeRx units 
in the current fiscal year. 

Overall, Kroger recorded a 
23.3% increase in net profits to 
$156.6 million, or $3.49 a 
share, from $127.1 million, or 
$2.76 a share, in 1983. 

Sales for the fiscal year in- 
creased 4.5% to $15.92 billion, 
despite the closing of 156 food 
stores during the year. 

The company said that the 
1984 sales momentum in- 
creased throughout the year, 
culminating in a record fourth- 


quarter performance, despite 
an approximate 5% decline in 
supermarket square footage 
during the year. Kroger said 
the sales momentum had car- 
ried through to the early part 
of 1985. 

In the fourth quarter, net 
earnings rose 34.3% to $56 
million, or $1.25 a share, from 
$41.7 million, or 93¢ a share, in 
the comparable year-earlier 
period. 

Sales for the quarter in- 
creased to $3.87 billion, 2% 
higher than the $3.78 billion 
recorded a year earlier. 

“To a degree, Kroger’s per- 


formance in 1984 was aided by 
more favorable operating con- 
ditions,’’ said Lyle Ever- 
ingham, Kroger chairman. 
“But the overriding factor be- 


hind Kroger’s turnaround was 
our ability to obtain better, 
more productive and more 
profitable performance from 
all of our retail operations.”

There are currently six 
firms making a market in

A SETTLEMENT WAS REACHED in the lawsuit against 
SmithKline Beckman Corp. and the National Wholesale Drug- 
gists’ Association filed by Northwesterr Drug, a wholesale sub- 
sidiary of Pay ’n Save, and Velocity Hospital Group. The suit 
arose last April after SmithKline & French and other drug man- 

-ufacturers terminated their agreements to supply legend drug 
products to Northwestern because the wholesaler had been pur- 
chased by a retail company and then NWDA dropped North- 
western as a member for the same reason. Under the agreement, 
SKF will supply Northwestern with products for Velocity’s more 
than 100 hospital accounts, and NWDA will readmit Northwest- 
ern as a member.

Four Sav-On execs fired 
as Skaggs tightens belt 


ANAHEIM, Calif. — Sam 
Skaggs has wielded the long- 
awaited ax at Sav-On with the 
dismissal of four top execs: 
Sam Parker, president; Carl 
Vitalie, vp-professional ser- 
vices; Gerald Hight, vp-mer- 
chandising, and Dale Short, 
vp-distribution. 

None of the four are being 
replaced. Instead, their duties 
are being absorbed by others. 
Dick George, president of 
Osco, is doubling as Sav-On’s 

resident; Russ Coon and Dan 

amirez, pharmacy buyers- 
supervisors, are dividing Vi- 
talie’s responsibilities; Larry 
LaRock, recently named vp- 
marketing, assumes oti 


Hight’s duties, and Ed 
McManus, former director of 
warehouse operations who re- 
placed Dale Short, is now 
wearing both hats. 

The shake-up is not surpris- 
ing in view of Sav-On’s lack- 
luster performance during the 
past several years. Jewel, 
which bought the chain late in 
1979 and then sold out to 
American Stores last year, 
tried to revive earnings by 
slashing labor costs and dra- 
matically cutting back inven- 
tory. Costs did come down, 
but so did sales, 2s out-of- 
stocks multiplied and house- 
keeping became a problem.

video business, Peoples is pro-

homes. Members then call the

pick — tape at their regis-

sion on each tape rented from 
its stores. Moreover, the 
chain benefits directly from 
increased store traffic.

Peoples’ corporate vp, the 
program \is ‘‘working out 
well,” sincé the chain began 
testing the video departments 
last year.

proach,” said Manton. “It was 
a business we weren’t sure we 
wanted to take the risk and 
get into.

Court rule on HMO status an 


WASHINGTON — Orga- 
nized pharmacy groups vowed 
to continue the fight to curb 
unfair Rx competition from 
HMOs in the wake of a key le- 
gal setback in the U.S. Su- 
preme Court. 

The setback came as the re- 
sult of the high court’s refusal 
to reconsider the status of the 
Kaiser Foundation’s Health 
Maintenance Organization as 
a charitable institution. 

The effect of the decision 
was to uphold a Federal Ap- 
peals Court ruling in the bitter 
dispute between the Portland 
Retail Druggists Association 
and Kaiser over the applica- 


tion of the Robinson-Patman 
antiprice discriminations act 
to HMOs. 

The central issue in that 
case involved whether the 
Kaiser HMO Rx dispensaries 
may legally compete with re- 
tail pharmacies after purchas- 
ing drugs at prices lower than 
those available to drug stores. 

Although the Federal R-P 
Act outlaws such discrimina- 
tion, the Federal Appeals 
Court ruled that Kaiser is a 
“charitable institution” under 
Federal law and thus exempt 
from the price discrimination 
provision of Robinson-Pat- 
man. The Supreme Court let

Arbor acquires Detroit Dale 


TROY, Mich. —Arbor Drugs has acquired the three Dale 
Drug stores in metropolitan Detroit, bringing the total num- 
ber of Arbor stores to 40. Two of the stores, located in St. 
Clair Shores and Union Lake, have opened new local markets 
for Arbor, and the Warren location is the second in that area 


for the company. 


Pay ’n Save appoints Shefveland 


SEATTLE — Pay ’n Save Corp. has named Ken Shefve- 
land to the newly created post of director of data processing 
operations services. Shefveland, former vp/manager of com- 
er processing services, at the Seattle First National 

ank, will be responsible for Pay ’n Save’s new data process- 


ing center.

Drug Systems revenues up 


PORTSMOUTH, Ohio — Drug Systems Inc., which oper- 
ates White Drug Enterprises, reported that third-quarter 
net income dropped 39% to $584,000 from $954,000. Net rev- 
enues for the quarter, ended Jan. 5, 1985, increased 5% to 
$28.9 million from $27.5 million during the same period in 
1984. Through the first three quarters of the year, net earn- 
ings at Drug Systems were down 28% to $1.14 million from 
$1.6 million last year. Net revenues for the first three quar- 
ters of the year rose 38% to $81.7 million from $59.3 million in 
1984, reflecting the White Drug acquisition during the sec- 


ond quarter last year.

N.Y. manufacturer to acquire 
major interest in Pantry Pride 


FORT LAUDERDALE, 
Fla. — Senior management at 
Pantry Pride Inc., the parent 
company of Adams Drug, will 
recommend to its board of di- 
rectors the sale of a controlling 
interest in the company to 
MacAndrews & Forbes, a 
New York-based manufactur- 
ing concern. 

The terms of the proposed 
sale call for Pantry Pride to is- 
sue as much as $50 million in 
9.5% convertible preferred 
stock to MacAndrews & 
Forbes. The shares could be 
converted into common stock 
at $5.625 a share. MacAn- 
drews & Forbes would receive 
voting rights on the shares as 
well as majority representa- 


tion on the Pantry Pride 
board. 

MacAndrews & Forbes, a 
privately held company that 
manufactures cigars, confec- 
tionery products and photo 
processing materials, already 
owns 8% of Pantry Pride’s 
common stock outstanding. 

In addition, the company 
has an option to purchase the 
10% stake in Pantry Pride 
owned by members of the 
Devon family, which acquired 
the shares last year following 
the sale of the Devon general 
merchandise chain to Pantry 
Pride. Late last year a group 
of dissident shareholders, led 
by the Devons, staged an un- 
successful proxy battle to gain 


control of Pantry Pride. 

A spokesman for Pantry 
Pride said that if proposed sale 
is approved by shareholders, 
MacAndrew & Forbes could 
control as much as 35% of the 
food, drug and specialty re- 
tailer. 

The company official added 
that MacAndrew & Forbes 
plans to retain the current 
management at Pantry Pride. 

Pantry Pride acquired Ad- 
ams Drug in November as 
part of a diversification pro- 
gram designed to take advan- 
tage of tax loss carryforward. 

The company said that it in- 
tends to use proceeds from 
stock sale to finance future ac- 
quisitions. 


Suppliers win price concessions 


WASHINGTON — Drug 
store industry suppliers will 
receive almost blanket anti- 
trust immunity to engage ina 
wide range of distributional 
trade restraints under contro- 
versial new Justice Depart- 
ment enforcement guidelines 
released late last month. 

Although the new Federal 
case-selection standards do 
not directly apply to fair 
trade-style resale price main- 
tenance violations, critics of 
Reagan Administration “lais- 
sez-faire antitrust policies” 
contend that the justice guide- 
lines will encourage manufac- 
turers to dictate retail prices 
for their products. 

In announcing the new case- 


selection procedure, justice 
antitrust chief J. Paul 
McGrath said that the guide- 
lines are necessary to “help re- 
duce the uncertainty associat- 
ed with enforcement of the 
antitrust laws” in order to “en- 
courage the use of lawful ver- 
tical [trade restraint] prac- 
tices” by manufacturers. 
Among other things, the 
guides establish a series of 
“safe harbors” which allow 
suppliers to impose a variety 
of “nonprice” distributional 
restrictions on retailers, in- 
cluding: 
© “territorial restrictions” 
which effectively prevent au- 
thorized dealers from trans- 
shipping the manufacturers 


products to drug chains or un- 
authorized retailers in other 
markets; 
® “customer allocation” re- 
straints which may be used to 
achieve the same objective by 
prohibiting wholesalers and 
retailers from selling to cer- 
tain “classes” of customers; 
@ “exclusive dealership” re- 
quirements preventing retail- 
ers from carrying products 
made by competing manufac- 
turers, and 
e “tying arrangements” un- 
der which pharmaceutical 
manufacturers and other in- 
dustry suppliers refuse to sell 
key products to retailers un- 
less other unwanted goods (or

Most OTC product recom- 
| mendations by pediatricians 
| are for sees HE remedies, 

analgesic and vitamins. 

That was one finding of a 
survey conducted by Medical 
Marketing Conference, a divi- 
| sion of Market Measures Inc. 

The nationally projectable 
survey of 100 pediatricians re- 
vealed that they recommend a 
wider variety of products in 
the cough and ee eategory 
than in any other classifica- 
tion. It also showed that 97% 
recommend at least one OTC 
analgesic and 92% a vitamin 
supplement for their patients. 

It has long been recognized 
by pharmacists that pediatri- 
clans’ product recommenda- 
tions have a significant influ- 
ence on buying habits of their 
customers. 

According to the National 
Disease and Therapeutic In- 
dex, 84 million patient visits 
were made to pediatricians 
last year. The number of pa- 
tient visits per day for the av- 
erage children’s physicians 
was Just over 22, and 47% of 
those visits were by children 
through the age of 2. Children 
5 years old through 9 account- 
ed for another 32% of all visits. 

A leading medical publica- 
tion recently indicated that 
99% of the patients visiting pe- 
diatricians will follow their 
recommendations for OTC 
products. 


In the Market Measures 
Survey, pediatricians were 
asked to evaluate 14 product 
categories and indicate which 
products they recommended 


and the average number of 


times a week they made that 
recommendation. 

The category with the larg- 
est variety of products was 
cough/cold, with a choice of 19 
products. The smallest cate- 
gory was teething products, 
with two dominating the cate- 
gory. 

It is estimated that 21 mil- 
lion visits were made to pedia- 
tricians last year for respira- 


tory problems, sore throat, or 
the common cold. Visits for 


ear problems, usually prompt- 
ing recommendations for anal- 
gesics, measured 11 million. 


Cough/cold 


Pediatricians recommend a 
greater variety of products in 
the cough/cold category than 
any other OTC grouping. 

The report uncovered 19 
cough/cold products recom- 
mended by anywhere from 1% 
of the pediatricians to as many 
as 87%. 

Triaminic, a product mar- 
keted primarily for use in 
fighting colds in children, 
lived up to its reputation by 
topping the list of most recom- 
mended cough/cold products.

for the average physician—a

Dental 


Pediatricians would rather 
leave the choice of what tooth- 
brush to use to dentists. Less 
than 20% of the pediatricians 
recommend toothbrushes for 
their patients. 

Among those recommend- 
ed, Oral B received the high- 
est number of endorsements. 
with 10% of the doctors mak- 
ing it their choice. 

Nuk, known for many baby 
products including pacifiers, 
received only 5% of the doctor 
recommendations. 

Like toothbrushes, tooth- 
paste is not high on the pedia- 
triclans’ recommended list. 
Only about 25% recommend 
any brand of toothpaste. 
Crest received the highest 


vote of confidence with 17% of 
the baby doctors giving it the 
nod. Close behind are Aim. 
Colgate and Aqua-Fresh with 
12%, 11% and 10%. 

In contrast to toothbrushes 
and toothpaste, the pediatri- 
clans do make recommenda- 
tions when it comes to teeth- 
ing pain.

DENVER — FoxMeyer Corp. has 
signed a letter of intent to acquire the 
drug wholesaling and pharmacy com- 
puter operations of McPike Inc., a 
closely held drug wholesaler. 

The terms of the deal were not dis- 
closed. However, sources close to Fox- 
Meyer said the company was paying 
$60 million in cash and another $20 mil- 
lion to $25 million in assumed liabil- 
ities. 

The acquisition thrusts FoxMeyer 
into a position as the leading drug 
wholesaler in western Missouri and 
Iowa. Moreover, it provides Fox- 
Meyer with a 300,000-sq.-ft. distribu- 
tion center that is widely acknowl- 
edged to be the highest volume drug 


Based in Kansas City, Mo., McPike 
is projected to generate na omer 
ly $225 million to $250 million through 
its one and only distribution center for 
the fiscal year ending April 30. 
McPike’s other revenue source, Camp- 
bell Development, a Colorado-based 
real estate development company, was 
not included in the purchase agree- 
ment. 

FoxMeyer will finance the acquisi- 
tion through a $75 million offering of 
convertible debentures, due 2010. 

Although FoxMeyer enjoys a lead- 
ing market position in Kansas, Ne- 
braska, Oklahoma, Arkansas and 
parts of Illinois, it had been unable to

New look, prices at Total Plus 
renew Dart’s deep-discount aim 


RICHMOND — Dart Drug 
is reviving its five-year-old 
experiment with deep-dis- 
count drug stores. 

Under the leadership of 
Dart’s chairman Al Towle, 
who acquired the 78-unit com- 
pany last June, Dart has re- 
modeled all five of its Total 
Plus deep-discount drug 
stores, restocked them with 
13,000 everyday sku’s plus 
“every decent brand we can 
buy on deal,” repriced them at 


30% to 50% below the local 
competition, and launched a 
brand new television, radio 
and print campaign to build 
visibility for the mini-chain. 
Towle says his goal is to 
double Total Plus’s average $3 
million to $4 million sales per 
store “within the year.” With 
the ad campaign just a few 
weeks old as Drug Store News 
went to press, sources for the 
company said they had 
achieved that for the month.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 1, 1985 


By Bruce Buckley 

_ NEW YORK — Jack Eckerd Corp. has reached 
into its bag for some new medicine to revive its ail- 
ing American Home Video division. 

he hoped-for cure centers on two new ware- 
house-style VideoConcepts stores that the compa- 
ny planned to open in Denver on March 22. 

tewart Turley, chairman and ceo, told financial 
analysts here that Eckerd is counting on the higher 
visibility and heavier promotional firepower of the 
warehouse stores to enhance the fortunes of the 
standard VideoConcepts stores, not only by bol- 
stering their promotional image, but also by acting 
as a centralized depot for inventory. 

Turley likened the concept to a “mother ship” 
feeding its satellites. If it is successful, he said, it 
will be rolled out to other markets in the 30 states in 
which AHV operates more than 200 video stores. 
Turley said the Denver experiment would weigh 
— y in any decision about the future of the video 
chain. 


Warehouse units: cure for Eckerd video ills? 


At the analysts’ meeting Turley also said that the 
yee ‘erage to sell off its 102-store Eckerd 
—s chain “within the next few weeks.” 

ince its acquisition in 1981, American Home 
Video has been a highly visible wart on Eckerd’s 
otherwise relatively unblemished fiscal record. Be- 
cause of its high profitability in the past, Eckerd 
had always been a darling of Wall Street. But the 
company’s insistence on sticking with a division 
that has been a continuing drain has turned ana- 
lysts into harriers seeking divestiture. 
_ Inthe most recent quarter, AHF o rating prof- 
its were up 17% to $1.4 million, but Teles conced- 
ed that the division was still lagging behind projec- 
tions and was not expected to ‘io better than break 
even for the year. 

The warehouse stores are aimed at providing a 
much-needed shot in the arm. The two test stores, 
one 10,000 and the other 12,000 sq. ft., are located 
in two Denver suburbs, Englewood and Aurora. 
Eckerd has chosen two high-traffic strip center 


sites dominated by price club-type outlets and 
— to promote the stores with weekly ads in the 
Denver market. Standard VideoConcepts stores, 
in contrast, are smaller and are located in shopping 
malls, which gives them a pricier image. 

Although the new stores’ prices on national 
brands will match those of the standard mall stores, 
Turley said the warehouse outlets will carry a wid- 
er variety of private label goods, which will enable 
the stores to “be competitive with anybody in the 
marketplace.” 

Jonathan Ziegler, an analyst for Dean Witter, 
said the concept “seems to make sense. The present 
stores are too small. The new stores will allow them 
to stock more inventory and give the customers a 
better choice.” 

As for a possible divestiture, Turley again said 
that the company will continue to “operate and de- 
velop that business” as long as there is a hope for a 
“respectable roi. Frankly, it’s been a disappoint- 
ment over the past three years.”

ATLANTA — About 1,400 wholesalers and manufactur-

In addition to the 171 OTC and H&BA manufacturers who 
exhibited at the show, there were also 114 pharmaceutical 
exhibits plus a series of workshops on HMO’s and PPO’s, the

stores, creative new marketing ideas to sell health & beauty

Gray Drug Fair breaks even in ’84 


CLEVELAND — Gray Drug Fair just managed to break 
even last year, according to company reports issued by Sher- 
win-Williams, parent of the struggling drug chain. For the 
year ended Dec. 31, 1984, Gray Drug earned only $82,000 on 
sales of $623 million. The 99% decline in earnings in 1984 was 
attributed to more aggressive promotional activity, distribu- 


tion inefficiencies and increased inventory shrinkage. Sales 
at the 423-unit drug chain advanced 7.8%.

Eckerd eyes deep-discount entry 


NEW YORK — Eckerd 
Drug “may very well test” a 
deep-discount drug-store for- 
mat, according to Stewart 
Turley, chairman and ceo of 
the Jack Eckerd Corp. 

Turley told analysts here 
that the company has been fol- 
lowing the deep-discount phe- 
nomenon “for some time. We 
think it’s a viable niche.” 

But Turley added that noth- 
ing definite had been decided, 
and Eckerd does not see deep- 
discount stores “in any way re- 
placing or superseding chain- 
drug stores. 

“T see a lot of chains experi- 
menting with the concept, but 
I see nobody embracing it 
widely,” the chief exec noted. 

Turley said Eckerd had 
faced some competition from 
deep discounters in Florida 
and Texas, but had not been 
hurt by them. “We get right 
down next to them in price,” 
he said. “They’re going to 
fight to get our market share.” 

Turiey and Harry Lambert, 
president of Eckerd Drug, 
also disclosed the following 
during the analysts meeting. 


The drug chain has begun to 
roll out a new higher gondola 
neg (54 in. to 68 in.), which 

as been tested in its experi- 
mental “race track” store in 


Florida and other units. The 
additional height allows a bet- 
ter merchandise presentation, 
according to Lambert. It also 
helps increase turnover.

Cough/cold dominates Top 100 OTC list 


pproximately one-third of the 

Top 100 over-the-counter prod- 

ucts moved through chain drug 
stores last year were items used to 
treat coughs and colds. 

Because of their heavy concentra- 
tion in the Top 100 unit listing, cough/ 
cold products also accounted for the 
highest dollar sales and gross profit 


That was one finding of Drug Store 
News 2nd Annual Study of Best-Sell- 
ing OTC’s. The study is based on 1984 
warehouse withdrawal data provided 
by a number of chains and weighted to 
account for regional variations. 

The study found that analgesics 
closely followed cough/cold on the Top 
100 list, with 25% of the places. Anal- 


dollars. gesics also accounted for 23% of the

Top 100 dollar products and 20% of the 
leading profit producers. 

The battle for third place in unit 
movement was won by the antacids, 
though fourth-place eye care catego- 
ry recorded higher dollar sales and 
gross margin dollars. Antacids won 
15% of the Top 100 places in unit move- 
ment, while eye care products—pri- 
marily contact lens solutions—came in 
with 9% of the top positions. 

The lower dollar sales and profit dol- 
lars of antacids relative to eye care was 
due mainly to the competitive nature 
and lower price points of that category. 

In the eye care category, consumers 
rely heavily on doctors’ recommenda- 
tions and remain brand loyal. Price, 
therefore, is not as big a factor as it is in 
some other categories, where there’s a 
higher degree of consumer switching.

The OTC drugs that made it 
to the Top 100 included most 
heavily advertised and pro- 
moted products sold by drug 
chains. 

According to Medi-Span’s 
OTC Pricing Guide, for exam- 
ple, the suggested selling 
price for Chapstick is 95¢. Ina 
recent sweep through the lat- 
est tear sheets from major 
chains, Drug Store News staff- 
ers found Chapstick to be 
among the most deeply dis- 
counted OTC products. The 
average promotional price 
charged for Chapstick by the 
chains was 52¢, actually 9¢ be- 
low AWP. At least one chain 
advertised the lip balm for as 
low as 39¢. 

Other OTC products selling 
below AWP price were Bayer 
aspirin 100’s, priced by most 
chains at around $1.78, 85¢ be- 
low AWP. The hottest price 
was $1.69. 

The most dramatic promo- 
tions were in OTC vitamin ad- 
vertising. Squibb’s Theragran 
M 100 + 30 was selling for an 
average price $7.32, $2.79 be- 
low AWP. The lowest price 
was $6.99. 

Lederle’s Centrum 100 + 
30 was selling for an average of 
$6.92 per bottle by the chains, 
$2.81 below its AWP.

Slim-Fast, the No. 1 diet aid 
among the Top 100 OTC prod- 
ucts may owe some of its popu- 
larity to the heavy discounting 
being done by the chains. 

On average, a 16-0z. can of 
Thompson Medical’s Slim- 
Fast was selling for $4.83 and 
as low as $3.99. At the promo- 
tional price of $3.99, Slim-F ast 
is a real bargain, $3 below 
AWP and $6.50 below the sug- 
gested retail. 


Cough/cold 


Almost one-quarter of all 
the cough/cold products in the 
Top 100 were Rx-to-OTC 
switched drugs. Burroughs- 


Wellcome did exceptionally 
well with its Actifed product, 
placing two popular sizes, 12’s 
and 24’s in the Top 100 accord- 
ing to unit movement, dollar 
sales and profit dollars. Bur- 
roughs’ Sudafed SA, a long- 
acting decongestant that was 
formerly prescription-only, 
also made it to the Top 100 in 
all three lists. 

Other switched OTC’s in- 
clude Schering’s Afrin Nasal 
Spray and Drixoral tablets, 
and Parke-Davis’ Benylin 
cough syrup.

Rx-to-OTC drugs were some 
perennial winners.

Bud’s will bloom in Indianapolis 


By Tim O’Brien 

ALEXANDRIA, Va. — In- 
dianapolis . . . this Bud’s for 
ycu. in fact, there will be two 
Bud’s for you by fall. 

Peoples Drug Stores will 
open two new “Bud’s Deep 
Discount Drug Store & More” 
locations in this central Indi- 
ana city of 700,000 during 
1985. The first is to open in 
mid-June, the other later this 
fall. 

Officials at Peoples said In- 


dianapolis was chosen for 
Bud’s expansion so manage- 
ment could get an idea of what 
it was like to operate a deep 
discounter in a market with 
less discretionary income than 
the original Bud’s. That store 
opened in December in highly 
affluent Greenbelt, Md. 

The market was also a logi- 
cal choice for expansion since 
Peoples already operates 40 
drug stores in the area, as well 
as a large warehouse facility.

Kaye resigns from Tangible Ind. 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — Leo Kaye abruptly resigned as 
head of Tangible Industries, the ma division of Odd 
Lot Trading Inc., less than two months after he joined the 
Reveo subsidiary. Revco named Peter J. Laitmon, for- 
merly vp of special products division of Media General 
Broadcast Services, to succeed Kaye. 


Harco expands hdgatrs., warehouse 


NORTHPORT, Ala. — A $4 million expansion project 
has been announced by Harco Drug. The plan calls for dou- 
bling the office space at corporate headquarters and for in- 
creasing warehouse space from 60,000 sq. ft. to 130,000 sq. 
ft. Fifty new jobs will be created for the warehouse opera- 
tion. 

“We are very excited about our expansion and the in- 
creased padre! Fs it will provide us. It will help us facili- 
tate opening new stores and make us much more efficient 
in our warehouse operation,” says Harco president Jim 
Harrison Jr. “It is a positive move to better equip us for 
the future.” 

The 44-year-old, privately owned drug store chain pres- 
ently operates 54 drug stores, 10 Carport auto part stores 
and 10 TotalCare home health care stores in Alabama and 
Mississippi. 


American appoints six to board 


SALT LAKE CITY — American Stores Co. has elected 
Richard E. George to its board of directors. George joined 
American Stores as president of the Osco drug store chain 
following the acquisition of the Jewel Companies last year. 
In addition to heading Osco, George was recently named 
president of American’s Sav-On Drugs division. American 
also named five other new board members, expanding its 
board of directors from 10 to 16.
