Continued on page 99 


Correction 


In the March 18th issue, 
Drug Store News erroneously 
reported that the National 
Wholesale Druggists’ Associ- 
ation had dropped Northwest- 
ern Drug as amember because 
Northwestern had been ac- 
quired by a retail chain, Pay ’n 
Save Corp. 

NWDA sources say that 
Northwestern was dropped as 
a direct result of NWDA’s by- 
laws on active members. Ac- 
cording to Article III, Section 
3, if the ownership or control 
of an active member is sold or 
transferred to another entity 
or corporation that is not an 
active member, the orginal 
membership must be termi- 
nated and there must be an ap- 
plication from the new owner 
for a new active membership. 

NWDA has since deter- 
mined that Northwestern, 
even though it is under the 
ownership of Pay ’n Save, the 
owner-operator of a chain of 
retail drug stores, is eligible 
for an active membership. 


DRUG STORE NEWS, April 15, 1985 


FINANCIAL 


ST. LOUIS — Medicare- 
Glaser said it expected to re- 
port a loss in the fourth quar- 
ter of its current fiscal year 
ended in March. 

Harlan Steinbaum, chair- 
man and ceo, said the previ- 
ously announced campaign to 
increase market share, partic- 
ularly in the St. Louis Metro- 
politan Area, had damaged 
gross margins and operating 


earnings. 


“New store openings and in- 
creased advertising, as well as 
expenditures for marketing 


and product development by 
Professional Drug Systems 
Inc., the company’s medical 
database subsidiary, have had 
a negative impact on our earn- 
ings,” Steinbaum said. 

The chief exec said that situ- 
ation was likely to continue 
into the new fiscal year, “but 
we remain convinced that the 
actions taken will result in 
longer term growth opportu- 
nities for our company and 
shareholders.” 

Steinbaum said the compa- 
ny will open four new Medi- 


care-Glaser drug stores in the 
St. Louis market in the cur- 
rent quarter. He said the new 
full-line stores will replace 
smaller Medicare-Glaser 
pharmacies. But Steinbaum 
noted that in addition to signif- 
icant expenses for new store 
equipment, inventory and 
opening costs, there is always 
a temporary loss of earnings 
when stores are relocated. 
Steinbaum said he was 
“pleased” that the drive for 
market share was “bearing 
fruit” in increased sales dur- 


ing the third quarter ended 

Dec. 31 and the first two 

months of the final quarter. 
“We believe that the compa- 


Med.-Glaser seeks expanded market share 


ny is laying a strong founda- 
tion for increased earnings 
growth in the years ahead,” he 
said. 


Bergen earnings increase 22% 


LOS ANGELES — Bergen 
Brunswig Corp. announced 
that net earnings for the sec- 
ond quarter increased 22% to 
$7.4 million or 58¢ a share, 
from $6.1 million, or 48¢ a 
share in the same year-earlier 
period. Sales for the quarter 
rose 42% to $594 million from 


$419 million. 

For the first half, earnings 
from continuing operations 
climbed 19% to $13.5 million, 
or $1.07 a share, from $11.4 
million or 90¢ a share, a year 
ago. Net sales and other reve- 
nues increased 33% to $1.09 
billion from $816 million.

chains spent more than $1 mil-

The Top 15 chain drug TV 
advertisers spent a combined 
$58.7 million on local spot tele- 
vision in 1984, a 7% increase 
over the 1983 expenditures, 
according to the Television 
Bureau of Advertising. 

Eckerd Drug, the nation’s 
top drug store advertiser, 
- more than $12 million in 
the 42 different television 
markets the drug chain serves 
in the Southeast and South- 
west. 

“We like to use TV to add 
reinforcement to our print ad- 
vertising,” says Eckerd’s su- 
pervisor of broadcast, Kevin 
Weinman. “It’s also a good 
break-through medium to

Sheets under 
lock and key 
at Thrifty 


LOS ANGELES — Thrifty 
Drug has installed locked 
cases for upscaled domestics 
in selected stores. 

The glass eases range in size 
from 9 to 12 ft. (depending on 
the size of store), and price 

oints are from $12.99 to 

4.99. 

Typical: three-piece twin 
set (one twin flat sheet, one 
twin fitted sheet and a stan- 
dard pillowcase), $21.99. 
Typical of the top-of-the-line 
is king or queen four-piece set 
(flat sheet, fitted sheet and 
two pillowcases), $44.99. 

The locked glass case ad- 
joins the regular domestics 
section. 

Demographics in the area 
determine whether the up- 
scale line is installed. For ex- 
ample, Thrifty’s No. 1 volume 
store, in a middle-income 
neighborhood, has a 12-ft. 
case; whereas the No. 2 vol- 
ume store in a low-income area 
does not. 

Principal drawback to the 
new locked-case section is that 
in today’s tight-labor-con- 
trolled store, it is sometimes 
time-consuming for shoppers 
to find a staff member to un- 
lock the case. However, a 
Thrifty district manager says 
that this has not been a soa 
lem thus far.

THE WALGREEN CO. announced a 2-for-1 stock split in the 
form.of a 100% stock dividend payable May 8 to stockholders of 
record April 24. This is the company’s third since 1982. 


McKESSON CORP. will acquire Spectro Industries for ap- 
proximately $161 million. The $20 a share bid for the Jenkin- 
town, Pa.-based drug wholesaler, which for the year ended 
March 31 had estimated sales of $450 million, has been ap- 
proved by the boards of both companies. The acquisition will 
mean that 60% of McKesson’s revenues and more than 50% of 
its net earnings willcome from health care-related businesses.

Osco banner 
to fly above 
108 Skaggs 


SALT LAKE CITY — 
American Stores has moved 
another step closer to central- 
izing its drug store division. 

From now until the end of 
fiscal 1986 next February, 
American will be converting 
all 108 of its super-sized 
Skaggs drug centers into Osco 
drug stores. The transforma- 
tion will give American over 
350 drug stores operating in 
more than 30 states under one 
name and one logo. 

It will eliminate duplica- 
tions in services and opera- 
tions while allowing American 
to reduce the cost of its vari- 
ous advertising programs. 

After the conversion is com- 
pleted, company executives 
will decide if they want to 
make the same change with 
the 176 Sav-On drug stores 
now operating in California. 

“We chose the Osco name 
because that division had the 
largest number of stores in the 
most states,’’ said Mike 
Miller, senior vp. 

Miller also said that all the 
signage and decor packages in 
the Skaggs stores will be 
changed to conform to the 
Osco format. The merchandis- 
ing mix, however, will proba- 
bly not be changed. 

“The merchandising 
schemes of Osco and Skaggs 
are already very similar,” “ 
said, “at least in terms of dis- 
play.”

quarter increased 14.8% to $875.3 mill

$46.6 million, or $1.52 a share, from $40.2 million, or $1.31 
a share, a year ago. Sales for the first half increased 15.6% 
to $1.59 billion, from $1.38 billion.

‘adhe of Pay ’n Save, which the

Skaggs, chairman of Ameri-

Save stores in Hawaii and has 
met with chain officials con-

Southland, owner of the 7-

reportedly negotiating for 
Pay ’n Save’s Schuck’s auto 
supply stores in order to add 
them to its Big Chief auto 
store holdings. 


The company’s Lamont ap- 
parel stores, its most profit- 
able division, appear to have 
already been sold. Inside 
sources say the chain has been 
purchased by Mervyn’s of 
Hayward, Calif. The company 
would not confirm the sale, 
but acompany officer asserted 
that “these rumors have been 
going on for three years.” 

Three separate brokerage 
firms are handling the possi- 
ble divestitures. Kidder, Pea- 
body is handling Schuck’s; Sal- 
omon Brothers has Bi-Mart 
drug stores and Goldman 
Sachs, the Pay’n Save stores. 

Trump Group officials told 
Drug Store News that “con- 
sistent with our strategic 


plan, it is true that we are con- 
sidering the possible sale of 
one or more of Pay ’n Save’s 
companies.”

Drug Store News’ report last 
October that Acquicorp., the 
Trump subsidiary that ac- 
quired Pay ’n Save in a lever- 
aged pon he late last year, 
might sell off the chain’s divi- 
sions piecemeal. At that time, 
an analyst noted that Pay ’n 
Save’s “parts are worth more 
than the whole.” 

“There’s a lot of rumors,”

attle, “but nothing definitive. 
The word is out that things

Chains remove certain tampons 
possibly linked to toxic shock 


NEW YORK — Drug 
chains nationwide are comply- 
ing with a voluntary recall is- 
sued by manufacturers of tam- 
pons that contain poly- 
acrylate, a highly absorbent 
substance that may be linked 
to toxic shock syndrome 
(TSS). 

The tampon products in 
egy ne are Playtex’s Slen- 

er, Super and Super Plus, 
and Tampax’s Super Plus. 

The recall follows on the 
heels of an $11 million lawsuit 
brought against Playtex by a 
Kansas family whose 21-year- 
old daughter died of TSS in 
1983, staaadly as a result of 
using a Playtex brand tampon 
made with polyacrylate. 

While the recall leaves sev- 
eral holes on retailers shelves, 
the consensus is that it will not 
have a major impact on the 
market. 

“We removed the product 
from our shelves as soon as we 
received notice,” said Ray 
Meissner, buyer at Fay’s 
Drug. “The recall went 
smoothly and we don’t expect 
much of a drop in sales. We’ve 
instructed our stores to fill in 
the holes with existing mer- 
chandise until the recailed 
goods are replaced.” 

Meissner said that Fay’s is 
giving refunds to consumers 
who bring in open packages of 


the recalled tampons. 

According to Jim Kyle, buy- 
er at Page Drug in Dallas, the 
recall did not come close to 
matching the impact of 
Procter & Gamble’s 1980 re- 
call of its Rely tampon. 

“Not too many people are 

etting excited about it,” said 
Kyle. “Both companies did a 
good job in notifying the public 
without any panic.” 

In Kentucky, the reaction 


from Begley buyer, Mike Tip- 
ton, was much the same. 
“We've started the process 
of pulling the tampons _in- 
volved and sending them back 
to the warehouse for credit,” 
said Tipton. “People will just 
have to buy another brand or 
another tampon from those 
manufacturers involved that 
has a little less absorbency.”

the company’s profits, but 
only 25% of its sales. In 1983, 
for example, Pneumo’s aero- 
space division accounted for 
$60.3 million of the company’s 
$81.1 million net profits.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 29, 1985 


Chains wrap up a blockbuster 


ineteen eighty-four was the 
year of the blockbuster. 
American-Jewel . . . Revco- 

Odd Lot . . . Peoples-Rea and Derick 
_.. Pay ’n Save-Trump . . . K mart- 
Pay Less Rite Aid-Hook 
Kroger-Hook . . . Adams-Pantry 
Pride. 

No sooner had one whopping stor) 
been digested, then another whopper 
was filling the mind with new details. 

It was a year that Drug Store News 
overshot its quota of banner headlines. 

It was also a year of growth for the 


chain drug industry, as consumer con- 
fidence continued to be buoyed by low 
inflation and a decreasing jobless rate 
While profits did not match the spec- 
tacular performance of the previous 
year, they were generally strong. 
Overall sales for the retail drug in- 
dustry increased 9% to $43.2 billion, 
but the chain drug segment again out- 
shone the industry as a whole with 
sales gaining 12% to $25.2 billion. 
Moreover, while the number of drug 
stores throughout the United States 
remained roughly the same as last year 


50,709), the chain drug portion of that 
total increased two percentage points 
to 35%. 

If the big acquisitions and mergers 

were the Himalayas of a breathless 
news year, there were other peaks that 
seemed only a little less important as 
1984 unfolded. Among them: 
@ With competition from supermar- 
kets, mass merchandisers and deep 
discounters growing increasingly heat- 
ed, several chains struck back with 
deep, across-the-board price cuts in se- 
lected markets. 


@ More and more chains rushed into 
new types of retail ventures as a way of 
insuring future growth, especially in 
markets saturated with traditional 
drug stores. The diversifications in- 
cluded retail book stores (Rite Aid and 
Encore); fast food (Peoples and Har- 
dee’s), and mega-optical stores (Eck- 
erd and Vision Works). 

® Chains continued to reach out for 
new technological advances to height- 
en efficiency and improve the bottom 
line. Perhaps the most important de- 


Continued on page 64 


64 


PERFORMANCE 


§ _ 


Continued from page 61 

velopment was the integration of phar- 
macy and front-end computers into to- 
tal store management systems. More 
chains also launched point-of-sale laser 
scanning tests. 

@ The year also had its share of prob- 
lems. Revco, for example, ran into sev- 
eral tough-luck situations that ended 
its run of sparkling performances. And 
Gray Drug Fair, after tasting the be- 
ginning of a turnaround in the begin- 
ning of 1984, found the year had turned 
sour in the second half. 

@ Finally, there were the milestones: 
Genovese reached its 60th year, White 
Drug its 100th, and Walgreens joined 
Reveo, Eckerd and Rite Aid in the ex- 
clusive 1,000-store club. 


Big deals 


: n 1984, the term shrinkage could be 


applied to a lot more than an unex- 

plained slippage in inventory. It 
also seemed the perfect way to de- 
scribe what happened to the chain 
drug industry as a whole. 

Specifically, the ranks of the large 
publicly traded drug chains dwindled 
as company after company was ac- 
quired by bigger firms or moved into 
private hands through leveraged 
buyouts. 

The biggest of these were Jewel 
Companies with its Osco and Sav-On 
drug chains (acquired by American 
Stores); Peoples Drug Stores (pur- 
chased by Imasco); Pay Less Drug 
Stores NW (K mart); Hook Drug 
(Kroger Co.); Adams Drug (Pantry 
Pride); Pay ’n Save (The Trump 
Group), and Dart Drug (a leveraged 
buyout by Dart executives). 

In addition to these large deais, 
there were others involving smaller 
companies whose acquisition in former 
years would have merited top atten- 
tion. Among them: Muir Drugs (ac- 
quired by Rite Aid); Apex (Perry 
Drug), and Rea and Derick (Peoples). 

In some issues of Drug Store News, 
the big acquisition stories competed 


for front-page placement. On May 14, 
for example, the top story concerned 
the offer by Al Towle and other Dart 
Drug executives to buy the 73-store su- 
perdrug chain for $160 million. (Towle 
and the group would later succeed in 
getting financing for the leveraged 
buyout, and then begin the job of solv- 
ing some of the problems that had been 
plaguing the chain under the former 
owners. ) 

On the same page was another top 
acquisition story, one which would lat- 
er erupt into a major problem for the 
acquiring company. It involved Revco’s 
decision to buy out Odd Lot, the close- 
out specialty retailer with whom the 
Twinsburg, Ohio-based company had 
been working amicably and profitably 
for two years. 

No one—certainly not Sid Dworkin, 
the chairman—suspected that Odd 
Lot’s owners would use their newly ac- 
quired 12% interest in Revco to try to 
wrest control of the company from 
Dworkin. They failed but the fight was 
damaging. 

Perhaps the biggest acquisition 
news of the year was the $1.2 billion 
takeover of the Jewel Companies by 
American Stores. Jewel had long been 
coveted by Sam Skaggs, the publicity- 
shy head of American Stores. The com- 
pletion of the merger brought together 
two food/drug giants operating four 
separate drug chains with stores from 
coast to coast. Only Walgreens could 
rival the breadth of their retail drug 
store coverage. 


In addition to the drug chains, 
American and Jewel separately were 
operating close to 250 food and drug 
combination stores, the one-stop shop- 
ping behemoths that American has 
targeted as its major growth vehicle. 
Combos, which can generate $1 million 
or more a week in sales and yield profit 
margins higher than the traditional 1% 
of foods stores, were operating under 
the various names of Skaggs-Alpha 
Beta, Jewel/Osco, Buttery and But- 
tery/Osco. In addition there were the 
Sav-On combos in California that 
American would later drop. 


To lighten its $700 million debt load, 
American began to sell off some of its 
parts, including Rea and Derick, which 
went to Peoples for $85 million. 

American then began the task of

welding the three remaining drug 
chains—Skaggs, Osco and Sav-On— 
into a single drug division that eventu- 
ally will carry one logo, Osco, and be 
headed by Dick George. George, presi- 
dent of Osco before the acquisition, 
quietly added the top Sav-On post to 
his responsibilities and is expected to 
take on Skaggs as well. 

The largest sum ever paid for a pure 
chain drug company was laid out by 
K mart for Pay Less NW, the super- 
drug store company headquartered in 
} Wilsonville, Ore. 

K mart had made no secret of its in- 
tention to diversify into the retail drug 
business and was looking for a chain 
that was well managed and profitable. 
Pay Less fit the bill, and then some. 

Operating in five Western states, 
the 164-store chain was averaging al- 
most $6 million a store, close to the 
best of the chain drug operators, and 
producing a net profit margin of more 
than 3% on sales greater than $900 mil- 
lion. 

In addition to the 30,000-sq.-ft. su- 
per stores, Pay Less had begun to open 
smaller Key drug stores in markets 
which could not support a full-line su- 
per store but which had growth poten- 
tial. 

K mart and Pay Less fit very well. 
The discounter, the second largest re- 
tail company after Sears Roebuck, had 
given emphasis to its pharmacy de- 
partments, with prescription services 
available in almost 1,000 stores. But 
there were no pharmacies in the Pacific 
Northwest or California, where Pay 
Less has its major strength. 

What’s more, Pay Less has consider- 
able resources to ensure its growth, 
but K mart’s pockets are almost bot- 
tomless. So far, the plans are to finance 
expansion out of Pay Less’ cash flow, 
but the K mart resources are there if 
needed. 

K mart chairman Bernard Fauber 
said the company has big plans for Pay 
Less, with expansion slated for contig- 
uous states as well as certain areas of 
central and southern California. 

Nineteen eighty-four was also a year 
in which one of the oldest companies in 
drug retailing, Hook Drug, was 
merged into the nation’s second larg- 
est food retailers, the Kroger Co. 

The chain drug industry, which had 
grown almost immune to shock over

the big mergers taking place last year, 
was nevertheless startled when Rite 
Aid made a $31 a share bid for Hook. 
The unfriendly takeover offer for the 
312-store Indianapolis-based chain 
sent Hook executives searching for a 
white knight who would guarantee the 
continued existence of the Hook name 
and at least some degree of indepen- 
dence for the management. 

Although Hook’s earnings had 
dropped 18% in the first nine months of 
the fiscal year, the chain was dominant 
in its home state of Indiana, and its dis- 
tribution center is considered first- 
rate, both very attractive features for 
the aggressively growth-minded Rite 
Aid. The Shiremanstown, Pa.-based 
drug chain then upped the ante to 
$36.50 a share. 

With aimost everyone convinced 
that Hook management would lose its 
battle, it was a shock when Kroger 
moved in at the 11th hour with a $37 a 
share offer. in addition, Hook granted 
Kroger an option to buy up to 1.3 mil- 
lion shares, which effectively locked 
out Rite Aid. 

Koger is expected to allow Hook its 
autonomy as long as it is able to reverse 
the earnings slide. 


Hitting back 


ckerd had not yet experienced 

major competition from deep-dis- 

count drug stores, but Stewart 
Turley, chairman and ceo of the Jack 
Eckerd Corp., earlier this year told an- 
alysts: 

“They’re going to have to fight to get 
our market share.” 

Turley said that when the stores get 
competition from deep discounters, as 
they had ina minor way in Florida, “We 
get right down with them in price.” 

Turley might have been setting the 
tone for other chains that decided dur- 
ing the year that “We’re mad as hell, 
and we’re not going to take it any- 
more.” 

Specifically, Revco and Fay’s both 
lowered prices on hundreds of sku’s of 
core drug store products in selected 
markets in which the two chains were 
feeling competitive heat from super- 
markets, mass merchandisers and 
deep discounters. Begley later fol- 
lowed suit.

price-slashing compaign, it was a mat-

The chain did no feature advertising

story.

tions that the price campaign was 
working. Same-store sales were run- 
ning ahead of last year in some mar- 
kets. But for the most part it was too 
early to tell if the sacrifice of gross 
margins would result in greater sales 
and gross profits dollars.

On the heels of Revco’s dramatic 
price-cutting, Fay’s Drug did some 
deep price cuts of its own in the rugged 
Rochester market. “We’re going as 


deep on prices as the best-run deep- 
discount stores,” explained Dan Herr- 


mann, president of the chain. 


Fay’s rolled back prices on 8,100 


H&BA and OTC products, every sku in 
stock, in 25 stores in the market. 

The campaign was also aimed direct- 
ly at food chains, mass merchandisers 
and deep discounters. They included 
Wegman’s, K mart and Freddie’s, a 
deep-discount store operated by CVS 
parent Melville Corp. 

Melville was about to open its second 
Freddie’s. “When you compete with 
one successful deep discounter, that’s a 
temporary phenomenon,” Herrmann 
said. “Two is a price war.” 

Begley recently joined the price-cut- 
ting trend with a campaign to make the 
chain’s 47 drug stores more aggressive 
on price. Begley chose 380 of the most 
visible H&BA, general merchandise 
and pharmaceutical products for “dra- 
matic” cuts.

yesterday continue to be popular. Drug 
chains opening auto stores, deep-dis- 
count units and home health care 
stores is common today.

variety of diversifications last year. 
They invested in burgers, glasses, pa- 
per goods, capability extenders and 
fact and fiction.

announced plans to venture into three 
new retail markets. In 1982, the chain 
acquired the Circus World toy store 
chain. In March 1984, it purchased 
ADAP, a discount auto parts chain, 
and in August, it picked up the Phila- 
delphia-based Encore discount book- 
store chain. 

At the time of the purchase of the 
bookstores, some industry officials 
were puzzled about why Rite Aid, with 
sales in excess of $1.2 billion, would 
bother with the 18-store book chain 
with sales just topping $10 million. 

Analysts concurred that this smal! 
acquisition alone would have no sub- 
stantial effect on Rite Aid’s perfor- 
mance, but combined with the other 
two diversifications, could raise the

| 4984: Chain stocks rally in second half 


hain drug stocks turned bear- 

ish during the first half of the 

year, but a second-half rally 
helped set the stage for a strong run-up 
in prices that has continued through 
the first quarter of 1985. 

Must chain drug stocks closed out 
1984 with mixed results. Eight of the 
15 leading public drug chains gained 
during the year. 

However, because of the broad sell- 
off of retail issues in general during the 
first six months of the year, publicly 
held drug chains posted increases that 
were substantially lower than in 1983. 

Among the biggest losers last year 
was Hook Drug, which plunged 31% in 
1984, Genovese Drug, down 28.3% 
from. the previous year and Fay’s 
Drug, off 23.6% from 1983. Big B, 
which registered a 104% increase in 
1983, fell 17.5% last year. 

Large institutionally held stocks 
fared somewhat better. Eckerd Drug 
closed the year up 3.6%. Rite Aid ap- 
preciated 14% from the previous year. 
The Los Angeles-based Thrifty man- 
aged to gain 13.6% over last year. 

But the widely publicized problem at 
Reveo sent the stock price spiraling 
downward in 1984. At year-end, Revco 
was selling at $24.37, more than 10 
points off from its 1983 close of $34.62. 

Pay ’n Save, the subject of a take- 
over, still closed the year down 9.4% 
from 1983. 


However, investors whose holdings 
included Peoples, Jewel Cos., Dart 
Drug and Adams found 1984 particu- 
larly rewarding. Each of those compa- 
nies also was a takeover target, but un- 
like Pay ’n Save, their individual stock 
prices soared. 

During the second half of 1984 as re- 
tailer profits strengthened, Wall 
Street turned the bulls loose with 
chain drug stocks, and they’ve been 
running ever since. 

Of the 15 leading public chain drug 
issues tracked by Drug Store News, 
only three—Revco, Hook and Geno- 
vese—failed to stage a recovery in the 
second half of the year. 

But Hook Drug investors were am- 
ply rewarded for their patience during 
the first quarter of 1985. An unfriend- 
ly tender bid by Rite Aid for $31 a 
share was later topped by Kroger’s of- 
fer of $37 a share, which Hook accept- 
ed. Inthe end, Hook investors realized 
a 75% gain from the stock’s closing 
price of $20.50 on Dec. 31, 1984. 

In addition, those savvy investors 
who held Pay Less NW stock also ben- 
efited from an outside takeover. After 
enjoying a 38% run-up in the price of 
their shares in 1984, they were treated 
to an additional 16% increase during 
the first month of the year when Pay 
Less accepted K mart’s $27 offer. 

With the exception of Revco, every 
publicly held drug chain rode the bull

Warehouse grades 


he trend toward warehouse mod- 

ernization and centralization con- 

tinued at full throttle in 1984 as 
chain drug companies strived to in- 
crease inventory turns and improve 
delivery time. 

Moreover, many chains also greatly 
expanded existing distribution facili- 
ties not only to support additional drug 
stores, but to furnish a growing num- 
ber of diversified ventures such as auto 
outlets and home health care centers. 

Overall, the state-of-the-art tech- 
nology installed in today’s warehouse 
is truly impressive. 

Eckerd Drug 

Eckerd Drug’s ninth distribution 
center, which opened last spring in 
Hammond, La., was the chain’s first 
fully automated and completely com- 
puter-controlled facility. The 216,000- 
sq.-ft. center has the capacity to pro- 
cess more than 15,000 pieces of 
merchandise over more than two miles 
of mechanized conveyors. 

One of the keys to the Eckerd sys- 
tem is a Rexnor Laser beam scanner, 
which can “read” laser-printed bar 
codes at a rate of three units a second. 
Eckerd is also using the sophisticated 
Alvey Zip Sorter to divert merchan- 
dise along conveyors to one of 28 ship- 
ping doors. 

Eckerd’s Hammond facility, accord- 
ing to some sources, should help boost 
its inventory turns from 12 to 15 times 
a year. The mechanized center should 
also help speed deliveries to about 116 
Louisiana stores. 

Perry Drug 

In another major expansion develop- 
ment, Perry Drug will soon open a $4 
million 155,235-sq.-ft. addition to its 
present 224,000-sq.-ft. distribution fa- 
cility in Pontiac, Mich. The addition 
will not only increase the facility’s 
space by 50%, but also significantly 
boost the percentage of merchandise 
shipped via the warehouse. Perry cur- 
rently ships 55% of its goods (by dollar 
volume) through the facility. 

In addition to its Pontiac facility, 
Perry now operates two auto supply 
warehouses, a 49,000-sq.-ft facility in 
Columbus, Ohio, and a 65,000-sq.-ft. 
facility in Muncie, Ind. 

Perry’s 224,000-sq.-ft. distribution 
center in Pontiac has a new high-tech 
system designed by William Semco, 


up at full throttle 


chairman of Semco, Sweet & Mayers. 
Semco has designed warehouses for 
Pay Less NW, Sav-On and Gray Drug.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 29, 1985 


1985 Annual Report 


_of the Chain Drug Indusiry 


87 


PERFORMANCE 


Combo units continue fo lure shoppers 


he marriage between food and 
drug stores grew stronger during 
1984 as the combination store con- 
cept continued to lure major food and 
drug retailers into profitable ventures. 

As the popular offspring of this 
union, convenient one-stop shopping, 
became more accessible to the public, 
more shoppers turned to their local 
foodAdrug combo stores. 

Another important offspring of this 
marriage is the increased profit poten- 
tial it provides the retailer. 

The reason for opening, and for con- 
verting to the food/drug combination, 
is a simple one—food, with an average 
profit margin of 1%, generates the 
traffic and drugs, with a margin of 3%, 
boosts the profits. 

“Supermarkets provide */ of the vol- 
ume and drug stores */3 of the profits,” 
notes one industry observer. 

The major combo store news in 1984 
was the acquisition of the Jewel Com- 
panies by American Stores. That $1.15 
billion deal stands as the largest merg- 
er ever in the history of the chain drug 
industry. 

The merger made American Stores 
the third largest food and drug chain in 
the country with a total of 2,200 food/ 
drug combos, supermarkets and free- 
standing drug stores spanning 43 
states. 

Specifically, at year’s end, American 
operated 245 food/drug combos: 118 
Jewel/Osco; 92 Skaggs Alpha Beta; 34 
Buttery, and one Buttery Osco. 

The five central California Sav-On 
combos that Jewel had big plans for 
were closed down by American Stores 
within a few months of the takeover. 

American Stores now ranks third in 
total number of combo stores operat- 
ed. Cincinnati-based Kroger Company 
was operating 420 combos at year’s 
end, and Safeway of Oakland, Calif., 
was operating 354. 

An industry first occurred in Octo- 
ber 1984, when Minyard Food Stores 
combined one of its food warehouse 
stores with a deep discount drug store. 
“Sack ’N Save” is a 76,000-sq.-ft. store 
combining for the first time warehouse 
selling of both food and drug items. 


The store, complete with pharmacy, 
has a ratio of 60% food to 40% drug 
items. It is open 24 hours a day. 

According to the company, the store 
must to a hefty $23 million in sales a 
year to break even. The company was 
so happy with the initial results of the 
store, that within a month of its open- 
ing, announced that it would open an- 
other in late spring of 1985. 

The store is located in Waco, Tex., 
just 100 miles south of Dallas. 

And speaking of Dallas. . . . 

The Metropolitan Dallas Area, in- 
cluding Fort Worth, is undisputedly 
the toughest combo market in the 
country. The area is served by the gi- 


ants in the combo world, including | 


Skaggs Alpha Beta and Tom Thumb/ 
Page. 

Albertson’s, which operates a total 
of 91 combos, made Dallas a bit tough- 
er in 1984 when it returned to the mar- 
ket after an absence of seven years. 
The company announced its plans to 
build 10 stores in the area. 

The chain is taking its new move 
quite seriously. Earlier this year, it 
sold its seven Alabama combos to Bru- 
no’s because it lacked market penetra- 
tion. Concentration will now be on 
Sunbelt markets. 

Prior to 1977, the Skaggs-Albertson 
food/drug combo stores dominated the 
Dallas market, but when the two com- 
panies broke up their partnership, 
Skaggs got the Dallas market where it 
kent expanding its Skaggs Alpha Beta 
combo stores. 

Albertson’s has returned with a new 
low price posture, and industry offi- 
cials predict that the company’s major 
target in this hot market is its old part- 
ner. 

In order to serve its Dallas combos 
better, Tom Thumb/Page increased its 
warehouse space by 24% during 1984 
by adding another 110,000 sq. ft. to its 
existing 467,000 sq. ft. Tom Thumb/ 
Page operates a total of 72 food drug 
combos. 

Albertson’s also returned to anoth- 
er market last year that it left about 17 
years ago—Tacoma, Wash.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 29, 1985 


Computer technology improves 


harmacy computers took a quan- 

tum leap in 1984 with an expan- 

sion in their versatility and con- 
tinuing reduction in cost. 

Pharmacy computer systems, intro- 
duced in the late 70’s, have steadily im- 
proved over the past five years. In- 
creased memory, more sophisticated 
software and a miniaturization of hard- 
ware are credited as being major fac- 
tors in the 80’s for what some manufac- 
turers are calling “third-generation” 
systems. 

“We reached a turning point in 
1984,” said Bill Lockwood, president 
and publisher of ComputerTalk. “The 
price of a computer system is now cost- 
justified. There is no excuse not to pur- 
chase a system.” 

Last year, several drug chains an- 
nounced tests of fully integrated phar- 
macy/store management systems. 
Now, not only will the computer handle 
the routine tasks of filling prescrip- 
tions and preparing patient profiles, 
but also inventory control, point-of- 
sale purchases, automatic ordering 
and a host of other electronic applica- 
tions necessary in evaluating store op- 
erations. 

Until now, pharmacy computers 
have concentrated on automating only 


the pharmacy, and, for the most part, 
have been a success. The new systems 
introduced in 1984 have taken that a 
step further by automating other de- 
partments throughout the store and 
feeding all the information through the 
pharmacy system. 

One major feature of the new sys- 
tems is the ability to communicate with 
a host computer. Data can be transmit- 
ted via telephone lines and collected at 
a central location for interpretation. 
Third-party claim submissions can be 
done by the main office instead of indi- 
vidual pharmacies for more accurate 
and faster reimbursement. 

While industry experts agree that 
inventory control and analysis of gross 
profits through point-of-sale scanning 
technology is still a year or two away, 
several chains began testing in 1984. 

Pay Less NW was one of the first 
chains to fully integrate its pharmacy 
system with the rest of the store, and 
Rite Aid is also testing an integrated 
front-end computer management sys- 
tem in severa! stores. 

While there has been a flurry of ac- 
tivity in the high-tech computer busi- 
ness, POS and scanning technology is 
expected to go through the same grow- 
ing pains the pharmacy computer sys-

tem experienced. 

“Many are taking the same ‘wait- 
and-see’ attitude,” said Computer- 
Talk’s Lockwood, “but rest assured, 
the industry is on its way to even great- 
er sophistication in computer technol- 
ogy.” 

Aside from the pharmacy/manage- 
ment benefits derived from computers 
in chain stores, retailers are realizing 
that the computer systems make ex- 
cellent marketing tools. 

In advertisements to their custom- 
ers, chains emphasize the computer in 
cutting down waiting time for pre- 
scriptions. The pharmacist does not 
have to look up prescriptions in a book. 
By merely pushing several keys, he can 
view the patient’s entire prescription 
history. 

In addition, the chains advertise the 
fact that a listing of prescriptions is 
available to customers for any period of 
time, especially during tax season. 
And even the pharmacist’s profession-

PERFORMANCE 
ZA» 


alism is heightened with the advent of 
drug interaction databases. 

At least one company is concentrat- 
ing on increasing the marketing capa- 
bilities of its pharmacy computer sys- 
tem. In its latest version, the 
pharmacist can access a word-proces- 
sor built into the computer and merge 
letters to a particular group of custom- 
ers he wants to reach. 

Another feature is the production of 
a multicolored label, making reading 
prescription labels easier for the elder- 
iy or sight-impaired. 

And finally, computers have been 
shown to lessen the pharmacist’s 
stress while filling prescriptions. 

Because of the computer’s speed, 
the pharmacist can fill more prescrip- 
tions faster, allowing him to spend 
more time consulting with patients. 
The computer eliminates writing 
third-party claim forms by hand and al- 
lows pharmacists to maintain better 
control over inventory.

PERFORMANCE 


he deep-discount drug field grew 
more crowded last year as major 
drug chains, food, discount and 
specialty retailers entered the multi- 
billion-dollar business. 

Although the deep-discount format 
continues to attract independent en- 
trepreneurs, more and more of the na- 
tion’s largest retailers have taken no- 
tice of the phenomenon. To be sure, the 
entry of such retail giants as the Mel- 
ville Corp., Supermarkets General 
Corp. and F. W. Woolworth are alter- 
ing the face of deep-discount drug re- 
tailing. 

Last summer, the Melville Corp., in 
a surprise move, became the first ma- 
jor corporation to enter the deep-dis- 
count business by acquiring an inde- 
pendently operated store. The 
purchase of Freddy’s deep-discount 
store in Rochester, in a deal worth an 
estimated $2 million, was viewed as a 
test project for Melville. 

However, it wasn’t long before the 
test was expanded. A second Freddy’s 
was scheduled to open in Rochester 
this month. In addition, as many as 
four more units are said to be in the 
planning stages. 

Only a year ago, Supermarkets Gen- 
eral, operators of Pathmark supermar- 
kets and drug stores, had yet to open 
its first deep-discount drug store. It 
now ranks as one of the biggest deep- 
discount operators. 

In midsummer, the company opened 
a deep-discount drug store in Balti- 
more. Two more Pathmark Super 
Drug deep-discount stores were subse- 
quently opened in that market. 

At about the same time the first 
Pathmark Super Drug was opening, 
Supermarkets General acquired 10 
Heartland deep-discount stores, New 


England’s leading discount chain, as 
part of the purchase of Purity Su- 
preme, owners of Heartland. 

The company intends to aggressive- 
ly expand both the Heartland and 
Pathmark Super Drug Stores over the 
next two years. 

Major retailing behemoths weren't 
the only ones to enter the high-flying 
deep-discount business via the acquisi- 
tion route. Fay’s Drug purchased the 
Syracuse-based Jay Jay’s store from 
S. M. Flickinger Co. 

Markets limited 

The driving force behind the rush to 
open deep-discount stores is the fact 
that most major markets around the 
country can only support a limited 
number of these stores, which can pro- 
duce up to $20 million in sales a year. 
Chains and independents are in a race 
to establish themselves in their mar- 
kets before the competition does. 

One such race is under way in the 
Philadelphia-southern New Jersey 
market. Drug Emporium, the nation’s 
largest chain of deep-discount stores, 
plans to open as many as 20 deep-dis- 
count units there over the next 18 
months. 

F. W. Woolworth Co. will join the 
ranks of the deep discounters when it 
premieres its first low-margin drug 
store called the Rx Place in southern 
New Jersey. Three more Woolworth 
deep-discount stores may be opened in 
the Philadelphia area in 1986. 

Meanwhile, in northern New Jer- 
sey, Community Distributors, opera- 
tors of Drug Fair of New Jersey drug 
stores, created a big splash by opening 
five deep-discount drug stores called 
Cost Cutters in the last 12 months. 

Baltimore has been another hotbed 
of activity for the deep discounters. In

In fact, competition heated up in the 
Baltimore market to the point that a 
price war erupted with Giant Foods 
slashing prices on greeting cards, cos-

gories. Safeway also cut prices on drug 
store items in its stores in the Balti-

The threat of deep discounters tak- 
ing market share has sparked price 
wars in other markets around the 
country. 

Revco D.S., which operates two Get 
It For Less deep-discount stores of its 
own in Memphis and Minneapolis, re- 
duced prices up to 40% on 3,000 health 
& beauty aids in 230 stores in six mar- 
kets. The action was taken, according 
to Marc Dworkin, the chain’s executive 
vp, marketing, in order to make a 
“statement” to the “deep discounters, 
the food and drug combo stores, the 
mass merchandisers, to anyone who’s 
been using traditional drug store prod- 
ucts to build a low-price image.” 

Fay’s Drug rolled back prices in 
Rochester in response to the opening 
of the second Freddy’s. Fay’s price 
cuts were instituted in 25 stores and in- 
volved more than 8,100 sku’s. 

The chain drug industry’s knee-jerk 
response to the growth of the deep dis- 
counters comes at a time when more of 
the conventional chain operators are 
rolling out deep-discount stores of 
their own. 

In addition to Peoples and Fay’s, 
several other drug chains entered the 
deep-discount business last year. 
Among the new players: American 
Stores’ FAD, Pay Less NW’s three 
Value Giant stores and Medicare Gla- 
ser’s Meg’s. They join a long list of 
chains, including Perry Drug, Shop- 
pers Drug Mart, SupeRx and Ribordy, 
which are already operating deep-dis- 
count stores.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 29, 1985 


~ Drug chain execs look to the future 


Charles R. Walgreen Iii 
chairman, ceo 
The Walgreen Co. 


In 1985, Wal- 
greens will con- 
tinue to run 
convenient, 
customer- 
oriented, prof- 
itable drug 
stores across 
the nation. We 
project 100 new 
stores for the 
year, chiefly 
within our existing major markets. 
Finding quality locations for those 
stores is perhaps our biggest chal- 
lenge. Our success will be based on 
flexibility—our 10,000- to 15,000-sq.- 
ft. store size allows us to take advan- 
tage of every kind of location, from 
densely populated downtowns to 
neighborhood corners to suburban 
strip centers. 

Store management development is 
another top priority. Our objective is 
to attract and train competent manag- 
ers who also will be leaders that will 
recognize the importance we place on 
the entrepreneurial spirit. 

Other challenges? The continued 
computerization of our stores and fur- 
ther productivity improvements in the 
distribution centers. 

The U.S. Commerce Department 
forecasts a 10% increase in drug store 
industry sales for 1985. Based on past 
performance, Walgreens should do 
even better. We're not a company 
hungry for diversification. We think 
our drug store industry has plenty of 
potential.

ters with grocery anchors for drug 
store locations. We are going to have 
to look at freestanding stores and small 
strip centers where we are the anchor. 
The price pressure from mass mer- 
chandisers and deep-discount stores 
will compress margins even more. 

Changes in the health care delivery 
system will have a tremendous impact 
on us in the future. HMO’s and pre- 
ferred provider organizations will cap- 
ture most of the prescription markets. 

Cost containment in hospitals is a 
whole new game for them. To compen- 
sate, hospitals will go into more and 
more outpatient services and off-site 
satellites and centers. They will ag- 


gressively seek outpatient prescrip- 
tion business. If pharmaceutical manu- 
facturers continue their two-tier 
pricing, it will put chains at a severe 
cost disadvantage. Cost containment 
and DRGs and PPOs will also encour- 
age physicians to dispense prescrip- 
tions as a means to supplement their 
income. 

Large chains will have the resources 
to withstand these challenges. Large 
chains’ drive for market share and 
market dominance will also have a big 
impact on small chains. Small chains 
are going to have to be innovative, ag- 
gressive and very cost-conscious to re- 
main viable in the next decade.

of managerial power. 

There was, for example, the situa- 
tion at Revco. The Board of Directors 
at the Twinsburg, Ohio-based chain, 
headed by Sid Dworkin, finally got fed 
up with the pot shots taken at the com- 
pany by the heads of its Odd Lot sub- 
sidiary, Bernard Marden and Isaac 
Perlmutter. 

Although the two execs held a 12% 
interest in the company as a result of 
Revco’s Odd Lot buyout, they were 
fired and replaced by Leo Kaye and 
Stephen Adler. Kaye; who had been 
president at Americore Ltd., would 
later resign for personal reasons and 
be replaced by Peter J. Laitmon, a vp 
at Media General. |

in the executive suite was Gray Drug 
Fair. Last summer, Gray parent Sher- 
win- Williams named Mac Allen Culver 
president and general manager of the 
drug chain after an eight-month execu- 
tive search. 

Culver, who had been a senior vp at 
Pay Less and an expert in merchandis- 
ing and distribution, stunned every- 
one when he suddenly resigned six 
months after his appdintment and took 
a job as president of Pay ’n Save’s

New producis, promos push up sales 


ew products and heavier pro- 
motional activity helped propel 
1984 chain drug sales to $25.5 
billion, 12% higher than in the previous 
year. 

Among the leading product depart- 
ments were pharmacy, toiletries, cos- 
metics, stationery and photo, all of 
which had growth rates higher than 
the industry as a whole. 

What follows is a breakdown of those 
departments and how they performed 
last year. 

Prescriptions—The number of 
scripts dispensed by chain drug stores 
increased almost 8%. That increase 
combined with higher pharmaceutical 
prices pushed up chain drug prescrip- 
tion sales to $6.7 billion in 1984. The 
price of the average script increased 
65¢ to $11.25. Prescriptions now ac- 
count for 26.4% of total chain drug 
sales. 

Drugs/Proprietaries—The trend to 
more self-medication as well as the ex- 
tensive promotion of new products 
were the biggest factors in an almost 
13% increase in OTC/proprietary de- 
partment sales last year. Some of the 
biggest category gains were generated 
by analgesics; cough/eold; eye care 
products; feminine hygiene and dental 
care. The success of heavily advertised 
Rx-to-OTC products, ineluding two 
new branded ibuprofens, again con- 
tributed to the increase. 


General merchandise 


Toiletries—One of the hottest new 
product categories to emerge in years 
was responsible for at least part of the 
record sales registered in the toiletries 
department. Mousse went from noth- 
ing the previous year to $48 million in 
1984 and succeeded in capturing 2% of 
all toiletries sales. Other strong gains 
were recorded in skin care; shampoos; 
body creams and lotions ethnic 
H&BA, and suntan/sun protection 
products 

Cosmetics—-F ragrances again were 
the dominant factor in chain drug cos- 
metics, capturing 31% of department 
sales and reaching $421.8 million in vol- 
ume. Body sprays, a new subcategory 
within fragrances, generated $22.8 
million in chain drug sales, almost 2% 
of the $1.35 billion cosmetics volume. 
Nail products also produced strong re- 
sults, increasing 14% to $117 million 
and capturing almost 9% of sales. 

Photo—With hefty gains in the film 
(especially still color) and film process- 
ing categories, chain drug photo sales 
increased more than 12% to $1.11 bil- 
lion in 1984. Film is considered an espe- 
cially important category, since it can 
generate three customer trips per 
roll—one to buy, one to.drop off for pro- 
cessing and a third to pick up the re- 
sults. Several chains experimented 
with one-hour turnaround on process- 
ing, but it remains to be seen whether 
the tests will grow into a full-blown

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 29, 1985 


Chain script sales 


n increase in the average pre- 
scription price combined with a 
gain in the number of scripts 
helped push chain drug store prescrip- 
tion sales up 13% in 1984 to $6.7 billion. 

Chains increased the number of 
scripts dispensed by almost eight per- 
centage points, filling over 600 million 
in 1984, almost 40% of the total retail 
drug store market. About 5% of that 
gain was the result of an increase in the 
number of chain stores. 

The average price of a prescription 
filled at a chain drug store was $11.25, 
representing a 65¢ jump in the average 
prescription price over a year ago. 

While that represents a 7.6% in- 
crease, the percentage increase is al- 
most two points lower than last year’s. 

One reason the price of prescriptions 
has risen at a slower rate is new substi- 
tution laws now mandated by many 
state Medicaid programs. 

Some security analysts predict that 
generic sales will be responsible for al- 
most two-thirds of all prescription 
drugs by 1988, almost triple the busi- 
ness they did in 1978. 

Partly responsible for the generic 
surge is the new Generic Drug/Patent 
Restoration law of 1984. The law is a 
trade-off between extended patents 
for branded drugs approved between 
Jan. 1, 1982 and Sept. 24, 1984, and ab- 
breviated new drug applications 
(ANDA) for companies wishing to 
manufacture generic equivalents of 
post-1962 branded drugs losing their 
patents. 

Generic manufacturers were quick 
to take advantage of the new law. On 
Nov. 26, the first day the ANDA bill 
went into effect, F.D.A.’s Generic 
Drug division recorded approximately 
200 ANDA applications from approxi- 
mately 15 to 20 manufacturers. 

While generic manufacturers were 
positioning themse!ves in pharmacies 
across the country, at least 18 major 


branded pharmaceutical companies 
launched new products in 1984 hoping 
to stave off the wave of generics en- 
croaching on their once-exclusive 
turfs. 

Recognizing that generic substitu- 
tion can lead to higher gross profits, 
several chains have begun to use ge- 
nerics to their marketing advantage. 
Several chains introduced programs 
that assure their customers that the 
generics they are dispensing are of the 
highest quality approved by a set chain 
standard. 

Indeed, branded drug companies 
will have their hands full in the battle 
for continuing market dominance. 
Cost containment has become the 
buzzword of the 80’s as third-party ad- 
ministrators join the bandwagon of 
cost-cutters, and every indication 
points to more and more generic sub- 
stitution. 

Wall Street analysts are estimating 
that the new generics will generate ap- 
proximately $1 billion in sales by 1990 
and could go as high as $4 billion by the 
end of this century.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 29, 1985 


1985 Annual Report 


Chains cash in on home health boom 


scalation of the nation’s health 

care bill fueled growth of the $6.3 

billion home health care market 
in 1984. 

By 1995, it is estimated that total 
health care spending will account for 
13.6% of the gross national product, 
with home health care expanding to 
$24.8 billion. 

Cashing in on the coming boom are a 
number of drug chains, which either 
opened new freestanding stores or ex- 
panded in-store departments. The list 
of companies in the market continues 
to grow, but some of the dominant play- 
ers are Hook, Harco, Begley, Peoples, 
Walgreens and Eckerd. 

While execs of chains that operate 
home health care centers agree that 
the campaign to shorten hospital stays 
and thus cut costs is responsible for the 
spurt in growth, they are quick to add 
that the greater life expectancy of 
Americans is also playing a major role. 

The number of people over age 65, 
the fastest growing segment of the 
population, stands at greater than 27 
million, up 43% over the past 16 years. 
It is projected that by 1995 this group 
will comprise 13% of the total popula- 
tion, reaching 34 million. Since the 
over-65 age group consumes twice as 
much health care as the population as a 
whole, the need for less costly home 
health care is clearly an imperative. 

As health care continues to move 
into the home, the need for specialty 
equipment and services will also con- 
tinue to grow. 

According to Predicasts, a Cleve- 
land-based market research firm, du- 
rable medical equipment accounts for 


the largest share of health equipment 
used in the home. Such items as hospi- 
tal beds, wheelchairs, walkers, toilet 
items and traction equipment account- 
ed for approximately $1 billion. Dura- 
ble medical equipment is expected to 
show an 11.8% annual growth rate and 
should reach $1.8 billion by 1988. 

One home health care item that all 
chains are cashing in on is incontinent 
products. Approximately eight million 
adults suffer from incontinence, creat- 
ing a nearly $700 million market with 
expected growth from Predicasts pro- 
jected to reach $1.9 billion by 1988. 

In a report to the health care indus- 
try, Predicasts affirms that home care 
will grow at a greater rate than general 
health care expenditures. 

“If only 5% of the elderly were par- 
taking of home care in 1995,” the re- 
port says, “this would amount to an av- 
erage patient expenditure of $14,618 a 
year or $40 a day. The potential for the 
home care market is scarcely being 
tapped.” 

Through all the good news, however, 
comes a word of caution from Teri 
Louden, president of Louden & Com- 
pany, a Chicago-based health care con- 
sulting and information service. 

“Such positive growth is also attract- 
ing new entrants and causing payors to 
more carefully scrutinize current reim- 
bursement payments,” said Louden. 
“The home care industry is sure to at- 
tract the attention of the regulators if 
the rest of the industry is any indica- 
tion. Evaluating the market, the com- 
petition and your own competitive po- 
sition are critical steps in planning 
future strategies.”

OTC comprises 14% === 
_ Of drug chain sales 


utside of the prescription de- 

partment, consumer purchas- 

es of proprietary products 
contributed the highest percentage of 
chain drug store sales in 1984. 

Sales of proprietaries accounted for 
14% of chain sales, while the category 
recorded an almost 13% gain over a 
year ago. 

Much of the increase can be credited 
to the trend toward greater self-medi- 
cation and extensive promotion of new 
products. 

According to one study done by Har- 
ry Heller Research Corp., proprietary 
products are used to treat 35% of tem- 
porary medical problems such as 
coughs, colds, sore throats, allergy 
symptoms and minor pain. While 9% of 
these problems were taken to a doctor, 
11% of the patients used prescription 
medication already in their home. The 
remaining either used home remedies 
or did not treat the condition at all. 

The average American suffers a po- 
tentially self-treatable health problem 
once every three days. Among the ma- 
jor ailments most likely to be treated 
with OTC medications are the common 
cold, fever and minor aches and pains. 

Within the total category, cough and 
cold products contributed the greatest 
share of sales (15%), while analgesics 
and vitamins each accounted for about 
10%. 

Helping fuel the growth of cough 
cold and analgesics was the success of 
the heavily advertised Rx-to-OTC 
switched products. 

Last year, for example, the F.D.A. 


approved ibuprofen, a proven and ef- 
fective prescription product long used 
to treat arthritis pain, for over-the- 
counter sale. 

Some consumers with prescriptions 
for Motrin or Rufen, the branded ver- 
sions of ibuprofen, opted to purchase 
the readily available, if less potent, 
OTC product, even though the OTC 
version has not been indicated for ar- 
thritis pain. 

The only drawback to the OTC ibu- 
profens was the package warning to as- 
pirin-sensitive individuals not to take 
the product. As a result, acetamino- 
phen OTC product sales suffered little 
from the new kid on the block, and the 
analgesic category as a whole in- 
creased a whopping 17%. 

Vitamins and nutritionals also had 
an excellent year, spurred by both the 
national emphasis on fitness and the 
promotional firepower used by the 
chains to boost sales. 

While there were few new vitamin 
entries, retailers said the 14% sales 
gain was due in large part to vigorous 
advertising for perennial branded best 
sellers and a special emphasis on the 
importance of calcium products to 
women. 

But favorite among drug retailers is 
still private label. Store brands can 
yield gross margins up to 60% while de- 
veloping store loyalty. In most chains, 
private-label vitamins account for al- 
most three-quarters of total category 
volume.

also contributed to increased sales in

for 5.3% of total drug chain sales, a 
slight increase over 1983.

thumping 18.7% increase, bringing in 
$421.8 million in total sales. That sub- 
stantial gain was sparked by the inclu- 
sion of body sprays for the first time as 
a category. The sprays made a big 
splash in 1984, capturing $22.8 million 
in sales.

Sprays—accounted for nearly one- 
third of the sales in the cosmetics de- 
partment.

every toiletry category produced a

nearly 2% of the sales in toiletries.

hit nearly $100 million in 1985, some 
buyers are concerned that the catego- 
ry is approaching saturation. Already 
there are about 10 brands of mousse on 
the market. Another new entry will be 
Jhirmack, which will launch a new line 
of professional styling mousses in May 
1985. How many more sku’s can the 
shelves hold? 

Ethnic health & beauty aids was also 
one of the hottest categories in toilet- 
ries last year. Sales soared 16.8% to 
$178.4 million, the highest dollar vol- 
ume this category has ever generated. 
That substantial gain was spurred by 
drug retailers’ increasing commitment 
to this category. 

More retailers, for example, added 
space and sku’s to their ethnic sections 
last year, and some major chains began 
promoting ethnic products on a chain-

stationery writes ‘exceptional’ gains 


hain drug stationery depart- 

ments turned in an exceptional 

performance last year as sales 
soared 13.9% to nearly $1.2 billion. 

Even more satisfying to retailers 
was the fact that nearly every major 
component of the drug store stationery 
department registered strong in- 
creases. 

School and home office supplies 
turned in the largest increase as sales 
rose 15.5% to $313.4 million. Although 
some of the increase was due to sub- 
stantially higher paper prices, retail- 
ers still enjoyed a banner year in back- 
to-school sales. Home and office also 
showed steady gains as retailers cap- 
tured a larger share of the expanding 
home office market. 

The other major element of the 
school and home office mix that scored 
well last year were writing instru- 
ments. Sales were up 14% to $84.6 mil- 
lion. 

Retailers say the writing instrument 
category has been bolstered by new 
pen introductions, as weil as greater 
market penetration by many of the im- 
ported pen lines. 

Chain drug stores experienced an- 
other impressive year with greeting 
cards. Sales of greeting cards rose 
14.8% to $405.3 million. Greeting cards 
accounted for nearly 34% of the statio- 
nery department sales last year. 

There are several reasons for the 
substantial run-up in greeting card 
sales. Competition from other retail 
channels, principally discount stores 
and supermarkets, has forced drug re- 
tailers to upgrade their departments 
in order to retain market share. Sever- 
al chains have expanded the depart- 
ments and moved them to higher-traf- 


fic locations. 
At the same time, drug store greet- 
ing card departments are generating 
more sales per square foot because of Greeting cards lead Stationery dept.

cated inventory control systems. Eck- 
erd Drug, for instance, last year ex- 
panded its test of electronic ordering to 
more than 400 drug stores.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 29, 1985 


9985 Annual Report 


of fhe Chain Drug Industry 


ne-stop trend boosts drink, snack sales 


otal sales for liquor and food 

topped $1.2 billion last year, an in- 

crease of 7.1% over 1983. Overall, 
food, liquor and soft drinks accounted 
for 4.7% of total 1984 chain-drug-sales 
volume. 

The lure of one-stop shopping conve- 
nience helped boost sales in one of the 
largest traffic draws in this depart- 
ment—liquor and wine. Sales in this 
category jumped 7.1% to $568.5 mil- 
lion. 

Moreover, the liquor and wine cate- 
gory alone generated nearly half of 
1984’s total sales volume in the food 
and liquor department. The category 
also benefited from introduction of 
wine coolers, a new item in 1984 that 
produced strong sales in many chain 
drug stores. 

Nineteen hundred eighty-four was 
also a big year for another alcoholic 
beverage—beer. Sales in this category 
rose 8.9% to $89.5 million. The nearly 
9% increase in beer sales over 1983 was 
larger than that generated by any oth- 
er segment of the food and liquor de- 


partment. Beer accounted for 6.6% of 


the department’s sales last year. 

Altogether, alcoholic beverages—li- 
quor, wine and beer—-brought in $648 
million in 1984. Considering that some 
states do not permit the sale of alcohol- 
ic beverages in drug stores, that total is 
even more impressive. 

Although typical gross margins for 
alcoholic beverages are only 15% to 
20%, the average number of turns can 
range from an industry average of nine 
to 10 to as high as 40 to 60. The number 
of turns depends on a chain’s pricing- 
merchandising strategies and its abili- 
ty to advertise the beverages. Accord- 
ing to some retailers, beer and liquor 


sales would skyrocket if state laws pro- 
hibiting the sale of those drinks were 
lifted. 


The second biggest performer in the 
liquor and food department came from 
another thirst quencher—soft drinks. 
In 1984, this category registered 
$172.2 million in sales for chain drug 
stores. Sales increased 7.3% over the 
previous year and generated 14.2% of 
the total 1984 drug chain sales in the 
food and liquor department. 

As with alcoholic beverages, case- 
stacked soft drinks are excellent traffic 
builders in chain drug stores. Last 
year, many chains also installed per- 
manent soft drink sections, which 
helped boost sales in this category. 

The upward trend in snack food such 
as chips, crackers and cookies contin- 
ued in 1984. These largely unplanned 
purchase items produced a 7.5% in- 
crease over 1983. 

Sales in snack food rose to $89.5 mil- 
lion in 1984, generating 7.4% of the to- 
tal sales volume in the food and liquor 
department. One snack food that pro- 
pelled sales in this category was the 
soft-baked cookie, which a number of 
manufacturers introduced last year. 
Soft-cookie lines, according to buyers, 
were one of the hottest items in conve- 
nience food departments last year. 

Another strong category in 1984 was 
nuts, up 6.9% to $98.2 million. Nuts 
contributed 8.2% of the total sales in 
the food and liquor department. 

Canned goods and condiments held 
steady in 1984, rising 6.1% to $55.2 
million. Despite flat sales, the catego- 
ry still produced 4.6% of the sales in 
the food and liquor department. 

Another category that held steady 
in 1984 was dry groceries. Last year 
dry groceries brought in sales of $47.9 
million, an increase of 7.4% over the 
previous year. 

Although interest in full-line conve- 
nience food stores may be waning, 
chains such as Perry report strong 
food sales, especially in markets where 
there are no large food stores. Indeed, 
more chains may enlarge their food se- 
lections in those markets where there 
is little competition from supermar- 
kets and grocery stores.

PRODUCTS 


Small electrics lead 
in housewares dept. 


hain drug retailers’ efforts to 

build sales in the housewares 

category paid off last year as 
sales advanced 8.5% to $1.6 billion. 

Drug stores placed a greater empha- 
sis on housewares because the catego- 
ry’s higher profit margins have helped 
offset eroding margins in some of the 
health & beauty aids categories. 

Chains recorded a 9.5% increase in 
the plastics and rubber housewares 
category as manufacturers price cuts 
and rebates sparked a resurgence of 
sales. Plastic and rubber products ac- 
counted for nearly 23% of the depart- 
ment sales, or $364.6 million. 

Small electrics scored the biggest 
gains in the housewares category last 
year. Sales rose 9.7% to $170.2 million. 

Many of the consumers who re- 
placed items such as can openers, cof- 
feemakers, blenders, toaster ovens 
end irons traded up to higher-priced 
products. Space-saving appliances, 
which frequently carry higher price 
tags, were again in hot demand in 1984. 

In addition, a number of chains, in- 
cluding Page Drugs and Pay Less NW, 
managed to cash in on the microwave 
oven craze. Last year, industrywide 
unit sales reached eight million. 

For those chains that found price 
points in the microwave category to be 
prohibitive, there was the microwave 
accessory category. Once strictly an 
in-out promotional item, microwave ac- 
cessories have become everyday items 
in many housewares departments. 

Kitchen gadgets remained an inte- 
gral part of the department last year. 


In addition to selling many of the high 
margin, fast-turning, pe gged gadget- 
ry, many chains were able to move into 
some of the pricey gourmet accesso- 
ries. Overall, kitchen gadget sales in- 
creased 8.5% to $105.8 million. 

Many chains increased the visibility 
of their lighting products last year. 
And the results were encouraging: Vol- 
ume picked up 8.8% to $84 million. The 
highly profitable lighting products cat- 
egory chipped in 5.2% to total depart- 
ment sales. 

The glass/dishware/cookware cate- 
gory performed steadily last year as 
sales rose 7.4% to $175.4 million. The 
category, measured collectively, con- 
tributed nearly 11% to total depart- 
ment sales. 

Consumers seeking relief from 
cramped closets and cabinets pushed 
sales in the storage device category up 
substantially. Sales increased 8.3% t 
$30.1 million in the bath and closet cat- 
egory. 

Sales of indoor/outdoor furniture 
also turned in a good performance in 
1984 as volume was up 8.2% to $45.8 
million. 

Despite fierce competition from dis- 
counters and supermarkets, drug 
stores still managed to keep sales in 
the household supplies and paper prod- 
ucts category growing at a good clip. 
Household supplies, which account for 
13.2% of the total department sales, 
posted an increase of 8.9% to $200.3 
million. The much-promoted paper 
products posted an increase of 7.3% to 
$137.5 million.

Photo processing 


ups Customer traffic 


he growing popularity of 35mm 

cameras and films, as well as drug 

chains’ eagerness to promote film 
processing, translated into another 
banner year for the chain drug photo 
department. 

With an increase of 12% in 1984, pho- 
to department sales reached $1.1 bil- 
lion and accounted for 4.4% of the total! 
sales of a typical store. 

Management’s eagerness to pro- 
mote film and film processing is easily 
explained. First of all, the combination 
of the two account for almost 70% of the 
department’s sales. Second, the mar- 
gins on these items average close to 
25% and third, each roll of film usually 
generates three visits by the customer 
to the drug store—one to buy the film, 
another to drop it off for processing 
and a third to pick up the finished 
prints or slides. 

Film sales, the traditional backbone

accounted for 55% of all film sales, at 
$231 million. Color still film, including 
the big selection of fast-moving 35mm 
films, was the hottest item in the photo 
department, growing at a 15% rate

million, was the second most popular 
film sold last year and accounted for 
42% of all film sales. However, the 6.3% 
growth rate of instant films lagged be- 
hind the average growth of total film 
sales by almost five percentage points.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 29, 1985

Impulse sales propel candy category 


he ever prevalent sweet tooth of 

the American consumer, com- 

bined with strategic marketing in 
high-traffic areas of the store, helped 
chain drug candy departments exper'- 
ence a sugar-coated 1984. 

Department sales reached $891.6 
million last year, a 14% increase over 
1983, and accounted for 3.5% of total 
chain drug sales in 1984. 

Candy items including gums aver- 
aged about 5.5 turns, with gross mar- 
gins averaging 25% to 30%. 

During 1984, candy and gum was the 
most purchased category in drug 
stores, accounting for 7.7% of all cash 
register ring-ups. The category also 
averaged 17.1 sales per 100 customers, 
according to the 1984 POPAI-DuPent 
Drug Store Shoppers Study. 

The study also showed that candy 
and gum was fourth in a list of catego- 
ries most affected by in-store decision 
making. Shoppers made 75% of their 
decisions to buy candy or gum while in 
the store. Candy bars, rolls, small box- 
es and bagged candies were most pur- 
chased without prior planning. 

According to several candy buyers, 
drug stores promoted candy more in 
1984 than they have in the past several 
years, thanks mainly to the availability 
of generous co-op advertising dollars 
from major manufacturers. “Every 
flyer and ad we printed last year fea- 
tured some kind of candy,” says one 
Midwest buyer. 

That fact, plus the basic truth that 
Americans LOVE candy, consuming 
an average of more than 18 lb. per per- 
son last year, helped the candy depart- 
ments grow at a brisk rate. 


Buyers say that Halloween 1984 was 
a very strong candy holiday for them 
and that those seasonal sales alone ac- 
count for almost 10% of their depart- 
ments’ annual volume. 

Bagged candy, the most popular 
Halloween packaging, led all candy 
categories in growth this year with a 
15.1% increase over 1983. Sales of 
bagged candies came close to $340 mil- 
lion last year, accounting for 38.1% of 
all candy sales. 

Boxed candies, traditionally choco- 
lates, sell best during holiday seasons, 
with Christmas being the best, fol- 
lowed by Valentine’s Day and Easter. 

According to the Chocolate Manu- 
facturers’ Association, 60% of the con- 
fectionery products consumed each 
year in America are chocolates. 

With boxed chocolates selling well 
throughout the year, boxed candies ex- 
perienced a 13% increase for 1984. To- 
tal sales reached $175.5 million. 

Candy bars, a traditionally popular 
high-margin impulse item in the chain 
drug’s candy department, had a 
healthy sales year with a 14.2% in- 
crease over 1983. Accounting for near- 
ly 30% of all candy department reve- 
nue, candy bars had sales in excess of 
$266 million. 

Chewing gum sales, buoyed by stra- 
tegic placement for impulse sales and 
by the addition of Nutrasweet by sev- 
eral manufacturers, experienced a 
12% increase in sales during 1984, to 
reach $93.3 million. 

The perennial favorites, Wrigley and 
Warner Lambert, according to buy- 
ers, continue to dominate the chewing 
gum field.

lighter market by effective point-of- 
purchase merchandising. Disposable 
lighters are also highly promotable. 

The tobacco and tobacco products 
segment continues to be a viable area 
for many chains. Sales for those prod- 
ucts were up 8.6% to $144.4 million.

DIY growth lags 


he heyday of soaring sales for 
T chain drug DIY departments ap- 
pears to be waning. 

Out of the 14 departments broken 
down for this year’s annual report, the 
DIY department ranks 14th, showing 
the slowest growth rate and the small- 
est sales totals. 

The DIY department—consisting of 
hardware, automotive, paint and paint 
supplies—registered 1984 sales of $420 
million, a 6% growth over 1983. Actual 
dollar sales increased by $24.6 million. 
Batteries, a category included in this 
department in the past, are reflected 
this year in the general merchandise 
figures. 

The sluggish showing this depart- 
ment made, however, does not mean 
there are fewer do-it-yourselfers out 
there. What it basically means is that 
consumers have a greater variety of 
stores to shop for their DIY items, and 
specialty discount home and auto 
stores are taking some business away 
from drug stores. 

With that in mind, it’s no wonder 
that many drug chains have diversified 
into auto parts stores. Several chains 
including Perry, Fay’s, Rite Aid, Pay’n 
Save and Malone & Hyde now own 
their own auto parts stores. 

Within the DIY department, the 
automotive category, showed the most 
vitality last year by growing 8.5% to 
$169 million. Automotive sales account 
for 40.4% of all department revenue. 

According to retailers, drug store 
auto departments have continued to 
grow for several reasons. One, drug 
stores are convenient and usually stay 
open longer than auto parts stores, and 
two, the new consumer-oriented pack- 
aging that manufacturers have devel- 
oped has aided in drug store merchan- 
dising. 

One buyer points out that there 
seems to be “a lot more people out 


010 SHOT - 


frigera 


behind other depts. 


there trying to do the simpler fix-its 
themselves. People try to save a few 
dollars any way they can, and changing 
your own oil or spark plugs is one way 
of doing it.” 

As manufacturers change packaging 
to provide more self-service items, 
more drug stores are expanding the 
number of auite sku’s they carry. “We 
especially like the high margins on 
auto parts and accessories,” says the 
buyer. That margin averages 35%- 
45%. 

As a traffic draw, most drug stores 
use items such as windshield washer 
solvent and major brand motor oils. 
It’s not uncommon to see quarts of oil 
selling for less than $1 in chain drugs. 

The hardware category accounted 
for $188.4 million in sales last year, 
44.8% of the revenues of the total de- 
partment. Although hardware was the 
sales leader, it showed a slow growth 
rate of 5%. 

“Hardware will always be an impor- 
tant department in the drug store,” 
says Ron Davis, a buyer at Perry’s. 
“But we have to switch from hard hard- 
ware and complete lines to more im- 
pulse-type, general hardware.” 

Davis says people don’t expect to 
find high quality and top-of-the-line 
hardware items in drug stores, but 
they do expect to find packaged 
screws, nails and bolts, drapery hard- 
ware, faucet washers, light switches 
and other types of “handy man” items. 

Paint and paint supplies accounted 
for about 15% of the department’s 
business last year, with sales of $62 
million and a growth rate of 4%. 

Large buckets of paint, mostly gal- 
lon containers, are becoming quite 
scarce in drug stores. According to Da- 
vis, Perry is getting out of the big 
bucket paint business but will continue 
to carry smaller containers of popular 
colors and various types of spray paint.

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 29, 1985 


Games, robots lead 
as toy sales Qrow 


hanks to GoBots, Transformers, 
trivia games and Cabbage Patch 
Kids, chain drug store toy depart- 
ments experienced one of their healthi- 
est years ever in 1984. 

Toy department sales in chain drug 
stores grew by 18% last year, with re- 
tail sales totaling $671.5 million, while 
the toy industry as a whole grew by 
20%, with retail sales topping $12 bil- 
lion. 

Much of that healthy growth in chain 
drugs can be attributed to the aggres- 
sive buying and merchandising by the 
stores. Drug stores proved in 1984, 
that no matter the price point, a hot toy 
will sell in a drug store. 

Toy sales accounted for 2.6% of chain 
drug stores’ overall volume. 

Games, once again, were the sales 
leaders in the toy department with to- 
tal sales of $118.8 million, an increase 
of 15.9% over the 1983 sales figures. 
The higher priced trivia games were 
the stars of the department, helping 
games account for 17.7% of all toys 
sold. 

One of the other hot toy categories of 
1984, the transforming robots, were 
mostly pegged, thus helping this area 
show an increase of 15.8%, with sales 
at $97.9 million. Tonka’s GoBots and 
Hasbro’s Transformers were the vic- 
tors, with no less than 10 lower-priced, 
mainly imported copycats doing well 
when the big two became scarce prior 
to Christmas. 

As drug store toy buyers expanded 
their departments, both in unit count 
and with higher priced, nationally pro- 


moted items, more boxed items found 
their way to the toy department 
shelves. In 1984, sales of boxed toys in- 
creased by 14%, compared with a 5.8% 
growth in 1983. Boxed items account- 
ed for $82.9 million in sales, 12.3% of 
the total sales of the toy department. 

Toy cars and trucks, always fast 
movers in the chain drug mix, regis- 
tered a 12% increase to $88.8 million, 
and accounted for 13.2% of toy depart- 
ment sales. 

Doll sales, thanks to Cabbage Patch 
and the ever popular Barbie, grew 
stronger than the department itself in 
1984 with a 14.9% growth rate. Dolls 
brought in $53 million in sales. 

Plush toys, led by Kenner’s Care 
Bear family, experienced sales of $52.4 
million, a 12.5% increase over 1983. 

Although becoming more popular 
with the consumer, educational and 
preschool toys, on the whole, grew at a 
slower rate than the total toy depart- 
ment last year. The 11.8% increase 
represented total sales of $52.4 million. 

People turned elsewhere to buy hob- 
by and craft kits and supplies during 
1984, and in turn, this category proved 
to be the slowest in growth at 9.6%. To- 
tal sales reached $41 million. 

One has-been category in the drug 
store toy department is electronic and 
video games. After several years of 
phenomenal growth, last year’s sales 
totals barely showed up on the charts. 
This category has been included in this 
year’s miscellaneous listing. 

Seasonal toy and game sales figures 
are also included in miscellaneous.

PRODUCTS 


eneral merchandise sales in 
chain drug stores rose 8.1% 
last year to $1.3 billion. 

The increase would have been sub- 
stantially higher had it not been for a 
slowdown in general merchandise 
sales during the fourth quarter. A 
number of chains reported that sales 
during the holiday period, traditional- 
ly the strongest for general merchan- 
dise, were not nearly as robust as the 
previous year. 

However, drug chains still regis- 
tered healthy increases in a number of 
general merchandise categories, in- 
cluding home electronics, watches and 
sunglasses. 

Sunglasses, in fact, were the biggest 
winner in the general merchandise de- 
partment last year. Sales jumped 
10.1% to $173.6 million. 

The gains in the sunglass category 
were particularly impressive in light of 
the fact that discounters and super- 
markets have gone after this market 
much more aggressively in recent 
years. 

Retailers said the high degree of 
consumer confidence in the economy 
earlier in the year and an influx of new 
styles on the market drove up sunglass 
sales, which accounted for 13% of the 
department’s total volume. 

The category leader in dollar sales 
did not fare as well. Personal care ap- 
pliance sales slipped during the Christ- 
mas quarter. Sales for the year were up 
7.1% to $217.6 million. 

However, things could have been 
worse. Retailers credited an aggres- 
sive rebate program from several man- 
ufacturers for sparking sales of hair 


dryers, curling irons and electric shav- 
ers. 

Watch sales registered a healthy 
9.2% increase in sales to $97.5 million. 
Gains were posted both in the low-end 
and high-end watches. 

Despite near-saturation in the per- 
sonal stereo market, drug retailers 
still benefited from a 9.1% increase in 
the home electronics category. Sales 
climbed to $89.9 million. 

Personal stereos last year finally 
showed signs of peaking after several 
consecutive years of double-digit sales 
gains. However, the “boom-box” radi- 
os continued to be hot sellers in many 
chains during 1984. 


Several chains, including Begley 


Drug, Pay Less NW, Pay ’n Save and 
Page Drug, carried video cassette re- 
corders—last year’s biggest-selling 
home electronic product. Industry- 
wide unit sales of video cassette re- 
corders in 1984 were up nearly 80% 
from the previous year. 

Batteries generated a steady 7.4% 
increase in sales last year with sales in 
chain drug stores closing in on the $150 
million mark. 

In addition to producing some of the 
highest sales per square foot in drug 
stores, batteries also are among the 
most profitable products in the chain 
drug mix. 

Another leading performer in the 
general merchandise category last 
year was the pantyhose/soft goods seg- 
ment. Pantyhose sales climbed 9.4% to 
$189.3 million. Drug stores have 
carved a substantial share of the panty- 
hose market by offering women low 
prices and convenience.
