Walgreens plans expansion drive for’ 85 


DEERFIELD, Ill. — Walgreens, 
which opened its 1,000th store last 
year, plans to continue its aggressive 
expansion drive in 1985. 

The company is opening another 100 
drug stores this year compared to 72 
last year. For 1984, Walgreens report- 
ed that comparable store sales (sales 
for all stores opened at least a full year) 
were up 11.2%. 

Pharmacy sales are still continuing 
to grow dramatically. Prescriptions, 
which currently account for 19% of all 
Walgreens’ drug store sales, increased 
a vibrant 22.8% in 1984, leading all oth- 
er categories. 

Much of the chain’s 1985 unit growth 
is being planned for what chairman and 
ceo Charles “Corky” Walgreen calls 
the “booming” states of California, 
Florida and Texas. 

Walgreens plans to add 10 more 
stores to the 44 now in California’s Bay 
Area including 19 in San Francisco. In 
Texas, where Walgreens already has 
164 stores including 107 in Houston, 24 
stores will be added, and in Florida, 
where Walgreens has 144 stores, 50 
new stores will be opened. 

This year, Walgreens will also re- 
model 70 stores while refurbishing an- 
other 200. 

In recent years, Walgreens has been 
filling in those major markets where 
the company has either a No. 1 or No. 2 
market share. Currently there are 
only five markets—about 10% of Wal- 
greens’ total market arenas—where 
the company’s stores don’t command 
first or second position. 

“Our. expansion strategy remains 
one of cptimum penetration,” Wal- 
green says. “California will be one oi 
the hottest retail markets in the Unit- 
ed States for the rest of the 80’s, and 
Texas will grow 32% through the year 
2000.” 

Florida, he points out, is expected to 
pick up 300,000 new residents in 1985 
alone. 

In other areas, Walgreens is ex- 
panding its merchandise mix to em- 
brace more high-margin “consumable 


categories” like video tapes, computer 
discs, computer paper, convenience 
foods and photo processing. 

The new technology lines like com- 
puter discs and video accessories are 
seen as good “growth businesses” by 
Fred Canning, the chain’s president. 

“Accessory business,” says Can- 
ning, “is all plus business. Much of this 
business didn’t even exist five years 
ago. Today 20% of all American house- 
holds have VCRs and personal com- 
puter sales are up by 50%.” 

Canning stresses that Walgreens is 
not planning to sell hardware, but 
rather the more consumable accesso- 
ries. Blank video tapes, computer 
discs and papers “are the consumables 
of the 80’s,” he says. 

Walgreens is also aggressively ex- 
panding its consumable convenience 
foods departments. Another 40 “full- 
selection” convenience food depart- 
ments will be added this year. Wal- 
greens projects a t ital of 153 “full-size” 
convenience food departments by next 
year. In addition, many Walgreens’ 
stores also sport limited lines of conve- 
nience and frozen prepared foods. 

“We’re building up consumable cate- 
gories with the goal of increasing our 
customers’ trips to Walgreens,” 
Canning. 

“We want to draw them into the 
store, not only for toothpaste and aspl- 


Says 


rin, but also for midweek purchases of 


milk, bread or tomato soup. 

In the area of retail store diversifica- 
tions, Walgreens will add another two 
home health care stores in 1985. The 
company currently operates three 
such stores, all in the Chicago market. 

The company will also add another 
10 Wags freestanding restaurants fora 
year-end total of 73. 

Canning says the plan is to expand 
the home health care stores 
finding our niche in this growing mar- 
ket.” He says the restaurants, too, will 
continue to grow “cautiously,” but he 
adds that it won’t be too long before 
Walgreens plans to enter some new 
markets with its Wags.

Eckerd bolsters 


CLEARWATER — Eckerd’s chair- 
man and president Stewart Turley 
calls 1984 “a year for significant im- 
provements for the company.” 

For the corporation as a whole, sales 
rose 13% to $2.62 billion during the 
year ended July 1984, while net profits 
increased 19% to $85.4 million. 

The drug-store division, which ac- 
counts for about 86% of corporate 
sales, generated a 12% sales gain for 
year-end sales of $2.2 billion. At the 
same time, operating profits for the di- 
vision surged ahead a lusty 23.5%, 
helping to offset losses at Eckerd’s 
American Home Video division as well 
as an earnings decline in the JByrons 
department store division. 

In setting strategy for 1985, Turley 
said that the corporation would try to 
strengthen the JByrons division by 
opening fewer new stores and by put- 
ting a stronger emphasis on the opera- 
tions in existing stores. He also pre- 
dicted that American Home Video, 
which has consistently operated at a 
loss, would show its first operating 
profit this year. The ceo has since re- 
vised that prediction to break even at 
best for the troubled chain of video 
stores. 

In the drug division, the company 
rebounded after two years of de- 
pressed sales and earnings by activat- 
ing a number of merchandising and op- 
erational strategies, including: 
® consolidating buying and all mer- 
chandising groups into the company’s 
headquarters in Clearwater; 
®@ grouping the company’s six drug di- 
visions under two executive vps as a 
first step in “nationalizing” the compa- 
ny; 

@ stepping up Eckerd’s image and vis- 
ibility as a health-care provider by in- 
creasing the number of ads and promo- 
tional programs stressing the 
pharmacy and the preservation of good 
health; 

® experimenting with new store de- 
signs and new layouts developed to im- 
prove merchandise presentation and 
shopping convenience; 


operating strategy 


® expanding the installation of phar- 
macy terminals to the point where 
about 900 stores, or 59% of the divi- 
sion, will have Rx terminals by the end 
of fiscal 1985 in July. 

® installing computerized point-of- 
sale registers in select stores to moni- 
tor transactions and inventory status, 
and 

® opening another 216,000-sq.-ft. dis- 
tribution center in Hammond, La. 

Earlier this year, president Harry 
Lambert consolidated the company’s 
13 division offices into eight district of- 
fices, and at the same time, redefined 
the responsibilities of Eckerd’s divi- 
sion managers. 

To make it possible for desk-bound 
division managers to liberate them- 
selves from paperwork and get into the 
field where the action is, Lambert re- 
lieved them of distribution and ac- 
counting responsibilities. 

Those responsibilities were trans- 
ferred to Curt Neel, Eckerd’s vp of dis- 
tribution for operations services, 
whom Lambert describes as the com- 
pany’s “distribution expert.” 

Freed from their distribution and 
accounting responsibilities, the divi- 
sion managers would now be able to 
concentrate more effectively on store 
sales and store operations, Lambert 
said. 

“Our strongest guys are at the divi- 
sion level,” he said, “and they felt, as 
we did, that they weren’t spending 
enough time in the field.” 

Under Eckerd’s old system, the dis- 
trict managers reported to Neel on a 
dotted line basis. According to Lam- 
bert, the system was similar to “oper- 
ating more like a regional chain.” 

Before, the distribution center could 
only service the stores in its region. 
Under the new system, Lambert says 
the distribution end of Eckerd’s busi- 
ness will be run more like a national 
chain. 

“If it’s cheaper for us to ship a store 
in North Carolina from Atlanta,” he 
said, “we'll ship from Atlanta. We’re 
going for the operational efficiencies

LOS ANGELES — For years 
Thrifty played catch-up. They were 
late in weaning away from service cos- 
metics; late in switching to self-service 
liquor and promotional foods. And 
they were testing two pharmacy ter- 
minal systems in a handful of stores 
long after Pay Less NW, Pay ’n Save 
and Longs were installing them chain- 
wide. 

But those days are faded memories 
because today’s Thrifty is a rejuvenat- 


are 


Thrifty sales up 9.4%

as Thrifty takes lead 


ed giant—from its Perfecto prototype 
to diversification into discount book 
and auto supply stores. 

And now the latest thrust forward: a 
$60 million in-store computer system 
being tested in the Los Angeles area. 
The system has five major compo- 
nents: POS registers, direct store de- 
livery, store inventory management, 
energy management and labor sched- 
uling. 

Thrifty is also beefing up its support 
systems. The corporation will add 35,- 
000 sq. ft. of mezzanine space to its 
400,000-sq.-ft. Anaheim distribution 
center and will install $1 million in new 
equipment. In addition, the chain will 
spend $2.5 million to open a new 20,- 
000-sq.-ft. film processing plant in 
northern California. The new plant 
will enable Thrifty to increase its film 
processing volume 250% in five years. 

The support systems will dovetail 
into Thrifty’s expansion program, 
which will see 25 new stores go on- 
stream in fiscal 1985. This is the larg- 
est number of new stores since 1976. 

The engine powering the revitalized 
Thrifty machine is its fiscal perfor- 
mance. For the 55th consecutive year, 
sales increased, and for the 30th con- 
secutive year, same-store sales (ex- 
cluding those opened during the past 
two years) have increased over the pri- 
or year. Also, it is the 28th year out of

Thrifty sales were $1.3 billion; net in-

The only dark cloud in Thrifty’s 
golden lining is Trak Auto West, 
owned 50% by Thrifty and 50% by the 
Dart Group of Landover, Md. 

As of May 1984, Thrifty was losing

that Trak is running one year behind 
expectations.

have 70-80 in operation by August 
1985, with a total of 90-100 by Decem-

Thrifty is expected to open more Giant

The chain continues its drug store

Record sales, earnings for Shoppers 


TORONTO — Although faced with 
increased competition throughout 
many of its operating regions in Cana- 
da, Shoppers Drug Mart is closing in 
on another year of record sales and 
earnings. 

Through the first nine months of its 
fiscal year, Canada’s largest drug 
chain generated systemwide sales of 
$1.1 billion (Canadian), up 12.3% from 
the $978.7 million the previous year. 
Operating income for the three-quar- 
ter period was up 14% to $29.6 million 
from $25.9 million the previous year. 

Revenues during that period, which 
includes franchise fees and other in- 
come but excludes sales by Shoppers 
stores, grew 11.7% to $52.5 million 
from $47 million. 

Shoppers’ performance this year, 
coupled with the strong gains posted 
by its sister chain in the U.S., Peoples 
Drug Stores, contributed heavily to 
the substantial increases in sales, rev- 
enues and earnings at the parent com- 
pany, Imasco Ltd. 

However, Shoppers’ fast-paced 
growth is no longer a given. Competi- 
tion from food/drug combo operators 
and high-volume deep discounters is a 
serious concern for chain officials. 

Shoppers’ stores in western Canada 
in particular have been plagued by the 


Shoppers Drug Mart 
nine-month sales* 


“Canadian dollars in millions 
Source: Company reports 


incursion of food/drug stores, which 
company officials acknowledge has 
heightened price competition and af- 
fected the bottom line in that region. 
Elsewhere, other Shoppers stores 
have had to deal with the invasion of 
the deep-discount format. Although 
deep discounters have not posed as 
great a problem in Canada as they 
have in many large U.S markets, the 


sprawling off-price stores are expect- 
ed to garner a larger share of the busi- 
ness over the next year. 

Shoppers has been quicker to react 
to the deep-discount threat than many 
of its U.S. counterparts. The 442-unit 
chain has followed the rise of the deep 
discounters in the U.S. for some time 
and one year ago opened its first true 
deep-discount store in Toronto. 

Dubbed Howie’s, the store has been 
a major success for Shoppers. Some 
chain officials predict that the store 
could generate $10 million in sales dur- 
ing its second year of operation. 

In March, Shoppers opened its sec- 
ond Howie’s in Toronto. The store also 
marked the chain’s first test of point- 
of-purchase scanning equipment. 

Earlier this month, Shoppers’ Phar- 
maprix division planned to open its 
first deep-discount drug store in Mon- 
treal called Pharmaprix Carnaval. A 
second Carnaval store also is slated to 
open this spring in Montreal. 

In addition, Shoppers plans to roll 
out the deep-discount format in other 
Canadian cities, including Winnipeg, 
Manitoba and Windsor, Ontario, later 
this summer. 

Two notable events occurred this 
year within Shoppers’ U.S. opera- 
tions. Shoppers pulled out of Seattle- 


Tacoma after it was unable to pene- 
trate the markets. 

In the chain’s Florida division, the 
news was more upbeat. Shoppers 
opened its first new store in the state in 
nearly four years. The opening of the 
31st store in Florida took place as the 
chain’s Florida division turned profit- 
able for the first time since Shoppers 
entered the state in 1974.

SupeRx momentum continues into 1985 


CINCINNATI — SupeRx, the 25- 
year-old, 621-drug store division of the 
Kroger Company, continued to devel- 
op into a strong regional drug retailer 
in 1984. 

The chain, after a soft first six 
months, rebounded and showed sales 
of $859.5 million for the year ended 
Dec. 29, an 8.8% increase over the pre- 
vious year’s sales of $789.6 million. 

Pretax operating profits grew 4.4% 
to $28.4 million, from fiscal 1983's 
$27.2 million. However, company offi- 
cials pointed out that the 1984 results 
included a $5.5 million pretax LIFO 
charge. 

SupeRx used the FIFO method in 
1983 and would have shown greater 
operating profits in 1984 had it not 
switched to LIFO. 

SupeRx’s parent, the Kroger Com- 
pany, reported its sales showed in-

Adams: Paniry Pride's surprise buy 


PAWTUCKET, R.I. — The acqui- 
sition of Adams Drug in November by 
Pantry Pride Inc. took many industry 
observers by surprise. 

Pantry Pride, a struggling super- 
market chain, emerged from Chapter 
11 bankruptcy proceedings three 
years ago considerably smaller and its 
future very much in doubt. It had re- 
treated from the New York and mid- 
Atlantic markets to concentrate its ef- 
forts primarily in the Sunbelt states of 
Florida and Georgia. 

The $100 million purchase of the 
New England-based Adams Drug 
seemed a strange fit. But clearly, Pan- 
try Pride’s strategy was to diversify 
into the mainstream of retailing. 

The company is currently negotiat- 
ing the sale of its 44-store Jacksonville, 
Fla., division, which would leave Pan- 
try Pride with only 36 supermarkets. 
And there is some speculation that the 
company is looking to abandon the su- 
permarket business entirely. 

Armed with sizable tax-loss carry- 
forwards from the bankruptcy pro- 
ceedings, Pantry Pride earlier in the 
year paid $82 million for Devon Stores, 
a chain of general merchandise stores 
that operate near military bases. 

Adams was an attractive property 
for Pantry Pride. The chain operates 
443 drug and health & beauty aids 
stores in Massachusetts, Rhode Is- 
land, Pennsylvania and New York. 

Through the first nine months of the 


fiscal year, sales increased 9.1% to 


$239 million from $219 million the pre- 
vious year. Net earnings were down 
19.6% to $2.05 million from $2.5 million 
in 1983. 

Pantry Pride said that if Adams had 
continued to finish out its fiscal year, 
the chain would have posted a 16.5% 
increase in sales to $332.1 million and a 
12% increase in net income to $18.5 
million. 

During the year, Adams consolidat- 
ed more of its stores under the Brooks 
name. The chain also accelerated the 
conversion of its health & beauty aids 
stores to full-service pharmacies. At 
the close of 1984, more than 70% of its 
stores contained pharmacies. 

In 1985, Adams plans to open ap- 
proximately 25 new stores. The chain 
also has slated 40 to 50 stores for re- 
modeling. An additional 20 health & 
beauty aids stores will be converted to 
pharmacy units this year as well. 

When the Salmanson family an- 
nounced their intentions to sell the 
drug chain, there was some specula- 
tion that another drug retailer would 
emerge as a Suitor, possibly signaling a 
change in management at the 52-year- 
old chain. 

However, Pantry Pride’s decision to 
purchase the chain has solidified the 
positions of several leading executives 
at Adams. 

New posts 

Earlier this year, Pantry Pride 
named James Salmanson, formerly ex- 
ecutive vp, to the post of vice chair-

Thrift cuts costs, 


remodels 27 units 


PITTSBURGH — Record sales and 
improved control over operating ex- 
penses combined to give Thrift Drug 
its highest profits ever in 1984. 

The J. C. Penney subsidiary 
showed a yearly sales figure of $591 
million, up 11% from $532 million in 
1983. The same-store increase was 
9.9%. 

Thrift Drug, also operating as Trea- 
sury Drug Centers, was operating 373 
stores in 20 states at year’s end. Dur- 
ing the year the company opened 16 
drug stores and closed six. In 1985, 20 
new stores are scheduled to open. 

Continuing its plan to upgrade exist- 
ing stores, the company remodeled 27 
units during the year, and plans to do 
the same with 25 stores in 1985. 

A typical Thrift, or Treasury, drug 
store is an 8,500-sq.-ft. unit averaging 
about $1.7 million in sales per year. 

The company’s annual sales per 
square foot was $180 in 1984. 

During the year, about 83% of the 
company’s total volume was handled 
through its three distribution centers. 
Overall, at year’s end, space in the 
warehouse distribution centers to- 
taled 781,000 sq. ft. 


The company dispensed 17.2 million 
prescriptions in 1984, an increase of 
16% over 1983. Thrift, one of the lead- 
ers in pharmacy computerization, had 
346 of 373 Thrift and Treasury stores 
equipped with terminals at year-end. 
Prescriptions accounted for 34% of 
Thrift’s total sales, the same as in 1983. 

Substantial growth also occurred in 
Thrift’s mail-order pharmacy busi- 
ness. During the year, this segment of 
the company teamed up with several 
major industrial companies to provide 
low-cost mail-order scripts to employ- 
ees of those companies. 

“The nature of this business is high 
volume,” a spokesman added. 

Two officials of the Pittsburgh- 
based Thrift Drug stores were also 
busy this year organizing chain drug 
store support to help save the Pitts- 
burgh School of Pharmacy. 

The school, experiencing financial 
difficulties, was in danger of closing its 
doors until Donald Bell, vp public af- 
fairs, and Francis Marasco, vp person- 
nel, stepped in to help. 

“The pharmacy school at Pitt is very 
important to the profession,” said Bell. 
“Most of the major chains depend on

which accelerated markdown and pro- 
motional activity. 


DRUG STORE NEWS, April 29, 1985 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — After 
reaching the climactic $2 billion sales 
nark during fiscal 1984, Revco D.S. 
seemed on the threshold of even great- 
2r growth in sales and earnings via ex- 
pansion of its drug stores and carefully 
salculated diversification moves. In- 
stead, the company that operates more 
jrug stores than any other drug chain 
in the U.S. stumbled. 

Through the first three quarters of 
the year, ended Feb. 9, 1985, net in- 
come plunged 33% to $42 million, or 
$1.14 a share, from $63 million, or 
$1.71 a share the previous year. Sales 
for the first three quarters of the year 
were up 9% to $1.64 billion from $1.5 
billion the previous year. However, 
when measured on a same-store basis, 
sales were up an anemic 5.6%. 

How did things turn from good to 
bad so fast? While no one factor was 
wholly responsible for Revco’s star- 
tling downturn, its fourth-quarter ac- 
quisition of Odd Lot Trading has been 
the biggest thorn in Revco’s side. 

After more than two years of joint 
ventures with Odd Lot, Revco in April 
purchased the close-out retailer and

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 29, 1985 


SALT LAKE CITY — Fiscal 1984 
was a year of dramatic consolidation 
for American Stores’ retail drug store 
subsidiaries. 

In addition to divesting itself of the 
134-unit Rea and Derick drug chain in 
mid-November, American also began 
taking steps to integrate its three re- 
maining drug store subsidiaries, Osco, 
Sav-On and Skaggs, into one unified 
division. 

American is in the process of con- 
verting all of its 108 Skaggs stores into 
Oscos. A few Sav-Ons have also been 
converted to Osco, but a company 
spokesman said a final decision on the 
remaining 176 Sav-On’s would not be 
made until the end of fiscal 1986. 

The Sav-On name is well established 
in southern California where the 
stores are concentrated, and Ameri- 
can must weigh the advantages of es- 
tablishing a common identity and a 
shared logo against the disadvantages 
of relinquishing an established name in 
a highly concentrated market. 

With 530 drug stores in 30 states, 
American could build a strong regional 
identity for its drug stores if it opted to 
go with a common name and format. 

There would be enormous savings 
from reduced overhead, plus the com- 
pany could eliminate many services 
now duplicated in the divisions. It 
would also be more efficient and cost 
effective to advertise for one company 


rather than two. 

The California stores as they are 
now run, however, are responsive to 
regional preferences and demographic 
trends. If the Sav-On stores were run 
as clones of Osco, they would inevita- 
bly lose some of their flexibility and re- 
sponsiveness. It would be much harder 
to create a merchandise mix that 
would work as effectively in California 
as it might in Chicago Osco’s headquar- 
ters or Salt Lake City, where Ameri- 
can’s corporate headquarters are lo- 
cated. 

Also, Sav-On is currently in the 
hands of relatively new management. 
Dick George, who heads the Osco sub- 
sidiary, was recently named president 
of the Sav-On subsidiary too. George 
replaces Sam Parker, who left the 
company last month. 

Sav-On also has a new vp of distribu- 
tion, Ed McManus, who is doing dou- 
ble duty as director of warehouse oper- 
ations; a new vp of marketing, Larry 
LaRock, who had been president of the 
Rea and Derick division, which was 
sold to People’s Drug last year, and 
there are two men, Ross Coon and Dan 
Ramirez, pharmacy buyers/supervi- 
sors, who were just promoted to share 
the responsibility of the office of vp of 
professional services. 

The new team will be trying to cen- 
tralize the Sav-On purchasing and 
computer systems plus identify and

At Skaggs, sources expect George

Like the managers of Longs stores,

When American acquired Osco

245 combos 

In addition to Osco, American’s 
strongest vehicle for drug store retail- 
ing is its chain of 245 food/drug combi- 
nation stores. 


The combination stores, which are 
operated under the names Skaggs/Al- 
pha Beta, Jewel/Osco and Buttery 
Food and Drug, are estimated to do 
somewhere between $4.9 billion and 
$6.3 billion a year in sales. Sources es- 
timate that anywhere from 25% to 35% 
of that business comes from sales of 
drug store-related products like phar- 
maceuticals, over-the-counter drugs, 
health & beauty aids and sundries and 
other general merchandise. 

The combination stores are expect- 
ed to be American’s major growth ve- 
hicle from now until at least the end of 
the decade. 

The company is also continuing to 
beef up its drug store-related products 
in its regular and super food stores. 
Currently there are a total of 731 food 
stores in the company operating under 
the various names of Acme, Alpha 
Beta, Buttery, Jewel and Star Mar- 
kets. 

American does not break down its 
sales volumes by division, but sources 
familiar with the company estimate 
that the 245 combination stores are do- 
ing nearly three times the annual dol- 
lar volume of the 530 traditional and 
superdrug stores and nearly twice the 
volume of the 731 food stores. 

For fiscal 1985 ended Feb. 2, Ameri- 
can generated sales of $12.1 billion and 
net earnings of $185.5 million.

RICHMOND — The Begley Drug 
Company ended its first three quar- 
ters of fiscal 1984 with sales 8% ahead 
of the same three quarters of 1983. 

Sales for the first nine months of the 
company’s year climbed to $50.1 mil- 
lion, up from last year’s $46.5 million. 

However, the sales increases were 
accompanied by an 11.7% drop in net 
income, from $726,000 last year to 
$641,000 for fiscal 1984. 

Making a turnaround from a poor 
second quarter, Begley showed sales 
for the three months ended Dec. 31, 
1984, at $19.1 million, compared to 
$17.6 million for the same period last 
year, an increase of almost 9%. 

Sales that fell short of projections in 
December are being blamed for the 4% 
decrease in the third quarter’s net in- 
come. 

The company explained that net in- 
come before taxes was slightly ahead 
of the figure recorded for the same 
quarter last year. Net income after 
taxes, however, was marginally lower 


than it’was for the same period last 


year because the company did not have 
the quantity of tax credits available to 
it that it had in the previous year’s 
quarter. 

Officials expect sales during the 
fourth quarter to come close to projec- 
tions with profits above those of last 
year. 

In fiscal 1983, the company earned 


$733,460 on total corporate sales of 
$61.5 million.

cludes the 123 Big B, Key and Superior 
dry cleaning stores in niné. states:

tributor of dry cleaning equipment and 
supplies, and Convenience Manufac-

Sales top $20M for Genovese 60th 


MELVILLE, N.Y. — The 76-store 
Genovese Drug chain celebrated its 
60th anniversary last year with a vari- 
ety of events and promotions. The 
chain also topped $20 million in sales 
for the first time. 

Sales for the company’s fiscal year 
grew to $220.3 million from the previ- 
ous year’s $193.7 million, a 13.7% in- 
crease. Profits showed a 7.2% increase 
during the year to $4.1 million, or $1.03 
a share, up from $3.9 million and 96¢ a 
share in fiscal 1983. 


Sales top $200 million mark 


For the fourth quarter, which ended 
Feb. 1, 1985, sales grew 4% to $56.8 
million while earnings decreased about 
1.5% from last year’s same quarter. 

“Overall, we had a strong year in 
1984,” says Don Gross, vp marketing 
and distribution. “But sales toward the 
latter part of the year were not as 
strong as we had anticipated.” 

Gross attributes those slow sales to 
the chain’s growing competition, 
which he describes as “getting tougher 
and tougher.” 

He points out that Genovese’s major 
competitors in the areas it serves, 
New York, Connecticut, New Jersey 
and Massachusetts, are the big super- 
market chains, especially Pathmark. 

“Strong competition is putting a 
tough squeeze on every retailer’s bot- 
tom line,” adds Gross. “And it’s going 
to be the same in 1985. This year is go- 
ing to really test the mettle of the re- 
tailer.” 

During 1984, Genovese opened four 
new stores, and since Jan. 1, has added 
two more. Gross says plans for the 
year include opening eight to 10 more 
stores in the markets in which the com-

Fay’s fares well despite competition 


LIVERPOOL, N.Y. — Despite a 
decline in fourth-quarter net earnings, 
Fay’s Drug Co. achieved record finan- 
cial results for the year ended Jan. 31. 

Sales for the year increased 17% to 
$367 million from $312 million in the 
previous fiscal year, while earnings 
rose 7% to $8.7 million, or 62¢ a share, 
from $8.1 million, or 60¢ a share. 

In the fourth quarter, however, 
earnings dipped to $3.3 million, or 24¢ 
a share, from $3.8 million, or 27¢ a 
share, in the same year-earlier period. 
Sales, meanwhile, increased 19% to 
$109 million from $92 million. 

Chairman Henry A. Panasci, while 
calling the year’s performance “re- 
warding,” noted that sales did not 
meet earlier expectations. 

“The last six months of the fiscal 
year,” Panasci said, “saw a very com- 
petitive retailing environment, which 
resulted in a slowdown in sales of gen- 
eral merchandise and increased pro- 
motion and advertising expenditures 
necessary to achieve the revenue re- 
sults that were obtained. 

“Additional promotions resulted in 
lower gross margins as a result of 
markdowns required to maintain a bal- 
anced inventory position.” 

Panasci said the competitive envi- 
ronment remained heated during the 
early part of the new fiscal year, and he 
anticipated “constrained results” 
through July. 

Although overall gains in the second 
half were muted, Panasci noted that 
the company’s “most important core 
category,” prescriptions, increased in 
sales by 29% for the year, “far surpass- 
ing national averages.” In contrast, 
chain drug prescription sales in- 
creased 13% in 1984. 

Panasci also noted that Fay’s 
achieved its store opening goal with 17 
new super discount drug units, three 
bantam drug stores and three special- 
ty stores, including the first discount 
auto parts store and the first office 
supply store. 

Panasci also pointed out that open- 
ing expenses for the new specialty 
stores had contributed to the “disap- 
pointing” fourth quarter earnings.

Expansion nets record year for Longs 


WALNUT CREEK, Calif. — 
Longs Drug Stores ended fiscal 1985 
with record sales and earnings, as well 
as a sharply increased store count. The 
indications are for more of the same 
this year. 

For the 53-week year ended Jan. 26, 
earnings were up 10% to $40.1 million, 
or $3.77 a share, from $36.4 million, or 
$3.43 a share, in the previous 52-week 
year. Sales for the year increased 
13.3% to $1.38 billion from $1.21 bil- 
lion. 

During the year, Longs opened 13 
new stores, sharply higher than the 
seven opening during the previous 
year. The company plans an even more 
aggressive expansion schedule this 
year, with 16 stores slated to open 
their doors. 

Part of that expansion includes a 
new market—Colorado—which the 
chain has targeted as a natural growth 
area because of its rapidly growing 
economy, its large and diverse labor 
pool and heavy home building activity. 

“Some of the fastest growing cities 
are in Colorado, and it appears that 
growth can be sustained,” said Robert 
M. Long, president and ceo of the 191- 
store chain. 

“When we add all of these plusses up 
and add the fact that we know we can 
compete in the Colorado market, we 
are anxious to begin serving customers 
in the Rocky Mountain State,” Long 
said. 


Long’s Colorado venture is being fo- 


cused on cities surrounding Denver, 
including Colorado Springs and Fort 
Collins, but not on the Mile-High City 
itself. Analysts say the strategy is to 


avoid Denver, where Eckerd and Pay 
Less both foundered, until Longs can 
establish a strong beachhead. 

The company’s strongest expansion, 
however, is taking place in its home 
state of California, and the reason is 
the state’s tremendous population 
growth. From 1970 to 1980, <3 exam- 
ple, California’s share of the U.S. pop- 
ulation grew by 16%. 

With an aggressive expansion 
schedule on the drawing boards 
Longs last year made several key man- 
agement changes designed to increase 


the overall effectiveness of merchan- 
dising, distribution and sales develop- 
ment and, at the same time, to identify 
potential new opportunities for 
branching out. 

Steve Roath, who had been vp of 
professional affairs, was named senior 
vp of marketing, and Ron Plomgren, 
vp of properties, became senior vp of 
development. 

The moves were seen as an effort to 
introduce more coordination into 
Longs’ decentralized approach to re- 
tailing. 

Photo processing is one area in 
which a coordinated approach was 
used to ensure more consistency 
throughout the chain. During the year, 
the company launched “Longs 
Photoworld.” Executive vp Richard 
A. Scott said that with the new chain- 
wide photo processing system, “cus- 
tomers can expect greater consistency 
in the products and services which are 
offered in every Longs store.’ 

The chain has also taken a more co- 
ordinated approach to what it calls its 
“redistribution” system. While Longs

DRUG STORE NEWS, April 29, 1985 


Owner Trump may trim Pay ’n Save 


SEATTLE — What a difference a 
vear makes! 

In fiscal 1984 (ended Jan. 28, 1984), 
Pay ’n Save had dramatically rebound- 
ed from two years of severe recession 
in the Pacific Northwest to boost net 
earnings 54% on a sales increase of 
12%. 

Pay ’n Save’s fortunes appeared to 
be on a rising continuum with two sub- 
sequent acquisitions: Schuck’s, the 
Northwest’s leading auto supply 
chain, with a profit-to-sales ratio dou- 
ble that of Pay ’n Save, and North- 
western Drug, which added $130 mil- 
lion in volume and a state-of-the-art 
distribution center. 

Then the clouds began to gather. 
The harbinger was the profit plunge of 
64% in the first fiscal quarter of 1985. 

The main source of the trouble was 
Ernst Home Centers. In an attempt to 
turn Ernst around, the stores were re- 
merchandised, with sporting goods be- 
ing phased out and new emphasis 
placed on DIY categories such as lum- 
ber, hardware, electrical, paint, 
doors, windows and plumbing. How- 
ever, the elimination of sporting goods 
necessitated markdowns, and to re- 
coup them, Ernst went to aggressive 
pricing on other lines, thereby reduc- 
ing margins. 

In addition, Ernst faced a firestorm 
of competition from Pay ’n Pak, opera- 
tors of more than 100 home centers in 
six western states. Early in 1983, Pay 
’n Pak dropped sporting goods and 
auto supplies and beefed up paint and 
hardware, thereby tightening the 
crunch. 

Not long after Pay ’n Save’s second 
quarter profits were announced (an- 
other decrease of 64%), came the offer 
from The Trump Group, a New York 
investment firm, for a leveraged buy- 
out. After a skirmish with Samuel 
Stroum and Stuart Sloan (former own- 
ers of Schuck’s who were Pay ’n Save’s 
largest shareholders), Trump bought 
Pay ’n Save. 

Inasmuch as Pay ’n Save is now a pri- 
vate corporation, sales and profits for 
the last two quarters of fiscal 1985 
have not been revealed. However, 


Pay ’n Save store count dips 


Includes Pay 'n Save and Bi-Mart 
Source: Company reports 


best estimates are that profits were 
down 75% to 80% in the second half, 
and that sales increased 8% to 10%. 
This contrasts with increased sales of 
18% and 14% for the first two quarters. 

Julius Trump, one of the principals 
of The Trump Group, has restructured 
the responsibilities of Pay ’n Save’s ex- 
ecutives so that Trump has more direct 
control of the operation. 

Meanwhile, problems remain. With 
high start-up costs and $30 million in 
volume needed to break even, Price 
Savers Membership Warehouse is in 
the red. 

Northwestern Drug’s basic prob- 
lems were engendered by the circum- 
stances of its acquisition by Pay ’n 
Save. That is, when a retail drug chain 
acquires a wholesaler, many pharma- 
ceutical manufacturers won't ship to 
the wholesaler—or will ship only at re- 
tail prices. 

Northwestern and its Velocity Hos- 
pital Group subsidiary received some 
relief when, after suing five manufac- 
turers and NWDA, the suit was set- 
tled prior to trial. However, there are 
“strings” attached to the settlement 
with Eli Lilly and SmithKline Beck- 
man, two major suppliers. 

Lilly has agreed to supply North- 
western with a half-dozen chargeback 
hospital products until June 30, 1985, 
but none of the 300 other pharmaceuti- 
cals manufactured by Lilly. Smith- 
Kline has agreed to supply Northwest- 
ern only with hospital drugs but with 
no time limit. 

By its own admission, Northwest- 
ern has lost 50 accounts since Pay ‘n 
Save bought the wholesaler. 

Even so, \»ere is a bright side to 
Northwestern: It is now servicing Pay 
’n Save and Bi-Mart drug stores as well 
as Ernst Home Centers, and this has 
resulted in cost and delivery savings. 

Still, Pay ’n Save faces some formi- 
dable obstacles. The principal one is 
the indebtedness incurred by the 
buyout. Total borrowing was $470 mil- 
lion ($370 million to take the company 
private and $100 million for working 
capital). That translates to annual pay- 
ments of $50 million just to cover the 
cost of interest. 

As a result of the debt burden, The 
Trump Group, through its Acquicorp 
subsidiary, might sell off Pay ’n Save’s 
divisions piecemeal. The Trump Group 
opened the door to this possibility in its 
tender offer by stating “Acquicorp is 
considering selling one or more of the 
company’s businesses and applying 
the proceeds to pay indebtedness ” 

Ernie Domas, security analyst for 
Piper, Jaffray and Hopwood, says that 
“the parts are worth much more than 
the whole,” and that “Trump has a 
good history of real estate manage- 
ment because that’s their specialty.” 

Domas adds that “there is a possibil- 
ity they would hold back on selling 
some of their divisions—particularly 
Pay ’n Save and Ernst—for two years. 
During that time they would turn them 
into lean and trim operations.”

chain’s 100,000-sq.-ft. Birmingham 
center.

adding computers to its stores. In Feb-

Dart focuses growth on deep discount 


LANDOVER, Md. — Since last 
year’s $160 million leveraged buyout of 
Dart’s 78-unit drug store division, the 
new owners have moved aggressively 
to bolster the company’s lagging oper- 
ations in the highly competitive Wash- 
ington and Richmond, Va., metro mar- 
kets. 

Under the leadership of Al Towle, 
chairman and principal stockholder of 
the privately held Dart Drug Stores 
Inc., and Stephen J. Hansbrough, 
president and coo, the company has 
opened five new stores in 1984 and 
plans to add an additionai five in 1985. 

Currently, the Dart chain has 17 
drug/home center combination stores, 
all averaging between 30,000 and 
40,000 sq. ft., five Total Plus deep-dis- 
count stores in Richmond, Va., and 56 
conventional Dart drug stores averag- 
ing between 10,000 and 20,000 sq. ft. 

Dart’s conventional and combina- 
tion drug stores will remain the chain’s 
growth vehicle in Maryland and Wash- 
ington, D.C., but the company expects 
to focus its growth on its mini-chain of 
deep-discount stores in Richmond and 
in all future markets. 

Recently, Dart remodeled all five of 
its Total Plus deep-discount stores, re- 
stocked them with more than 13,000 
sku’s and repriced them at 30% to 50% 
below the local competition. And to 
build visibility for the mini-chain of 
deep-discount stores, a brand new 
television, radio and print campaign 
was launched. All of this activity cen- 


ters around Towle’s goal of doubling 
Total Plus’s average $3 million to $4 
million sales per stores “within the 
year.” 

In an earlier interview with Drug 
Store News, Towle noted that the 
chain’s previous owners were only 
“half-heartedly” into the new ventures 
like deep-discount stores. Before the 
buyout, the former management had 
put most of its efforts into the rapid ex- 
pansion of its Crown Book and Trak 
Auto companies. The drug store divi- 
sion had languished and operational 
problems like frequent out-of-stocks 
and poor housekeeping were increas- 
ingly becoming endemic to almost all 
the drug stores. 

To solve those problems, Al Towle 
was hired last March as president of 
Dart’s drug store division. Towle had 
previously served in upper manage- 
ment positions in two of the three lead- 
ing drug chains in Washington, D.C. 
Before joining Dart, Towle was presi- 
dent of Gray Drug Fair and earlier in 
his career he was senior vp of market- 
ing for Peoples. 

About three months after Towle 
joined Dart, he and Hansbrough, who 
was then senior vp of distribution and 
data processing, led the management 
group’s leveraged buyout of Dart’s re- 
tail drug division. 

Both men immediately sought to re- 
vise the chain’s entire merchandise 
mix, particularly the core depart- 
ments, which had suffered the most 


under previous management. Along 
with revamping the merchandise mix, 
the new management team worked to 
reduce frequent out-of-stocks, cleaned 
up the stores and put in more clerks at 
checkout stands. 

By most accounts, these efforts paid 
off. Currently, Dart’s conventional 
drug stores do about $3 million a store, 
while its combos ring up about $5 mil- 
lion. According to Towle, the remod- 


eled Total Plus deep-discount stores 
now generate between $4 million and 
$5 million. 

In other developments, Dart is scal- 
ing down the size of its Washington, 
D.C., stores. In that market a smaller 
prototype, from 15,000 to 20,000 sq. 
ft., will become the norm, rather than 
the 40,000- to 50,000-sq.-ft. drug/home 
center giants that once characterized 
the chain.

WILSONVILLE, Ore. — If, in a 
flight of fancy, K mart execs ever 
imagined a “dream” drug chain to ac- 

quire, the vision would have fit Pay 

Less NW. 

On Feb. 2, 1985, the dream became a 
reality when K mart bought Pay Less 
for $500 million in cash, the largest 
sum ever paid for a pure chain drug 
company. 

Pay Less more than justified the 
deal with its virtuoso performance 
during the last two years. In the fiscal 
year ended Jan. 31, 1985, Pay Less 
hiked profits 26% (from $24.7 million to 
$31 million), on a sales increase of 7.8% 
(from $852.9 million to $919 million). 

- That came on the heels of an equaily 
- impressive fiscal 1984 when earnings 
jumped 28% on a sales rise of 9%. 

With the infusion of fresh capital 
from K mart, Pay Less is expected to 
break out of its five-state territory 
(Oregon, Washington, California, Ida- 
ho, Nevada) and eventually become a 
national chain. The timetable is to first 
gain strong market position in all 
states west of the Rockies, concentrat- 
ing on those states which are contigu- 
ous to its present operations. Most 
likely are Arizona, Montana, Wyo- 
ming and New Mexico. 

Currently, Pay Less has three retail 
entities: the 30,000-sq.-ft. superdrug 
store, its cornerstone with 159 stores. 
Then there are three Value Giant deep 
discount stores which are conversions 
of Pay Less superdrug stores. Finally, 
there is Key Drug, the scaled-down 
version of the Pay Less superdrug 
store, which is geared for towns with 
5,000 to 10,000 population. 

Key to expansion 

Key Drug is literally the key to rapid 
expansion. Even before the K mart ac- 
quisition, Pay Less had planned to 
open 100 Key stores over the next 
three or four years. And since K mart 
has indicated it is interested in more 
numbers, Key is in the catbird seat. 

The size of Key varies according to 
available space. The first store was 
17,000 sq. ft.; the second, 8,500 sq. ft. 
| The chain prefers 10,000 to 12,000 sq. 
ft. In getting locations for Key, Pay

leased 400,000 sq. ft. of warehouse 
space in the Portland area several 
years ago. 

Distribution plan 

With adequate land available at Wil- 
sonville, the present distribution cen- 
ter was slated for expansion in 1984. 
However, further review of operating 
and transportation costs, coupled with 
heavy future expansion in northern 
California, led management to plan a 
distribution center in Stockton. The fa- 
cility was blue-printed at 640,000 sq. 
ft., plus 200,000 sq. ft. of interior racks 
on four levels (50,000 sq. ft. per level). 

However, costs for the proposed 
Stockton d.c. bailooned from $21 mil- 
lion to $35 million, so Pay Less down- 
scaled to 500,000 sq. ft. and decided to 
build in Woodland (near Sacramento). 
However, that building will not be 
completed until 1986. In the interim, 
Pay Less has leased a 347,000-sq.-ft. 
distribution center in Sacramento. 

At present, Pay Less operates 72 
stores in northern California. The new 
Woodland d.c. will be able to service 
twice as many stores, thereby confirm- 
ing northern California as a region tar- 
geted for growth. 

With expansion-minded K mart 
now in command, drugmen are now 
wondering how long before the new 
Woodland facility will reach capacity.

SHIREMANSTOWN, Pa. — Rite 
Aid Corp. last year added another egg 
to its basket of specialty retail outlets, 
and at the same time forged new mar- 
kets with its drug store division. 

Rite Aid chairman Alex Grass’s lat- 
est effort into specialty retailing is En- 
core Discount Books, an 18-store chain 
based in Philadelphia. Since acquiring 
Encore, Rite Aid added three new out- 
lets and plans to open as many as 14 in 
fiscal 1986. The chain contributed ap- 
proximately $14 million in sales since 
becoming part of Rite Aid. 

In addition to Encore, Rite Aid’s di- 
versified holdings include ADAP (auto 
parts chain), Circus World (toy 
stores), Heaven (variety stores), and 
Sera-Tec (a plasmapheresis business). 
The drug retailer owns a 28% share in 
Superdrug Stores P.L.C., a British 
drug chain. Rite Aid also owns 46.8% 
of Super Rite Foods, a U.S. grocery 
wholesaler and retailer. 

For the year, ended March 2, Rite 
Aid posted net earnings of $69.9 mil- 
lion, down 6% from $74.3 million the 
previous year. However, fiscal 1984 in- 
cluded a $12 million earnings gain from 
the partial sale of Super Rite througha 
public offering at the close of calendar 
1983. 

Sales for fiscal 1985 were up 18% to 
$1.45 billion from $1.2 billion the previ- 
ous year. 

Super Rite Foods enjoyed a strong 
year in its first year as an independent 
company. The company posted a 30.7% 
gain in net earnings to $5.2 million 
from $3.9 million on sales of $375.6 mil- 
lion, up 31% from $286.8 million the 
previous year. 

During the year, Super Rite ex- 
panded into grocery retailing by ac- 
quiring the 48-store Food-A-Rama 
chain in Baltimore, leaving the door 
open for Rite Aid to test the food/drug 
combo format. 

While specialty retailing will play a 
bigger role in the profit picture at Rite 
Aid over the next few years, growth in 
the drug store division has hardly 
missed a beat.

store count to 32.

parent company also beefed up the 
management of its $40 million auto 
parts chain. Frank Corella, a former 
vp of merchandising at SupeRx Drugs, 
was reassigned to ADAP after joining 
Rite Aid last fall. 

The results were not as encouraging 
with Rite Aid’s 191-unit Circus World 
chain. Company officials acknowl- 
edged that sales from the toy chain did 
not meet expectations during the all- 
important third quarter.

Ailing Gray moves fo reverse decline 


CLEVELAND — Despite a prom- 
ising start, 1984 turned out to be Gray 
Drug Fair’s worst year since its acqui- 
sition by Sherwin-Williams in 1981. 

After a relatively strong first two 
quarters when operating profits 
reached $8 million on a sales rise of 
11%, the division went into a nose dive 
and finished up the year with operat- 
ing profits declining 99% to a mere 
$82,000. 

Sherwin-Williams chairman, presi- 
dent and ceo John G. Breen called the 
division’s performance “disappoint- 
ing” and blamed it on the company’s 
“inability to maintain margins.” 

“Problems continued to plague us in 
1981,” he said. “Poor inventory man- 
agement, inefficient operations at the 
distribution centers, poor gross mar- 
gins due to lack of merchandising skills 
and shortages that affected service 
levels and, therefore, margins. We 
also had problems balancing our gross 
margins, sales and inventory.” 

Breen also conceded to security ana- 
lysts that Sherwin-Williams had over- 
estimated its ability to “turn the com- 
pany around” when it first acquired 
Gray Drug Fair. 

However, Breen also said the drug 
chain’s record to date is not dissimilar 
to the Paint Store Division's experi- 
ence during the early part of its turn- 
around. 

Back in 1978, the paint stores lost 
more than $14 million. Last year, they 
generated $55.8 million in operating 
income. 

The paint stores currently account 
for nearly 41% of Sherwin’s sales and 
the drug stores, 30%. The paint stores, 
however, account for 39% of Sherwin’s 
operating income, while the drug 
stores account for just 0.1%. 

In the past year and a half, Sherwin 
Williams has tried to improve the situ- 
ation by downsizing most of the larger 
Washington D.C./Maryland/Virginia- 
based Drug Fair stores while simulta- 
neously trying to sharpen their com- 
petitive pricing. 

The company has also worked hard 
to improve the stores’ chronic out-of- 
stock problems and to improve its ad- 


vertising campaigns by locking into 
more of the “exciting new national 
brands that come along.” 

In the beginning of the year, some of 
the remedies seemed to be working, 
but in the third quarter, there was an 
operating loss of $1.1 million. Shortly 
after that, Mac Allen Culver, who had 
been recruited to head the division just 
six months before, resigned to return 
to his home in the Pacific Northwest 
and a job with Pay ’n Save, leaving the 
423-unit chain rudderless again. 

New turnaround plan 

Breen almost immediately appoint- 
ed Carl A. Bellini president and gener- 
al manager of Gray. He was formerly 
group vp for Gray and for the paint 
store division. 

Breen also announced a new strate- 
gic turnaround plan for 1985. To im- 
prove its control over inventory, Gray 


will now count its inventory three 
times a year instead of two. The com- 
pany will also mechanize its Alexan- 
dria, Va., distribution center, which 
services the Drug Fair stores. It will 
also open a new 150,000-sq.-ft. distri- 
bution center in Florida later this year 
to service Gray stores in that state. 

Also in 1985, Gray will test POS in- 
stallations in 25 stores and will install 
pharmacy computer stand-alone ter- 
minals in at least 100 stores. Gray had 
been using on-line computers in about 
100 stores, but after a test, the stand- 
alones seemed to promise a more effi- 
cient and less costly service. 

Gray also announced plans to open 
45 new stores in 1985 while remodeling 
another 40. Ten more Drug Fair stores 
in the Atlantic region will also be 
downsized. 

In 1984, Breen said, Gray downsized 
a total of 57 Drug Fair stores, taking 
them from an average of 18,000 to 
25,000 sq. ft. to 12,000 to 14,000 sq. ft. 

To build sales, the chain also plans to 
increase its number of circulars by 28% 
in 1985. There are also plans to pro- 
mote more items per circular and to en- 
sure that there are more of the “better 
branded items” included in the ads. 

Jim Mastrian, vp of marketing, was 
also said to be sending a team of mer- 
chandisers into the field to help restock 
and replanogram stores so they could 
accommodate expanded sku’s in select 
lines. 

Shrinkage was also under attack, 
and one security analyst who follows 
the company, said that for their more 
recent quarters, shrinkage did seem to 
be improving. For one period, he said, 
it had been reduced from a high range 
of between 5% and 6% of sales to be- 
tween 3% and 4%.

INDIANAPOLIS — Nineteen 
eighty-four was the last complete year 
of independent ownership for the 85- 
year-old Hook Drug sture chain. 

In February 1985, the Kroger Com- 
pany acquired Hook Drugs Ine. in a 
friendly takeover. The cash and stock 
transaction was valued at approxi- 
mately $161 million. 

The ck ain will retain its Hook’s name 
and will operate separately from 
Kroger’s other drug chain, SupeRx. 

Industry officials and analysts felt it 
was a good merger. “It’s a good fit from 
both points of view,” said Elizabeth 
Shiels, an analyst with Hilliard Lyons. 
“Kroger dominates the food business 
in Indiana, and Hook dominates the re- 
tail drug business.” 

Hook currently operates 298 drug 
stores and 14 convalescent aids centers 
in Indiana, Illinois, Kentucky and 
Ohio. 

The year started out weak for 
Hook’s. “We definitely had our prob- 
lems,” says a Hook’s spokesman. “We 
entered 1984 with the supposition that

Highest gross margins 

Hook, which has gained a reputation 
for its consistently high gross margins, 
registered 34% in that area for 1984, 
making it the highest among all chains. 

The company’s return on invest-

1983’s 20.3%. 

Sales per store increased slightly in 
1984 to $1.2 million with sales per 
square foot of $170, up from $163 last 
year. 

During 1984, Hock’s opened 16 new 
drug stores and four new Convalescent 
Aids Centers. 

The chain continued computerizing 
its pharmacies at a rate of six per 
month during 1984, ending the year 
with 158 installations completed. Ac- 
cording to officials, that same schedule 
of six per month will be followed dur- 
ing 1985.

gram where the stand-alone pharmacy 
computers are able to communicate 


with the headquarters mainframe but 
remain independent with their own 
program. “They are not on line,” says 
an official. “They can only communi- 
cate with each other to get third-party 
information. All script and family in- 
formation is kept in the store’s comput- 
er.” At year’s end, 84 pharmacy com- 
puters had this communicative 
capability. 

More than 10 million prescriptions 
were filled last year by the chain’s 
pharmacists, accounting for $123 mil-

_ NEWS IN BRIEF — 


Insulin nasal spray proven effective 


BOSTON — A new insulin delivery system, a nasal 
spray, may replace injections as the best way to adminis- 
ter insulin to some diabetics. 

A team of Boston University researchers reported in 
the New England Journal of Medicine that they success- 
fully treated diabetes for up to three months by adminis- 
tering insulin in a nasal spray. More studies, however, are 
needed before the spray could be put into widespread use. 

According to Renate Kimmerle, M.D., one of the Bos- 
ton researchers who condueted the study, the spray con- 
tains a concentrated form of fast-acting insulin, which 
“very quickly” enters the bloodstream where it breaks 
down sugar. Because the insulin spray works so quickly, 
she said, diabetics can use it immediately before a meal. 

Insulin administered by injection usually requires about 
30 to 45 minutes to enter the bloodstream, but the absorp- 
tion time varies widely between individuals. 
® See related stories on page 43. 


NACDS rejects proposed beer bill 


WASHINGTON — Chain drug industry leaders are 
urging Congress to & gr proposed legislation designed to 
eliminate virtually all price competition among distribu- 
tors of beer and other malt beverages to drug stores. 

The “Beer Bill” would create an exemption to the Fed- 
eral antitrust laws enabling brewers to enforce exclusive 
territory restrictions on beer wholesalers. 

Despite the widespread opposition, Congressional 
backers of the bill contend that such territorial restraints 
are essential to prevent malt beverage “diverters” from 
“undercutting” the prices of local distributors to capture 
chain accounts. 

NACDS vp Ty Kelley called the measure “one of the 
most anticompetitive pieces of legislation now before Con- 
gress.” : 

Allowing brewers to close off supply sources to drug 
chains and other malt beverage retailers would “eliminate 
price competition altogether” and “inevitably increase the 
cost of beer to consumers,” Kelley told Drug Store News. 


Pri¢e Mart launches third store 


MINNEAPOLIS — Prig¢e Mart, the new deep discount 
chain, which opened its first two stores last month, opened 
its third on May 4 in Davenport, Iowa. 

The 17,000-sq.-ft. store features a race track design and 
will carry about 50% deal merchandise. The rest will be ba- 
sic, everyday stock. ; 

Douglas Bablitch, president and ceo of the chain says 
that “we are so happy with business at the new stores, that 
we are going ahead with our plans.” 

Those plans include a May 31 opening of a Madison, 
Wis., store, an opening in South Bend, Ind., on July 15, an 
Elgin, Ill:, store this fall, and three more Minneapolis 
stores before the first of the year. 


SW launches distribution center 


SAN ANTONIO — Southwestern Drug Corp., a whole- 
saler serving Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico and Louisi- 
ana, has unveiled a 100,000-sq.-ft. distribution center 
here. The facility, which has 90,000 sq. ft. of warehouse 
space and more than 9,000 sq. ft. of offices, replaces an out- 
moded 76-year-old building in the downtown section of the 
city. The new state-of-the-art warehouse incorporates 
high bay pallet rack storage, effective flow rack/gravity 
flow shelving, order processing equipment and over a 
quarter mile of conveyor systems. The new center ser- 
vices more than 500 community and hospital pharmacies in 
southern Texas.

Chains unite in educating public 
on how to prevent child abduction 


NEW YORK — Several 
drug chains have joined the 
nationwide effort to locate 
missing children and to edu- 
cate the public on how to pre- 
vent child abduction. 

Peoples, Hook’s, Giant 
Foods, The Medicine Shoppes, 
LaVerdiere’s and Pay Less 
NW, are among the retailers 
that have developed chainwide 
programs. 

Peoples Drug recently be- 
or a program called Missing. 

n the program, a two-sided 
oster with photos of six miss- 
ing children is displayed in 
each of Peoples’ 750 stores. 
The photos have short de- 


scriptions and biographies of 
the children. 

ster is located on a 
isplay rack near the 


The 
candy 


registers. According to Jim 
Coyle, director of advertising, 
that location was chosen be- 
cause “most kids are found by 
other kids.” 

Hook’s Child Safe program 
began on April 29 in conjunc- 
tion with the rerun of TVs 
‘““Adam.”’ According to a 
Hook’s spokesman, that 
chain’s efforts are aimed at the 
prevention of abduction and 

uick action if an abduction 

oes occur. “There are so 
many organizations in our 
area printing photos of miss- 
ing children, we thought we’d 
provide a program that might 
prevent children from getting 
to that point,” said the spokes- 
man. 

Child Safe provides parents 
with small packets to be com- 


pleted with photos and bios of 
their children. Then, if a child 
does disappear, the informa- 
tion is immediately available 
to law enforcement officers. 

The Landover, Md.-based 
food and drug retailer, Giant 
Foods, has also directed its ef- 
forts toward prevention. The 
chain’s 74 pharmacies have 
started inserting “Guides to 
the Prevention of Child Abuse 
and Abduction” in each bag 
along with the prescription or- 
der. 

Sue Challis, Giant’s public 
affairs coordinator, says that 
prevention is the key to abduc- 
tion and that education is the 
key to prevention.

Ethnic items outshine general H&BA 


espite the relatively slow 
growth of the market for toilet- 

ries and cosmetics over the past 

two decades, the market for ethnic 
health & beauty aids has mushroomed. 
And the ethnic segment of the mar- 
ket will continue to grow and, some an- 
alysts say, even explode during the 
next decade. According to Business 
Trends Analysis, blacks spent over $2 
billion in 1983 for toiletries and cosmet- 
ics ($1.3 billion of which was spent on 
hair care). By 1998, sales are projected 


to skyrocket to $5.6 billion, or 24% of 
the total dollars spent on all toiletry 
and cosmetic items. 

What will fuel this astounding 
growth? Much of the answer can be 
found in the fact that blacks spend a 
significantly greater percentage of 
their per capita income on H&BA than 
whites. Although blacks comprise only 
12% of the population, for example, 
they purchased 34.1% of the hair preps 
sold in this country in 1983. Such a dis- 
proportionate amount of money is 


spent by blacks on H&BA especially 
formulated to meet their hair care 
needs—from easy breakage to exces- 
Sive dryness. 

In general, black women, who out- 
number black men in the population, 
spend as much as five times more on 
hair care items than the general popu- 
lation on a per capita basis. 

And blacks will spend even more 
money on H&BA in the next decade 
because the black population is grow- 
ing nearly 75% faster than the general 


population, according to the U.S. Cen- 
sus Bureau. By 1993, blacks will com- 

prise 12.8% of the U.S. population. 
Moreover the median age for blacks, 
23.5 years, is over six years younger 
than that of whites, according to Cen- 
sus estimates. This younger popula- 
tion spends more on total grooming 
compared to their older counterparts. 
The black youth market also sparks 
many of the trends in ethnic hair care. 
As the black population’s buying

DRUG STORE NEWS, May 13, 1985 


MERCHANDISER 


special report: 
Ethnic eatin 


17 


Continued from page 15 

power has expanded, retailers have 
tried to keep pace with the demand for 
ethnic products. Because blacks spend 
such a high percentage of their per cap- 
ita income on H&BA, stores with as lit- 
tle as 5% black traffic can generate 
15% of H&BA sales, according to Busi- 
ness Trends Analysis. 

Drug store chains, in particular, 
have been steadily increasing their 
commitment to the ethnic category, es- 
pecially hair care, the largest ethnic 
category. 

In 1983, according to A. C. Nielsen, 
drug chains held a 54% share of the 
black hair prep market, while mass 
merchandisers had a 17% share, and 
food outlets a 29% share. 

Moreover, while drug chains range 
up 58% of all drug sales in 1983, the 
chains generated over 80% of the black 
hair prep sales. In contrast, indepen- 
dents with over $500,000 in sales annu- 
ally rang up 19% of all drug sales, but 
only 11% of black hair prep sales. 

Despite drug chains’ and wholesal- 
ers’ commitment to the ethnic catego- 
ry, there is still a continuing struggle 
to achieve adequate distribution and 
shelf space for ethnic products. 

But, those drug chains that have 
made inroads into the ethnic category 
have seen sales soar. Many drug chains 
contacted by Drug Stores News report 
that gross margins for the category av- 
erage 40% and turns can run as high as 
19. 

Drug Emporium is one chain that 
has been very successful in ethnic 
H&BA. Says Mike O’Brien of Harris 
Beauty Supply, an ethnic H&BA sup- 
plier in Atlanta, ethnic sections aver- 
aging 12 ft. in a Drug Emporium can 
generate over $3,000 a week at retail. 


O'Brien says that an average store 
does about $50,000 a year in ethnic 


products, but some Drug Emporiums 


can pull in over $150,000 per year. 

Walgreens also has continued to ex- 
pand its ethnic sections, which range 
from 3 ft. to 21 ft. Says Richard Robin- 
son, ethnic products buyer at Wal- 
greens, “We are very committed and 
positive about the ethnic category and 
many stores are receiving increased 
promotional space.” 

Another chain that has increased its 
commitment to the category is Perry. 
Perry new has ethnic sections in 62 
stores ranging from 4 ft. to 36 ft., and 
the chain is expanding and adding eth- 
nic sections in stores where there is a 
lot of black traffic. Steve Lund, Perry’s 
ethnic H&BA buyer says the section is 
“extremely profitable,” but adds that 
there is no chainwide program to ex- 
pand or add ethnic departments. 

Fay’s also has increased its commit- 
ment to the category. About 30 stores 
now have ethnic sections ranging from 
4 ft. to 8 ft. and the category has re- 
cently been put on an MSI system to 
track product movement. 

And SupeRx, one of the leaders in 
the ethnic category, has created its 
own ethnic planograms ranging from 3 
ft. to 48 ft. Hook Drug also does its own 
planograms ranging from 6 ft. to 18 ft., 
and the chain also warehouses over 
80% of its ethn:c products. According 
to a Hook spokesman, “we’re probably 
not expanding our ethnic sections as 
fast as we should to keep up with de- 
mand.” 

Because the lion’s share of the ethnic 
market is hair care, most of the inter- 
est in new trends focuses on this cate- 
gory. The big question is whether the 
curl has run its course. 


U.S. population ad ethnic group 


Source: Bureau of the Census 


3 Black (Hispanic (_) Other 


Because of the ever changing ethnic product lines, ethnic H&BA buyers must stay 


on top of trends. 


Hair care 

In 1983, blacks spent $1.3 billion on 
hair care and over $138 million was 
generated in drug outlets. Overall, be- 
tween 1978 and 1983, curl activators 
brought in $143 million in sales and kits 
ran up $79 million in sales. 

However, many industry sources 
say that the curl has peaked and the 
wave is slowly emerging as the next big 
trend in ethnic hair care. Perhaps a 
harbinger of such a trend is the recent 
move by Worlds of Curls, a leading curl 
manufacturer, into the hair straighten- 
er market. 

Revlon’s Lou Roppollo, a marketing 
executive, says that the curl look has 
plateaued and the trend is toward a 
more natural and relaxed look. Revlon 
will be following up on this trend when 
it launches Finisheen, a maintenance 
spray product used in salons for re- 
laxed hair. The product is scheduled to 
hit the shelves July 1 and will retail at 
$4.95. 

Despite the emergence of the re- 
laxed look, many observers say that 
the ethnic H&BA business is regional. 
Says Kent Humphreys of Jack’s ser- 
vice, a supplier of ethnic H&BA in 
Oklahoma City: “People do not realize 
that just because an ethnic product is 
among the 10 best-selling items nation- 
wide, it is not necessarily going to be a 
top 10 item in their region.” 

Moreover, many observers stress 
that while the curl was suitable for 
both men and women, the wave will be 
more popular among men. Says Hair- 
lox’ Marcus Griffith: “The curl activa- 
tor market has run its normal cycle, 


but it is here to stay, just like relaxers. 
However, the wave could never be as 
big as the curl because women with 
long hair will not be able to wave their 
hair.” 

Notes Bob Scott, director of sales for 
Pro-Line: “I don’t know when the curl 
will bottom out, but I don’t see the 
market growing.” He adds, however, 
that there will “always be a cur! mar- 
ket.” 

Rocky Piccirillo, director of opera- 
tions for Beauty Enterprises, an ethnic 
products distributor in Hartford, 
agrees. He reports that although the 
kit category has peaked, the mainte- 
nance curl products remain very 
strong, accounting for 49% of his com- 
pany’s total dollar sales. 

Humphreys also notes strong sales 
in the maintenance category. “Sure the 
wave is out there, but eight or nine of 
my 12 best-selling items all have to do 
with the curl. There is still an awful lot 
of dollars out there for the curl,” says 
Humphreys. 

But relaxers, expecially no-lye prod- 
ucts, are making significant inroads in 
the ethnic market. Piccirillo projects 
relaxers to account for 10% of Beauty 
Supply’s total dollar business in 1985, 
up from 7% in 1984. 

And Ken Hall of the Savannah, Ga.- 
based Carson Products says that the 
increased sales from relaxer products 
have yet to show up in the Nielsen num- 
bers. But, he notes that retailers, sup- 
pliers and distributors generally agree 
that the relaxer category will be pick- 


ing up.

DRUG STORE NEWS, May 13, 1985 


Continued from page 17 

The trend toward straighter, 
shorter hair among blacks was 
expected to fuel the ethnic 
mousse market. However, most 
industry analysts say that eth- 
nic mousses account for less 
than 1% of sales in the ethnic 
category and, in general, the 
products have failed to ignite 
the category. 

However, another category 
in ethnic hair care that is ex- 
pected to blossom is hair color. 
“The minority-owned compa- 
nies will have to go into hair co- 
lorings if they want to main- 
tain a hold on the black 
market,” says Julia Wilson, 
beauty editor of the Los Ange- 


les Sentinel. 

Armand Jackson, senior 
product manager for Alberto 
Culver’s professional product 
division, says that Culver, 
makers of TCB, “is looking 
closely at hair colorings in the 
ethnic marketplace.” Other 
manufacturers such as John- 
son Products, M&M Products 
and Soft Sheen are reportedly 
following suit. 

It is still unknown, however, 
whether the minority-owned 
companies can get the ethnic 
hair color market from Revlon 
and Clairol. 

Another area that is still rel- 
atively untouched is shampoo. 
Although shampoos account 
for 40% of the overall U.S. hair 
care market, the category ac- 
counts for less than 9% of eth- 
nic hair care sales. But, as 
more manufacturers of ethnic 
products venture into sham- 
poo lines, the category is ex- 
pected to expand during the 
next decade. 

Cosmetics 

The prestige ethnic cosmet- 
ics and skin treatment prod- 
ucts by Fashion Fair, Flori 
Roberts and Barbara Walden 
have made a big impact on the 
department store level. But, 
with the exception of Posner, 
Honey & Spice, and Zuri, eth- 
nic cosmetics are limited in 
most chain drug stores. 

Says Griffith of HairLox: 
“It’s harder to make cosmetics 
for the ethnic market because 
black women readily buy cos- 
metics for the general mar- 
ket.” He adds that the same 
holds true for fragrances— 
black women identify best 
with general market prod- 
ucts. 

However, most observers 
say there is a big market for 
ethnic brands, especially as 
more cosmetics companies 
discontinue the darker shades 
popular among black women. 

Johnson Products is one 
company that has added some 
new sparkle to its line of Ultra 
Sheen cosmetics with new lip 
and nail shades ranging from 
“rambunctious red” to “cop- 
per sensation” and with new 


crayon colors in blue and fuch- 
sia. However, Johnson is one of 
only a handful of manufactur- 
ers of ethnic products that pro- 
duces both hair care preps as 
well as cosmetics for the mass 
market. 

Skin treatment lines are 
also targeted for expansion as 
the market for total grooming 
expands. Says Melvin String- 
er, sales manager for Standard 
Drug, a supplier of ethnic 
H&BA in Detroit: “Manufac- 
turers are going to have to look 
more closely at hypoallergenic 


products to see if they have a 
niche in the ethnic market- 
place.” 

Most analysts agree that 
ethnic cosmetics seem to work 
better when merchandised 
near the ethnic hair care sec- 
tion. 

Overall, however, the ethnic 
cosmetic category appears to 
lack a secure niche in the mar- 
ketplace. Some chains cross 
merchandise ethnic cosmet- 
ics, while others prefer to sell 
the items in the ethnic hair 
care section.

DRUG STORE NEWS, May 13, 1985 


Regional tastes affect black hair care sales 


espite growing sales and in- 
D creased profits, drug retailers 

have moved cautiously to ware- 
house their own black, health & beauty 
aid products. 

Although many chains could justify 
buying leading black hair care prod- 
ucts direct from manufacturers, based 
on their sales volume, the regional na- 
ture of the business and the volatility of 
the market has led many chain execs to 
continue with distributor arrange- 
ments. 

Only a handful of drug chains have 
opted to buy direct from the manufac- 
turer. They include Walgreens, Revco, 
Rite Aid and Hook. Most chains rely on 
either store-to-store deliveries or 
warehouse-to-warehouse deliveries 
from distributors. 

At the heart of the direct vs. distrib- 
utor issue is the fact that many of the 
black ethnic products have widely 
varying degrees of regional appeal. 

“People do not realize that just be- 
cause an ethnic H&BA item is among 
the top 10 selling items, it’s not neces- 
sarily going to be a top 10 item in their 
region,” said Kent Humphreys, presi- 
dent of Jack’s Service in Oklahoma 
City. 

Product-movement studies from 
Jack’s Service indicate, for instance, 
that Long Aid Gel is its third biggest 
seller in the Southwest. 

However, at Johnson Drug Supply 
Co. in Detroit, Mich., Long Aid Gel 
places 27th on the list of leading sell- 
ers. 

The problems become increasingly 
difficult for chains that have stores in a 
number of regions. While a chain such 
as Hook Drugs, which has stores pri- 
marily in the state of Indiana, can feel 
comfortable that what’s selling in one 
part of Indiana is probably selling in 
other areas of the state as well, chains 
with stores that span several states 
have to be aware of regional differ- 
ences. 

Some of the larger chains such as 
Walgreens and Revco that have gone 
the direct supply route have attempted 
to compensate for the regional swings 
in the business by getting product- 
movement information from their 
store district offices. 

Still, many industry insiders say 


that a case can be made for going di- 
rect. “I don’t think that anyone would 
question the fact that a product like 
Soft Sheen has the largest share of 
market in the country,” said one indus- 
try source. “But are the distributors 
going to be happy with the dregs while 
the chains take the jewels for them- 
selves?” 

There also is the question of whether 
chains want their buyers putting all 
the effort and time into an ethnic pro- 
gram when only 25% of a chain’s stores 
may feature ethnic departments. 

Ray Perrone, a buyer at Adams 
Drugs in Pawtucket, R.I., notes that 
the ethnic department is one of the 
most profitable areas in the store. But 
the chain uses a distributor because it 
has ethnic products in only about 85 of 
its 423 stores. 

Other chains including Medi Mart, 
Genovese Drugs and CVS have also 
opted for distributors. 

In addition, warehouse-to-ware- 
house programs such as those offered 
by Beauty Enterprises, based in Hart- 
ford, and Ben Sheftall in Savannah, 
Ga., are also being used much more 
widely by drug chains. 

Many drug retailers point out that at 
best they would ‘gain a few points” by 
going direct. Moreover, distributors 
make the case that chains benefit from 
increased volume in a distributor ar- 
rangement. 

One drug retailer for a chain on the 
West Coast likened the current situa- 
tion with ethnic products to sunglass- 
es. “We could buy ethnic products di- 
rect from manufacturers and as we 
could start a private-label sunglass 
program,” he noted. “But the question 
vou have to ask yourself is do you want 
vo be stuck servicing the department, 
and can you st#y on toy<! the trends in 
the business? 

“As it stands, we’re already making 
35% to 40% m=rgins, what’s the point 
in risking thai” 

However, in the long term, as more 
retailers test the ethnic department 
waters, drug chains may be forced to 
go direct with manufacturers. Up until 
now, the market has not been overly 
price sensitive. But chains may take a 
more competitive stance if the market- 
place heats up. 


Distribution of U.S. black population

Source: U.S. Department of Commerce, Bureau of the Census 


1980 


H&BA 


space allocation 


fied to local needs 


nlike the space allocated to gen- 
eral health & beauty aids de- 
partments, the size of ethnic 
H&BA departments varies from store 
to store, depending on the ethnic 
makeup of a particular store area. 

Consequently, input from store per- 
sonnel can be a crucial element in the 
success of an ethnic H&BA depart- 
ment. 

The general rule of thumb is that a 
store with a 10% black customer base 
should allocate no more than 3 ft. to 
ethnic H&BA products. 

However, as the percentage of black 


customers increases, it becomes much 
more important to allocate larger sec- 
tions to ethnic departments. A store 
with a black customer base of 15% to 
25% should feature an ethnic depart- 
ment ranging from 4 ft. to 6 ft. 

At least 8 ft. to 12 ft. for ethnic prod- 
ucts is recommended for stores with a 
40% ethnic makeup. And those stores 
in which 50% or more of the customers 
are black frequently can support de- 
partments of 16 ft. and up. 

But, however useful these formulas 
are in determining the size of a store’s 
ethnic department, most chains rely 


heavily on store personnel to advise 
hedquarters if a department should ei- 
ther be cut back or expanded. 

In addition to fine tuning space allot- 
ments, drug chains also are doing a 
better job promoting and merchandis- 
ing their ethnic departments than in 
the past. Until recently, many chain 
ethnic departments were relegated to 
outpost areas of the store and little 
consideration was given to developing 
the departments around the needs of a 
store’s ethnic customers. 

“We believe that the ethnic depart- 
ment is up and coming,” said Bobby 
Little, Big B’s vp of store operations. 
“For some time, it’s been a department 
that has been neglected, but we realize 
that there is a real need for these prod- 
ucts.” 

Big B is one of the few chains with 


ethnic departments in all of its stores. 
Little said the departments range in 
size from 4 ft. to 48 ft., with the aver- 
age totaling 8 ft. to 12 ft. Its largest de- 
partment is a 48-ft. section in the pre- 
dominantly black city of Montgomery, 
Ala. 

Another chain that has been aggres- 
sive in expanding ethnic H&BA’s is 
Revco. Several years ago, Revco typi- 
cally allocated 3-ft. and 4-ft. sections 
for ethnic departments in stores with a 
50% or more black customer base. To- 
day, Revco allocates 10 ft. to 12 ft. to 
ethnic H&BA’s in similar stores. 

Reveo’s commitment to ethnic de- 
partments has paid off. The chain is 
now doing as much business with its 
ethnic health & beauty aids as it does 
with general market hair conditioners 
in its more than 1,800 drug stores.

one-two Philly punch

Swinging against Drug Emporium, which entered 
this market last month, by converting two conven-

format.

eight.

Giant sales up almost $7M

fourth quarter, ended Feb. 23 were $691.8 million, up 
9.4% over the same period last year. Total sales for the 
year increased 9.3% to $2.1 billion. Net income for fiscal 
1985 rose to $45.2 million, up 11.6% over fiscal 1984.

Drug Mart, Canada’s No. 1 
drug store retailer, is testing 
scanning in one of its two deep 
discount drug stores and plan- 
ning to initiate a similar test 
this summer in about three of 
its conventional drug stores. 

At the beginning, the test 
will be limited to stores with 
about average volume so that 
Shoppers can realize as much 
of a return on its initial invest- 
ment as possible. 

The company will be using 
slot scanners, which generally 
cost between $3,000 and 
$5,000 each, at all of its regis- 


ters. The ave Shoppers 
—— has six registers, 
ut some stores can have as 
many as 10. 

According to David Bloom, 
president and ceo, ty ome 
expects to realize both hard 
and soft savings through the 
scanning installations. Hard 
savings should come in the 
form of productivity improve- 
ments in cash register 
throughput and labor schedul- 
ing, and soft savings should 
come from improvements in 
merchandising allocations 
based on data obtained from 
the scanners tracking. 


“We expect the greatest 
savings to come from mer- 
chandising changes that affect 
our gross in return on in- 
vestment,” said Bloom. “With 
scanning, we'll be in better 
control of our inventory, and 
we'll be able to reduce inven- 
tory investment based on 
turns.”

probably continue the test for 
about six months before ex- 

ding it to other stores. The 
irst scanners went into Shop-
