ers eying Computer accessory potential 


Retailers race clock to sell 


low-priced fashion watches 


hain drug buyers are hoping 

that there is still some life left 

in the plastic fashion watch cat- 
egory as the market floods with low- 
priced Swatch watch knockoffs. 

Last year drug chains and mass mer- 
chandisers could only watch from the 
sidelines as the trendy Swatches 
turned the watch market upside down. 


Under $10 29% 
Over $50 19% 


“| 
ye 


Swatch U.S.A., in a move that has 
been described by its competitors as a 
“stroke of marketing genius,” by- 
passed many of the conventional chan- 
nels of distribution and directed its col- 
orful line of $30 plastic watches to 
department and specialty stores. 

Swatch supported the line with a 
hefty ad budget that hammered home 
the trendy fashion theme to consum- 
ers, who propelled the product into po- 
sition as one top selling gift item dur- 
ing the ’84 holiday season. Since being 
introduced in 1984, industry insiders 
say that more than two million Swatch- 
es were sold. 

Although unit sales of Swatches rep- 
resented only a small percentage of the 
estimated 60 million watches sold in 
the U.S. last year, the Swatch has had 
a major impact on the industry. 

Given the Swatch’s tremendous suc- 
cess, it’s no surprise that manufactur- 
ers are gearing up their production 
lines to turn out plastic fashion watch- 
es. Such companies as Timex, Lorus, 
Armitron and Parker Watch, to name a 
few, are looking to capitalize on the 
growing market for inexpensive fash- 
ion watches. 

Drug retailers are excited by the 
fact that this year they will have more 
ammunition to compete with the de-

s the penetration of 
home and small busi- 
ness computers deep- 
en, anew merchandising cate- 
gory is emerging in chain drug

ries. 

Accessories, mainly floppy 
disks, are quickly becoming 
mass-market items and are 
starting to be merchandised in 
major drug chains such as 
Longs, Eckerd, Perry, 
Hook’s, Osco and Fay’s. 

Other than the floppy disks, 
or diskettes, the computer ac- 
cessories currently available 
to drug stores and other mass 
merchandisers include stor- 
age racks, paper, labels, mail- 
ers, forms, head-cleaning kits, 
stationery and cards. 

Unlike many other catego- 
ries, computer accessories can 
be cross merchandised in sev- 
eral departments—station- 
ery/office, business supplies 
and back-to-school. 

In a spot check, Drug Store 
News found that while most 
manufacturers felt optimistic 
about the category being mer- 
chandised in drug stores, buy- 
ers were somewhat cautious in 
their optimism.

Continued from page 15 

“We keep hearing that it’s a 
great item, and I think it could 
be in the future, but right now 
our sales are miserable,” says 
one buyer for a Midwest drug 
chain. 

On the other hand, Kerr 
Drug Stores in Raleigh, N.C., 
experimented with accesso- 
ries in ore of its stores and was 
delighted with the results. 
“We sent all of the samples we 
had received to our store near 
the university, and the manag- 
er made it into a nice display, 
and it turned very quickly,” 
says Steve Osborne, Kerr’s 
stationery buyer. “We know 
the business is out there, we 
just have to figure exactly 
what the public wants and how 
to get its business.” 

Tom Burke, director of sales 
dev.:lopment for Kodak’s con- 
sumer electronics division, 
Says now is the time for buyers 
to act. “The market is in its in- 
fancy. It’s a very good time for 
drug stores to enter it.” 

Currently, most of the ma- 
jor chains carry from one to 


four sku’s of floppy disks. 


Most carry only the 5%-in. 
single sided mini-disks that 
are compatible with the low- 
tech home computers like 
Atari, Commodore and Apple. 
Ony a few chains carry the 
new 3.5-in. micro-disk used by 
the new Apple McIntosh, and 
the 5'4-in. mini double-sided, 
used by the IBM amd other 
small business computers. 
Floppy disks are still con- 


sidered service counter items 
by most drug stores and are 
sold next to the film and video 
tape. Most disks are manufac- 
tured by consumer electronic 
suppliers, namely 3M, Fuji, 
Kodak and Maxwell, who mar- 
ket the products via estab- 
lished drug store channels. 
The stores that earry other ae- 
cessories usually do so in their 
stationery departments. 
Space requirements for 
computer accessories, espe- 
cially the disks, are quite mini- 
mal, and usually take up less 
space than film does. 
Retailers retain margins 
As is the case for most tech- 
nologieal newcomers, the re- 
tail price of the floppy disk has 
decreased by about 10% dur- 
ing the past year, and in some 
markets is footballed in ads 
quite frequently by the dis- 
count merchandisers. 
Margins in drug stores for 
all computer accessories are in 


the 35%-45% range. “During . 


the price decreases, the manu- 
facturers. gave up margin so 
retailers could keep theirs,” 
says Mark Welland, national 
sales manager for Maxell com- 
puter products. 

Originally, floppy disks 
were able to be purchased one 
at a time by the consumer, but 
most manufacturers have dis- 
continued that packaging, and 
now offer 2-, 5- and 10-packs 
with retail price points rang- 
ing from $3 to $48, depending 
on manufacturer. 

All Perry Drug stores carry 


two sku’s of floppy disks. “We 
carry them strictly as an ac- 
commodation for our custom- 
ers,” says a Perry buyer. “We 
haven’t promoted them much, 
but we do plan to do so in the 
future. Most people don’t 
know we carry them.” 
Cultivate your garden 

“I see a shift in volume from 
computer stores to mass mer- 
chandisers,” says Welland. “A 
trend is developing as a result 
of the natural growth cycle ofa 
product. In the beginning, 
only specialty computer shops 
carried floppy disks and other 
computer supplies, and now as 
the industry is experiencing 
strong growth, there’s a shift 
to sales in mass merchandis- 
ers.” 

Welland says that about 
30% of all blank floppy disks 
are now being sold by mass 
merchandisers. “And by all in- 
dications, that will increase 
dramatically within the next 
couple of years, especially if 
the mass merchandisers pro- 
mote,” he added. 


Buyers eying computer accessory potential 


Maxell, which holds about a 
22% share of the floppy disk 
market, has doubled its busi- 
ness every six months since 
1980. Seotch-brand floppy 
disks, by 3M, also hold a 22% 
market share. 

“It’s a very competitive 
market, especially on the 
West Coast,” says Kodak’s 
Tom Burke. “The floppy mar- 
ket is very price-oriented and 
is very promotable.” 

The Perry spokesman says 
it is quite different in his mar- 
ket. “I haven’t seen floppies 
advertised much by any retail- 
er in our area, so there’s really 
no need for me to promote 
price on the item. I wouldn’t 
be able to buy enough custom- 
ers to make it worthwhile.” 

By far, the greatest market- 
ing potential at this time is 
with the personal home com- 
puter user. 

Another important market- 
ing area is the ever-growing 
small business computer own- 
er, who uses a different floppy 
disk than the home computer 


user. “As the price of comput-_ 

ers comes down, more small 
businesses will get them and 
the need for double-sided: 
disks will increase,” says Fu- 
ji’s Solomon. 

“The growing market as I © 
see it,” says the Midwest buy- 
er, “is the small business com- 
puter user. I can easily see the - 
boss sending his secretary 
down to the drug store for a 10- 
pack of floppy disks and a pack 
of cigarettes.” 

Several other buyers ex- 
pressed that same prediction, 
based on the convenience of 
the drug store. “We’ve seen an 
increase in our stationery/of- 
fice supply department be- 
cause of that reason,” says one 
buyer. 

“Children are now being 
asked to buy their own disks 
for school use,” says Maxell’s 
Welland, pointing out that 
disks are also a back-to-school 
item. “Now, the kid’s back to 
school list reads, ‘pencils, 
crayons, scissors, ruler and a 
box of floppies.’”

Ss costume jewelry becomes 

more of an accepted fashion item 

among women, chain drug 
stores are upgrading their jewelry de- 
partments in an attempt to snare a big- 
ger share of this highly profitable busi- 
ness.

Suppliers, which service nearly 80% 
of the chain drug jewelry departments

“The chain drug industry has just

into the fall,” said Ron Goldman, a buy-

Some buyers believe that as the mar-

down, Swatch customers, who are pri-

Costume jewelry has long been con- 
sidered an excellent impulse item, par- 
ticularly among teenage girls. Howev- 
er, concern over pilferage led many 
chains to approach the category cau- 
tiously. Some chains limited their jew- 
elry business to in and out promotions. 


However, better-quality jewelry 
pieces that complement today’s fash- 
ion trends have expanded the tradi- 
tional customer base beyond the teen- 
age set. And drug retailers have been 
hard pressed to ignore the expansion of 
the market and the improvement in the 
merchandise. 


Several chains that two years ago 
had no formal jewelry programs have 
since gone chainwide. 


Medicare-Glaser, the St. Louis- 
based chain, last fall launched a chain- 
wide jewelry program through Marle 
Creations. According to Medicare-Gla- 
ser buyer Constance Curran, early re- 
sults from the program have prompted 
the chain to increase some of its projec- 
tions for some stores. 


“The whole category has really come 
around,” said Curran. “At one time, 
costume jewelry departments in drug 
stores were just. that—costume. But 
the category has really been upgraded. 
I’m really pleased with what I see out. 
there.”

clined.

WASHINGTON — Does 
the conversion of prescrip- 
tion-only drugs to over-the- 
counter status mean reduced 
demand for other Rx versions 
of those products? 

Not necessarily, accordin 
to market statistics release 
by the Proprietary Associa- 
tion. 

In the case of 0.5% hydro- 
cortisone ppp nenie for ex- 
ample, F.D.A.’s decision to al- 
low the non-Rx sale of these 
drugs created a new $70 mil- 
lion market for OTC versions, 
according to the proprietary 
drug manufacturers group. 


But instead of cutting into 
the market for Rx hydrocorti- 
sone products, the shift to 
OTC status has been accompa- 
nied by a parallel increase in 
the number of prescriptions 
filled for these drugs annually, 
PA said. 

In addition, consumers 
have the benefit of broader 
choices and greater conve- 
nience, the association main- 
tained. 

In a position paper on Rx- 
to-OTC switches, the Propri- 
etary Association said the 
practice has already “won the 
endorsement of Government, 


industry, health profession- 
als, consumer leaders and con- 
sumers themselves.” 

Nearly 40 drugs in 16 differ- 
ent categories have already 
been recommended for the 
shift from prescription-only 
status and “dozens of . these 
new products are coming onto 
the OTC market, where they 
are available conveniently and 
economically,” the association 
said. 

Some other examples of 
products that have enjoyed 
the new status are the brand- 
ed versions of the aspirin sub- 
stitute ibuprofen. This drug is 


SAMI tracks OTC, H&BA sales 


NEW YORK — SAMI 
(Selling Areas Marketing 
Inc.) is introducing a new di- 
mension to its marketing ser- 
vices—tracking the move- 
ment of over the counter 
drugs and health & beauty 
aids through chain drug stores 
and independent drug outlets. 

SAMI, a subsidiary of Time 
Inc., is well known in the 
cery business. Founded in 
1966, the company tracks the 
movement of 460 categories of 
grocery products from food 
operator warehouses to retail 
stores in 54 markets. 

The company plans to track 
the movement of drug store 
merchandise in much the same 
way. It will use computer data 
collected every 28 days from 
drug chain and drug wholesal- 
er warehouses in SAMI mar- 
kets. The data will be sold to 


U.S. manufacturers whose 
products are sold in drug 
stores. 

According to Barbara J. 
Lippard, vp Dinachan of corpo- 
rate development, the first 
four markets to use SAMI are: 
Chicago, New York, Los An- 
geles and San Francisco. Ini- 
tial data from these markets, 
which collectively ring up 
about 24% of U.S. drug store 
sales, is beginning to come in. 

The company ultimately 
plans to. operate in all 54SAMI 
markets, covering about 88% 
of drug stores’ product move- 
ment. It expects to reach that 
goal by December 1987. 

Currently, about 100 cate- 
gories, the majority of which 
are health & beauty aids, are 
being tracked. “It’s a little bit 
of trial and error right now be- 
fore we determine the exact 


categories we are going to cov- 
er,” said Alan B. Miller Jr., 
SAMI’s vp of sales and ser- 
vices. 

According to Miller, the 
company wanted to track drug 
store sales years ago but 
couldn’t, because drug stores 
were not as highly computer- 


ized as food stores and drug 
stores also had a higher de- 
gree of drop shipments. That 
Situation has changed, said 
Miller, making it feasible to 
track products from ware- 
houses to drug stores. 

Miller noted that SAMI will 
eventually track merchandise 
movement into mass mer- 
chandisers, but the company 
is still formulating these 
eae He said that ultimately 

AMI will pool data from food 
outlets, drug store chains and 
mass merchandisers.

DRUG STORE NEWS, May 27, 1985 


Rising script demand parallels OTC switch 


the first new OTC pain reliev- 
er in 30 years, and “the impact 
on self-medication from this 
one switch alone is expected to 
be substantial.” 

In spite of these benefits 
that have emerged from the 
F.D.A.’s review of the OTC 
drugs, the Proprietary Asso- 
ciation is calling for new guide- 
lines. 

Currently the drugs recom- 
mended for the switch to OTC 
status must go through the 
F.D.A.’s “new drug” review 
system, which is “already 
overburdened with other, 
more demanding work.” 

The association offered an 
example of one drug that was 
submitted for review and re- 
classification to OTC status, 
and 35 months later, “it had 
still not been addressed in de- 
tail by the New Drug Adviso- 


ry Committee.” 

Not only are drug compa- 
nies which face competitive 
pressures finding this situa- 
tion “distressing,” but the PA 
says, “it may also be unfair to 
consumers who might benefit 
from a favorable decision, ei- 
ther in relief from pain or dis- 
comfort or from lower medical 
bills, or both.” 

PA called for support of a 
“switch petition” in the form of 
supplemental new drug appli- 
cation. 

The proposal has been of- 
fered, but “is in limbo and has 
been for almost three years.” 

Such “procedural snags” 
must be removed for the “con- 
tinued transfer of appropriate 
ingredients and dosage 
strengths from prescription to 
OTC,” the association rea- 
soned.

NEWS IN BRIEF 


Eckerd opens third Visionworks 


TAMPA — Eckerd Corp. has opened its third “super” 
eyewear/eyecare store. The company’s latest, Vision- 
works, opened late last month ina cians center in Tam- 
pa. 
Eckerd’s first Visionworks opened last year in Clearwa- 
ter, Fla., and Charlotte, N.C., respectively. 

The new store is located in Visionworks Plaza in Tampa, 
opposite the University Square Mall. Like its predeces- 
sors, the unit stocks over 10,000 fashion eyeglass frames 
plus sunglasses, sports glasses, contact lenses, etc. The 
staff includes licensed opticians and optical technicians 
plus independent doctors of optometry and ophthalmolo- 
gy. Eckerd also operates 153 optical centers in five South- 
eastern states. 


Perry to offer $1.5M common stock 


PONTIAC, Mich. — Perry Drug Stores has filed a reg- 
istration statement with the Securities and Exchange 
Commission relating to the proposed offering of 1.5 million 
shares of common stock. 

Perry sources said that upon completion of this offering, 
it intends to effect a 5-for-4 stock split in the form of a 25% 
stock distribution. 

Proceeds of the offering will be used to repay a portion of 
short term bank indebtedness incurred in connection with 
several recent acquisitions by Perry. 

The offering will be co-managed by Prudential-Bache 
Securities, E. F. Hutton & Company, and Prescott, Ball 
& Turben. 


Buyers flock to Affil./Assoc. show 


NEW YORK — Buyers and executives from 75 drug 
chains converged on ds Omni Park Central Hotel here 
from May 20-23 to attend the spring buying show jointly 
sponsored by Affiliated Drug Stores and Associated Chain 
Drug Stores. 

Members of both organizations had an opportunity to 
visit 113 exhibiting vendors showing about 500 various 
lines for the back-to-school and Christmas buying seasons. 

The combined fall show is scheduled for Oct. 7-9, also at 
the Omni Park Central Hotel in New York City. 


Acme launches 3 combos 


PHILADELPHIA — Acme Markets plans to convert 
three existing supermarkets here into the company’s first 
combination food and drug stores. 

The conversions will be modeled after the Skaggs-Al- 
pha Beta combo stores operated by Acme’s parent, Ameri- 
can Food Stores headquartered in Salt Lake City. 

The first combo will open this fall in Kennet Square, 
Philadelphia. The existing 33,000 sq. ft. store will be ex- 
panded to 48,000 sq. ft. with 35,800 space allocated for sell- 


ing. 

in addition to pharmacy and extensive lines of H&BA 
and OTC products, the unit will also feature Acme’s first 
photo processing department plus a large assortment of 
general merchandise such as TVs, video recorders, small 
appliances, electronics, jewelry, film and watches.

NEW YORK — Are traffic- 
building, scratch give-away 
games the industry’s newest 
and possibly best answer to 
soft sales and declining mar- 
gins? 

With the first scratchoff 
game (Gray’s) just a few 
weeks into action and with the 
next two, Dart and People’s, 
slated to launch in the late 
summer and fall, it is too soon 
to give definitive answers, but 
an informal survey of chain ex- 
ecutives and agency represen- 
tatives say it may be the start 
of a new trend that holds “con- 
siderable promise.” 

‘““Everyone feels more 
threatened today,” says Gary 
Wilber, vice president of op- 
erations for Drug Emporium. 
“What you see emerging now 
is a determination to get more 
traffic without reducing the 
gross margin. 

“TI think you're going to see a 
lot more promotions like this. 
You're probably also going to 
see more promotions modeled 
after what the airlines are do- 
ing, frequency promotions, 
like, “buy 10 bottles of sham- 
poo from us and get the 11th 
one free.” “If a promotion like 
this can get a shopper to visit a 
store three times a week in- 
stead of two, you’ve got a po- 
tential winner.” 

Sources at Gray Drug Fair, 
which launched its first 
scratch off promotion in late 
April, said they were attract- 
ed by two things: the opportu- 
nity to build store traffic and 
consequently market share

At Gray, jury still out 
on scratch card game 


CLEVELAND — Gray Drug Fair, which has been using a 
sweepstakes-scratch-off game since late April to build sales and 
store traffic, isn’t sure how well the promotion is working. 

Store managers and other sources say the initial results are 
promising, but it is still “too soon to tell” if the game will suc- 
ceed. One source said average store sales were up about 8% to 
9% which he called “very encouraging.” 

Sweepstakes are not new to Gray, the company has tried 
them before to build traffic, but this is the first time the compa- 
ny has launched a promotion built around a scratch-off game. 

Customers who play the Gray “Lucky Labels game” can win 
prizes ranging from credit card size calculators to a round trip 
for two to the European city of their choice. 

Gray is giving away a total of $100,000 in prizes including four 
grand prizes (the European trips), 10 first prizes, a 19-in. G.E. 
color television with remote and video recorder; 25-in. G.E. 
black and white TVs with AM/FM radio; 100 Black & Decker 
Dust Busters, and 15,000 Aurora calculators. 

The promotion is chainwide and will last until the end of June. 

Although the company says that the co-op monies raised 
through the promotion don’t “really” filter down to the bottom 
line, neither does the promotion impact negatively on existing 


profit margins. 


McKesson’s latest buy:S-P Drug 


McKesson Drug, the nation’s largest volume 
drug wholesaler, has signed a definitive merg- 
er agreement to acquire Brooklyn-based S-P 
Drug. In 1984, S-P had sales of $164 million 
making it the country’s 17th highest volume 


wholesaler. 


The acquisition, which has been approved by 
the board of directors of both companies, will 
be McKesson’s third major takeover in the last 
six months. Earlier McKesson had acquired 
the $450 million Spectro Industries and the 


$120 million Johnson Drug. 


The current transaction is valued at $80 mil- 
lion based on the current number of outstand- 
ing shares for S-P. McKesson is paying $18 a 
share for S-P. Over the past four years, S-P 
Drug reported a compounded growth rate of 
22% in sales and 45% in net income. Net income

DRUG STORE NEWS, June 10, 1985 


Nn performance marks checkstand regulars 


hile most drug store 
checkstands carry a 
wide assortment of 


products, all of the items found 
in the front-end share the 
same three basic characteris- 
tics: high impulse appeal, good 
gross margins and fast turns. 

Competition among manu- 
facturers of the widely sought 
front-end location is fierce, 
even for those seeking only a 
three- to four-week run on the 
checkstand. However, a num- 
ber of product categories have 
managed to win a permanent 
home in the drug store check- 
stand. These high-performing 
front-end items include the 
following: 

Candy/gum 

The candy and gum assort- 
ment at the checkstand varies 
from chain to chain. Nearly 
every drug store features a 
rack at the checkout for gum 
and mints. However, an in- 
creasing number of drug 
chains are bringing single size 
candy bars into checkout loca- 
tions. 

Studies such as the Po- 
pai/Du Pont Drug Store Shop- 
per Study revealed that candy 
bars are among the most fre- 
quently purchased impulse 
items in drug stores. More- 
over, buyers point out that 
candy bars, which typically 
generate profit margins of 
30% and turn at a rate of more 
than 10 times a year, deliver 
some of the highest return on 
inventory investments of any 
checkstand item. 

The checkout configuration 
frequently dictates how much 
room a chain can provide for 
the candy section. Generally, 
chains with a front-end 
counter checkout configura- 
tion can allocate more space to 
single-size candy. 

Many Eckerd and Rea and 
Derick stores, for instance, 
merchandise candy bars and 
gum alongside the checkout 
counter on angled shelves. 

In some of the Los Angeles- 
based Thrifty drug stores, 


candy is merchandised verti- 
cally along with gum at the 
end of the checkstand counter. 
Industry studies have re- 
vealed that when candy and 
gum are merchandised verti- 
cally on a display rack, as op- 
posed to horizontally with 
gum at one level and candy at 
another, the consumer tends 
to scan the entire rack and is 
more likely to make a multiple 
purchase. 

While many chains mer- 
chandise candy at the check- 
stand, there are still some that 
have kept single candy bars in- 
line with bagged and boxed 
candy. One chain exec noted, 
“We can sell as much candy in- 
line as we could by the cheek- 
out.” 

However, there seems to be

a move afoot among more 
chains to cross merchandise 
some of the best-selling single 
candy bars in the front-end 
checkout area to take better 
advantage of impulse sales. 

In contrast to candy bars, 
most drug retailers agree that 
gum and mints belong at the 
checkstand. In addition to pro- 
ducing margins that range 
from 40% to 43%, gum and 
mints turn more than eight 
times annually. Retailers also 
point out that manufacturers 
such as the William Wrigley 
Co. have been extremely flexi- 
ble in designing display fix- 
tures that can carry a variety 
of other merchandise. 

At Peoples Drug Stores, for 
instance, the chain uses a 
Wrigley countertop display 
fixture to merchandise high- 
margin items such as key 
chains, nail clippers and 
combs. 

In addition to checkstand lo- 
cations, a number of chains 
have begun merchandising 
multipacks of chewing gum on 
endcaps directly across from 
the checkout. 

Tobacco and accessories 

Only candy and gum are 
merchandised more frequent- 
ly at the checkout area than 
cigarettes, according to a re- 
port compiled by Lebhar- 
Friedman Research. The sur- 
vey revealed that 77% of the 
chains regularly merchandise 
cigarettes at the main check- 
out area. 

Unlike many other front- 
end products, cigarettes are 
more of a planned purchase 
than an impulse buy. However, 
convenience is a key factor in 
placing cigarettes in the front- 
end. Drug stores have built a 
reputation among cigarette 
consumers as a primary retail 
outlet where they can pur- 
chase a pack of cigarettes at a 
good price and as quickly as 
possible. 

As with most other check- 
stand categories, the size of

of the back wall of the check-

Self-serve countertop dis-

cluttering the checkstand, Bill

“With tobacco you get about

found in the checkstand area, 
merchandising decisions are 
also a shared responsibility in 
many cases. 

A study of checkstand mer- 
chandising strategies, con- 
ducted by Lebhar-Friedman 
Research, revealed that oper- 
ations personnel were most 
heavily involved in the deci- 
sion-making process involving 
checkstand merchandise. Of 
the chains surveyed, the vp of 
operations played a major role 
in the checkstand merchandis- 
ing decisions in 47% of the 
cases. In addition, other key 
participants in the decision- 
making process included vps 
of merchandising and buyers, 
according to 37% of the chain 
respondents, district/regional 
managers (30%), merchandise 
managers (23%) and general 
merchandise managers (17%). 

While there is the potential 
for confusion in the front end 
with so many people assuming 
some responsibility for the 
section, most chains manage 
to keep a firm handle on things 
in the checkstand area by ad- 
hering closely to planograms. 
In addition, some chains have 
delegated one person to act as 
a type of “traffic cop” for the 
buyers and operations person- 
nel, tracking and scheduling 
the movement of merchandise 
into and out of checkstand dis- 
plays. 

Concern over the front end 
extends far up the corporate 
chain drug ladder. In one in- 
stance, a West Coast chain 
drug ceo was actively involved 
in the decision to merchandise 
single size candy bars at a 
checkstand position. 

At the same time, chains en- 
courage store managers to in- 
volve themselves in the front 
end as much as possible. The 
Lebhar-Friedman research 
study revealed that 53% of the 
respondents involve store 
managers and assistant man- 
agers in the decision-making 
process for front-end mer- 
chandise.

by the likes of Dart, nor would 
it be the victim of any green- 
mail attempt. 

The suit alleged among oth- 


er things that Dart had violat- 
ed the Federal securities law 
in acquiring 5% of Jack Eckerd 
stock and had filed a “false and 
misleading” statement with 
the Securities and Exchange 
Commission. 

Eckerd charged that Dart 
had claimed the stock acquisi- 
tion was for investment pur- 
poses, when Dart was actually 
seeking to gain control or to

NEWS IN BRIEF 


Genovese net earnings down 64% 


MELVILLE, N.Y. — Genovese Drug Stores cited 
“lackluster” same-store sales increases and “generally 
poor consumer spending” in reporting a 64% decline in net 
earnings for the 16-week first quarter ended May 24. Net 
income for the period was $317,000, or 8¢ a share, com- 
pared to $880,000, or 22¢ a share, a year earlier. Sales in- 
creased 11% to $68.6 million from $61.8 million. 


Perry launches 4th A. L. Price 


LANSING, Mich. — Perry Drug opened its fourth 
A. L. Price drug store here on June 6. 

The deep discounter, featuring cut case, stacked and 
high-tech warehouse style merchandising, marks Perry’s 
first presence in Michigan’s capital city. 

“It’s an important new market for us,” explained a com- 
pany spokesman. “We’re happy we were able to find a 
good location.” Future growth for the company in this par- 
ticular market is expected. 

The original A. L. Price (always low price), opened in 
1983 in Dearborn, followed by locations in Grosse Pointe 
Farms and Southfield. Two more deep discounters are 
planned for fiscal 1985.

Jones named exec. vp at Big B 


BIRMINGHAM, Ala. — Anthony 
J. Bruno, president of Big B Inc., an- 
nounced the promotion of Arthur M. 
(“Mac”) Jones as executive vp. 

Jones, 37, acertified public accoun- 
tant who joined the drug store chain 
in 1975, was previously vp of finance. 
Jones will continue to serve as secre- 4 
tary and treasurer of the corporation Arthur M. Jones 
and member of the board of directors. 

Before coming to Big B, he was employed by Arthur An- 
dersen & Co., a Big 8 accounting firm. He is a 1969 ac- 
counting graduate of Mississippi State University. 


Albertson’s income up 3.4% 


BOISE, Idaho— Albertson’s, the food and drug retailer 
based here, reported that first quarter net income rose 
3.4% to $18.7 million from 18.2 million the previous year. 
Sales for the quarter, ended May 2, increased 6% to $1.2 
billion from $1.13 billion during the same quarter last 
year. Earnings per share were up 3.6% to 57¢ from 55¢.

American sells shuttered Sav-On’s 


FRESNO, Calif. — Ameri- 
can Stores has sold four of its 
five shuttered Sav-On food/ 
drug combos in the San Joa- 
quin Valley to two major 
southern California food 
chains. 

The two 47,000-sq.-ft. Fres- 
no units were sold to Vons, 
and the Merced (47,000 sq. ft.) 
and Atwater (38,000 sq. ft.) 
combos to Lucky Stores. 

Vons calls its combos Value 
Centers, while Lucky’s combo 
loge is Lucky Discount Cen- 
ter. The pharmacy depart- 
ments are being retained. 

Still unsold is the Porter- 
ville property, former site of a 
47 ,000-sq.-ft. Sav-On combo. 

Sav-On opened the first 
store in Merced in the fall of 
1983 when Jewel Cos. owned 
the chain. Original plans were 
to open 10 food/drug combos in 
the San Joaquin Valley by the 
end of 1985.

DRUG STORE NEWS, June 24, 1985 


By Marjorie Shaffer 

rug stores are gearing up to de- 
fend their share of the $7 billion 
cosmetics and fragrance indus- 
try, as mass merchandisers and food 
stores continue to grab an increasing 

number of cosmetics customers. 
It’s going to be an uphill battle. Ac-

cording to the most recent A.-C. Niel- 
sen figures, drug stores held a 60% 
share of the color cosmetics market, 
which includes eye, lip, nail and facial 
makeup, losing two market share 
points to mass outlets. In 1984, mass 
merchandisers carved out a 24% share, 
up from 22% the previous year, while 
food stores held steady at 16%. 

Breaking it down by category, drug 
stores lost three percentage points to 
mass merchandisers in the eye makeup 
market in 1984. Drug stores held a 56% 
share, or $235 million, down from 59% 
in 1983. Mass merchandisers had a 26% 
share last year, up from 23% in 1983, 
while food stores held steady at 18% 
share. 

In lip, drug stores held onto their 
commanding share of the market with 
a 65% share, or $195 million, according 
to Nielsen. In facial makeup, drug 
stores held a 60% share, or $240 mil- 
lion, but lost over one market share 
point to mass merchandisers since 
1983. In facial creams and lotions, drug 
stores still command the lion’s share of 
the market with a 58% share, or $240 
million, but lost almost one point to 
mass merchandisers since 1983. 


While the battle rages for the cos- 
metics dollar, drug stores are creating 
a more upscale image, while also ap- 
pealing to the low end of the market. 
By covering all bases, retailers are 
hoping to offer increasingly price-con- 
scious consumers the best of every- 
thing, and, by most accounts, they are 
succeeding. 

At Genovese, for example, buyer 
Stephanie Hayter told Drug Store 
News that the chain is upgrading its 
planograms and expanding its entire 
cosmetics department to about 84 lin- 
ear feet. Pegged cosmetics are target- 
ed for expansion and a separate skin 
treatment area of about 8 ft. is also in 
the works. And the chain is also testing 
two prestige makeup lines, Arden and 
Lancome, in 12 stores. “Our customers 
expect to find prestige products,” says 
Hayter. 

At Carl’s, buyer Tom Neville says 
that the 42-store chain based in Rome, 
N.Y., is making a major push to up- 
grade all cosmetics departments. 
“We've decided to heavily promote our 
image as a cosmetics store,” says Nev- 
ille.

Lip 

The big news in lip is “mood” sticks. 

Pat Duckworth, buyer at Peoples re- 
ports that the sticks, which change col- 
or after application, are the hottest 
items around. Other buyers concur, 
but everyone is skeptical that the prod- 
uct will “stick” around for a long time. 

One buyer for a large western chain 
says that the lipsticks are “very suc- 
cessful, but are just a fad.” And Vikki 
Williams at Shoppers wonders wheth- 
er today’s sophisticated cosmetics cus- 
tomers are going to take to such novel- 
ty items. 

Helen James at Hook’s notes that 
the quality of some of the lipsticks is 
questionable, and she terms the prod- 
uct an “in and out item.” But Shirley 
Northrop, a buyer for British Colum- 
bia-based Londen Drugs notes that the 
lipsticks, which have just come into the 
stores, is a “terrific idea,” though she 
also wonders how long the fad will last. 


Fragrances 


Vanderbilt remains the best-selling 
women’s fragrance in drug stores, ac- 
cording to Smith Barney. Over 70% of 
the buyers surveyed for the report 
gave Vanderbilt top honors, and a huge 
lead over second-placed Forever Krys- 
tle, which received 25.7% of the vote. 
Tied for third place was Ciara and Hal- 
ston, each with 13.3% of the vote.

But the real story in fragrance is 
prestige brands, often diverted, which 
account for as much as 30% of volume in 
some chain drug stores. Not only have 
prestige fragrances brought an up- 
scale look into drug stores, they have 
also been a terrific traffic draw. In- 
deed, the fragrance selection in many 
drug stores rivals that of many of the 
finest department stores. 

Peoples’ Duckworth, for example, 
Says that prestige fragrances are con- 
sistently strong sellers, particularly 
during Christmas when sales dramati- 
cally increase. Last August, Peoples 
began planogramming prestige brands

Body sprays 


Body sprays, which showed 
strong sales in 1984, may be 
flattening out because of too 
many introductions. The ma- 
jor brands, Body Flowers and 
Impulse, are strong in some 
markets, but weak in others. 

Greg Ostroff, a cosmetics 
analyst with Goldman Sachs, 


says that the category will not 
last. “It never really took off,” 
he notes. “Lots of ad bucks 
were spent for nothing in re- 
turn.” 

Other observers, however, 
disagree. One buyer from a 
Seattle, Wash.-based chain, 
for example, reports that body 
sprays, in general, have fared 
poorly, but that the Parfums 
de Coeur line of fragrances 
has shown some strength. 

Super D’s Pratt agrees. She 
notes that while Impulse sales 
are slowing down, the Design-

American’s aim for 86: 


20 new combo stores 


SALT LAKE CITY — American 
Stores expects to open about 20 combo 
stores during fiscal 1986. 

The combos, which security ana- 
lysts say yield the company a 20% re- 
turn on investment, will be located in 
Wichita, Kan., and Wichita Falls, 
Tex.—both markets identified by 
chairman L. S. “Sam” Skaggs as hav- 
ing plenty of “growth potential.” 


@ See related story page 3 


The new combos will be pperenes ei- 
ther under the Skaggs/Alpha Beta 
banner or as Jewel/Osco stores. 

With about 262 combos now in oper- 
ation, American is the country’s lead- 
ing operator of pure combination 
stores. Some chains define combo 
stores as any food store with a pharma- 
cy department, but American’s com- 
bos literally include a full size drug 


store with pharmacy, cosmetics and 
expanded health & beauty aids, under 
the same roof as its food store. As of 
March 31, 1985, American had 92 
Skaggs Alpha Beta combos, 116 Jewel- 
Osco combos and three Buttrey-Osco 
combos, all in a total of 28 states. 

In fiscal 1986, American tentatively 
will open 36 combination food and drug 
stores. American will not comment on 
growth plans for 1987 and beyond but 
the common expectation is that the 
company will continue to expand. 

henever American talks about fu- 
ture growth prospects, it always iden- 
tifies combo stores as well as “super” 
sized drug stores and expanded food 
stores as preferred growth vehicles. 

The company has targeted some 
$280 million for capital expenditures in 
1986 and analysts are estimating that 
approximately 30% will be spent on

SGC’'s growth agenda calls 
for more deep-discount units 


SECAUCUS, N.J. — Supermar- 
kets General Corp. will open 12 to 15 
freestanding drug stores this year, 
half of which will operate under a deep- 
discount format, including the compa- 
ny’s first in Albany, N.Y. 

Leonard Lieberman, SGC’s presi- 
dent and ceo, told shareholders at the 
company’s annual meeting here that 
with 15 deep-discount units already in 
operation, “SGC has rapidly become 
one of the largest operators of deep- 
discount drug stores in the country.” 

The deep-discount stores include 
the recently acquired Heartland units 
and the Pathmark Super Drug units 
which were unveiled in Baltimore last 
year. 

However, rapid store growth has 


temporarily put a dent in the drug 
store division’s operating income, said 
Lieberman, who added that its perfor- 
mance “has declined principally as a re- 
sult of the new store expansion.” 
Three of the new deep-discount 
units will be Heartland drug stores, 
the off-price chain that SGC acquired 
as part of the Purity Supreme pur- 
chase last year. The remaining three 
deep-discount stores will carry the 
Pathmark Super Drug banner. 
Underscoring the importance of the 
company’s growing drug store and 
nonfood sales in its grocery stores, 
Leonard Lieberman, SGC’s president 
and ceo, told shareholders here that 
drug and nonfood sales represented

IN BRIEF _ 


FoxMeyer acquires Calif. supplier 


DENVER — FoxMeyer has acquired Devco Medical 
Industries of Santa Fe Springs, Calif., a supplier of medi- 
cal and SS. supplies to hospitals. 

Devco will be FoxMeyer’s fifth hospital supply division 
and the first in the Golden State. Others are in Denver, 
Oklahoma City, Kansas City and St. Louis. 

“This department is not big historically,” said Richard 
Bard, president of the wholesale company, “but we expect 
it to grow into the $200 million range in the next couple of 
years.” 

Bard conceded that “breaking into California with a 
small drug division [Devco does $25 million a year] will 
make it easier for FoxMeyer to enter California as a 
wholesaler, but not right now. We need time to assimilate 
our two most recent acquisitions—McPike and Yahr- 
Lange of Wisconsin—before contemplating our next 
move.” 

Bard denied rumors that FoxMeyer was negotiating 
with Pay ’n Save to buy Northwestern Drug asa way 
to break into the West Coast wholesale drug market. 


SupeRx expands food/drug sections 


CINCINNATI — Kroger is expanding its convenience 
food/drug sections inside its freestanding SupeRx drug 
stores. 

Kroger executives said that SupeRx is adding a “limited 
assortment of convenience foods to its larger stores, while 
in new facilities and in remodels, as many as 1,000 grocery 
and perishable items are being offered in addition to the 
typical drug store selection.” 

Sales in 1984 for SupeRx drug stores rose 8.8% to $859.5 
million, even though the chain’s total square footage re- 
mained “virtually” unchanged since4983. SupeRx plans to 
open 24 new stores in 1985, and will remodel about the 
same number of existing stores. 

SupeRx currently operates 620 stores in 20 states, in- 
cluding 24 SupeRx food and drug stores in Florida. 


NACDS name Welsh as exec vp 


ALEXANDRIA, Va. — The National Association of 
Chain Drug Stores Inc. has named William Z. Welsh Jr. 
executive vp and chief operating officer. Welsh, who 
joined the NACDS in 1975, was most recently corporate 
secretary. Welsh will report directly to Robert J. Bolger, 
president and ceo of the NACDS.

ALCO Standard revenues up 5% 


VALLEY FORGE, Pa. — 
ALCO Standard Corp.’s sec- 
ond quarter figures showed 
that revenues, net income and 

rimary earnings per share 
rom continuing operations 
were all ahead of the same 
quarter last year. 

Net income rose 13% to 
$15.5 million, or 70¢ per share, 
from last year’s $13.8 million, 


and 62¢ per share. Revenues 
were up 5% to $872 million, 
from $829.3 million. 

For the six months ended 
March 31, the figures were 
also ahead of last year’s. Net 
income grew by 13% to $32.1 
million, up from $28.4 million 
in 1984, 

While ALCO’s other opera- 
tions were affected by “soften- 


ing business conditions” dur- 
ing the second fiscal quarter, 
the company’s health services 
showed a 20% rise in revenues 
to $247.9 million while income 
before taxes grew 24% to $5.7 
million. 

ALCO Standard is the 
country’s third largest whole- 
sale drug company with 1984 
revenues totaling $3.4 billion.

For the nine months, net in- 
come rose 3% to $18.3 million 
(LIFO), or $1.45 a share, from 
$17.8 million (FIFO), or $1.41 
a year ago. 

Under the LIFO method, 
last year’s earnings for the 
nine months from continuing 
operations would have in- 
creased 25%. 

Sales and other revenues 
for the nine months increased 
40% to $1.75 billion from $1.26 
billion in the same period last 
year. 

Commenting on the results, 
Emil P. Martini Jr., chairman 
and ceo, said that although 


“acquisitions completed earli- 
er in the fiseal year had a ma- 
jor impact on sales growth for 
the quarter, the results from 
existing operations exceeded 
internal growth targets. 
Earnings contributions from 
these acquisitions are also 
meeting objectives.” 

Martini said the company 
was “pleased with the integra- 
tion of the medical supplies 
units of Synergex.” He said 
the medical supply division 
was continuing to show signs 
of renewed sales growth. 

In Bergen’s consumer elec- 
tronics division, Commtron 
Corp., Martini said sales 
should exceed $300 million for 
the current fiscal year.

TC conversions 
to bolster healtn 
of cough/cold 


ith two more top-seiling prescription cough/coid 
and allergy products going over the counter this 
year, drug retailers are expecting another block- 
buster year from the cough/cold category. 

This year’s new entries include Dimetapp, the cold and 
allergy product from A. H. Robins, and Benadryl, the an- 
ee and antihistimine/decongestant from Parke- 

avis. 

Both Dimetapp and Benadry] join a cough/cold/allergy 
category that has undergone a radical transformation in 
recent years as a resuit of the Rx to OTC conversions of 
such hot-performing prescription drugs as Actifed, Drix- 
oral and Sudafed. 

So successful have these conversions been that last year 
Actifed and Drixoral each had two of the top 10 selling OTC 
products in dollar sales, according to the Drug Store News 
Top 100 OTC List. 

Retailers are betting that Dimetapp and Benadry] will 
follow in Actifed and Drixoral’s footsteps. But their grand 
entry may also accelerate the passing of a number of pe- 
rennial favorites in the department. Some buyers already 
have begun weeding out some of the unproductive cough 
and cold products to make room for the newcomers. 

Since its introduction in 1961, Dimetapp has racked up 
an impressive record as one of the most frequently pre- 
scribed cold remedies for both adults and children. Ac- 
cording to Robins, approximately 146 million prescrip- 
tions were written for Dimetapp from 1973 to 1983, 
compared with 123 million for Actifed and 55 million for 
Drixoral. 

Robins expects that as an OTC drug, Dimetapp will 
probably generate four times the estimated $54 million it 
did in sales as an Rx product. The company believes that 
Dimetapp’s market share after its first year as an OTC 
product, coul:. fall somewhere between Actifed’s 5.1% 
share and D~ixoral’s 7.4% after their first year as OTC. 

To capture that kind of market share, Robins will sup- 
port Dimetapp with an extensive television and print bud- 
get during the cold season that will well exceed $5 mitlion.

Differing plans used to raise feminine hygiene sales 


n 1984, according to A. C. 

Nielsen, food stores com- 

manded 60% of the sani- 
tary napkin market, down 2 
share points since 1983, while 
drug stores trailed, a distant 
second, with 25.5% share, up 
0.5% over the previous year. 

With the flurry of new sani- 
tary napkin products on the 
market and limited shelf 
space, chain drug stores are 
going in two directions to 
maintain their share of the 
market. Some are cutting 
back drastically on slow-mov- 
ing sku’s and hoping to lure 
shoppers looking for conve- 
nience, while others are pro- 
viding a huge selection in an 
attempt to nab shoppers who 
would otherwise buy pads in 
food stores. 

Major surgery is now being 
carried out at Fay’s, where 
buyer Ray Meissner last year 


added 33 sku’s of pads. He is 
now cutting back on slow-mov- 
ing sku’s like minipads and 
some of the 12 and 48 sizes, in 
other pad lines. Other buyers 
agree that the sku’s they add- 
ed last year are beginning to 
thin out on their own and cut- 
backs are being made based on 
consumer response. 

But Ribordy Drugs based in 
Valparaiso, Ind., buyer John 
Weal has taken a different 
tack. “We believe that selec- 
tion is the key because the cus- 
tomer is so confused by all of 
the various types of napkins on 
the market,” he told Drug 
Store News. “Until we can 
make some wise decisions, we 
don’t want to cut out any 
wrong sku’s, and lose part of 
our business,” he added. 

In order to accommodate 
95% of all the sku’s on the mar- 
ket—about 87 according to 


Weal—Ribordy has reduced 
all pad products, except pri- 
vate label, to one facing. 

Currently the $930 million 
sanitary napkin market 
breaks down into four catego- 
ries: superabsorbent thin 
maxis; pantyliners; full-size 
thick, and minipads. Accord- 
ing to a report by Salomon 
Brothers, superabsorbent 
thins are the growing market 
with a 30% share, while the 
market for minipads is steadi- 
ly declining. 

A survey of buyers at Ri- 
bordy, Sentry, Page and Fay’s 
and other chains confirmed 
that the minipads are dying 
while the superabsorbent-thin 
pads are moving well. But 
buyers agree that the public 
needs to be more educated 
about the convenience of the 
superthin maxi pads.

Tambrands. The metal in- 
creases production of the bac-

shock syndrome.

Now it’s

from its products, while Tam-

Super Plus brand.

share of the tampon market, 
have recently launched new 
products. Tambrands brought 
out its three-sku line, Petal 
Soft, which has a plastic appli- 
cator, in January. And Playtex 
fought back with its early 1985 
launch of Slender Regular for 
younger women. Retailers re- 
port fairly good sales in both of 
these lines.

Revco launches 3rd Get It For Less 


TULSA, Okla. — Revco opened its third Get It For 
Less deep-discount store here on July 15. 

Revco’s second Get It For Less opened earlier this year 
in Minneapolis. The first unit opened in Memphis in 1983. 

In an earlier interview with Drug Store News Budd 
Dworkin, sr. vp marketing, said that the chain would open 
three more Get It For Less stores this year in markets 
where the format will not compete with conventional 
Revco outlets. Memphis, Minneapolis, and now Tulsa are 
all areas where the company does not operate Revco drug 
stores. 

Sidney Dworkin, Revco’s chairman and ceo, said the 
Tulsa store will be similar to the 23,000-sq.-ft. Minneapolis 
mall location. 

In Tulsa, only one other deep-discount store is currently 
operating—The Drug Warehouse run by Tulsa-based 

ay’s Drug. 


Walgreens: June sales up 12.1% 


DEERFIELD, Ill. — Walgreen Co. said June sales in- 
creased 12.1% to $254.8 million from $227.2 million in the 
same month last year. “Our June prescription sales were 
excellent,” said Charles R. Walgreen III, chairman. “The 
category continues to benefit from the Intercom pharma- 
cy computer system and strong generic sales.” 

Walgreen said that customer counts have been “steadi- 
ly increasing in established stores”—those open two year's 
or more. Calendar year-to-date sales were up 15.1% to 
$1.54 billion. 


Sentry moves Ways & Means merch. 


ROMULUS, Mich. — Sentry Drug Stores is injecting 
merchandise from its Ways & Means specialty store, a 
joint venture with Citrin Corp., into 10 of its conventional 
drug stores. Sentry opened the Ways & Means outlet ear- 
lier this year in Birmingham, Mich. 

The Ways & Means merchandise being placed in the 
drug stores consists of up to 300 of the best-selling items 
specifically designed to help people perform everyday 
tasks more easily. 

According to Chuck Fugate, Sentry’s vp of operations, 
the merchandise is being placed in sections ranging from 
32 linear feet to 64 linear feet. The Ways & Means depart- 
ment is being placed adjacent to pharmacy. 

_ Sentry plans on opening five drug stores this year bring- 
ing the total store count to 22. The store now operates 18 
drug stores and one Ways & Means outlet.

Peoples eyes mega-optical unit 


ALEXANDRIA, Va. — Peoples Drug 
Stores, which has already diversified into 
deep-discount drug stores, freestanding and 
in-store optical departments, and fast-food res- 
taurants, is considering opening a mega-optical 
store featuring hundreds of high-priced fashion 


eyeglass frames. 


The concept, similar to Eckerd’s Vision 
Works, which opened last year in Tampa, is un- 
der consideration now, and a possible test unit 
may open before the year is out. 

“We've done very well with our eyeglass cen- 
ters per se,” says Peoples vp of advertising Joe 
Pollard, “and we can see that there’s a potential 
to make money with a mega-store. People are 
more fashion-conscious today, and many peo- 
ple buy more than one pair of eyeglasses.’

Harrison seeks support 


m for Reagan tax proposal 


HOUSTON — Jim Harrison, president of Harco Drug and 
chairman of the National Association of Drug Stores, speaking 
from th podium of this year’s NACDS cosmetics show, called 
on industry members to strongly support President Reagan’s 
proposed income tax reforms. 

alling the proposed reforms “a needed program whose time 
has surely come,” Harrison said it was particularly a. 
for the industry to be assertive in support of the president be- 
cause his proposed reforms “will surely receive heavy criticism 
from many special interest groups.” 

Harrison reminded the audience of chain executives and cos- 
metics H&BA manufacturers that the president’s proposal 
would “lower tax rates by eliminating or reducing many exist- 
ing tax credits, deductions and exclusions that would set indi- 
vidual tax rates at 15, 25 and 35%.” Corporations, he also point- 
ed out, would be taxed at a flat 33%. 

He said these amendments would create “a level playing field 
for all American industries” and would also be a “welcome relief 
to retailers who have long been among the highest effective tax 
rate payers in this country.” 

Harrison stressed that the average effective tax rate for all 
industries in this country is 16.7%. “Compare that,” he said, “to 
our industry where the ighest effective tax rate exceeds 40%. 

“It is obvious,” he said “that tax preferences for the few cre- 
ate higher taxes for the many.” 

Harrison concluded by saying that the NACDS “strongly 
supports a fairer and simpler tax code for all Americans and is 
playing an active role through its lobbying and coalition efforts 
to achieve that objective.”

Congress urged to reject beer territory bill 


WASHINGTON — Con- 
sumer activists and antitrust 
enforcement officials joined 
representatives of the nation’s 
drug chains in urging Con- 
gress to reject legislation 
which could prompt sharp 
price increases for ae and 
other malt beverage products. 

_ Testifying at Seeate Judi- 
clary Committee hearings late 
last month, officials from the 
Consumer Federation of 
America warned that propos- 
als legalizing anticompetitive 
exclusive territorial restric- 
tions on beer distributors 
could result in overnight price 
hikes of 20% to 30% to retail- 


ate hearings—including anti- 
trust policy makers from both 
the Federal Trade Commis- 
sion and the Justice Depart- 
ment—called the beer indus- 
try proposal a “dangerous” 
attempt to “weaken competi- 
tion... by facilitating collu- 
sion among [malt beverage] 
distributors.” 

Those charges echoed earli- 
er criticisms from the Nation- 
al Association of Chain Dru 
Stores, which is working with 
other retail groups to short- 
circuit the pending legislation. 

According to NACDS offi- 
cials, the Beer Bill would ef- 
fectively eliminate competi- 


ers to force retailers to pur- 
chase only from a single desig- 
nated distributor. 

Similiar “exclusive territo- 
ry” laws have already been 
adopted in a number of states, 
and studies of the impact of 
those statutes support the 
chain drug industry’s con- 
cerns. 

One government price sur- 
vey found that the cost of beer 
or tg 30% in 10 months fol- 
owing the adoption of exclu- 
sive territories in New York 
City, while a separate study 
reported that Indiana beer 
prices dropped 20% since 
wholesale territorial restric- 


beck told Congress. 

The Justice Department’s 
acting antitrust chief, Charles 
Rule, stressed that his opposi- 
tion to the Beer Bill does not 
reflect opposition to exclusive 


territories in general, howev- 
er. 

State antitrust officials also 
testified against the Beer Bill 
at last month’s Senate hear- 
ings, 


ed March 31.

ho are the drug store 
market makers’ 
The Triple A list- 


ings of the Top 100 products in 
units, dollars and profits give a 
fair indication. 

This year’s 16th annual 
study shows the diversity of 
products that make up the 
best-selling lists. It also gives 
a reading of how top market- 
ers like Procter & Gamble, 
Richardson Vicks, Johnson & 
Johnson, Kodak and Pola- 
roid—to name just a few— 
continue to dominate drug 
store shelves. 

For retailers, the study 
showcases the products that 
add promotional power to the 
merchandise mix. These are 
products that can pull traffic 
because of their national repu- 
tation. Consumers look for 
value in these products and 
shop the stores that promote 
them. 

To compile this study, Drug 
Store News gathered and 
blended 1984 warehouse with- 
drawal figures from a geo- 
graphically diverse group of 
medium to large chains. 

This year, for the first time, 
Drug Store News broke out 


general merchandise products 
from the traditional health & 
beauty aids and over-the- 
counter best-seller lists to see 
how they would fare on their 
own. 

While breaking out general 
merchandise did open up the 
H&BA/OTC list for more 
items, the newly created 
places tended to be taken by 
different sizes and flavors of 
the strongest sellers—not 
surprising in light of the na- 
tional ad support given the top 
products. 

The breakout did add diver- 
sity of the Top 10 H&BA and 


OTC product lists. Take the 
Top 10 unit movers, for exam- 
ple. On that rarefied list, there 
were two baby products, but 
only one each of laxatives, skin 
care, shaving, analgesics, eye/ 
lens, antacids, feminine hy- 
giene and cough/cold. 

Among the Top 10 dollar 
generators, there were two 
each of diet aids, skin care and 
baby products, and only a sin- 
gle sku each of vitamins, femi- 
nine hygiene, dental and anal- 
gesics. A similar diversity was 
found among the Top 10 profit 
generators. 

In contrast, the Top 10 


places on the general mer- 
chandise lists were dominated 
by just two product catego- 
ries: film and batteries. In unit 
sales, for example, there were 
five battery items, three film 
sku’s, a household supply item 
and a paper product. In dollar 
sales it was all film and batter- 
ies. Film took seven places and 
batteries the other three. The 
story was no different for the 
Top 10 profit generators—five 
battery items and five film 
items. 

The Top 100 lists in the 
H&BA/OTC area were domi- 
nated by four categories— 


Triple A products deliver profits to chains 


dental, cough/cold, analgesics 
and baby products—followed 
by three others slightly less 
dominant—diet aids, eye/lens 
care and feminine hygiene. 

Cough/cold products, for 
example, took 15 places on the 
dollar list, 13 on the unit list 
and 21 on the profit list. Anal- 
gesics accounted for 16 places 
on the dollar list, 13 on the unit 
list and 14 on the profit list. 
And dental products took 11 
places on the dollar list 19 on 
the unit list and 10 on the prof- 
it list. Not surprisingly, the 
highly promoted baby prod- 
ucts, which accounted for 11 
places on the dollar list and 14 
on the unit list, managed only 
three on the profit list. 

Five categories alone— 
cough/cold, analgesics, den- 
tal, diet aids and eye/lens— 
took 51% of the places on the 
Top 100 dollar list, 52% of the 
places on the Top 100 unit list 
and 58% of the Top 100 profit 
generator places. 

In considering the Triple A 
study, it is apparent that the 
Top 100 lists are dominated by 
highly consumable products 
whose sales are driven more 
by demand than impulse.

10, with positions two, four 
and five.

price points, Polaroid film

retail sales, with three sku’s 
holding positions one, two and 
eight.

10, up one from last year, but it 
gave up second position to Po- 
laroid’s hot SX-70 film.

Revco takes $98 million ~ 
Odd Lot headache remed 


By Marjorie Shaffer 

TWINSBURG, Ohio — Revco has washed 
its hands of a long and bitter dispute which 
rocked the 1,900-store chain and embroiled 
management in expensive litigation. 

Bernard Marden and Isaac Perlmutter, the 
two Odd Lot principals who owned nearly 12%, 
or 4.4 million shares, of Revco stock, have been 
sent packing. 

In an agreement struck with Revco, Marden 
and Perlmutter are allowed to enter the whole- 
sale distribution business through a new com- 
pany by paying Revco $3 million in cash. But 
they are prohibited for 10 years from purchas- 
ing Revco stock and from retailing close-out 
merchandise. 

In exchange, Revco repurchased all of the 
former Odd Lot owners’ 4.4 million shares for 
$22.50 per share, or $98.2 million. The day be- 
fore the agreement was completed, Revco 
shares closed on the New York Stock Ex- 
change for $23.25 per share.

Walgreens earnings up 12% 


DEERFIELD, Ill. — Walgreens reported that net 
earnings for the third quarter ended May 31 increased 12% 
to $21.5 million from $19.2 million in the comparable year- 
earlier period. Sales were up 15.7% to $792.6 million. 

For the nine months, net earnings rose 14.6% to $68.1 
million, or $1.11 per share, from 
share, in the same period last year. Sales increased 15.7% 


During the nine months, the company has opened 87 
stores and plans to open 21 more during the final quarter. 
The company also anticipates a 6¢ a share gain from the 
sale of its Mexican affiliate during the fourth quarter.

By Tim O’Brien 

CLEARWATER, Fla. — 
Eckerd Drug will launch a new 
dimension in point-of-pur- 
chase promotion next month 
when it goes “on the air” with 
a complete in-store radio 
broadcasting system. 

“We're rolling into our 115 
stores in the Houston market 
first,” said Eckerd’s advertis- 
ng manager, Mel Ardelean. 
“Then we'll roll out the con- 
cept on a controlled chainwide 
basis.” Ardelean said all 1,525 
Eckerd stores will be 
equipped with their own POP 
radio station by the year’s 
end. 

Point-of-purchase radio is 
an in-store radio entertain- 
ment concept that uses a pro- 
fessional announcer and car- 
ries paid advertising. To the 
consumer, it sounds more like 
a traditional radio station than 
a custom made selling tool. 

The concept got its original 
test at CVS in iy and June of 
1984. “We called it WCVS Ra-

Radio, the company that de-

poned. The new management 
wanted to look at alternatives 
before making a commitment,

eau, CVS’s vp of advertising 
and sales promotion. 

Peoples Drug is currently 
testing the concept, and ac- 
cording to Joe Pollard, vp of 
advertising, management 
likes what it hears so far.

ing called, was tested by the 
chain in its Tampa-Clearwa-

ber and December, and the re-

Shoppers launches Winnipeg Howie’s 


WINNIPEG, Canada — Shoppers Drug Mart, the 400- 
store Canadian drug chain, has opened its first “Howie’s— 
More Than a Drug Store,” in the city of Winnipeg. 

Howie’s, a separate division of off-price drug stores, 
also operates two stores in Montreal and two in Toronto. 
According to David R. Bloom, president and ceo, there 
will be “as many as 25 Howie’s locations spread across 
Canada within the next five years.” 

This particular store is the first drug store in Manitoba 
Province to be fully scanner equipped. 


Perry converts 27 Apex units 


PONTIAC, Mich. — Perry Drug Stores has completed 
the conversion of the 27 Apex stores acquired in March. 
All the Metro Detroit Area stores now have the Perry 
name and format. 

As special employee training sessions were being held 
for the 750 Apex employees with Perry policies, workers 
remerchandised, refixtured and resigned all the stores. 

Pharmacy computer terminals were installed in all 27 
stores in three days. 

Apex stores are now serviced by Perry’s Pontiac ware- 
house and are included in Perry’s advertising and promo- 
tional programs. 


Harris to purchase Narco 


CLEVELAND — Harris Wholesale Co., the largest 
privately held drug wholesaler in the country, has signed 
an agreement to purchase Narco Drug Co. of St. Louis. 

Narco, a major supplier of pharmaceuticals to retaiiers 
and hospitals in the St. Louis area, will operate as a subsid- 
iary to Harris. Narco’s management team, headed by Eu- 
gene T. Luning, chairman, will remain in place. 


Valu-Rite management reorganized 


SAN FRANCISCO — In a move to 
strengthen support services to its 1,600 Valu- 
Rite pharmacies, McKesson Corp. has institut- 
ed major changes in the organization structure 
of the voluntary co-op program. 

The biggest change is that Valu-Rite, for- 
merly 1 of 19 independent operating units of 
the Drug & Health Care Group, has now been 
integrated into McKesson Drug. 

And rather than reporting to Rex Malson, 
president of the group, Valu-Rite’s manage- 
ment will report to McKesson Drug’s excutive 
vp, Joe Polastri. 

In addition, promotional account managers 
have been relieved of some of their service 
functions, including merchandising, signage, 
displays and decor, and will be free to concen- 
trate on advertising. 

The service functions will be taken over by 
newly appointed zone service sales managers. 
To date, dienes has appointed such manag- 
ers in four of its nine regions: Northeast, 
Southeast, northern California, and Pacific 
Northwest, with the remaining five regions 
due to be implemented by the end of the cur- 
rent fiscal year next March. 

Ron Bone, president of Valu-Rite, told Drug 
Store News: “Because we are now working 
closer with McKesson, we can draw on their 
marketing resources; it wasn’t as easy when we 
were not at the same management meetings.” 

An exec with a wholesale drug competitor 
says: “The zone sales manager move makes 
sense. As a self-standing company, the Valu- 
Rite sales force was selling against the McKes- 


son sales force to some extent.” 

However, the wholesaler also notes that 
“Valu-Rite has lacked variety in merchan- 
dise—they had some of the same items—such 
as k.d. desks—for five years. If you don’t 
change every two years, your promos go sour.” 


A veteran drug supplier, who competed 
— Valu-Rite when he owned a promotion- 
al sundries company, told Drug Stores News: 
“Valu-Rite has not made money for years. The 
reason McKesson keeps it alive is that it pro- 
vides the drug retailer with a total resource for 
goods and services. And McKesson wants the 
drug business.” 


Arthur Lichtendorf, New York security an- 
alyst, says: “Valu-Rite has been overinventor- 
ied, and they’ve taken some writeoffs. To cor- 
rect the situation, they’ve changed their 
buying patterns. Before, they first bought the 
goods and then arranged the promotion. Now 
they have a prebooking system before order- 
ing. I also expect to see Valu-Rite expand their 
private label program because Tom Field 
(McKesson president) is experienced in private 
label and committed to quality products.” 


McKesson purchased Valu-Rite—then oper- 
ated by Super Specials—from Hyatt Hotels in 
1977. Before the acquisition, Valu-Rite was 
strictly a promotional sundries company, and 
its main vehicle was the circular. McKesson 
broadened the program to include private la- 
bel, coupon redemption, magazine rebates, 
sunglasses, store fixtures, photo finishing, and 
signs, in addition to circulars.

Harrison: two-tier drug prices 


TORONTO — Jim Harmri- 
son, chairman of the National 
Association of Chain Drug 
Stores, responding to allega- 
tions about the proliferation of 
counterfeit drugs within the 
diversion marketplace, called 
the existence of counterfeit 
products within the retail 
drug store industry a “totally 
unacceptable phenomenon 
that cannot be tolerated.” 

Speaking to about 270 chain 
retailers and manufacturers 

thered here for the annual 

ACDS General Merchandise 
show, Harrison called for 
“stricter and more rigid en- 
forcement of laws regulating 
the distribution of illegally di- 
verted and counterfeit 
drugs.” 


Asserting that legislative 
reforms are needed, atten 
said that part of the problem 
with counterfeit drugs and il- 
legally diverted drugs arises 
from the existence of a two- 
tier pricing structure for phar- 
maceuticals in this country. 

He described the existing 
two-tier system as one 
“racked with abuse” and said 
that it is “a major contributing 
factor to the illegal diversion 
of drugs.” 

Harrison said that to coun- 
teract the situation, NACDS 
is currently developing a com- 
prehensive set of statutory 
recommendations for Con- 
gress. 

The centerpiece of those re- 
forms, he said, is a strong call 


factor in Rx counterfeit stream 


for a “major overhaul of the 
Non Profit Institutions Act.” 

Pointing out that it is often 
difficult, it not impossible, for 
a retailer to know the “true 
source” of a drug, given the 
current state of affairs, Harri- 
son urged retailers to be “ever 
vigilant” in their buying prac- 
tices. 

He warned that offers and 
promotions must be “carefully 
scrutinized to be sure of their 
legitimacy and integrity.” 

arrison said that if the di- 
verter market is going to con- 
tinue to “have a place in the 
distribution system,” that it 
“must find a way to be sure it 
has ‘not itself, purchased for 
redistribution counterfeit or 
illegally diverted drugs.”

Sales set records 
at Thrifty Drug 


LOS ANGELES — For the first nine months of fiscal 
1985, Thrifty reported record-high sales and earnings. 

Sales for the period ended May 31 increased 8.4% to $1.04 
billion compared to $961 million over the same period last 
year. Sales for the third quarter ended May 31 increased 9% 
to $342 million from $313.6 million for last year’s quarter. 

Net earnings for the third quarter increased 18% to $5.6 
million compared to $4.8 million for the same period last 
year. For the nine-month period, net earnings were up 16% 
to $23.5 million from $20.3 million last year. 

Same-store sales for the third quarter increased 6%. 

Thrifty now operates 546 drug and discount stores and 82 
sporting goods stores plus it owns 34% of Crown Books, a 
profitable chain of 181 book stores. Thrifty also owns a 50% 
interest in the Trak Auto parts chain. The combined results 
of these companies reduced Thrifty’s income before taxes 
for the nine-month period by $1.03 million.

275,000- to 300,000-sq.-ft. 
range.

a cost of $41 million.

Rite Aid rolls out scanners chainwide 


By Bruce Buckley 

SHIREMANSTOWN, Pa. — Rite Aid 
Corp. has begun a chainwide rollout of one of 
the most sophisticated new in-store computer 
systems in the retail drug industry. 

Rite Aid, which operates more than 1,300 
drug stores, expects to complete the installa- 
tion at a rate of about 50 new stores a month. 

The system, designed by Bensalem, Pa.- 
based SASI (Stores Automated Systems Inc.), 
integrates point-of-sale scanning cash regis- 
ters with a powerful computer located in each 


store manager’s office. 


A separate pharmacy computer system with 
its own central processing unit is also linked to 
the central computer in the manager’s office. 

According to Duane Ruble, senior vp, Rite 
Aid anticipates that scanning alone will gener- 
ate an overall saving of one-half to three-quar- 
ters of a percentage point, mainly from the la- 
bor savings in eliminating item price marking 
and from weeding out cashier ring-up errors. 

Thai is not a negligible saving for a company 
whose drug stores generated aimost $1.3 bil- 

Continued on page 38 


Faster checkout has not been a big factor in Rite 
Aid’s scanning system, but price accuracy has.

NEWS IN BRIEF 


Medi Mart launches two units 


BOSTON, Mass. — Medi Mart Drug Stores opened its 
64th and 65th stores simultaneously on Saturday, Aug. 10. 
The new stores are located in Enfield, Conn., and Wake- 
field, Mass. The stores feature the chain’s new bold and 
colorful graphics package and new planogramming, in- 
cluding wider aisles. The Wakefield store also has a small 
convenience food department featuring bakery and dairy 
products, frozen foods, snacks and drinks. 


Begley sales up in 1st quarter 


RICHMOND — Begley company reported an increase 
in sales and net profits for the first quarter ended June 30. 
Sales climbed 6% and earnings 9% compared to the same 
period last year. During the quarter the company opened 
one drug store, one home health care center and five dry 
cleaning stores. Begley now operates 43 drug stores and 
six home health care units. Robert Begley, chairman and 

resident, said the company plans on opening two more 
ome health care centers by the end of the year. 


Commtron acquires Cibcoa 


LOS ANGELES — Bergen Brunswig Corp. has an- 
nounced that its wholly owned subsidiary, Commtron, a 
leading distributor of prerecorded video tapes, has signed 
an agreement to acquire Cibcoa Inc., a nationwide distrib- 
utor of consumer electronics. 

Under the terms of the agreement, Bergen Brunswig 
will pay Cibcoa an undisclosed amount of cash and notes. 
The closing will take place at the end of August. 

Cibcoa’s anaineed sales volume totals about $80 mil- 
lion, while Commtron expects to have revenues in excess 
of $300 million when the fiscal year closes on Aug. 31. 

“The combination of Commtron’s expertise in prere- 
corded video tapes and Cibcoa’s strength in consumer 
electronics should provide a convenient source for most of 
the requirements of the customers served by both compa- 
nies,” said Emil P. Martini Jr., chairman and ceo of Ber- 
gen Brunswig. 


Hook’s launches Mich. unit 


INDIANAPOLIS — Hook’s, the 303-store drug chain, 
has expanded its market area into Michigan. The chain re- 
cently opened its first in that state in a new strip center in 
downtown Niles, Mich., a community of 13,000, just five 
miles north of South Bend, Ind. 

The new store, in the new state, is not the beginning of a 
grand plan for expansion into Michigan, but just “a logical 
extension of a market in which we already have seven 
stores. The new store just happens to be in a different 
state,” said Hook’s Tom Dingledy. 

The 7,500-sq.-ft. store is a “typical Hook’s prototype” 
and will be able to benefit from the South Bend’s market’s 
efficiencies in advertising and distribution.

store manager was eager to 
experiment and the store’s 
proximity to Liverpool, N.Y., 
the headquarters of the 129- 
unit chain, made it an even 
— desirable site, said Da- 
ey. 

In New York, the fate of 


computerized point-of-sale 
scanning in drug stores will 
depend on the extension of a 
state law stipulating that all 
merchandise in certain retail 
establishments must be price 
marked. 

Although this law, which 
expires at the end of 1985, is 


primarily directed at food and 
mass merchandise retailers, 
Daley said that Fay’s legal 
counsel felt that it might even- 
tually affect drug stores. Con- 
sequently, scanning would not 
be financially feasible if all 
items in a drug store had to be 
price marked, said Daley. 


Revco launches 
Ohio scanning test 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — 
Reveo expects to launch its 
first “pure” in-store scanning 
test in the Cleveland area lat- 
er this month. 

The scanning test will prob- 
ably be followed in five or six 
months with a one-store test 
of a full blown in-store com- 
puter integration system. 

Both tests will initially con- 
centrate on cost justification. 
Revco executives hope to 
break even on the scanning in- 
vestments within six months 
to a year. 

Revco has already had posi- 
tive results from its test of 
scanning in its Get It For Less 
deep-discount drug stores, 
and the company has been re- 
ceiving product-movement re- 
ports and other types of scan- 
ning data from the marketing 
research company Informa- 
tion Resources. Executives at 
I.R. have been monitoring 
and collecting product-move- 
ment data from scanners they 
installed in a handful of Revco 
stores. However, in the I.R. 
program, known as Beha- 
viorScan, Revco does not own 
the scanners and does not ¢con- 
trol the program. 

The scanning test will en- 
able Reveo’s vp of systems 
Scott Leeseberg to tailor the 
scanner programs to Revco’s 
needs. 

The initial test will be very 
basic, using a price look-up 
system that ha pies capture 

roduct movement. Leese. 
erg expects results from the 
test to allow the program to be 


expanded to three or four 
stores “relatively quickly.” 

The computer store inte- 
gration test will also be done in 
a store located close to Revco 
headquarters, but it will prob- 
ably not be in the same stores 
as those testing scanners. 

Over the past few years, 
Revco has gradually been re- 
placing most of its cash regis- 
ters with those that are up- 
gradable to both scanning and 
store integration. 

In the store integration 
test, a personal computer will 
link the front-end registers to 
Reveo’s main frame at head- 
quarters. The intregration 
will enable Revco to automate 
a series of functions including 
direct store deliveries, inven- 
tory control, electronic mail, 
price updates, product dele- 
tions and additions and mark- 
downs. 

In the scanning part of the 
experiment, Revco will be us- 
ing a combination of both slot 
scanners and hand guns. 
Leeseberg thinks that if scan- 
ning does justify its cost, the 
pee will probably use a 
combination of both systems 
in future stores, but the test is 
also designed to see if one sys- 
tem is superior to the other. 

Leeseberg does not expect 
to have to make any major de- 
sign modifications in Revco’s 
store layout to accommodate 
the slot scanner. It will proba- 
bly just be incorporated into 
the counter or directly next to 
the front-end counter as it cur- 
rently exists in Revco stores.

Vol. 7, No. 18 August 19, 1985 


By Lou Karney 

RICHMOND, British Columbia — London 
Drugs, the first Canadian drug chain to install 
checkout scanners, has installed them in 11 
stores, with four more scheduled by Novem- 
ber. The remaining nine stores will be complet- 
ed by June 1986. 

Scanners are the first step in London’s five- 
year $17 million to $20 million long-range sys- 
tems plan. 

Currently, 55% to 60% of all items stocked 
are UPC-coded at the source. This represents 
80% of merchandise sold. Of the remaining 
40%-45%, all but 12%-15% are UPC-coded at 
the store, with the balance—accounting for 
about 7% of store sales— rung up manually. 

London’s checkout scanners are NCR 
T9020. At headquarters, a model 19020 tele- 
communications processor pulls sales and fi- 
nancial data from the stores at the end of each 
rs | and transmits the information to a Wang 
VS/100 for storage in a master file. The Wang is 
the storage center for merchandising, ware- 
housing, accounting, and office functions. 

Tied to the Wang in the main office are desk 


terminals for employees in all departments at 
all levels—executive, office, warehouse, ac- 
counting. Buyers use the Wang to generate 
purchase orders, while the warehouse process- 
es receiving and shipments to the stores. 

Eventually, London will install an in-store 
system which will pull together all existing and 
future systems in the stores, such as time/at- 
tendance, pharmacy, POS, and direct store de- 
livery. 

London is no stranger to store-level comput- 
erized systems—pharmacy terminals were in- 
stalled eight years ago. 

Pat Fisher, London’s manager of informa- 
tion systems, told Drug Store News that the 
short-term priority of the program is to get im- 
poe merchandising information to buyers. 

ong-term, it is to build an improved manage- 
ment information system for executive and 
store-level management. 

“We are in an increasingly competitive mar- 
ketplace,” says Fisher, “and we feel these sys- 
tems will enable us to get the required informa- 
tion on time, as well as helping us keep a lid on 
support costs.”
