McKesson profits rise 21%, revenue up 19% 


SAN FRANCISCO — For 
the first quarter of fiscal 1986 
which ended June 30, McKes- 
son Corp. increased revenues 
19% to $1.4 billion, while in- 
come from continuing opera- 
tions was up 15% to $16.9 mil- 
lion. 

Operating profit increased 
by 21% to $44.5 million. The 
record results reflected 
strong performances by the 
company’s Drug & Health 
Care, Beverage and Develop- 
ment groups, according to 
Neil E. Harlan, chairman and 
chief executive officer. 

After deducting corporate 
expense and interest expense, 
which increased because of 
borrowings to finance the re- 


cent acquisition of Spectro In- 
dustries, pretax income rose 
17% to $32.5 million from 
$27.8 million. 

Harlan said the company’s 
cash flow would enable it to re- 
duce its debt quite rapidly and 
operating profit will drop to 
tne bottom of the income 
statement. 

Net income was $16.9 mil- 
lion compared with $15.4 mil- 
lion, a year earlier. The re- 
sults last year included a profit 
of $691,000 or 3¢ a share from 
discontinued operations. 

The company’s Drug & 
Health Care Group, which ac- 
counted for 64% of first quar- 
ter revenues and 48% of oper- 
ating profit, reported a 29% 


rise in revenues to $878.7 mil- 
lion and a 28% gain in operat- 
ing profit to $21.5 million. The 
gains were led by the group’s 
wholesale drug distribution 
operations, which now in- 
cludes Spectro, acquired in 


May, and Johnson Drug, ac- 
, aii last December. Drug 

roup results were adversely 
impacted by continuing losses 
by the group’s 3PM unit, a de- 
veloper of pharmacy comput- 
er systems. 


Bindley net income up 14% 


INDIANAPOLIS — Bind- 
ley Western Industries has re- 
ported that net income for its 
second quarter ended June 30 
increased 14% to $1.4 million, 
up from $1.26 million for the 
same period in 1984. Earnings 
per share increased to 22¢ 
from 20¢ a year ago. 

Sales for the second quarter 


were up 7% from the 1984 fig- 
ures, to $142.8 million. 

For the first half of 1985, the 
company’s net income in- 
creased 17% to $2.66 million, 
up from $2.3 million. Earnings 
per share rose to 41¢ from 36¢ 
during the first half of 1984. 
Sales for the first two quarters 


totaled $296.9 million, up 12%.

Antacids remain ‘profit center’ - 


rug stores once again led all 
other retailers in the market 

place in the sale of antacids. 
Last year, according to A. C. Niel- 
sen, drug stores accounted for 50% of 
the dollar volume in the $700 million in- 
dustry. Food stores were next with a 
42% share, and mass merchandisers 
were far behind with 8% of the market. 
The 8.7% growth rate of the antacid 
sections in chain drug stores iast year 
came mainly from inflationary growth 


and not unit movement. 

“Antacids have been a good profit 
center for us in the past,” said Begley’s 
Dennis Osborne, “Even though there 
appears to be a decline in the user base, 
department margins in the low 30% 
range makes it an important category 
for us.” 

Osborne, and most of the other buy- 
ers Drug Store News talked with, sees 
nothing dramatic happening, or about 
to happen, in the antacids department, 


Stephen Lund of Perry’s predicts the 
category will stay somewhat static. “It 
doesn’t look like it has much growth po- 
tential because when a new product 
does come out, it grows at the expense 
of the older products, so all we’re get- 
ting is a user shift within the catego- 
ry.” 

On the other hand, Raymond Free- 
man, a buyer with the Southwest Drug 
store chain in Jackson, Miss., sees his 
antacid section on an upward swing. 
“It’s a growing category for us,” he 
said. “I think the faster life style and 
the hustle and bustle of everyday life 
contributes to upset stomachs and gas. 
In turn, there’s a greater demand for 
products.” 

Whether they agreed on its growth 
potential or not, the buyers all agreed 
that the category in general has lacked 
some pizazz in recent years. 

“It’s still profitable, but it’s not a 
very exciting category anymore,” said 
a spokesman for Maalox. “In fact, it’s 
been somewhat boring lately.” 

The spokesman was referring to the 
fact that while most drug store catego- 
ries have super star products or prom- 
ising rising stars, the antacid section 
has been void of innovations for several 
years. 

Unlike the neighboring laxative de- 
partment that’s having a good year 
with bulk-fiber laxatives, there are no 
real runaway products in the antacid

are doing well, but the stimu- 
lant varieties are still the sales 
leaders in the category,”’ 
pointed out Stephen Lund, a 
buyer for Perry. “While the 
stimulant segment is holding 
its own, the new bulk products 
are bringing added sales into 
the category.” 

In the traditional laxative 
area, “Fleet enema is by far 
the unit movement leader,” 
said Lund, “and our private la- 
bel and Ex-Lax are the !ead- 
ers among the stimulant 
types.” 

Dennis Osborne, a buyer at 
Begley, agrees that “bulks are 
steadily increasing their mar- 
ket share within the laxative 
category.” 

As the health aspects of fi- 
ber and bulk are publicized, 
Osborne sees the segment 
growing even further. “People 
are buying the bulk forming 
laxatives as a fiber supple- 
ment, and not solely as a laxa- 
tive,” he said. 

The fiber that forms that 
bulk in most of the products is 
the hulk and seed from the 
Psyllium plant, grown primar- 
ily in India. 

“Calling these high fiber 
products laxatives is really a 
misnomer,” said Bill Steiber, 
sales and marketing director 
for Lafayette Pharmacal, 
makers of Konsyl. “They are 
really bowel normalizers that 
work equally well on diarrhea 
and constipation.” 

Steiber pointed out that his 
products, Konsyl and Konsyl- 
PD, as well as the other prod- 
ucts in the category, are not 
used for quick acting relief of 
constipation as the stimulant 
type laxatives are. “We make 
it clear that several days’ use 
will probably be needed to es- 
tablish reglarity. In fact, these 


products should be used on a 
daily regimen to work efiec- 
tively.” 

One Midwest pharmacist, 
after observing and talking 
with shoppers in his store, 
concluded, “It appears that 
bulk-forming products appeal 
more to the person who wants 


to prevent future problems.” 


Even with the publicity bulk 
fiber products are getting, the 
old standbys remain impor- 
tant in the drug store product 
mix. “Sure, fiber is big now 
and the price point is much 
greater, but we are still doing 


great numbers with Ex-Lax 
and Correctol,” claimed Os- 
borne. 

Fad or just a healthful ap- 
proach to one’s diet, the bulk 
laxative is an emerging and 
important segment of the cat- 
egory. “The funny thing,” one 
buyer commented, “is that 
Metamucil has been around 
for about 50 years and really 
had no major competition. 
Now it seems everybody is 
getting into the bulk laxative 
area.” 

Industry sources all agree 
that Metamucil controls “at 


least” 75% of bulk laxatives . 

Originally, manufacturers 
of most of the bulk laxatives 
shied away from consumer ad- 
vertising, and relied solely on 
doctor and pharmacist detail- 
ing, as well as some limited 
trade advertising. Now, most 
of the major products are be- 
ing featured in consumer print 
advertising as well as some 
TV promotion. 

On the retail level, many 
buyers said that their chains 
were somewhat hesitant to ad- 
vertise and promote laxatives 
in the past because of the low- 


er price points on most of the 
stimulant variety laxatives. 
Now, with the popularity of 
the bulk fiber variety, the 
same margin of 30% to 35% ex- 
ists, but the higher price 
points make it more feasible to 
promote and give in-store dis- 
play space. 

“We've been promoting the 
bulk laxatives quite heavily,” 
said Perry’s Lund. “Primarily 
because of their current popu- 
larity and because of their 
higher price points, they’ve 
become quite a promotional 
item for us.”

Fixers carving out niche as HMO’ 


Pharmacists nationwide are 
+ “1 y for a place in the $10 
billion HMO industry business 
that some analysts say could 
reach as high as $70 billion by 
1990. 

According to a report by the 
National Association of Chain 
Drug Stores, health mainte- 
nance organizations have en- 
joyed a remarkable growth 
pattern in the last 12 years. 

Since 1973, the year federal 
legislation was introduced of.- 
ficially recognizing the HMO 
aS an alternative form of 
health care delivery, the num- 
ber of HMO’s increased from 
30 to 270. NACDS reports 
that the growth rate is expect- 
ed to continue with more than 
a 250% increase in the number 
of HMO’s over the next seven 
years. 

Many drug chains, alarmed 
by the rapid growth, have set 
out to capture their share of 
the prescription business gen- 
erated by HMO’s by becoming 
contract providers. 

Most commonly known as 
independent practice associa- 
tion (IPA) HMOs or Pre- 
ferred Provider Organizations 
(PPO’s), those HMO’s that do 
not have their own pharma- 
cies offer the greatest oppor- 
tunities for community or 
chain pharmacists to cash in on 
this booming market. 

According to the American 
Medical Care and Review As- 
sociation, a national organiza- 
tion representing these types 
of HMOs, there are 160 IPA- 
type HMO’s, encompassing 
04,000 participating physi- 
clans and a combined enroll- 
ment of over 2.8 million enroll- 
ees. 

While industry sources Say 
it is nearly impossible to esti- 
mate the number of pharma- 
cies currently enrolled as pro- 
viders to these HMO’s. they 
do say that the list is growing. 

As part of a PPO, a pharma- 
cy agrees to offer a variety of 
Services outlined in a contrac- 
tual agreement with a particu- 
lar HMO. Aside from filling 
prescriptions based on a spe- 
cific pricing schedule, these 
may include mandatory pa- 
tient profiles, home delivery 
of prescriptions and consulta- 
tion. 

Chain drug stores are in the 
best position to provide these 
services because HMO’s 
would typically rather send 
their patients to a drug chain 
that has several locations near 
the HMO’s address. 

Pharmacists view the IPA- 
type HMO less threatening 
than the staff HMO, where 
rescriptions are filled in- 
eae

eryone visiting an HMO for 
medical treatment will have 
his prescription filled at the

marketplace.

retail pharmacy, chain or in- 
ushiont. by the end of the 
century.”

action to lift the dark cloud 
hanging over the profession. 

Maryiand pharmacists are 

lobbying state legislators to

chain, from their benefit pro-

agreements are met. The goal 
is to eliminate exclusive con- 
tracts by HMO’s with certain 
providers.

0.”

bership are that many custom- 
ers consider service and con-

the money saved by being in-

from an HMO,” said Granat.

Continued from page 29 

While pharmacists believe 
that bid purchasing and pref- 
erential pricing gives HMO’s 
an unfair advantage in the 
marketplace, Miller’s study 
shows differently. 

According to his results, 
82% of the HMO’s studied said 
the most effective method of 
cost containment was limiting 
the amount of medication dis- 
pensed. Eighty-one per cent 
said the use of copays was the 
second most effective method 
in keeping costs down. Only 
11% of the respondents cited 
bid purchases as an important 
factor in cost containment. In 
fact, bid purchases ranked 
eighth out of a possible nine 
methods for keeping costs toa 
minimum. 

Other methods included a 
maximum allowable cost pro- 
gram (24%), drug bulletins 
(53%), co-insurance (14%), 
physician peer review (43%), 
patient drug use review (57%) 
and capitation (6%). 

Miller’s study also found 
prescriptions were offered by 
06% of the HMO’s as part of 
their basic benefit program, 
while 44% made it optional. In 
38% of the HMO’s, prescrip- 
tions were listed on a formu- 
lary, 69% said that there was 
no prescription formulary in 
use. 

Three-quarters of the re- 
spondents said that oral con- 
traceptives were covered, 
23% said they were not. When 
it came to coverage of OTC 
drugs, the results. were just 
the opposite. Three-quarters 
said they were not covered, 
while 25% said that certain 
OTC drugs were covered.

NEWS IN BRIEF 


Bindley stock drops to 914 per share 


INDIANAPOLIS — Following charges by the FBI 
that three former Bindley Western executives were alleg- 
edly involved in drug diversion schemes, the price per 
share of Bindley stock plummeted to a low of 9% from 
around 13 on the New York Stock Exchange. The stock 
had previously reached a high of 15% this year. At pres- 
stime, Steve Asher, a former vice president for Bindley, 
pleaded guilty to charges of fraud in the acquisition of di- 
verted pharmaceuticals. 


Alco sells 40% health service stock 


VALLEY FORGE, Pa. — Alco Standard sold 40% of its 
stock in Alco Health Services to the public, generating $68 
million. According to financial analyst Bill Jellin, a securi- 
ty analyst who follows the drug wholesaling industry, Alco 
will use the proceeds from the sale to acquire other drug 
wholesaling companies. Alco isa diversified $4 billion com- 
pany with about $1 billion generated through drug whole- 
saling. Aleo Health Services is the third largest drug 
wholesaler in the country after McKesson and Bergen 
Brunswig. 


Medicare-Glaser suffers $138,000 loss 


ST. LOUIS — Although Medicare-Glaser’s first quar- 
ter net sales increased to $21.1 million, an 8.9% increase 
over last year, the company experienced a first quarter 
loss of $138,000, or 5¢ per share. For the same three 
months of last year, the company showed a profit of $114,- 
000, or 4¢ per share. 


Begley income rises 14.6% 


RICHMOND — The Begley Co. reported that net in- 
come for the first quarter, ended June 30, was $229,390, an 
increase of 14.6% over the same period last year. Earnings 
per share increased to 42¢ from 36¢. 

Total sales and operating revenues increased 6.1% to 
$16 million-$9 million from $15.9 million. A quarterly cash 
dividend of 18¢ per share was declared. ~ 

Begley currently operates 43 retail drug stores in Ken- 
tucky, and has 131 Big B, Key and Superior dry cleaning 
stores in nine states. Additionally, the company operates 
six home health care centers in Kentucky. 


Walgreens sales up 15.1% 


Walgreens reports that its July sales rose 15.1% to 


$224,728,000. For the year to date, management says July 
sales were up 15% to $1.795 billion.

Chains report sales surge 


NEW YORK — After a 
sluggish six months, chain 
drug executives are reporting 
that comparable store sales 
are finally on the upswing. 

Executives for chains like 
Reveo, Medicare Glaser, Dart 
Drug, Adams, Perry, etc., re- 
port that consumer confidence 
seems to be rebounding, and 
as a result year-to-date same- 
store sales are up anywhere 
from 6% to 20% depending on 
the chain and the market. 

Some executives say the 
primary surge seems to be 
coming from seasonal and gen- 
eral merchandise categories, 
but others are also seeing 
strong trends in H&BA and 
OTC products as well. 

Prescription sales for most 
of the chains surveyed always 
were strong. 

“Sales are definitely perk- 
ing up,” says Revco’s senior 
vp of marketing Mare Dwor- 
kin. “We noticed it in June, 
but the trend has been even 
stronger in July.” 

Dworkin said that Revco, 
which had been struggling 
with flat sales for the early 
part of the year, enjoyed com- 
parable store sales increases 
of 8.8% for all of June and they 
were exceeding 10% last 
July. 

Harlan Steinbaum, presi- 
dent of Medicare Glaser, re- 

orted a similar trend in the 
St. Louis metro market. 

“July has been better than 
April or May or June,” he said. 
“July sales have also been 
stronger than July sales last 
year. It’s a good trend line, 
and we're hoping it’s an indica- 
tion of even better things to 
come.” 

In the Baltimore, D.C. mar- 
ket, Al Towle, chairman of 
Dart Drug, also reported 
stronger sales, particularly in 
seasonals and general mer- 
chandise lines. Towle said 
part of the surge seems to be 
due to weather-related fac- 
tors. 

“It was colder than expect- 
ed up here and people seemed 
to hold off buying seasonals,” 


he said, “but now they seem to 
be making up for lost time.” 

Most executives said they 
hoped the stronger sales were 
the result of their latest adver- 
tising programs, but most also 
said they weren't sure that 
they were doing anything that 
different. 

“Primarily, I think. it’s the 
economy,” said Dwrkin. “I'd 
like to take credit for it, but I 
think people just feel a little 
more comfortable with the 
government and with infla- 
tion.” 

Steinbaum felt that some of 
the stronger sales may be due 
to Medicare’s latest TV/radio 
campaign launched last 
month, but he also said that at 
least some of the surge has to 
be due to “increased consumer 
confidence in the economy.” 


performance could be im- 
proved by the economies and 
the programs FoxMeyer of- 
fers. 

Bard pointed to McPike, 
which FoxMeyer acquired last 
spring, as an example. He said 
the Kansas City, Mo.-based 
wholesaler was a good compa- 
ny whose sales were more 
than $225 million. Neverthe- 
less, McPike stood to gain 
from FoxMeyer’s Health Mart 
drug store franchising pro- 
gram, its trucking and com- 
puter companies, and from a 
streamlining of its sales force. 

Bard added that the price of 
many acquisition targets had 
now risen to a point where it 
made the economics doubtful. 
“Clearly,” he said, “we’re not 
going to be jumping at those 
prices.” 

As a result, he said, Fox- 
Meyer would probably be 
looking at opportunities out- 
side of the drug industry. He 
said that when prices in the 
drug distribution industry are 
so high, “one has to look at oth- 
er distribution opportunities 
because the concepts are not 
so different.” 


Kroger to Hook: Manage 
SupeRx home health unit 


NASHVILLE — Kroger 
Co., parent of SupeRx Drug 
and Hook Drug, has effected 
the first synergistic consolida- 
tion of its two drug divisions. 

Kroger has transferred the 
management of SupeRx’s only 
Home Health Care store here 
to the Hook division which op- 
erates 16 home health care 
stores. 

The reorganization immedi- 
ately gave the store access to 
the vast buying economies 
that the Hook Convalescent 
Aids Centers already had 
available. 

“We'll gain access to several 
suppliers that we weren't able 
to deal with before,” said 
Steve Babineaux, the manag- 
er of the 4,000-sq.-ft. facility 
in the Nashville suburb of 
Madison. 

The management transfer 
was a logical move for The 
Kroger Company, since Su- 
peRx’s home health care staff 
was at a point on the learnin 
curve that Hook’s staff mie 
about seven years ago. 


“It gives us a better chance 
for success and less waste of 
our staff’s time,” said one Su- 
peRx source. “It all adds up to 
a more efficient operation.” 

Since the midsummer 
switch, the manager has al- 
ready seen his cost of goods re- 
duced. “Our acquisition costs 
have already been reduced,” 
he claimed. “And I’m sure 
we'll find more advantages.” 

The store is expected to 
keep the SupeRx name be- 
cause of the strong presence 
SupeRx already has in the 
Nashville market. This is 
Hook’s first venture into Ten- 
nessee. 

The Madison store fits into 
the Hook’s concept of a home 
health care center quite nice- 
ly. It’s a bit smaller than 
Hook’s standard 6,000-sq.-ft. 
store, but the line of durable 
and nondurable goods is quite 
similar as are the services of- 
fered and overall standard op- 
erating procedures. The ratio 
of sales vs. rentals is also quite 
similar.

DRUG STORE NEWS, September 2, 1985 


VALLEY FORGE, Pa. — 
Alco Standard Corp., one of 
the country’s largest distribu- 
tors of drugs and health ser- 
vices, reported that revenues 
for the third quarter ended 
June 30 increased 16% to $1.01 
billion from $876 million in the 
comparable period last year. 

ird-quarter net earnings 
from continuing operations in- 
creased ae"! to $18 million 
from $17.5 million. Earnings 
per share from continuing op- 
erations were 79¢ vs. 75¢ (pri- 
mary) and 75¢ vs. 73¢ (fully di- 
luted). 

For the first nine months 
revenues increased 11% to 
$2.79 billion from $2.50 billion 
in the same period last year. 

Nine-month net income 


from continuing operations 
was up 9% to $49.8 million 
from $45.9 million. Earnings 
per share from continuing op- 
erations increased to $2.24 
from $2.02. 

The company took a write- 
down of $1.5 million on discon- 
tinued operations in the first 


— and $3.97 million on 
iscontinued operations for 
the nine months. 

Revenues from Alco’s 
health services business in- 
creased 22% to $236.6 million 
in the first quarter and 26% to 
$697.8 million during the first 
nine months. 


Perry plans stock split 


PONTIAC, Mich. — Perry Drug Stores declared a 3-for- 
2 stock split, the third such split in the past four years. The 
split increased the number of shares outstanding to 9.8 mil- 


lion from 6.5 million. 


“This stock split continues to reflect the exceptional rec- 
ord of our company,” said Jack Robinson, chairman and ceo. 

The additional share will be distributed Sept. 10 to share- 
holders of record Aug. 22. Holders of Perry common stock 
will get one share for each two held. 


Alco Standard hits $1B in sales Medicine Shoppe 


net income up 17% 


ST. LOUIS — Medicine 
Shoppe International, the 
leading franchiser of drug 
stores in this country, report- 
ed that its net income for the 
third quarter ended June 30 
increased 17% to $742,345, or 
21¢ ashare, from $633,566, or 
18¢ a share, in the same period 
last year. 

Revenues for the first quar- 
ter were also up 17%, to $3.4 
million from $2.9 million last 
year. 

For the first nine months, 
net income increased 36% to 
$2.1 million, or 61¢ a share, 
from $1.6 million, or 49¢ a 


share, in the same year-earli- 
er period. 

ales for the nine months 
rose 23% to $10.2 million from 
$8.3 million. 

The company also reported 
that the number of new fran- 
chises rose during the first 
quarter to a record 55, com- 
pared to 14 for last year. 

Pharmacies in operation in- 
creased by 65 for the first nine 
months, a figure equal to the 
total number of pharmacies 
opened in fiscal 1984. 

The company said operating 
earnings for the third quarter 
increased 41%.

Product mix 


According to the study, 
chains and independents both 
try to stock a broad variety of 
OTC products to give their 
customers as much of a selec- 
tion as possible. Chains were a 
little more likely than inde- 
pendents to stress variety in 
their mix while independents 
were a little bit more likely to 
stock only the major three to 
five brands in each of the dom- 
inant OTC product categories. 

Oddly enough, however, 
the independent OTC buyer 
was more likely than the chain 
buyer to use an everyday com- 
er pricing strategy to 

ring in customers. Fifty-sev- 
en per cent of all independent 
responses agreed with the 
statement “we stay competi- 
tive with other drug stores in 
our market” compared to just 
40% of all chains. 

Chains, however, were four 
times as likely to use low pro- 
motional prices to lure in cus- 
tomer traffic. Some 43% of the 
chain respondents said that 
they relied on sales and low 
promotional prices to attract 
traffic rather than staying 
competitive overall with other 
stores in their market. Only 
10% of the independents fol- 
lowed that strategy. No one 
had a “we are never undersold 
policy,” and independents 
were twice as likely as chains 
to use their full-service fea- 
tures to justify that pricing. 


Advertising 

Print ads were an important 
vehicle for OTC advertisers. 
In print ads which featured 
OTC products, those OTC 
brands advertised constituted 
an average 43.2% of all the 
preducts featured. 


The ads run by drug chains 
tended to be larger than ads 
run by independents and to 
numerically feature more 
OTC products. But, the inde- 
pendents in their ads gave the 
OTC category a more impor- 
tant role: 51.3% of all products 
in an average independent ad 
were OTC items compared to 
just 36.3% for all products in 
an average chain ad. 

The average drug chain 
tended to mention 84.2 prod- 
ucts in their typical ads while 
the average independent ads 
generally totaled about 36 

roducts. Of the 84 products 
eatured in an average chain 
ad, some 22 or 36% were OTC 
items while for those average 
independent ads which fea- 
tured 36 products, some 15 or 
51% were OTC items.

a week compared to 37% of all 
independents. A third of all 
chains and all indys, however, 
did promote OTC’s at least 
once or twice a month.

had climbed. Four out of 10 
said it was because of pricing 
strategies. Many buyers said

which operate seven and 13

state of Indiana. 

The 30-year-old Ribordy 
drug chain is headquartered in 
Valparaiso—about a two-hour 
drive from Walgreens head- 
quarters.

Centralized distribution is new tack for American 


By Lou Karney 

SALT LAKE CITY — In 
consolidating its three drug 
divisions—Osco, Skaggs and 
Sav-On—into a single super- 
drug chain, American stores is 
centralizing its distribution 
center. 

The move to centralized dis- 
tribution, following the acqui- 
sition of Jewel Companies in 
1984, represents a 180-degree 
turn, since American’s chair- 
man, Sam Skaggs, has always 
been an advocate of supplying 
stores through drug wholesal- 
ers. 

A security analyst who 


tracks the company says that 
Osco changed Eanoy think- 
ing. “Osco, the most profitable 
of the drug divisions, has been 
a centralized operation for 
ears,” the analyst said. “And 
ick George, president of 
Osco—who in essence is the 
president of all the drug 
stores—is calling the shots.” 
At the core of the new align- 
ment are four distribution 
centers that will supply drug 
store merchandise and phar- 
maceuticals to American drug 
stores. 
Of the four centers, only the 
one in Payson, Utah, is a com-

WILSONVILLE, Ore. — 
Pay Less NW has installed 300 
new on-line POS registers and 
expects to have 3,000 in place 
by the end of 1986. 

A major benefit of the new 
registers is their adaptability, 
according to Jim Baer, vp of 
data processing. “Every com- 
pany has different priorities. 
Ours is on-line processing of 
bank and debit cards through 
direct hook-up with the bank.” 

Baer said that it will now 
take only six seconds to pro- 
cess a bank transaction, as op- 
posed to a minimum of three 
and a half minutes. “That 
speeds up the checkout opera- 
tions,” he explained. 


Osco’s Dick George 
*. . calling the shots 


Hardware for the new reg- 
isters is being manufactured 
by a company in Portland, 
Ore., under contact with Pay 
Less. Software was designed 
in-house. 

When a debit card is used to 
pay for a transaction, funds 
are transferred electronically 
from the customer’s account 
to the Pay Less account. 
When a credit card is used, the 
customer’s credit is first 
checked electronically. Thus, 
losses from bad checks, poor 
credit, or fraudulent cards are 
eliminated. 

Another major benefit of 
the register, according to 
Baer, is that it is software-

Perry reduces prototype by 2,000 sq. ft. 

PONTIAC, Mich. — Perry is reducing its prototype 
drug store about 2,000 sq. ft., to 10,880 sq. ft. from 12,500 
sq. ft., according to Mickey Kole, president of the compa- 
ny’s drug store division. 

The chain, which currently operates 183 drug stores, 
decided to downsize its drug stores to decrease occupancy 
costs and improve productivity. 

Kole said that “marginal merchandise” will be eliminat- 
ed in the smaller stores. Such merchandise includes non- 
traditional, exotic items such as paint and — sup- 
plies and, in some locations, live animals and boats. Perry, 
which may have the distinction of being the only drug 
chain to carry pets, is currently conducting a study to de- 
termine the viability of that department. 

In line with the elimination of exotic merchandise, Kole 
said that Perry would expand traditional drug store de- 
partments like cosmetics and health & beauty aids. 


Big B’s 2nd quarter sales rise 


BIRMINGHAM, Ala. — Big B reported that earnings 
for the second quarter increased 3% to $959,000, or 15¢ a 
share, from $930,000, or 14¢ a share, in the same period 
last year. Sales for the quarter, which ended Aug. 3, were 
up 17.5% to $38.3 million from $32.5 million. 

For the first half, profits increased 7.8% to $2.2 million, 
or 34¢ ashare, from $2.1 million, or 31¢ ashare, in the com- 

arable period a year ago. Sales for the half rose 20.2% te 
$83.3 million from $69.3 million. 

Big B, which operates 113 drug stores, five combos and 
three home health care centers, is in the midst of a heavy 
capital expansion program, with 20 new units set to open 
during the current year. Work is also under way on the 
company’s new 240,000-sq.-ft. office and distribution cen- 
ter, which will open this fall 


Rite Aid names Auchey vp 


HARRISBURG, Pa. — Rite Aid announced that Don- 
ald Auchey has been named vp of store planning. Auchey, 
who had been vp of facility engineering for Smith Manage- 
ment Corp., the Salt Lake City-based food and drug retail- 
er, will oversee design and construction of new stores as 
well as the remodeling of existing ones. He is also in charge 
of the purchase and manufacture of equipment and fix- 
tures used by Rite Aid. 


Alco acquires Valdosta 


VALLEY FORGE, Pa. — Alco Health Services Corp., 
the nation’s fourth largest drug wholesaler with sales of al- 
most $1 billion, has acquired Valdosta Drug Co., Valdosta, 
Ga., for an undisclosed amount of cash. Alco said that the 
95-year-old Valdosta, a full-service drug wholesaler with 
annual sales of more than $20 million, will remain under 
the management of president Bobby G. Kent. Alco al- 
ready does business in the region through Duff Brothers in 
Chattanooga, Tenn., and Geer Drug in Charleston and 
Greenville, S.C. 


Drug chains sell Calif. lottery tickets 


SACRAMENTO — Among the 5,996 California retail 
chain stores authorized to sell California’s new lottery 
tickets are three drug chains: Longs, Thrifty and Pay 
Less. The lottery will begin in late September or October.

ALEXANDRIA, Va. — 
Drug wholesalers recorded a 
banner year in 1984, following 
a year in which operating re- 
sults suffered a slignt decline, 
according to the National 
Wholesale Druggists’ Associ- 
ation. 

According to NWDA’s 1984 
Operating Survey, the perfor- 
mance was particularly strong 
in expense reduction and pro- 
ductivity gains. 

The survey found, for ex- 
ample, that operating ex- 
penses as a percentage of net 
sales dropped to a record low 
of 6.84% from 7.21% in 1983 
and 7.79% the previous year. 

Personnel productivity also 
hit a record, according to the 
NWDA, as lines per ware- 
house picking manhour 
reached 59.01, up from 55.32 
last year and 58.60 in 1982. 

In addition, gross profit per 
employee was $72,280 on a 
FIFO basis in 1984 vs. $64,570 
in 1983 and $56,410 the previ- 
ous year. 

LIFO net margin also 
reached a new peak at 1.42%, 
compared to 1.37% in 1983 and 
1.41% the year before. On a

CHICAGO — NACDS may file a lawsuit 
against the Health Care Financing Adminis- 
tration (HCFA) to stop an Oct. 1 change in 
Medicaid policy that would lower pharmacy re- 
imbursements. 

Jim Harrison, chairman of the National As- 
sociation of Chain Drug Stores, made the an- 
nouncement before a general business session 
at this year’s NACDS Pharmaceutical Confer- 
ence. 

Harrison reaffirmed NACDS’ commitment 
to “leaving no stone unturned in our efforts to 
stop the Oct. 1 target date.” 

“Hopefully, such action will not be needed,” 
said Harrison, “but it may be our last recourse 
if HCFA does not relent.” ; 

Under HCFA‘s proposal, Medicaid reim- 
bursements to pharmacists, currently based on 
drugs purchased at the average wholesale 
price, would shift to reimbursements based on 
the actual acquisition cost, eliminating any 
“earned” discounts between the two cost-bas- 
ing methods. 

Another issue considered by Harrison to be 
responsible for eroding profits on prescription 
sales, that NACDS will follow closely, is pref- 
erential pricing and the misinterpretation of 
the Non-Profit Institutions Act. 

“The act is looked upon by many in pharmacy 
as the root cause of ever spahiom we have, 


from halitosis to athlete’s foot,” said Harrison. 

Although Harrison admits that it may be 
somewhat of an exaggeration, he believes the 
issue of preferential pricing “deserves the rep- 


utation it has due to its potentially devasting 
effect on many aspects of pharmaceutical deliv- 
ery in America.” 

arrison told the attendees that the NACDS 
will offer constructive suggestions and legisla- 
tive recommendations to Congress in the hope 
of “eliminating the widespread abuses that are 
—_—— under the Non-Profit Institutions 

ct.” 

The NACDS will recommend to Congress 
that only bona fide charitable hospitals caring 
solely for indigent patients be »'lowed to pur- 
chase drugs at svaliaendtel prices. 

In addition, the chain organization will ask 
Congress to require stronger regulatory en- 
forcement, including “greater surveillance of 
all imports, exports and re-imports by the 
Food and Drug Administration and the U.S. 
Customs Service to guard against counterfeit 
medications entering the domestic market. 

“Also, we will work to educate the Congress 
that the current drug distribution system 
works well and efficiently in bringing quality 
medications to consumers,” sai arrison. 
“NACDS will devote a significant amount of 
energy to this issue.” 


Correction 


In the article “OTC buyers detail their dis- 
satisfaction with manufacturers’ reps” (Sept. 2 
issue), the manufacturer of Lensept was incor- 
rectly identified. Lensept is manufactured by 
American Optical.

Perry reports sales, earnings up 


PONTIAC, Mich. — Perry 
Drug reported record sales 
and earnings for the third 

uarter ended July 1. The 
chain said the results reflected 
“continued progress in the 
consolidation and integration 
of its latest acquisitions.” 
_ Net earnings for the period 
increased 69% to $2.7 million 
from $1.6 million in the compa- 
rable year-earlier quarter. 
Earnings per share, restated 
to reflect a 3-for-2 split an- 
nounced earlier, would be 27¢ 
vs. 18¢ last year. 

Third quarter sales in- 
creased 48% to $140 million 
from $95 million a year earlier. 

For the nine months, net 
earnings increased 30% to 


$7.2 million from $5.5 million 
in the same period last year. 
Earnings per share for the 
nine months were $1.09, com- 
pared to 92¢ a year ago. 

Sales for the nine months in- 
creased 37% to $377 million 
from $275 million. Nine- 
month sales are already high- 
er than all of last year’s, the 


company said. 
“We are obviously pleased 
erfor- 


by our continued oe o 
. Robin- 


mance,” said Jac 

son, chairman and ceo. 
At the end of the third quar- 

ter, Perry was operating 183 

drug stores and five health 

care companies in addition to 

the auto parts stores. 


SGC net earnings up 15% 


WOODBRIDGE, N.J. — 
Supermarkets General, oper- 
ator of Pathmark and Purity 
Supreme supermarkets and 
drug stores, reported that net 
earnings for the second quar- 
ter increased 15% to $18 mil- 


lion or $1.01 a share, from 
$15.7 million, or 88% a share, 
in the same period last year. 
Supermarkets General re- 
ported that sales in its free- 
standing drug stores contin- 
ued strong during the quarter.

DRUG STORE NEWS, September 16, 1985 


MERCHANDISER 


29 


Combo operators accelerate growth plans 


ynergism may be one of 
the most overworked 
buzzwords of the 80's. 
But it seems as if it were in- 
- vented to describe combos: 
Huge food and drug stores, 
the food pulling enormous 
traffic and the drug/gm por- 
tion boosting narrow food 
margins. One and one make 
three. What could be better? 
Not much, in the estimation 
of the nation’s biggest food re- 
tailers, who have invested 
heavily in the development 
and expansion of these one- 
stop shopping behemoths. 

Consider the following: 

—American Stores, whose 
chairman, Sam Skaggs, has 
long been the leading expo- 
nent of the format, plans to 
open 36 in fiscal 1986. Ana- 
lysts say that fully 30% of 
American’s capital expendi- 
tures will be sunk into their 
development. With the acqui- 
sition of Jewel Companies, 
American now operates some 
250 combination stores. 

—The Kroger Co. expects 
to have more than 500 combos 
in operation by the end of 
1987. The number may be mis- 
leading, however, since Sam 
Skaggs would undoubtedly 
call many of Kroger’s combos 
“superstores’ with pharma- 
cies. Whatever the definition, 
Kroger says that combos by 
1987 will make up 45% of its 
food stores but will deliver 
65% of food store sales. 

—Albertson’s, which oper- 
ates combos in some of the 
most attractive Sunbelt mar- 
kets, has scheduled 30 to 32 
new stores for 1985, one-third 
of them in the 47,000-67,000- 
sq.-ft. combo range. The com- 
pany has looked at other types 
of retail ventures, including 
drug stores, but vice chairman 
Gary Michaels says the Boise, 
Idaho-based retailer is “going 
to stay in the food and drug 
combo business. We like the 
stores we’re building.” 

—Giant Food, the Lan- 
dover, Md., based food/drug 
retailer, has 23 food and drug 
combos set to open within the 
next three years. The addi- 
tions will boost total store 
space by 25% or more than 1.1 
million sq. ft. 

These represent just a 
handful of the companies that 
are committing themselves to 
expanding what Bill Bishop, a 
leading supermarket consul- 
tant, calls “one of the two pri- 
mary vehicles for selling gro- 
cery and drug products in 
urban areas.” The other vehi- 
cle, of course, is the ware- 
house-style store. 

Bishop says there are “a lot 
of reasons” why combos have 
proven so attractive, “but 
probably the most important 
is that these stores can be 
price competitive on a lot of 
items and still return a reason- 


able profit because of the 
mix.” 

Another important reason, 
Bishop says, is that the combo 
stores are the most resistant 
to attacks from deep-discount 
stores. 

Beyond all the talk of vari- 
ety and selection, of one-stop 
shopping and of food/nonfood 
synergism is the sheer beauty 
of these stores. They are se- 
ductive. Customers find them 
fun to shop. There are cosmet- 
ics departments that can com- 
pete with department stores 
for attractiveness and chic; 
colorful produce and floral de- 
partments that act as power- 
ful magnets to the eye, and a 
variety of boutique-style spe- 
cialty departments including 
delis and cheese islands and 
even lobster pounds. 

The one key element that 


dinary supermarket is the 
pharmacy department. It is 
the one essential ingredient in 
all of the definitions. 

In a recent study, the Food 
Marketing Institute found 
that the median size of a super- 
market with pharmacy was 
45,000 sq. ft., compared to the 
average supermarket without 
pharmacy, which measures 
28,000 sq. ft. 

According to the study, the 
typical supermarket pharma- 
ey accounts for 1% of total 
square footage and generates 
1.2% of sales. That additional 
two-tenths of a percentage 
point may not seem like much, 
but prescription drug volume 
is just one part of the story. 

The real strength of the 
pharmacy is as a powerful ac- 
celerator of health & beauty 


chairman of Safeway, has said, 
in fact, that the addition of 
pharmacy can increase a su- 
permarket’s H&BA sales by 
as much as four times. 
Kroger is a prime example

Higher profits expected 
in second half of 1985 


NEW YORK — Many drug 
chains have been flying 
through what might be de- 
scribed as an economic wind 
shear, but Wall Street experts 
predict that the ride will level 
off in the second half of the 
year. 

With some notable excep- 
tions, after-tax profits have 
been down or flat, even those 
of some former] mg PP gine 
companies like Rite Aid an 
Longs. 

Analysts say the reasons for 
the falloff vary, but there are 
some overriding factors, 
among them the sluggish 
economy, the easing of infla- 
tion and the heavy competi- 
_ for limited consumer dol- 
ars. 


“The biggest factor is a real 
slowdown in general merchan- 
dise sales across all segments 
of the retail industry,” said 
Rodert Roth, retail analyst 
for Merrill Lynch. 

Roth said he expects the 
drug chains’ performance to 
be “moderately better” in the 
second half, with an im- 
proved Christi.as season. 

Elaine M. Garzarelli, sector 
strategist for Shearson Leh- 
man Brothers, agreed. “We 
expect profits for the drug 
chains to be up 11%-12%. 
That’s not fantastic, but cer- 
tainly better than the 2% 
we're predicting for the S&P 
(Standard & Poor’s 500 list- 
ing].”

Kroger shutters 23 Ohio stores 


CLEVELAND — Kroger Co. closed all 23 of its north- 
eastern Ohio stores, including four Barney Food & aaa 
Warehouse outlefs ranging from 55,000 sq. ft. to 72,( 
sq. ft., and two Kroger super stores with pharmacies. 
Kroger plans to seil the stores. 

All of the stores’ pharmacies, however, have remained 
open, said Jim McIntire, a company spokesman, to allow 
customers to continue to get their prescriptions filled. 

McIntire said that stores had to be closed due to “unsat- 
isfactory return on assets coupled with excessive demands 
by labor negotiators on a new contract.” 

The union representing Kroger workers denied that the 
stores were unprofitable. 


Perry sells bonds 


PONTIAC, Mich. — Perry Drug Stores Inc. has recent- 
ly completed the sale of $50 million of convertible deben- 
ture bonds, priced at par to yield 8.5%. They are due on 
Sept. 15, 2010, and are convertible at a rate of $18.125 of 
debentures for each common share. 

Proceeds from the sale will be used to reduce short-term 
debt, and for general; unnamed, purposes. 


Stop & Shop suffers $1.2M loss 2nd atr. 


BOSTON — The Stop & Shop Companies, the food, 
drug and department store operator, reported a “very dis- 
appointing” second quarter. Pased partly on “sluggish 

es and heavy clearance markdowns” in its Bradlees de- 
partment stores, Stop & Shop experienced a loss of $1.2 
million in the quarter compared to last year’s profit of $9.7 
million. Sales for the 12 weeks ended Aug. 17 were up 9% 
to $776 million. 

While the 65-store Medi Mart drug store chain was prof- 
itable, the company said, earnings were still below those 
of last year’s second — 

For the 28 weeks, Stop & Shop’s earnings fell to $5.7 
million from $16.1 million, while sales rose to $1.75 billion 
from $1.58 billion. 


Parker appointed Lucky div. pres. 


DUBLIN, Calif. -— Samuel J. Parker, former president 
of Sav-On Drug, wiil join Lucky Stores Sept. 30 as presi- 
dent of the company’s automotive division. 

Parker, 42, served as president of the California drug 
chain from 1981 through February 1985. He left Sav-On, a 
subsidiary of Jewel Companies, following Jewel’s acquisi- 
tion by American Stores. 

Leaky automotive division operates 378 Kragen and 
Checker auto parts stores in 12 states in the West and 
Southwest.

FDA lifts Rx consumer 


WASHINGTON — The 
Food and Drug Administra- 
tion abruptly withdrew its 
two-year-old “moratorium” on 
direct-to-consumer advertis- 
ing of prescription drugs—a 
move likely to encourage some 
brand-name pharmaceutical 
manufacturers and dru 
chains to resume earlier ef- 
forts to promote Rx medicines 
to the public. 

But at:the same time, feder- 
al drug regulators bowed to 
pressure from physicians, 

harmacists, consumer activ- 
ists and other critics of direct- 
to-consumer Rx ads by refus- 
ing to relax existing FDA 
es requiring advertisers of 
prescription gs to inform 
consumers about the “risks” 
as well as the benefits of their 
products. 

The ad moratorium was im- 
posed in 1983 by former FDA 
Commissioner Arthur Hull 
Hayes in response to predic- 
tions that pharmaceutical 
manufacturers are “on the 
brink of the exponential 
growth phase of the direct-to- 
the-consumer promotion of 
prescription products.” 

Although the advertising of 

Rx drugs to the public has nev- 
er been prohibited by federal 
law, an informal “gentlemen’s 
agreement” among pharma- 
ceutical manufacturers coupled 
with FDA requirements for 
risk disclosures effectively 
short-circuited such direct-to- 
consumer promotions for 
years. 
During the early 1980’s, 
however, several manufactur- 
ers launched limited consumer 
Rx ad campaigns, others in- 
formed FDA officials of plans 
to follow suit, and drug chain 
ads for prescription herpes 
salves began appearing in dai- 
ly newspapers. 

Hayes—who initially char- 
acterized such consumer Rx 
advertising as a major new 
“opportunity” for the pharma- 
ceutical industry but later 
adopted a neutral stand on the 
issue—called for the volun- 
tary moritorium to allow time 
for research and “dialogue” on 
the subject of consumer Rx 
promotions. 

Although the research con- 
ducted since then suggested 
that many consumers would 
be in favor of direct advertis- 
ing of prescription products, 


the “dialogue” received by 
FDA from consumer organi- 
zations, pharmacy leaders, 
physicians and many drug 
manufacturers was sharply 
critical of such promotional ac- 
tivity. 

In a terse announcement 
aborting the moratorium ear- 
liey this month, FDA Commis-

Peoples names coo for Fla. 


BOCA RATON, Fla. — 
Peoples Drug Stores has 
named John C. Cain vp and 
chief operating officer of its 
30-store Shoppers Drug Mart 
Division in Florida, according 
to Sheldon W. Fantle, Peoples 
chairman, president and ceo. 

The appointment comes at a 
time when Peoples is gearing 

up for a major expansion of its 
Florida drug store division. 
Four stores are scheduled to 
open by the end of the fiscal 
year in March, and another 


eight to 10 the following year. 

Cain, who has been with the 
chain since 1976, said the Sun- 
shine State had been targeted 
for growth because of the tre- 
mendous population gains 
that are projected. 

“The Census says that Flor- 
ida is expected to add 6.5 mil- 
lion to seven million people by 
the end of the century,” Cain 
told Drug Store News. “That 
will bring the state’s popula- 
tion to about 17 million.”

Gloria takes toll at Genovese 


MELVILLE, N.Y. — Almost half of the Genovese drug 
stores in Long Island, N.Y., lost power for at least one day 
as a result of Hurricane Gloria. Although the stores es- 
caped extensive damage, the hurricane knocked out elec- 
trical power in about 16 units. 

In some stores, the power outage lasted throughout the 
peak weekend sales days, said Don Gross, Genovese’s vp 
of marketing and distribution. At presstime, four stores 
remained without power and Gross said he expected those 
units to be without electricity for up to one week. 

Gross noted that sales were beginning to pick up in Sep- 
tember and that the storm-related store closings repre- 
sented a “temporary setback.” 


SDM appoints 2 senior execs 


WILLOWDALE, Ontario — Shoppers Drug Mart, 
Canada’s leading drug chain, named two senior executives 
to executive vp positions. Fred Van Laare has been ap- 
pointed executive vp, operational services, and Louis 
Goelman, has been named executive vp, purchasing and 
distribution. 

Van Laare, who joined Shoppers in 1971, has also been 
assistant director of advertising and operations coordina- 
tor, both posts in SDM’s Western Region; vp of operations 
for Alberta-Saskatchewan, and executive vp of the chain’s 
Florida division. 

Goelman, who has had extensive experience in the food 
and drug industry, will be responsible for purchasing and 
distribution for more than 400 Shoppers Drug Mart/Phar- 
maprix retail pharmacies throughout Canada. 


Alico agrees to buy Meyers 


VALLEY FORGE, Pa. — Alco Health Services Corp., 
the nation’s fourth largest drug wholesaler, has agreed in 
ncaa to acquire Meyers & Co. of Tiffin, Ohio, from 

illman Securities Inc., for 1.11 million shares of Alco 
Health Services common stock. 

The acquisition is subject to final approval by the boards 
of both companies, the execution of a definitive agreement 
and appropriate regulatory filings. 

Meyers is a distributor of pharmaceuticals, H&BA, 
medical and surgical supplies and home health products 
and has annual sales of more than $100 million. It will con- 
tinue to operate from its existing location under the same 
management led by Robert W. Meyers, president. 

The acquisition will put Alco over the billion-dollar mark 
in revenues. 


Cardinal acquires Daly for $31.8M 


DUBLIN, Ohio — Cardinal Distribution Inc. has 
signed an agreement in principle to acquire James W. Daly 
Inc., a $140 million drug wholesaler based in Peabody, 
Mass., for $31.8 million in cash and convertible debenture. 

Under the agreement, Cardinal, a food and yes | whole- 
saler with annualized sales of $400 million, will either pur- 
chase or lease Daly’s new 250,000-sq.-ft. distribution cen- 
ter in Peabody, Mass. 

The agreement calls for Daly to continue operating inde- 

endently under the present management headed by ceo’s 
Joseph L. Daly and William J. Daly.

WASHINGTON — Law- 
yers for the nation’s drug 
stores, wholesale druggists 
and pharmacists scored a 
stunning first round knockout 
in their courtroom battle to 
block “disastrous” new Medi- 
caid Rx reimbursement cuts 
scheduled to take effect this 
month. 

Faced with the prospect of a 
federal court order barring 
implementation of the contro- 
versial plan, officials at the 
Health Care Financing <Ad- 
ministration reversed course 
abruptly and announced that 
state Medicaid programs will 
not be barred from reimburs- 
ing pharmacies for drug prod- 
ucts based on “average whole- 
sale prices” on Oct. 1 after all. 
(See earlier story, page 85.) 

Inastatement filed with the 
federal district court in Wash- 
ington, HCFA officials 
announced their decision to 
“rescind the Oct. 1, 1985, 
‘deadline’ for states to make 
potentially needed changes in

regional officials at the agency 
for giving state Medicaid ad- 
ministrators the “erroneous” 
impression that AWP pay- 
ments to drug stores sods be 
outlawed. 

HCFA’s surprise reversal 
surfaced late last month in re- 
sponse to a lawsuit filed by an 
unprecedented coalition of in- 
dustry and professional 
groups including the National 
Association of Chain Drug 
Stores, the National Retail 
Druggists Association, the 
American Pharmaceutical As-

‘ation of Wholesale Druggists, 


the American Society of Hos-

can Society of Consultant

ceutical Manufacturers Asso- 
ciation.

isting Medicaid Rx reimburse- 
ment formulas without first

House approves polygraph ban 


WASHINGTON — The 
House Employment Opportu- 
nities Committee ignored 
warnings from chain drug in- 
dustry leaders and approved 
new legislation flatly prohibit- 
ing polygraph testing of em- 
ployees. 

The bill passed by the sub- 
committee would impose civil 
penalties of up to $10,000 on 
drug chains and other private 
employers who even “‘sug- 
gest” that an employee submit 
to a “lie detector” test. 

The measure also allows the 
Labor Department to secure 
injunctions preventing indi- 
vidual firms from conducting 
polygraph “screens” of work- 
ers or job applicants, and en- 
ables employees (or ‘abor 
unions) to file civil damage 
suits against employers who 
violate the act. 

Although .similar — 
graph laws have already been 
enacted in a number of states, 


drug chain lobbyists are op- 
posed to a nationwide ban 
against workplace lie detector 
testing because such exams 
are considered necessary to 
prevent “internal diversion” 
of controlled substances. 

In testimony before the 
House subcommittee earlier 
this year, Rite Aid’s Govern- 
ment Relations vp, James 
Krahulee, told Congress that 
“employees are stealing be- 
tween 500,000 to one million 
dosage units of dangerous 
drugs each year from pharma- 
cies’ and,chain warehouses, 
and that without the poly- 
graph, drug stores would be- 
come even more “vulnerable 
to internal diversion.” 

During the subcommittee’s 


, 


“markup” of the bill late last 
month Etec nts concerns 
were echoed by Rep. Robert 
Livingston (R-La.). 

Noting that “up to a million 
doses of legal drugs vanish 


despite drug chain protests 


from pharmaceutical company 
inventories each year,” Liv- 
ingston maintained that the 
drug store industry needs lie 
detectors “to help protect its 
inventories and to ferret out 
internal theft rings.” 

Despite the setback at the 
subcommittee level, chain 
drug industry leaders told 
Drug Store News that they 
still hope to head off final pas- 
sage of antipolygraph legisla- 
tion this vear. 

“We plan to ask the full 
House ale and Labor 
Committee to adopt an 
amendment to the bill specifi- 
cally exempting the drug 1n- 
dustry from the polygraph 
ban.” National Association of 
Chain Drug Stores vp Ty Kel- 
ley said. 

‘If that maneuver fails, 
NACDS will continue the bat- 
tle when the bill reaches the 
House floor for a vote, he add- 
ed.

Ethnic H&BA: $2.3 b 


s the profitable ethnic health & 

beauty aids market continues to 

expand, more retailers, whole- 
salers and manufacturers are tapping 
into the category. 

Everyone is hoping to grab a piece of 
a $2.3 billion market that is projected 
to skyrocket to $5.6 billion by 1993. In 
the next decade, according to Business 
Trends Analysts, ethnic H&BA will 
generate nearly 24% of the total dollars 
spent on all toiletry and cosmetic 
items. 

And on a profit per unit basis, black 
hair preps, the traditional backbone of 
the category, outpace any other 
H&BA item. According to A. C. Niel- 
sen, the dollar profit per year on a unit 


of black hair preps—based on a 40% 
margin, an inventory turn of six and an 
average retail of $3.85—is $9.26. In 
contrast, the average general market 
shampoo yields only $4.78. In other 
words, black hair preps are profitable. 
Amid such profitability, the catego- 
ry has continued to grow. Among the 
major developments: 
® The $50 million ethnic hair color 
market is set to explode with the intro- 
duction of new products, including 
semipermanent colors, from a number 
of major manufacturers. 
@ The black men’s market is pegged 
for expansion as manufacturers target 
this fashion-conscious consumer 


group. 


@ McKesson is rolling out its first coor- 
dinated national program for ethnic 
products in 40 distribution centers. In 
mid-1986, the giant wholesaler will 
supplement its current planograms of 
ethnic hair and skin care products with 
4-ft. to 8-ft. sections of cosmetics, hair 
accessories, and hosiery targeted for 
the ethnic market. 

@ The American Health and Beauty 
Aids Institute, a Chicago-based con- 
sortium of 20 manufacturers of ethnic 
H&BA products, will conduct the first 
buyers school for the category. At the 
two-and-a-half day seminar, buyers 
will receive an operations manual, di- 
rectory of products and their use and 
other educational information. The 


lion and growing 


AHBATL is also developing a set of plan- 
ograms for the category based on 
quantitative data from leading re- 
search organizations. 

@ Perry is expanding and adding eth- 
nic sections in stores where there is a 
lot of black traffic. The Pontiac, Mich.- 
based chain now has ethnic sections in 
over 60 stores ranging from 4 ft. to 36 
ft. 

@ Fay’s is tracking the category’s 
movement on a computerized system 
in those stores with ethnic sections. 

@ Hook’s and SupeRx have both creat- 
ed their own ethnic planograms. 
Hook’s is warehousing over 80% of its 


ethnic product mix.

Ethnic H&BA: $2.3 billion and growing 


Continued from page 71 

e Eckerd is taking a closer look at the 
category and is said to be slashing 
prices on ethnic items in highly com- 
petitive markets. 

@ Revco is continually broadening its 
ethnic mix and now carries cver 250 
sku’s. 

What all this activity revolves 
around is a burgeoning black popula- 
tion that is projected to grow nearly 
75% faster than the general popula- 
tion. By 1993, blacks will comprise 
12.8% of the U.S. population. 

Because blacks spend as much as 
five times more on hair care items than 
the general population on a per capita 
basis, stores with as little as 5% black 
traffic can generate 15% of H&BA 
sales in the ethnic section, according to 
Business Trends Analysis. 

Drug chains have always led the 
pack when it comes to the ethnic cate- 
gory. In 1984, for example, drug stores 
generated 44% of 25 H&BA category 
sales, but a 54% share of ethnic hair 
care s2'es, according to A. C. Nielsen. 
In contrast, food stores generated 47% 
of general H&BA sales, but only 28% 
of ethnic hair care sales. 

But, there are signs that mass mer- 
chandisers and food stores, in particu- 
lar, are starting to realize the catego- 
rvs potential. 

Diana Warren of Judith Lynn notes 
that more food stores are beginning to 
put in ethnic H&BA sections. And La- 
fayette Jones, executive director of 
AHBA\|, says that drug stores were in 
the category early, but “there is tre- 
mendous opportunity in other retail 
outlets.” 

While retail outlets battle for the 
ethnic H&BA dollar, a number of 
trends are emerging. 

Hair color 

In 1984, hair care products generat- 
ed 41%, or $920 million, of all ethnic 
H&BA sales, according to Business 


Trends Analysts. However, the one 
subsegment primed for growth is the 
$50 million hair color business, includ- 
ing permanent, semipermanent and 
highlighting formulations. 

Rocky Piccirillo, director of opera- 
tions for Beauty Enterprises, an ethnic 
products distributor in Hartford, 
Conn., says that “1986 will be the year 
of hair color.” While only 3% of his com- 
pany’s total dollar sales are now reiat- 
ed to hair color, he says that the seg- 
ment is “growing.” 

Indeed, as the trend toward a more 
relaxed and natural look continues, 
hair colors, especially, semipermanent 
formulations, will become more popu- 
lar. 

Notes Kent Humphreys of Jack’s 
service, a supplier of ethnic H&BA in 
Oklahoma City: “Temporary hair col- 
ors are an exciting category.” But he 
also stresses that permanent hair col- 
ors are very strong. For example, sales 
of Carson’s Dark & Lovely hair color 
have more than doubled in the last 12 
months, says Humphreys. 

At least four major manufacturers, 
including Clairol and Soft Sheen, are 
launching, or plan to launch, hair color 
products. 

Clairol’s Born Beautiful division has 
already unveiled a semipermanent hair 
color targeted for black and hispanic 
women with relaxed or permed hair. 
And Soft Sheen is reportedly gearing 
up to launch a temporary hair color for 
the ethnic market in retail markets. 
Other manufacturers are reportedly 
following suit. Several manufacturers, 
including Soft Sheen, Worlds of Curls, 
and Lustrasilk; have also recently in- 
troduced professional hair colors. 

In other areas of the hair care arena, 
buyers and distributors note that Soft 
Sheen’s Snap Back has been an unqual- 
ified success. Notes Humphreys: 
“Snap Back is the product of the year. 
Sales are increasing 15% to 20% every 


The AHBAI recommends seven 
ways for retailers to reap more dol- 
lars from ethnic H&BA: 

1. Wider distribution. 

2. Carry broader, deeper lines; ex- 
pand shelf space. 

3. Feature ethnic H&BA more fre- 
quently in ads. 

4. Offer better discounts. 

5. Promote the entire category 
more aggressively and consistent- 
ly. 

6. Use profit-generating end-aisle 
displays. 

7. Improve in-store presentation 
with better housekeeping. 


month.” 

The trend toward the “light look” 
has also increased sales of gloss and 
sheen sprays. 

And at Drug King in Oakland, Calif., 
a store with 30-ft. ethnic section, store 
manager Joe Martinez, has spotted an 
interesting trend. He says that activa- 
tors are selling to anyone with perms. 
Although it would be difficult to track, 
many observers agree with Martinez: 
products for the ethnic market indeed 
sell outside of that market. 

Men’s market 

Black men, of course, have always 
used oil sheens, conditioners, hair 
sprays and gels. For example, as much 
as 70% of Atlanta-based M&M Prod- 
ucts’ sales are generated by products 
specifically formulated for men. 

However, the emergence of the wave 
and the more natural look have cata- 
pulted men’s product sales. Says Mike 
O’Brien of Harris Beauty Supply, an 
ethnic H&BA supplier in Atlanta: 
“There has been a big increase in sales 
in the pomade category.” 

Pat Marr, account manager for 
Hanes DSD/Sav-A-Stop, one of the na- 
tion’s largest nonfoods distributors,

agrees. “The curl activator market is 
turning like a big battleship toward the

Many manufacturers have also re- 
cently introduced hair care lines for 
men. For example, Johnson Products 
unveiled Ultra Style for men in 1984. 
This year the company signed Chicago 
Bulls’ superstar and Rookie-of-the- 
Year Michael Jordan to a multiyear en- 
dorsement contract. 

According to Johnson, the hefty con- 
tract is the largest for a celebrity en- 
dorsement in the ethnic H&BA catego- 
ry” “It’s substantial, lucrative and on 
par with his other contracts,” says 
George E. Johnson, founder and presi- 
dent of Johnson Products. Jordon, the 
dynamo who led the U.S. basketball 
team to an Olympic gold medal, has 
signed a seven-year $6 million contract 
with the Bulls. 

Another company which has recent- 
ly introduced a hair product for men is 
Pro-Line. The Dallas-based ethnic 
H&BA producer is launching a no-rod 
wave and curl kit called Players. Ac- 
cording to the company, “market re- 
search proves that men prefer no-lye 
by a margin of over 5 to 1.” 

Says Comer J. Cottrell, president 
and chairman of Pro-Line: “Players 
was designed with the fashion-con- 
scious active black male in mind.” 

Johnson Publishing Co. is also tap- 
ping into the fashion market for black 
men with the first of Johnson’s black- 
oriented magazines targeted specifi- 
cally to men. 

Called Ebony Man, the magazine, 
which will debut in November, is aimed 
at the more than 13 million black men 
looking for a “commonsense, funda- 
mental approach to fashion, grooming 
and fitness,” says John H. Johnson, 
publisher. Alfred Fornay, the maga- 
zine’s executive editor, adds: “Simply 
put, EM is the fashion, grooming, fit- 
ness and successful living magazine for 
contemporary black men.” 

With all the attention black men are 
receiving, retailers should look for- 
ward to increased sales of those prod- 
ucts targeted specifically for this 


group.

Hispanic products: big potential, slow sales 


lion Hispanics regularly passing 

through the nation’s drug stores, 
but retailers are not experiencing a 
sales explosion of products aimed at 
this substantial population segment. 

Retailers including Walgreens, Eck- 
erd, K mart and Standard have tested 
Hispanic departments. Although 
these tests are on-going, sales to date 
have been only modest. 

“It is growing, slowly, but surely,” 
reports Diana Warren of Judith Lynn 
Sales Inc., one of the first suppliers of 
Hispanic items. 

The mediocre success to date does 
not mean a boom is never going to 
come, cuggests Joe Potocki of the Pro- 
motion Marketing Association of 
America. Like the ethnic category 10 
years ago, the Hispanic market will 
take cultivating, he says. 

Several issues have kept the Hispan- 
ic market locked up, say experts. One 
problem is the language barrier. 

Marketers are currently battling 
over whether Hispanics prefer Spanish 
labeling on packages or not. While 
many believe Hispanics feel more com- 
fortable finding products with Spanish 
lahels, Lionel Sosa, president and cre- 
ative director of Sosa & Associates, in- 
sists Hispanics prefer to feel part of the 
American family. To that end, he says, 
advertising and packaging should be in 
English. 

Yet, Strategy Research finds that 
the primary language spoken by His- 
panics in this country is Spanish. In 
fact, most of the current rack jobber 
programs include products wrapped in 
Spanish or bilingual packaging. 

Many manufacturers are following 
suit. Jason Products, for example, has 
a new line of natural shampoos with 
Spanish labeling. The “Primavera Flo- 
ra” line is aimed at what Jason calls a 
category that has been neglected. 

Another hitch in efforts to perk up 
the Hispanic market is the lack of a ma- 
jor advertising medium comparable to 
the black market’s Ebony and Es- 
sence, the bibles of ethnic marketing. 
A relatively new magazine, Latina, 
however, may be the answer. Many 
marketers such as Sophisticolor with 
its new Paradise Cosmetics line, will 
use this new publication in hopes of 
wooing Hispanic shoppers. 

A final hurdle has been retailers’ and 
marketers’ lack of knowledge about 
the Hispanic customer. Although most 
know about the promising demograph- 


T here may be as many as 17.6 mil- 


ics, many have been confused by the 
market. Retailers originally thought 
they had to market to three distinct 
groups: Mexicans, Puerto Ricans and 
Cubans. In 1984, areport by Yanke- 
lovich, Skelly & White Inc. proved 
that theory wrong. The study conclud- 
ed that marketers should consider all 
Hispanics “in aggregate as a consumer 
segment.” 

If retailers do finally find the key to 
unlock the market, the sales potential 
is astonishing. The Hispanic popula- 
tion has increased 440% since 1950%. 
In the last five years, the Hispanic pop- 
ulation zoomed up another 20%. And 
the Commerce Bureau of the Census 
puts the total of Hispanics in 1990 at 21 
million. 

It is also a market gaining in income 
and educational level. The percentage 
of college graduates has doubled since 
1981, and the annual family income is 
up. Thirty-six per cent currently earn 
$20,000 or more, and Strategy Re- 
search estimates overall median in- 
come in 1985 will hit $19,900—that’s 
compared with only $14,712 five years 
ago. 

Strategy Research finds Hispanic 
shoppers dedicated to chain environ- 
ments. “It is another method for them 
to feel they fit into society,” explains 
one expert on these shoppers. This 
suggests drug chains will become fa- 
vorite shopping spots. 

What is also interesting about His- 
panic shoppers is that males partici- 
pate in shopping more often than their 
Anglo counterparts. 

Like black shoppers, Hispanics be- 
come very loyal to an outlet. Also re- 
sembling the black population is His- 
panics’ high consumption of health & 
beauty aids. For instance, over 76% of 
Hispanic men use after shave com- 
pared to 62% of non-Hispanics. 

According to Warren, the products 
gaining the most acceptance in chains 
are soaps, ointments and shampoos. 
She adds that Judith Lynn executives 
constantly travel to Mexico to discover 
other items favored by Hispanics. 

A buyer for a large Southern chain 
adds he has seen increasing sales to 
Hispanics of vanilla used as a fra- 
grance. “Now that is a product I'd nev- 
er expect to move. That’s the differ- 
ence between blacks and Hispanics. 
Blacks need certain products for their 
special skin and hair. Hispanics just 
like certain items they are familiar 
with or those from their homeland.”

Vendors pitch cosmetics 
to swelling Asian market 


cosmetics line, Paradise Cosmet- 

ics of Beverly Hills, touts the line 
as perfect for not only blacks and His- 
panics, but Orientals as well. When 
Gazelle International debuts, next 
year, its line will be pitched at “women 
of color,” including Asians. 

It is no surprise marketers are tar- 
geting the swelling Asian market. Ac- 
cording to the latest available U.S. De- 
partment of Commerce Bureau of 
Census figures, there are 3.7 million 
people from Asia now living in Ameri- 
ca. 

Although these figures cannot be 
compared with incomplete earlier Cen- 
sus data, the population is indeed 
growing, according to Karen Mills of 
the Census Bureau. 

The bulk of this group, 58.5%, live in 
western states. In fact, 35.2% reside in 
California. Hawaii, New York, New 
Jersey, Texas, and Illinois are also 
home to a significant portion of this 
population. 

Will Asians be the next ethnic group 
retailers and manufacturers attempt 
to lure? Many marketers already see it 
as a viable option. 

Like Hispanics and blacks, the 
Asian group likes to shop well-known 


T he press release from a new ethnic 


chain stores. But Asians also enjoy 
finding products they are familiar with 
from their homes. Shiseido Cosmetics, 
for instance, got its entry into the U.S. 
market based on its overwhelming suc- 
cess in Japan. Japanese-American 
women started looking for the prod- 
ucts here. It has since become a best 
seller among all women. 

Royce Cates of Sophisticolor expects 
his Paradise Cosmetics line to appeal 
to Oriental women because of the col- 
ors available in the pegged offering. 
Sophisticolor’s color expert Vicki Bar- 
neck, discovered all Asian women have 
“cool” skin tones meaning they fall into 
the winter classification. 

Cates believes Asian women will see 
the Paradise colors suit their natural 
skin tones. “Color analysis is just going 
to keep growing. You see Joan Col- 
lins—she is always in her colors and 
looks great. Linda Evans doesn’t know 
her proper colors and goes wrong.” 

While colors aimed at the Asian mar- 
ket may work, several retailers are still 
not sure the market requires any other 
special attention. 

But with the population exploding, 
retailers say they will stay on top of it 
and be ready if it becomes the next 
trend.

To Our Friends In the 
Retail Drug Trade 


Once again it is our pleasure to recognize our friendships within the 
Drug Industry with this presentation of key trends in drug store re- 
tailing and merchandising of health & beauty aids. This annual publi- 
cation is one way we find to express our thanks to you, the retailers 
who are such an important ingredient in the development of these in- 
dustry statistics. 

This year finds us well along in the implementation of a plan that 
will strengthen our support of drug retailers through our new ex- 
panded Trade Services Department. These marketing, merchandis- 
ing and research specialists are at the service of your industry as well 
as our cooperating stores and organizations. We think this enhanced 
Nielsen commitment wil! contribute to your industry’s success in the 
future. 

We hope all of our readers will find the 1985 review both informa- 
tive and interesting. We welcome your questions and comments. Just 
give our Trade Services group a call. 

We would also like to thank the staff at Drug Store News for their 
advice in assembling this review and including it in their Oct. 14, 1985, 
issue. 


Cordially, 


Broli @ Me 


Donald R. MeCurry

Product availability at the retail 
level is crucial to the success of both 
manufacturers and retailers: out of 
stocks cause both consumer dissat- 
isfaction and the loss of retail sales. 

The chart on this page illustrates 
how pipeline inventory levels 
change as a typical new item is in- 


DRUG STORE NEWS 


troduced. 

Kor the product traced here, a 
nonseasonal health care item, total 
inventory levels appear to have sta- 
bilized at the end of the sixth month. 
At that point, retail inventories rep- 
resent approximately 50% of total 
retail/wholesale inventory levels. 


Months supply, which is a mea- 
surement of how long it would take 
to deplete inventories at the current 
rate of retail sales, appears to be 
leveling off at 2.5 months at the re 
tail level and at a similar 2.6 months 
at the wholesale level.

Automated future to ease retail Rx operations 


NEW YORK — The drug 
store industry, which is close 
to making the use of pharmacy 
computers standard in most 
stores, is now on the threshold 
of a new technology evolution: 
the use of in-store computers 
to automate the entire retail 
operation. 

Most of the industry’s major 
data processing information 
executives think that the 
yharmacy computer will be a 
fact of life in all stores that 
need them within the next 
three to five years. 

Within 5 to 10 years, most 
data processing executives 
believe that the computer’s 
functions will be expanded to 
include controlling the front 
end, monitoring individual 
product movement and inven- 
tory status, grinding out pay- 
roll and other accounting pro- 
grams, and eventually 
supplying data that will lead to 
an entire merchandising revo- 
lution: the allocation of shelf 
and warehouse space based 
entirely on sku movement out 
of individual stores. 

According to Drug Store 
News first Computer Tech- 
nology Survey, approximate- 
ly 27% of retailers responding 
are engaged in some form of 
experimentation with in-store 


computer link-ups to point-of- 
sale terminals. Nine out of 10 
said they believed that in- 
store computers had to be 
linked to the point-of-sale ter- 
minals for retailers to realize 
the maximum benefits from 
their technology investments. 
More than half the respon- 
dents estimated that they 
would have pharmacy com- 
puters in 75% to 100% of their 
stores by the end of April 
1986. A third indicated that 
they would have electronic 
point-of-sale terminals in 50% 
to 100% of their stores and 
that they would be integrating 
their computers to their front 
ends by the end of April 1986. 
“The technology is changing 
so rapidly,” says Bob Rams- 
den, vp of operating systems 
for Eckerd note “that every 
day the equipment gets more 
cost efficient. The same 
amount of disc storage today 
costs about a fourth less than 
it did, say, five years ago. 
“We think there are major 
savings to be secured from us- 
ing the computer to do such 
things as register checkouts, 
mail transfers, price lookups, 
payrolls and scheduling, etc.” 
“There is no question that 
POS is up and coming,” says

Next revolution: fully automated drug stores 


Continued from page 95 

Norm Everett, vp of manage- 
ment information systems for 
Dart Drugs in Landover, Md. 
“A POS system would be par- 
ticularly important to us be- 
cause our average register 
sale is several items and it 
would improve checkout effi- 
ciency. But also we advertise 
about 600 items every week, 
so it would be a great help just 
to download those price 
changes right through the 
computer.” 

At Rite Aid, where 175 
stores are already fully inte- 
grated with the front end, the 
chain is already realizing what 
Duane Ruble, sr vp of admin- 
istration, calls “significant 
savings” from the link-up. 

“The system is giving us re- 
ports by department. We can 


compare cashier to cashier. 
We are downloading price 
changes for ads. We’re very 
positive about our savings to 
date, but we won’t have our 
maximum savings until the 
whole system is up and until 
we have fully automated the 
stores. 

“We have the capacity ior a 
lot of things that we’re not do- 
ing now. We feel there are 
more basic things to do first, 
so we're prioritizing the sys- 
tems we put in, but down the 
line we'll be doing inventory 
control, gross profit dollar and 
margin analysis, ad sell 
throughs and so on. 

“In three to five years, the 
POS/computer link-up will be 
in place with all the big guys,” 
says Don Gross, vp of market- 
ing and distribution for Geno-

vese Drug Stores. “It’s a ne- 
cessity.” 

Most chain drug executives 
believe that the POS/in-store 
computer integration will 
spread through the industry 
even faster than pharmacy 
computers have. 

Justifying cost 

In the first place, the cost of 
the technology is falling rapid- 
ly while the efficiency of the 
various hardware and soft- 
ware systems now available is 
improving almost daily. 

At presstime, as a matter of 
fact, NCR was preparing to 
introduce an in-store personal 
computer that could handle 
pharmacy applications as well 
as store and front-end man- 
agement and would cost a 
proximately $7,000. N spmalts 
such systems sell for between 
$20,000 and $35,000. 

“Today, it probably costs 
the average chain about 
$35,000 to automate a store,’ 
says Eckerd’s Ramsden, “five 
years ago, it would have cost 
$60,000 to $70,000. Today 
we're probably just about 
$10,000 away from the point 
where automation will be cost 
justifiable for just about any 
store doing over $2 million a 
year in sales.” 

“Tf it’s not cost justifiable at 
this point, then we'll wait for 
prices to come down some 
more, but we won’t know what 
our savings will be until we 
put the system up;”said Bruce 
Waterman, asst. vp and direc- 
tor of management informa- 
tion for Hook Drug in Indiana. 
Waterman says that Hook will 
probably launch its first com- 
puter/POS test in late 1986 so 
the chain can begin developing 
the right software. “We want 
to be in position with our soft- 
ware so we can take advan- 
tage of the hardw are when the 
price is right,” he says. 

Another reason to believe 
that the evolution will happen 
quickly is because most of the 
major chains already have 
various pieces of the puzzle in 
place within their stores. Most 
chains already have pharmacy 
computers in many, if not the 
majority of their stores, and

Tape to tape 

Both Waterman and Ruble 
say their goal is to go tape to 
tape whenever possible, “to 
eliminate as much paperwork 
coming to and from the stores 
and corporate as possible.” 

“Eventually,” says Ruble, 
“we'll get to the point where 
there will be no paperwork at 
all involved in third-party 
claims. Today there are agen- 
cles, usually smaller ones, 
that require paperwork with 
doctors’ signatures, but that’s 
a small percentage of the total 
universe.” 

At Eckerd, Bob Ramsden 
estimates that about 50% of 
the company’s third-party 
claims are submitted on com- 
puter tape. “We’re working 
our way now down to the 
smaller companies on a tape- 
to-tape system,” he says. 

“It may take another five 
years to get everyone on it, 
but the trend is for companies 
to get more efficient, to auto- 
mate their systems, so we ex- 
pect that ultimately 90% of all 
carriers will be on tape-to- 
tape with us. Submitting 
claims electronically is just a 

articularly valuable function 
or us to have.” 

Neck and neck with third- 
party claims in terms of their 
perceived value to retailers 
are price updates. Every 
chain that uses pharmacy 
computers reported they 
were also using the system to 
notify the store management 
of price changes going into ef- 
fect. 

Chains that had stores with 
point-of-sale terminals hooked 
up to computers also report ed 
this function as a benefit.
