Scanning skepticism 
At Revco, where a pro- 
osed one-store scanning test 
as again been postponed, 
Management Information 
Systems vp Scott Leeseberg 
has similar reservations. 

“We're not sure all dru 
stores should go to scanning,” 
he says. “The benefits the food 
stores got the most were from 
learning about their business 
in terms of product movement 
and improving their through- 
at the front end. But we 

ave good controls on our 
movement from the ware- 
house and we don’t handle as 
many items per sale through 
the front end as food stores do.’ 

There may be benefits from 
scanning, says SupeRx’s Jim 
Sinclair, director of account- 
ing, “but we need to recognize 
the costs vs. the value of the 
information.”’ 

System integration 

With 27% of respondents 
reporting that they were link- 
ing at least some in-store per- 
sonal computers to front ends 
and with &8% saying they be- 
lieved such links were neces- 
sary for stores to recognize 
maximum benefits, the ques- 
tion becomes how many in- 
store computers does a typical 
drug store need and can the 
computer that runs the phar- 
macy department also run the 
front end. 

Among the chains in the 
survey who were already link- 
ing pe’s to front ends or plan- 
ning to make the linkage by 
April 1986, 22% were testing 
both types of systems: phar- 
macy computers in some 
stores linked to the front end 
and separate nonpharmacy 
computers in other stores 
linked to the front end; anoth- 
er 33% each were using either 
the pharmacy computer exclu- 
sively or two separate in-store 
computers, respectively, and 
the rest still hadn’t decided 
what approach they would fol- 
low in 1986.

Management takes control of Jack Eckerd 
$1.2 billion leveraged buyout 


By Marjorie Shaffer 

CLEARWATER, Fla. — 
Jack Eckerd Corp., the na- 
tion’s second largest drug 
chain, has agreed to be pur- 
chased by an investment 
group that includes 25 mem- 
bers of the company’s man- 
agement and 32,060 employ- 
ees. 

The leveraged buyout, val- 
ued at $1.2 billion, is the larg- 
est in the history of the chain 
drug industry.

Walgreen first chain to clear $3B sales hurdle 


DEERFIELD, Ill. — The 
Walgreen Co. broke the $3 bil- 
lion sales barrier in fiscal 1985, 
becoming the first pure drug 
chain to reach that milestone. 

Sales for the year ended 
Aug. 31 hit $3.16 billion, a 
15.2% increase over the $2.74 
billion rung up in fiscal 1984. 

At the same time, Wal- 
greens also maintained its 
strong profit growth record. 
While the earnings of other 
drug chains faltered, Wal- 
greens drove up net income by 
10.2% to $94.2 million from 
$85.4 million in 1984. Last 
year’s results included a gain 
of $3.6 million on the sale of 
the company’s Mexican opera- 
tions.

Walgreen III managed to con- 
vey a hint of apology in de- 
scribing why earnings were 
not ep 

He noted that profits were 
affected by an accelerated 
store opening schedule—106 
stores vs. 72 in fiscal 1984. 


“This quickened pace af- 
fects near-term profits,” he 
said. “But it also means we're 
building our business. It gives 
us stronger market penetra- 
tion and economies, and posi- 
tions us for long-term growth. 
It indicates we're optimistic 
about the strength and future 
of drug stores.” 

Market penetration and 


economies of scale have been 
two of the main keys to Wal- 
greens’ phenomenal success in 
recent years. The chain’s 
overall strategy has been to 
achieve No. 1 or No. 2 status 
in every market entered.

and development of the deep- 
discount Saienon. In this 
series, Drug Store News will 
look at the problems of finding 
the right locations, coping 
with competition and the fu- 
ture of deep discounting. 

NEW YORK — Two years 
after the chain drug industry 
discovered the lucrative po- 
tential of deep-discount drug 
stores, that segment of the in- 
dustry is still “sprouting,” but 
today prospects for growth 
are a bit more speculative, and 
sources say there could soon 


Special feature 


be as many “shake-outs” in 
this segment as there are 
sprouters. 

Most analysts put the seg- 
ment’s current size at approx!- 
mately 300 stores and some $2 
billion in sales. On the basis of 
its own surveys, Drug Store 
News agrees with the store 
count, but its research indi- 
cates that total dollar volume 
today may be closer to $1.5 bil- 
lion, or about 3% of total drug 
store industry sales. 


The research also indicates 
that more than 90% of all deep- 
discount drug stores are oper- 
ated by established chain re- 
tailers, including about 30 
major food, drug and mass- 
merchandise chains as well as 
the industry’s two largest 
“pure” deep-discount drug 
store chains, F & M in Detroit 
and Drug Emporium in Co- 
lumbus, Ohio. 

The rest of the stores in this 
segment are operated by high- 
volume independents includ- 
ing particularly successful en- 
trepreneurs like Mare

REX banquet honors outstanding leaders 


NEW YORK — Vern Brun- 
ner, who began his career with 
the Walgreen Co. as a part- 
time college student in 1962, 
has been awarded the 1985 
Drug Store News REX Mer- 
chandiser of the Year award. 

Brunner, who is currently 
senior vp of marketing for 
Walgreens, accepted his 
award at a special REX ban- 
quet held in New York earlier 
this month in conjunction with 
the Associated/Affiliated 
shows. 

Speaking before an over- 
flow crowd of more than 650, 
Brunner thanked his staff and 
associates at Walgreens, his 
mentor and friend Walgreens’ 
president Fred Canning and 

articularly his wife, Sharon, 
or the support and help that 
has “sustained me over the 
years.” 

Brunner, the runaway 
choice for Chain Drug Mer- 
chandiser of the Year, was se- 
lected by popular vote among 
hundreds of manufacturer 
suppliers. 

n making the presentation, 
Drug Store News publisher 
Jay Forbes noted that both

Forbes said that many of 
the programs instituted by 
Brunner “insured the nation-

merchandise mix and store 
identity.” 

In fact, the same manufac-

Vern Brunner chain merchan-

Dworkin optimistic despite earnings slump 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — 
While Revco’s first-quarter 
earnings declined 39%, Sidney 
Dworkin, chairman and ceo, 
noted some encouraging 
trends that he believes will set 
the stage for improved results 
in the future. 

Dwerkin noted, for exam- 
ple, that the quarter's com- 
parable drug store sales in- 
creased 8.7%, compared to a 
6.9% increase in the same 
quarter last year and a 5.8% 
gain for all of fiscal 1985. 

In addition pharmacy sales, 
which have been fueling 
growth throughout the indus- 
try, rose 11.7% ona quarter-to 
quarter basis, compared to 


11% growth in the same period 
last year and 11.1% for the 
year as a whole. 

Dworkin said the 39% de- 
cline in first-quarter earnings 
was the ‘neak of lower gross 


margins in the drug store divi- 
sion, higher interest costs and 
continued losses from Odd 
Lot. 

He noted that interest ex- 
panse for the quarter more 


than doubled to $4.5 million 
from $2.1 billion, reflecting in- 
creased borrowings to finance 
the acquisition of the 42-store 
Carls Drug in July as well as 
the purchase of 4.4 million 


shares of common stock from 
the former Odd Lot owners. 

In addition, Odd Lot oper- 
ated at a loss for the quarter, 
reducing corporate earnings 
by 4¢ashare. 


Bergen posts record earnings and sales 


LOS ANGELES — Bergen 
Brunswig Corp., the nation’s 
second largest drug wholesal- 
er, announced record sales 
and earnings for the year end- 
ed Aug. 31. 

The company reported that 
net earnings increased 27.4% 
to $23.3 million from $18.3 mil- 
lion in the previous fiscal year. 


Earnings per share rose to 
$1.91 from $1.86. 

Last year’s earnings results 
included a loss of $5.2 million 
from discontinued operations. 

Sales and other revenues in- 
creased 43% to $2.43 billion 
from $1.70 billion. 

In the fourth quarter, net 
earnings increased 5% to $5.9 


million from $5.7 million in the 
same period last year. Earn- 
ings per share were 46¢. 

Sales and other revenues 
for the quarter increased 52% 
to $680.3 million. 

Bergen Brunswig said that 
the company decided, based 
on certain provisions in the 
Deficit Reduction Act of 1984, 


to switch to LIFO. 

The change permitted re- 
taining $21 million in cash. 

Commenting on the results, 
Emil P. Martini Jr., chairman 
and ceo, said that acquisitions 
had a “major impact on sales 
growth, together with the re- 
sults from existing operations 
exceeding internal targets.”

DRUG STORE NEWS, October 28, 1985 


Cosmetics biz booming, but fragrances off 


Cosmetics sales are 
climbing high in inde- 
pendent and chain 
drug stores while fra- 
grance sales are slug- 
gish or down. 

That information 
comes from the latest 
survey by Goldman 
Sachs of fragrance 
and cosmetics buyers 
at chain and independent drug 
stores. 

This important survey is 
the third such report from an- 
alysts Jack Salzman and Greg 
Ostroff. They polled buyers 
responsible for over 3,000 out- 
lets in this survey, and, in con- 
trast to the last survey, 88% of 
the buyers were from chains. 

The major conclusions of 
the study were: 

@ Unit and dollar sales 
growth in fragrances is lower 
than six months ago. 
® Cosmetics sales are up in 
both dollars and units. 
@ Consumers are more will- 
ing to trade up in price, espe- 
cially for fragrances. 
@ Manufacturer price in- 
creases are slowing down, but 
many buyers report that pric- 
ing is 6% to 10% ahead of last 
year. 
@ Inventories for fragrances 
and cosmetics are still above 
target. 

he best selling fragrances 
remain Stetson in the men’s 
category and Vanderbilt in 
the women’s arena. Vander- 
bilt expanded its lead over sec- 
ond place Forever Krystle. 
However Chaps from Ralph 
Lauren place d a solid second 
in the men’s market, moving 
from runnerup in the last sur- 
vey. 
@ Cover Girl and Revlon still 
hold the biggest rank in make- 
up and treatment, respective- 
ly. Almay again scored high on 
- this survey as the second best- 
selling treatment line in drug 
outlets. 
e Superior ratings were giv- 
en to Cosmair’s L’Oreal and 
Warner fragrance divisions, 
and L’Oreal perhaps on the 
coattails of its successful Vi- 
suelle launch, placed as the 
third ecg make-up 
line behind the dominant ae 
er Cover Girl and the second 
ranked Revlon. Maybelline 
moved down one notch to run-

DRUG STORE NEWS, October 28, 1985 


Deep discount drug industry grows rapial y 


Continued from page 1 
Glassman in Ohio and Cecilie 
and Sonny Raichlen in De- 
troit. 

In the two years since 1983, 
when this segment began to 
clearly manifest its dramatic 
growth potential, sources es- 
timate that the universe of 
deep-discount drug stores 
grew by some 150-plus stores. 

Both of the two major 
chains in this segment doubled 
in size. By the end of this year, 
Drug Emporium should have 
ney to 90 stores, compared to 
34 in 1983, while F & M 
should have 28, compared to 
14 in 1983. 

The rest of the expansion 
was, and, still is, coming from 
well-funded major retail play- 
ers finding their way into this 
new market to “test out” the 
concept. 

Supermarkets General, the 
supermarket company that 
also operates Pathmark drug 
stores, now has over 15 deep- 
discount drug stores, includ- 
ing 12 Heartland stores re- 
cently acquired from Purity 
Supreme. $ afeway is still test- 
ing Drugs For. Less and 
Kroger is giving SupeRx, its 
drug store division, the go- 
ahead to expand Drug World. 


In the chain drug segment, 
Rite Aid has begun a major 
expansion of its Drug Palaces, 
while Revco seems set to ex- 
pand Get it For Less. Perry is 
expanding A. L. Prige and 
Melville, parent of CVS, is ex- 
pected to expand Freddy’ S. 


So far, only a handful of 
chains have chosen to stop 
testing deep-discount drug 
stores: Medicare-Glaser shut 
down its Megs after just six 
months, American stores did 
the same with its FAD and so 
did Fay’s with its Jay-Jay’s. 


However, although most of 
the companies still experi- 
menting with the format have 
positive things to say about 
the segment “officially,” many 
are still having what can only 
be described as mixed results 
with their tests and only a few, 
like Rite Aid, Perry Drug, 
Shoppers and SupeRx, are of- 
ficially committed to opening a 
significant number of new 
stores. 

Future growth 

Moreover, although some 
sources have predicted that 
this segment will top $15 mil- 
lion in sales by the end of this 
decade, a number of execu- 
tives for the established 

“pure” deep-discount drug 
companies feel that the major 
retailers are not suited, either 
temperamentally or by train- 
ing, to make deep-discount 
drug stores work. 

Almost all cite the growing 
complexity and competitive- 
ness of the market as factors 
that will eventually discour- 
age the more traditional re- 
tailers, particularly the drug 
and food chains, from continu- 
ing to pursue this avenue of 
growth. 

They 


also say there is a 


“learning curve” that deep- 
discount drug store retailers 

must master before their in- 
vestments can prove lucra- 
tive. This curve can be partic- 
ularly painful to negotiate, 
they point out, because it in- 
volves committing millions to 
the experiment for one, two, 
maybe three years,” before 
the investment begins to 
prove profitable. 

“That’s very hard for most 
traditional public companies 
to do,” says a source for one of 
the two major deep-discount 
drug chains. “Can you imagine 
an executive for one of the 

ublic drug chains going to the 

oard of directors to explain 
that this store which will stock 
more than $1.5 million in in- 
ventory and which will proba- 
bly cost $300,000 a year or so 
to occupy plus labor costs and 


other related costs, that this 
store is probably going to lose 
$300,000 its first year and 
maybe $100,000, the next, and 
possibly will begin making 
money its third year? They’re 
going to say, ‘Why should we 
do that when we can open a 
conventional store at about a 
quarter the investment and 
probably start making money 
the second year?’” 
Profitability 

“It is not as lucrative as the 
industry thinks,” says another 
executive for one of those 
same two drug chains, “and it 
takes a lot more work than 
many people realize. Too 
many people think that all you 
have to do is open one of these 
stores and you start making 
money. That isn’t true. What 
is true is that the business gets 
harder evey day.”

In addition to getting hard- 
er, those involved in deep dis- 
counting also say the business 
is changing every day. That if 
someone like Fred and Marga- 
ret Cohen or Bernie Shulman 
or Mare Glassman—the 


names associated with the pio- 
neering of deep discounting in 
the late 50’s and early 60’s and 
70’s were to start up today, 


they would probably still 
make it, but not with the high 
double- digit stores that some 
of them have achieved. 

“If Bernie or Mark were to 
start up today,’ says one 
source, “they’d make it, but 
they wouldn’t make it with the 
$30 million store. Today 
they’d cap out at around $10 
million or $15 million.”

NEW YORK — Drug man- 
ufacturers have stepped up 
their detailing efforts to the 
chains, with an almost 20% in- 
crease in chain drug store de- 
tailing visits in the past year. 

In a nationwide study of 
pharmaceutical manufactur- 
ers’ detailing efforts, Drug 
Store News has learned that 
although company reps have 
beefed up their visits to the 
chains, pharmacists complain 
they are receiving less infor- 
mation than they would like 
with each visit. 

However, the study cited 
new product introductions as 
one area pharmaceutical de- 
tail people are doing a good job 

According to the data, 61% 
of the chain pharmacists ques- 
tioned said they were visited 
by a detail person once every 
two months this year com- 
pared to 52% the previous 
year. 


Rx detailing study 


On the other hand, of the 43 
manufacturers cited in 
DrSN’s survey questionnaire, 
only four were mentioned by 
at least 25% of the chain and 
independent pharmacists as 
maintaining scheduled visits 
of once every two months. 
They were: Lilly/Dista, Wy- 
eth, — and Parke-Davis. 

At the independents’ level, 


visits by manufacturers’ reps | 


showed no change over last 
year; 71% of the independents 
reported they were seen by a 
drug detail person once every 
two months. 

Furthermore, it was shown 
that an astonishing 86% of the 
pharmaceutical manufactur- 


ers were likely never to visit a | 


chain drug store. 


(verall, the study showed | 


that drug manufacturers have 
increased the frequency of de- 
tail visits to the chains. Some 
chain execs say that one rea- 


son for the increase is the so- | 


weeps of the medications 
eing developed today.

buying offices,” said Roland 
Knocke, prescription drug 
buyer at Medicare-Glaser, St. 
Louis. “For the most part, de- 
tail people are not allowed in 
our stores. Anything they 
want our pharmacists to know 
about their product is con- 
veyed to our stores through a 
newsletter we send our phar- 
macists. But we realize that 
the recent development of cer- 
tain new drug delivery sys-

cated through a newsletter, so 
we have begun to let the reps 
visit our stores and detail our 
pharmacists on selected prod- 
ucts.”

ample in a new inhaler intro- 
duced by Glaxo.
